jsc.cli.msd.about: Takes the whole terminal and shows what the machine is made of, a button for each part with what it found beside it. LPT Ports and COM Ports open the list of the ports with what is attached to each and whether it is on, where a device is enabled or disabled. A disabled device keeps its port, and the computer neither reads nor writes it.
jsc.cli.msd.about.keys: Arrows move between the buttons and Enter opens one; L opens the LPT ports and C the COM ports. In the list, E enables the picked port's device, D disables it, and Enter puts the list away. F3 gives the terminal back.

jsc.cli.netfile.copy.summary: a second file with the same content
jsc.cli.netfile.delete.summary: take a file off the disk
jsc.cli.netfile.listfiles.about: Lists every file the disk holds, with how big it is and when it was written.
jsc.cli.netfile.listfiles.about.flat: This disk keeps no folders, so there is nothing to list the contents of: what you see is the whole of it.
jsc.cli.netfile.seefile.about: Writes the whole file to the glass at once. A file longer than the glass runs off the top of it; read shows a long one a page at a time instead.
jsc.cli.netfile.seefile.summary: put a file on the glass
jsc.cli.netfile.write.about: Writes the text after the name into that file, replacing whatever was there. The kind of file is read from the end of its name.
jsc.cli.netfile.write.example.notes: a file with that line in it
jsc.cli.netfile.write.summary: make a file out of what you type
jsc.cli.netmachine.end.about: Stops the thing of that number, which tasklist tells you. What it was doing stops where it stands, and what it had not finished stays not done.
jsc.cli.netmachine.end.example.fourth: stop the fourth thing tasklist shows
jsc.cli.netmachine.end.no_job: this machine was left with no job %s
jsc.cli.netmachine.end.summary: stop something this machine is running
jsc.cli.netmachine.findcommand.about: Says whether a command is on this machine at all and what put it there: the system itself, or a package installed over it, which is the one to remove if it misbehaves.
jsc.cli.netmachine.findcommand.summary: say where a command comes from
jsc.cli.netmachine.format.about: Erases a disk and everything on it. A shell that remembers nothing between lines cannot ask you twice, so saying yes after the drive is how you mean it.
jsc.cli.netmachine.format.example.ask: what it would destroy, and nothing done
jsc.cli.netmachine.format.would_lose: Everything on drive %s would be lost.
jsc.cli.netmachine.memory.about: Three numbers, and they are not the same one. Fitted is the memory in the machine. Promised is what has been set aside for the things it agreed to run. Held is what those things are really using at this moment, which is the one that moves while you watch.
jsc.cli.netmachine.memory.summary: what this machine's memory is spent on
jsc.cli.netmachine.run.summary: run a stored script against the network
jsc.cli.netmachine.tasklist.about: Lists what the machine is running, the number each answers to, and what each is holding of the memory it was promised. Stop one with end.
jsc.cli.netmachine.worldtime.about: There is one clock here and everything on the machine is timed by it: a line left for an hour, a file's stamp, a log. This is that clock.
jsc.cli.netmachine.worldtime.summary: the day and hour of the world
jsc.cli.netsoftware.runbackground.about: Leaves the machine with the line and hands the prompt back at once. This machine runs one thing at a time, so it takes them in the order they were left.
jsc.cli.netsoftware.runbackground.exampl: ask for them and carry on
jsc.cli.netsoftware.runbackground.summar: run a line without waiting for it
jsc.cli.netsoftware.schedule.about: With nothing after it, says what this machine is already set to do. With an hour and a line, leaves that line to run at that hour, every day unless days are named. The shortest anything repeats is an hour of the world's clock.

jsc.configuration.boot.show_boot_menu.to:
Whether a machine whose system brings a boot manager stops at it every time it starts: GRUB on a Linux, the loader on FreeBSD, the Midsoft Boot Manager with two systems.
Turning this off boots the chosen system at once, the way a machine with the menu hidden does.
jsc.configuration.boot.tooltip: How the machines come up: whether they stop at their system's boot manager.
jsc.configuration.client.desktop_cursors: Whether the desktops draw their own pointer over the monitor's glass: each system's arrow, and its hourglass, ring or watch while it is busy. Off, the game's own pointer stays.
jsc.configuration.client.outside_compone:
Whether this game draws the components of programs' windows that reach outside the game, such as one showing a web address or a file on this computer.
Off, each shows a placeholder naming it, whatever the server allows.
jsc.configuration.client.reduce_motion.t:
Whether every desktop acts at once: no window, menu or boot moves, everything is drawn where it ends.
Each system's own settings page turns its motions off one by one; this turns them all off for this player.
jsc.configuration.client.tooltip: How the desktops look on this game: whether they move, whose pointer they draw, and what of the world outside the game they show.
jsc.configuration.install_by_hand.arch_e:
Whether installing Arch by hand asks for every step of the installation guide.
Off, only the steps a system cannot boot without are asked for. On, the hardware clock and a name for the machine are asked for as well.
jsc.configuration.install_by_hand.gentoo:
Whether installing Gentoo by hand asks for every step of the handbook.
Off, only the steps a system cannot boot without are asked for: the disk, the stage 3, the package tree, a kernel, the filesystem table and the bootloader.
On, the rest are asked for as well: the bind mounts, a profile, the @world update, the kernel link and a name for the machine.
Every step answers the way the real tool does either way; this only decides which of them a restart refuses to go on without.
jsc.configuration.install_by_hand.toolti: Installing a system by hand: how much of its guide the machine insists on.
jsc.configuration.programs.outside_compo:
Whether a program may put in its windows a component of a kind that reaches outside the game, such as one showing a web address or a file on the player's own computer.
Such kinds come only from other mods, which say so when they add them. Off, a program making one is stopped and told; on, each player still sees them only if their own settings turn them on as well.
jsc.configuration.programs.tooltip: What the programs players write may put in their windows.
jsc.configuration.prompt.list_commands.t:
Whether every computer has the 'listcmd' command, which lists absolutely everything that computer can run right now: its commands, whatever family they belong to, and the programs installed on it.
Off, it is nowhere at all: not in help, not in a manual, not in what a half-typed name completes to, and typing it is an unknown command. Each system then teaches what it has in its own way, which is the experience those systems really gave.
On, it is on every computer and shows up everywhere like any other command, for whoever would rather read one list than learn each system's own habits.
jsc.configuration.prompt.tooltip: What every computer's command line has, whatever system it runs.
jsc.configuration.soundfoundry.catalog.t:
Whether the server offers its music catalogue: the albums put in config/jstech/soundfoundry/catalog/, a folder each, and those the data packs carry in soundfoundry/catalog/.
Off, neither is read and the catalogue is empty. A change is taken up by '/soundfoundry catalog reload' or the next start.
jsc.configuration.soundfoundry.ethernet_:
How fast a song comes over the network into a computer, in kilobytes a second, by the slowest cable on its way. A song from the catalogue comes at the speed of the cable the computer itself is plugged into; the songs coming in at once share it.
Every other cable, in every era, carries songs in proportion to what it carries in items a tick, so the faster the cable the faster the song.
jsc.configuration.soundfoundry.tooltip: The music service: the catalogue the server offers, and how fast a song travels over each kind of cable into a computer.

jsc.guide.achievements.definition1: A step the game records once for each player, when that player does something worth noting.
jsc.guide.achievements.definition2: The player a machine's own achievements are credited to: the last player who placed or used the machine.
jsc.guide.achievements.fix1: Check who did the action. Your own actions earn it for you, and a machine's achievement goes to its operator. If you were offline, it appears at your next login.
jsc.guide.achievements.fix2: The operator is the last player who placed or used that machine. Use the machine yourself, and its later achievements are yours.
jsc.guide.achievements.problem1: An achievement you earned did not appear.
jsc.guide.achievements.problem2: A machine's achievement went to another player.
jsc.guide.achievements.table1_1_2: Building computers, racks, datacenters and clusters.
jsc.guide.achievements.table1_2_2: Installing and booting systems, and the programs you run on them.
jsc.guide.achievements.table1_3_2: Bringing a network to life, and running its Operations, the query language IQL, and autocrafting.
jsc.guide.achievements.table1_4_2: Writing, compiling and running Sigma and Sigma# programs.
jsc.guide.achievements.text1: An achievement is a step the game records for you the first time you do something worth noting, such as building a working computer or booting your first system. You earn each one once, and the game lists them in four tabs: Hardware, Operating Systems, Networks & Operations, and Sigma.
jsc.guide.achievements.text2: Each tab starts with a root, its first achievement, and the others hang from it. Every achievement has a kind. A task is a plain step, a goal is a larger milestone, a challenge asks for several separate things, and a secret stays hidden in its tab until you earn it. Once you earn a secret, its description shows too.
jsc.guide.achievements.text3: The game credits you for what you do yourself: when you do the thing, the achievement is yours. A machine that works on its own, such as a computer that finishes its power-on self-test, or a job that runs at a set time, credits its operator instead.
jsc.guide.achievements.text4: If you were offline when it happened, the achievement waits for you and appears at your next login. The game keeps up to 128 waiting achievements for each player.
jsc.guide.achievements.title: Achievements
jsc.guide.achievements_hardware.fix1: The last unit must be placed by a player. A rack filled by other means does not earn it.
jsc.guide.achievements_hardware.fix2: Only monitors linked to the computer count. Link four monitors to it.
jsc.guide.achievements_hardware.fix3: It hangs from Moore's Law Isn't Dead, so earn that first.
jsc.guide.achievements_hardware.problem1: Rack 'Em Up does not appear after you fill a rack.
jsc.guide.achievements_hardware.problem2: Battlestation does not appear with four monitors near the computer.
jsc.guide.achievements_hardware.table1_1: Build a working computer of each of the five eras: Vintage, Legacy, Transition, Standard and Advanced.
Each of those five eras is built once, with a valid build.
Fill every unit of a Server Rack.
The rack's 8 units are all used, and a player filled the last one.
Form a datacenter section behind a Server Router.
A Server Router goes from no datacenter section to at least one.
Run a whole cluster from a Cluster Management Computer.
You power on at least one node of the cluster, or you send an install to every node and it takes effect.
Bring a supercomputer online: Supercomputer Racks on High Compute Cable.
The HBW Interface is on a network and has parallel crafts (more than zero).
Get your hands on a computer.
You hold any computer item in your inventory: a computer case of any era, or a Mainframe.
jsc.guide.achievements_hardware.table1_2: Watch a computer pass its power-on self-test.
A computer finishes its power-on self-test (POST).
jsc.guide.achievements_hardware.table1_3: Have You Tried Turning It Off and On Again? (task)
Restart a running computer from its power menu.
You choose restart in the power menu of the desktop. Shutting down does not count.
jsc.guide.achievements_hardware.table1_4: Fill every RAM slot on a motherboard.
The random-access memory (RAM) installed fills every RAM slot of the motherboard, checked whenever the parts change.
jsc.guide.achievements_hardware.table1_5: Save a file to a floppy disk.
A file is written to a floppy disk in a media slot.
jsc.guide.achievements_hardware.table1_6: Link four monitors to one computer.
Four monitors are linked to the same computer; monitors merely placed near it do not count.
jsc.guide.achievements_hardware.table1_7: A computer of the Vintage era is built and its build is valid.
jsc.guide.achievements_hardware.table1_8: A computer of the Legacy era is built and its build is valid.
jsc.guide.achievements_hardware.table1_9: A computer of the Standard era is built and its build is valid.
jsc.guide.achievements_hardware.text1: The Hardware tab rewards building. Its root is the first step, and the others ask you to build working computers, fill racks, link monitors and run whole clusters. The table says what each one asks, and how the game checks it.
jsc.guide.achievements_hardware.text2: Time Traveller asks for the five eras that have a build achievement: Vintage, Legacy, Transition, Standard and Advanced. The eras Exa and Singularity have no build achievement.
jsc.guide.achievements_hardware.text3: Each build hangs from the one before it: 640K Ought to Be Enough comes first, then Party Like It's 1999, then Moore's Law Isn't Dead, and Time Traveller hangs from the last.
jsc.guide.achievements_hardware.title: Hardware achievements
jsc.guide.achievements_networks.fix1: It needs a machine to run a step of the craft. The Factory Must Grow counts any autocraft.
jsc.guide.achievements_networks.fix2: Place the other kind of bus on the same network: an Import Bus with an Export Bus.
jsc.guide.achievements_networks.fix3: It needs ComputerCraft and a Network Gateway that hears one of its computers.
jsc.guide.achievements_networks.problem1: Machine Learning does not appear although autocrafts finish.
jsc.guide.achievements_networks.problem2: Just-in-Time does not appear with one bus.
jsc.guide.achievements_networks.problem3: Talking to the Neighbours is missing.
jsc.guide.achievements_networks.table1_1: Machine Learning (goal)
Finish an autocraft through a machine.
A machine finishes a step of an autocraft, or an autocraft runs one of its steps in a machine.
Supply Chain Issues (challenge)
Finish an autocraft of ten stages or more.
An autocraft with ten or more stages finishes.
Just-in-Time (task)
Put an Import Bus and an Export Bus on one network.
A bus cable part is placed on a network that already has the other kind of bus.
Who Unplugged the Server? (secret)
Cut the last cable between a running computer and its Mainframe.
A running computer loses its last route to a Mainframe.
There Can Be Only One (secret)
Put two Mainframes on one network.
A network conflict starts. The chat announces it too.
Talking to the Neighbours (goal, with ComputerCraft only)
Hear a ComputerCraft computer through a Network Gateway.
A Network Gateway receives a message from a ComputerCraft computer.
Networks & Operations (root)
Bring a Mainframe onto a network.
A Mainframe joins a network for the first time.
jsc.guide.achievements_networks.table1_2: Join a computer to a Mainframe's network.
A computer joins a network that has a Mainframe.
jsc.guide.achievements_networks.table1_3: Take items out of network storage with an Operation.
jsc.guide.achievements_networks.table1_4: An IQL statement you type completes without error.
jsc.guide.achievements_networks.table1_5: Have an IQL JOB run on its own.
An IQL job runs on its own, and the Mainframe's operator is credited.
jsc.guide.achievements_networks.table1_6: Two Out of Three Ain't Bad (secret)
Have an Operation finish only partly done.
An Operation ends PARTIAL, as the terminal shows it.
jsc.guide.achievements_networks.table1_7: Have an Operation give up waiting on a locked resource.
An Operation ends RESOURCE LOCKED, as the terminal shows it.
jsc.guide.achievements_networks.table1_8: A Pattern Encoder encodes a pattern.
jsc.guide.achievements_networks.text1: The Networks & Operations tab follows the work of a network: a Mainframe on a network, computers joining it, Operations and IQL (the network's query language), autocrafting, and the trouble a network can get into. The table says what each one asks, and how the game checks it.
jsc.guide.achievements_networks.text2: An Operation you asked for credits you. A scheduled Operation credits the operator of the Mainframe ([](jsc:mainframes)), and so does an IQL job that runs on its own.
jsc.guide.achievements_networks.text3: Two Out of Three Ain't Bad and Deadlock name two of the ways an Operation can end: [the eight states of an Operation](jsc:operation_states) explains all of them.
jsc.guide.achievements_networks.text4: Talking to the Neighbours appears only when the ComputerCraft mod is installed with J's Computers, and the achievement needs a [Network Gateway](jsc:network_gateway).
jsc.guide.achievements_networks.title: Network and Operations achievements
jsc.guide.achievements_sigma.fix1: Any failed compile earns it, whichever error it is. Read the error line to find the real problem ([](jsc:sigma_reading_an_error)).
jsc.guide.achievements_sigma.fix2: Calls went more than 1,024 deep: a method may be calling itself without end. Look for a method that calls itself ([](jsc:sigma_runtime_stops)).
jsc.guide.achievements_sigma.fix3: Check the divisor before you divide. A program that halts this way earns Undefined Behaviour.
jsc.guide.achievements_sigma.fix4: The program must run without a stop for 168,000 ticks. The game checks once every 1,200 ticks, so it can appear up to a minute later.

jsc.guide.achievements_sigma.table1_8_2: Open a window from a program.

jsc.guide.achievements_sigma.text1: Sigma and Sigma# are the two programming languages of the computers, and the Sigma tab rewards you for writing them, compiling them and running them. The Book of Sigma explains both languages from zero ([](jsc:sigma_two_languages)).
jsc.guide.achievements_sigma.text2: Most Sigma achievements of a program credit the operator of the machine it runs on. The compile and run commands credit the player who typed them.
jsc.guide.achievements_sigma.text3: Five Nines counts ticks, not seconds: 24,000 ticks make one in-game day, so seven days make 168,000 ticks. A tick is the game's basic unit of time, one twentieth of a second ([](jsc:units_and_ticks)).
jsc.guide.achievements_sigma.text4: Works on My Machine needs the game to remember where you ran a program: it keeps up to 64 program names for each player.
jsc.guide.achievements_sigma.title: Sigma achievements

jsc.guide.achievements_systems.table1_17: Run screenfetch on every system it installs on.

jsc.guide.achievements_systems.text1: The Operating Systems tab rewards the systems you install and how you use them. Its root is the first boot of any system. Each system has a step of its own, and a few are hard ones, such as installing by hand or building from source.
jsc.guide.achievements_systems.text2: Most install steps count the first boot: the first time an installed system starts through a monitor. The game marks the disk when it welcomes the system, so the mark stays with the disk. A live installer session does not count.
jsc.guide.achievements_systems.text3: The Frames install steps hang from one another in the order of the editions, from Frames 95 to Frames 11, and the FreeBSD step hangs from the UNIX one.
jsc.guide.achievements_systems.title: System achievements
jsc.guide.after_reboot_checks.definition: The start-up test that the firmware runs first each time the computer starts, before any system starts.
jsc.guide.after_reboot_checks.fix1: The kernel file boot/vmlinuz is gone from the disk. Install over the system from an installation medium ([](jsc:installing)).
jsc.guide.after_reboot_checks.fix2: The disk has no system, or its folder boot is gone. Install a system on the disk from an installation medium ([](jsc:installing)).
jsc.guide.after_reboot_checks.heading1: The firmware's lines when nothing starts
jsc.guide.after_reboot_checks.problem1: The screen says "kernel panic - not syncing: no init found" and waits.
jsc.guide.after_reboot_checks.problem2: The screen shows the firmware's no-device lines and waits.
jsc.guide.after_reboot_checks.table1_1_1: The folder boot and the kernel file are both there.
jsc.guide.after_reboot_checks.table1_1_3: The machine starts the system. With more than one system on the disk, it may show the Boot Menu first.
jsc.guide.after_reboot_checks.table1_2_1: There is no folder named boot, or no system on the disk at all, and no installation medium is in a drive.
jsc.guide.after_reboot_checks.table1_2_3: The machine stops at the self-test and waits.
jsc.guide.after_reboot_checks.table1_3_1: The folder boot is there, but the kernel file is gone, and no installation medium is in a drive.
jsc.guide.after_reboot_checks.table1_3_3: The machine stops at the self-test and waits, with the repair line below.
jsc.guide.after_reboot_checks.table1_hea: What the check finds on the disk
jsc.guide.after_reboot_checks.table2_1_2: "Non-system disk or disk error", then "Replace and press any key when ready"
jsc.guide.after_reboot_checks.table2_3_2: "No bootable device found", then "Press any key to enter Setup"
jsc.guide.after_reboot_checks.text1: When the machine starts, it runs the power-on self-test (POST) first. At the end of the test, the machine checks the system disk once, and then it decides what to do next.
jsc.guide.after_reboot_checks.text2: The check looks for two things on the disk: a folder named boot, and the kernel file boot/vmlinuz inside it. The kernel file is the one file that starts a Linux system. If both are there, the machine starts the system.
jsc.guide.after_reboot_checks.text3: The lines depend on the look of the machine's firmware, which follows its era. Linux systems start on Legacy machines and later.
jsc.guide.after_reboot_checks.text4: When the machine stops with a complaint, the big header on the screen shows the complaint. Without a complaint, the header reads "No bootable device". With a complaint, the screen also shows the line "Put in an installation medium and install over it to repair."
jsc.guide.after_reboot_checks.text5: A stopped machine keeps its message on the screen, and a monitor you open later still shows it. The machine checks the disk again once a second. It starts again by itself when the disk is whole, or when an installation medium is in a drive.
jsc.guide.after_reboot_checks.text6: To repair a wrecked system, put an installation medium in a drive and install over the system ([](jsc:installing)). The install writes the folder boot and the kernel file back onto the disk, so the machine can start again.
jsc.guide.after_reboot_checks.text7: If you take the installation medium out of the drive that the machine started from, the machine restarts and finds nothing to start from.
jsc.guide.after_reboot_checks.text8: A computer can also refuse to start for lack of power, which is a different refusal ([](jsc:power_supplies)).
jsc.guide.after_reboot_checks.title: What the machine checks when it starts

jsc.guide.apt.step3: Type apt install and the command name, then press ENTER.
jsc.guide.apt.step4: Wait until the progress bar of the install is full.

jsc.guide.apt.text1: apt is the package manager of Ubuntu and Debian. You type apt, a verb such as install, then the name of what it works on, and it fetches from the Mirror. On Fedora the word is not a command: use dnf ([](jsc:dnf)).
jsc.guide.apt.text2: Words that start with a dash are skipped, so apt install -y vim installs vim.
jsc.guide.apt.text3: An install prints these lines, in this order, before its progress bar.
jsc.guide.apt.text4: A remove prints the same first two lines. Then it prints "The following packages will be REMOVED:" and "After this operation, <MB> disk space will be freed."
jsc.guide.apt.title: apt, verb by verb
jsc.guide.arch_base_system.definition1: The package manager of Arch Linux: it finds, downloads and installs packages.
jsc.guide.arch_base_system.definition2: The package server of a network. A Mainframe that runs it serves packages to every computer of the network.
jsc.guide.arch_base_system.fix1: Nothing is mounted on /mnt. Mount the root partition there, after its file system is made ([](jsc:mounting)): mount /dev/sda2 /mnt.
jsc.guide.arch_base_system.fix2: This computer cannot reach a Mirror. Put it on a network whose Mainframe runs the Mirror ([](jsc:mirror)).
jsc.guide.arch_base_system.fix3: The step is not recorded as done. Run pacstrap again from the start.
jsc.guide.arch_base_system.problem1: The screen says "==> ERROR: /mnt is not a mountpoint!".
jsc.guide.arch_base_system.problem2: The screen says "error: failed retrieving file 'core.db' from mirror://mainframe : Could not resolve host: mainframe", and then "error: failed to synchronize all databases (unexpected error)".
jsc.guide.arch_base_system.problem3: You stopped pacstrap with [[Ctrl]]+[[C]] before it finished.
jsc.guide.arch_base_system.step1: Make sure the root partition is mounted on /mnt.
jsc.guide.arch_base_system.step2: Type pacstrap -K /mnt base linux linux-firmware and press [[Enter]].
jsc.guide.arch_base_system.step3: Wait until the prompt comes back. The step takes as long as your connection and your disk need.
jsc.guide.arch_base_system.text1: The base system is the core of Arch Linux: the kernel ([](jsc:kernel_gentoo)), the core tools and the package manager, pacman. The command that installs it is pacstrap. It puts the packages on the disk, under /mnt, the folder where the new system is built.
jsc.guide.arch_base_system.text2: Pacstrap is the first step that writes the new system, so the disk must be ready before it runs. The root partition has to be mounted on /mnt ([](jsc:mounting)).
jsc.guide.arch_base_system.text3: On a real Arch install, pacstrap downloads the packages from the internet. Here the packages come from the Mirror, the package server of your network. A Mainframe must run it, and this computer must be on that network. Without a Mirror, pacstrap cannot start.
jsc.guide.arch_base_system.text4: Then come the download bars, the checks of the packages, one line for each package it installs, and the last steps of the install. Pacstrap asks you nothing: it does not stop to ask you to confirm, and it installs straight away.
jsc.guide.arch_base_system.text5: The 48 packages include base, linux, linux-firmware, pacman, systemd, bash, coreutils and mkinitcpio. The last steps of the install also build both boot images, so you do not need to build them again.
jsc.guide.arch_base_system.text6: When pacstrap finishes, the new system has its folders for /etc, /boot, /root, /usr, /var, /proc, /sys, /dev and /run. Its kernel and its two boot images ([](jsc:arch_mkinitcpio)) are in /boot. The step is recorded as done only at that moment.
jsc.guide.arch_base_system.text7: Running pacstrap again starts over. The steps you did before, such as the file system table and the boot steps, are forgotten, and you do them again. The clock setting is kept.
jsc.guide.arch_base_system.title: Installing the base system (pacstrap)
jsc.guide.arch_bootloader.definition1: The program on the motherboard that starts the computer, before any system runs.
jsc.guide.arch_bootloader.definition2: The program the firmware starts first, which then starts the kernel.
jsc.guide.arch_bootloader.definition3: The boot loader that Arch uses.
jsc.guide.arch_bootloader.fix1: The GRUB package is not installed yet. Install it first: pacman -S grub efibootmgr.
jsc.guide.arch_bootloader.fix2: You are on the live medium. Step in first with arch-chroot /mnt ([](jsc:arch_chroot)).
jsc.guide.arch_bootloader.fix3: The EFI system partition is not mounted where the command looks. Mount it at /mnt/boot before you step in ([](jsc:mounting)), then run grub-install --efi-directory=/boot.
jsc.guide.arch_bootloader.fix4: On older firmware, name the disk: grub-install /dev/sda.
jsc.guide.arch_bootloader.fix5: The boot loader goes on the disk, not in a partition. Name the disk: grub-install /dev/sda.
jsc.guide.arch_bootloader.problem1: The screen says "zsh: command not found: grub-install", with a line that says the boot loader is a package.
jsc.guide.arch_bootloader.problem2: The screen says "grub-install: command not found (it is the new system's: step into it first)".
jsc.guide.arch_bootloader.problem3: The screen says "grub-install: error: /boot/efi doesn't look like an EFI partition."
jsc.guide.arch_bootloader.problem4: The screen says "grub-install: error: install device isn't specified."
jsc.guide.arch_bootloader.problem5: The screen says "grub-install: error: cannot find a device for" and the name of a partition, such as /dev/sda2.
jsc.guide.arch_bootloader.step1: Make sure you are inside the new system.
jsc.guide.arch_bootloader.step2: Type pacman -S grub efibootmgr and press [[Enter]].
jsc.guide.arch_bootloader.step3: Press [[Enter]] or type Y at the question, and wait until the install finishes.
jsc.guide.arch_bootloader.step4: Type the grub-install command for your firmware, from the table below, and press [[Enter]].
jsc.guide.arch_bootloader.table1: The packages for the boot loader
jsc.guide.arch_bootloader.table2_1_1: UEFI, in the Standard era and later
jsc.guide.arch_bootloader.table2_2_1: BIOS, in the Legacy and Transition eras
jsc.guide.arch_bootloader.text1: When the firmware starts a disk, it starts the first program on it: the boot loader. The boot loader then starts the kernel with the boot images. Arch uses GRUB for that job. GRUB shows a menu, or starts its only entry, and loads the kernel.
jsc.guide.arch_bootloader.text2: The boot loader comes as two packages, and you install both with pacman. The efibootmgr package is the tool that tells the firmware where the boot loader is. The grub-install command refuses until the grub package is installed.
jsc.guide.arch_bootloader.text3: There are two kinds of firmware: the older Basic Input/Output System (BIOS) and the newer Unified Extensible Firmware Interface (UEFI). The table shows the install for each.
jsc.guide.arch_bootloader.text4: Which row is yours depends on your computer's firmware ([](jsc:firmware_for_install)). On older firmware, the boot loader goes on the whole disk, not in a partition. On UEFI, mount the EFI system partition at /mnt/boot before you step in ([](jsc:mounting)), so that /boot inside the new system is that partition.
jsc.guide.arch_bootloader.text5: On UEFI the screen says "Installing for x86_64-efi platform.", and on BIOS it says "Installing for i386-pc platform.". Both end with "Installation finished. No error reported." The install does not write the boot list. That is the next step ([](jsc:arch_grub_config)).
jsc.guide.arch_bootloader.title: Installing the boot loader
jsc.guide.arch_chroot.definition1: Running a program with a different folder as the top of the disk, so that the program sees that folder as its whole system.
jsc.guide.arch_chroot.fix1: The folder is not /mnt. Type arch-chroot /mnt.
jsc.guide.arch_chroot.fix2: The base system is not on the disk yet, so there is no shell to start. Install it first ([](jsc:arch_base_system)).
jsc.guide.arch_chroot.fix3: You typed pacman on the live medium. Step in first with arch-chroot /mnt.
jsc.guide.arch_chroot.fix4: You are on the live medium. Step in first with arch-chroot /mnt.
jsc.guide.arch_chroot.problem1: The screen says "chroot: cannot change root directory to '/mnt/x': No such file or directory".
jsc.guide.arch_chroot.problem2: The screen says "chroot: failed to run command '/bin/bash': No such file or directory".
jsc.guide.arch_chroot.problem3: The screen says "error: you cannot perform this operation unless you are root in the new" and then "system (arch-chroot /mnt first)".
jsc.guide.arch_chroot.problem4: The screen says "mkinitcpio: command not found (it is the new system's: arch-chroot /mnt first)".
jsc.guide.arch_chroot.step2: Check the prompt. It must read [root@archiso /]#.
jsc.guide.arch_chroot.step3: Do the steps of this chapter inside. Type exit when you are done.
jsc.guide.arch_chroot.table1: Commands that work only inside the new system
jsc.guide.arch_chroot.table1_1_2: Refused: you are not root in the new system yet.
jsc.guide.arch_chroot.table1_5_2: Refused: you cannot change the name of the live medium.
jsc.guide.arch_chroot.text1: Until now you have typed on the live medium, and your commands reached the disk from the outside. To finish the new system, you step inside it. From then on, the folder /mnt is the top of the system, and every path you type means a path inside the new system.
jsc.guide.arch_chroot.text2: The Arch tool for this is arch-chroot. Running a program with a different folder as the top of the disk is called a chroot, and arch-chroot makes one for the new system.
jsc.guide.arch_chroot.text3: Outside the new system, the prompt reads root@archiso ~ #. Inside, it reads [root@archiso /]#, with the folder you are in between the brackets.
jsc.guide.arch_chroot.text4: If you name a folder other than /mnt, the tool refuses, and you stay outside:
jsc.guide.arch_chroot.text5: Leaving is done with exit. Nothing is lost when you leave: the work you did stays, and arch-chroot /mnt takes you back in.
jsc.guide.arch_chroot.title: Stepping into the new system (arch-chroot)
jsc.guide.arch_clock_and_name.definition: The clock on the motherboard, which keeps the time while the computer is off.
jsc.guide.arch_clock_and_name.fix1: You are on the live medium, not in the new system. Step in with arch-chroot /mnt first ([](jsc:arch_chroot)).
jsc.guide.arch_clock_and_name.fix2: The name breaks a rule in the table, or it has more than one word. Use letters, digits and hyphens, at most 15 characters, starting with a letter or a digit.
jsc.guide.arch_clock_and_name.problem1: The screen says "hostname: you cannot change the host name of the live medium".
jsc.guide.arch_clock_and_name.problem2: The screen says "hostname: the specified hostname is invalid".
jsc.guide.arch_clock_and_name.step2: Type echo jarch > /etc/hostname, with your own name in place of jarch, and press [[Enter]].
jsc.guide.arch_clock_and_name.step3: Type hostname and press [[Enter]]. It prints the name you chose.
jsc.guide.arch_clock_and_name.table1: The rules for the machine's name
jsc.guide.arch_clock_and_name.text1: Two settings make the new system yours: the clock and the machine's name. The installer asks for both before the reboot only when the server setting Every step of Arch is on ([](jsc:installing)). You can always set them with the commands below.
jsc.guide.arch_clock_and_name.text2: The command hwclock --systohc copies the system's clock into the hardware clock, so the time is kept while the computer is off.
jsc.guide.arch_clock_and_name.text3: The name goes with the new system when the install finishes. The installed machine keeps it, and the network shows it.
jsc.guide.arch_clock_and_name.title: The clock and the machine's name
jsc.guide.arch_fstab.definition1: The file in /etc that lists which partitions to mount where, and how, when the system starts.
jsc.guide.arch_fstab.definition2: A long identifier that a file system carries on its disk, so the system finds the partition whatever its device name is.
jsc.guide.arch_fstab.fix1: The command does not name /mnt. Type genfstab -U /mnt >> /mnt/etc/fstab.
jsc.guide.arch_fstab.fix2: Pacstrap has not run yet. Install the base system first ([](jsc:arch_base_system)).
jsc.guide.arch_fstab.problem2: The screen says "==> ERROR: /mnt/etc does not exist".
jsc.guide.arch_fstab.step1: Make sure the base system is installed.
jsc.guide.arch_fstab.step2: Type genfstab -U /mnt and press [[Enter]]. The table is printed, and nothing is written.
jsc.guide.arch_fstab.step3: Type genfstab -U /mnt >> /mnt/etc/fstab and press [[Enter]]. The table is written into the file.
jsc.guide.arch_fstab.table1_1_2: A comment: the partition the line is about.
jsc.guide.arch_fstab.table1_2_2: The partition's UUID, then the folder it mounts on.
jsc.guide.arch_fstab.table1_3_2: The folder the partition mounts on: the top of the system.
jsc.guide.arch_fstab.table1_4_2: The file system type of the partition.
jsc.guide.arch_fstab.table1_5_2: The options: the disk is read and written, and access times are recorded in a lighter way.
jsc.guide.arch_fstab.text1: A system must know which disk to mount, and where, every time it starts. That list lives in one file, /etc/fstab, the file system table. The tool genfstab writes that file for you, from the disks you mounted.
jsc.guide.arch_fstab.text2: Most lines name a partition by its universally unique identifier (UUID), which the file system carries on its disk. The UUID stays the same when the disk gets another letter, so a renamed disk still boots. Here the same disk always gives the same UUID.
jsc.guide.arch_fstab.text3: Print the table first if you want to check it. The printed table is the same text the redirection writes, so what you see is what the file gets.
jsc.guide.arch_fstab.text4: If you mounted the boot partition, a second line follows after a blank line. It names that partition by its serial number, the identifier of the File Allocation Table (FAT) file system, and the folder it is mounted on, such as /boot.
jsc.guide.arch_fstab.title: Writing the file system table (genfstab)
jsc.guide.arch_grub_config.definition1: The file the boot loader reads when it starts. It says which kernel to start, and how.
jsc.guide.arch_grub_config.fix1: The boot loader is not installed yet, so its folder does not exist. Install it first ([](jsc:arch_bootloader)).
jsc.guide.arch_grub_config.fix2: The command has no -o. Type grub-mkconfig -o /boot/grub/grub.cfg.
jsc.guide.arch_grub_config.fix3: You are on the live medium. Step in first with arch-chroot /mnt ([](jsc:arch_chroot)).
jsc.guide.arch_grub_config.problem1: The screen says "/usr/bin/grub-mkconfig: /boot/grub: No such file or directory".
jsc.guide.arch_grub_config.problem3: The screen says "grub-mkconfig: command not found (it is the new system's: step into it first)".
jsc.guide.arch_grub_config.step1: Make sure you are inside the new system.
jsc.guide.arch_grub_config.step3: Wait for done at the end of the output.
jsc.guide.arch_grub_config.text1: The boot loader needs a list of what to start. That list is a file, and the tool grub-mkconfig writes it. It finds the kernel and the boot images in /boot, and writes one menu entry for them.
jsc.guide.arch_grub_config.text2: The file is always written to /boot/grub/grub.cfg, whatever you type after -o.
jsc.guide.arch_grub_config.text3: The first line of the output says the configuration file is being generated. A warning follows, and it is expected. os-prober is a tool that looks for other systems on other disks, and here it does not run, so no other system gets an entry. On UEFI, the output also says it adds a boot menu entry for the firmware settings.
jsc.guide.arch_grub_config.text4: The file has one menu entry, named Arch Linux. It loads the kernel and the boot images, and it tells the kernel which partition is the root, by its UUID.
jsc.guide.arch_grub_config.title: Writing the boot list (grub-mkconfig)
jsc.guide.arch_mkinitcpio.definition1: A small temporary system that starts before the real one, to load the drivers for the disks.
jsc.guide.arch_mkinitcpio.definition2: One step of building a boot image.
jsc.guide.arch_mkinitcpio.fix1: You are on the live medium. Step in first with arch-chroot /mnt ([](jsc:arch_chroot)).
jsc.guide.arch_mkinitcpio.problem1: The screen says "mkinitcpio: command not found (it is the new system's: arch-chroot /mnt first)".
jsc.guide.arch_mkinitcpio.step1: Make sure you are inside the new system.
jsc.guide.arch_mkinitcpio.step3: Wait until the prompt comes back.
jsc.guide.arch_mkinitcpio.text1: Before the real system starts, the kernel needs a small temporary system that loads the drivers for the disks. That system is the initramfs. Arch builds two of them, called boot images: a normal one, and a fallback for when the normal one does not start.
jsc.guide.arch_mkinitcpio.text2: The tool that builds them is mkinitcpio. Type mkinitcpio -P to build both images again. The tool works on the new system, so you must be inside it.
jsc.guide.arch_mkinitcpio.text3: Each image is built in steps called hooks. There are twelve: base, udev, autodetect, microcode, modconf, kms, keyboard, keymap, consolefont, block, filesystems and fsck.
jsc.guide.arch_mkinitcpio.text4: The fallback image skips the step autodetect. Pacstrap has already built both images in its last steps, so this command is for when you want them built again. On a slow processor it takes longer.
jsc.guide.arch_mkinitcpio.title: Rebuilding the boot images (mkinitcpio)
jsc.guide.arch_pacman_in_system.fix1: The Mirror has no program by that name for Linux, or this machine cannot run it. Check the spelling, and look at the programs on the Mirror ([](jsc:programs)).
jsc.guide.arch_pacman_in_system.fix2: You typed only flags, and no name. Add the name of a program after -S.
jsc.guide.arch_pacman_in_system.fix3: The command must start with -S and name a program. Type pacman -S, a space, then the name.
jsc.guide.arch_pacman_in_system.fix4: You are on the live medium. Step in first with arch-chroot /mnt ([](jsc:arch_chroot)).
jsc.guide.arch_pacman_in_system.fix5: This computer cannot reach a Mirror. Put it on a network whose Mainframe runs the Mirror ([](jsc:mirror)).
jsc.guide.arch_pacman_in_system.heading1: pacman on the system you installed
jsc.guide.arch_pacman_in_system.problem1: The screen says "error: target not found:" and then the name you typed.
jsc.guide.arch_pacman_in_system.problem2: The screen says "error: no targets specified (use -h for help)".
jsc.guide.arch_pacman_in_system.problem3: The screen says "error: no operation specified (use -h for help)".
jsc.guide.arch_pacman_in_system.problem4: The screen says "error: you cannot perform this operation unless you are root in the new" and then "system (arch-chroot /mnt first)".
jsc.guide.arch_pacman_in_system.problem5: The screen says "error: failed retrieving file 'core.db' from mirror://mainframe : Could not resolve host: mainframe".
jsc.guide.arch_pacman_in_system.step1: Make sure you are inside the new system.
jsc.guide.arch_pacman_in_system.step2: Type pacman -S and the names, for example pacman -S grub efibootmgr.
jsc.guide.arch_pacman_in_system.step3: Answer the question with Y or press [[Enter]] to install, or type n to stop.
jsc.guide.arch_pacman_in_system.table1: What pacman does on the installed system
jsc.guide.arch_pacman_in_system.table1_1: Installs the package from the Mirror.
jsc.guide.arch_pacman_in_system.table1_2: Searches the Mirror for packages whose names hold the term.
jsc.guide.arch_pacman_in_system.table1_3: Lists the packages installed on this computer.
jsc.guide.arch_pacman_in_system.table1_5: Brings every installed package up to the version the Mirror serves.
jsc.guide.arch_pacman_in_system.text1: Inside the new system, pacman -S installs programs from the Mirror, so that they are on the new system when it starts. A program you install this way is a package, with its files and the names of what it needs.
jsc.guide.arch_pacman_in_system.text2: Type pacman -S, a space, and then the names of the programs you want. Each name is the command name of a program that the Mirror has for Linux.
jsc.guide.arch_pacman_in_system.text3: Pacman asks "Proceed with installation? [Y/n]" before it changes anything. An answer that starts with n stops it, and nothing is installed. Any other answer, even an empty one, goes on.
jsc.guide.arch_pacman_in_system.text4: Each program you name is remembered, and it is installed on the new system when the install finishes. The package grub is also what the boot loader needs ([](jsc:arch_bootloader)).
jsc.guide.arch_pacman_in_system.text5: Once Arch Linux starts from your own disk, pacman stays as its package manager. Then pacman -S installs a package at once, and pacman has words to search, list, update and remove your packages too. Searching, installing and updating reach the Mirror over the network, while listing and removing work on the packages already on this computer.
jsc.guide.arch_pacman_in_system.title: Installing packages with pacman
jsc.guide.arch_reboot.fix1: You are still inside the new system. Type exit, then reboot.
jsc.guide.arch_reboot.fix2: Do each listed step, then reboot again.
jsc.guide.arch_reboot.fix3: The disk that holds /mnt has no room for the system, or it is not there. Check the disk, then install again.
jsc.guide.arch_reboot.problem1: The screen says "reboot: you are inside the new system. exit first."
jsc.guide.arch_reboot.problem2: The screen says "The new system will not boot:" and lists the missing parts.
jsc.guide.arch_reboot.problem3: The screen says "The installation could not be written to the disk (no space or no disk)."
jsc.guide.arch_reboot.step1: Type exit and press [[Enter]]. The prompt shows the live medium again.
jsc.guide.arch_reboot.text1: Before it reboots, the installer checks that the new system can start. If a part is missing, the machine lists what is missing, and it refuses to reboot until you add the part.
jsc.guide.arch_reboot.text2: When the check passes, the installer copies the new system onto the disk that holds /mnt. Then the machine reboots into it. The copy also takes the file system table you wrote, the name you chose, and the programs you asked for with pacman -S.
jsc.guide.arch_reboot.text3: The boot images are not on this list. If the server setting Every step of Arch is on, the list also checks the hardware clock and the machine's name ([](jsc:arch_clock_and_name)).
jsc.guide.arch_reboot.text4: If a part is missing, the reboot stops and lists what is missing:
jsc.guide.arch_reboot.text5: After a refusal, do each listed step, in this chapter, and then reboot again. The firmware starts the installed disk first, and the boot list shows the entry Arch Linux.
jsc.guide.arch_reboot.title: Checking and rebooting
jsc.guide.archiver.definition1: One file that holds other files, packed to weigh less. It ends in .ark.
jsc.guide.archiver.definition2: To put files into an archive, which stores them in less room.
jsc.guide.archiver.definition3: To copy files back out of an archive.
jsc.guide.archiver.fix1: Open only a file that ends in .ark.
jsc.guide.archiver.fix2: Pack the files into two archives.
jsc.guide.archiver.problem1: 67ark says that file is not an archive.
jsc.guide.archiver.problem2: 67ark says an archive holds at most 512 files.
jsc.guide.archiver.step1: Open an archive, or start a new one with New.
jsc.guide.archiver.step2: Press Add, and choose the files you want to pack.
jsc.guide.archiver.step3: Press Pack. The server does the packing, so the saving on disk is real.
jsc.guide.archiver.step4: Press Extract for the files you chose, Extract all for every file, or Take out into a folder.
jsc.guide.archiver.table1_1_2: The name of the file inside the archive.
jsc.guide.archiver.table1_2_2: The size of the file, in bytes, kilobytes or megabytes.
jsc.guide.archiver.table1_3_2: The percentage by which the archive is smaller than the files.
jsc.guide.archiver.text1: 67ark packs many files into one archive that weighs less, and it takes them back out again. That is how a small disk is made to stretch: the archive takes less room than the files it holds.
jsc.guide.archiver.text2: The window does one of two jobs, and it says which one you are doing. Either an archive is open, and its contents are listed, or you are putting an archive together from files you chose on the disk.
jsc.guide.archiver.text3: After packing, the window asks whether to delete the original files or keep them.
jsc.guide.archiver.title: 67ark

jsc.guide.asking_for_a_craft.fix2: Another operation held what it needed. Ask again once that operation has settled.

jsc.guide.asking_for_a_craft.text1: You ask for a craft the way you ask for anything else: in the Network Interactor, or in IQL, the network's query language, with CRAFT 512 piston ([](jsc:iql)).
jsc.guide.asking_for_a_craft.text2: The network plans the craft from the bottom up: what it has, what it must make first, in which order and on which machines. Then it runs the steps. Bench steps run on the Crafting Computer, as many stages at once as its threads allow. Machine steps run on the Crafting Interfaces, each on its own machine ([](jsc:crafting_computers)).
jsc.guide.asking_for_a_craft.text3: Before you ask, the Craft Planner shows you the same plan, with what it needs and what is missing ([](jsc:craft_planner)). When you open a craft from the Network Interactor's catalogue, the popup asks for the plan at once.
jsc.guide.asking_for_a_craft.text4: The quantity, the number of items to craft, starts at 1 item and can go up to 99,999 items.
jsc.guide.asking_for_a_craft.text5: The computer remembers your choice of recipe for each item, so you choose once.
jsc.guide.asking_for_a_craft.text6: The craft popup of the terminal has the buttons CRAFT and PARTIAL. CRAFT makes the whole craft. PARTIAL makes what the network can make now, and the popup shows that largest amount as "max now". CLOSE closes the popup.
jsc.guide.asking_for_a_craft.text7: The Craft tab of the terminal lists what is RUNNING and what is JUST MADE. It reads "nothing being made" when the network is idle. A pattern must be loaded before the terminal can craft: without one, the terminal reads "no patterns loaded" and asks you to load one from a medium under Patterns.
jsc.guide.asking_for_a_craft.text8: You cancel a craft in the Network Manager. Open the details of the craft there, and press Cancel. A craft cancelled while its plan is still being worked out is discarded ([](jsc:network_manager)).
jsc.guide.asking_for_a_craft.title: Asking for a craft

jsc.guide.assembly_screen.definition5: The part that draws the picture for the monitors. GPU stands for graphics processing unit.
jsc.guide.assembly_screen.definition6: The part that gives power to the other parts. PSU stands for power supply unit.
jsc.guide.assembly_screen.definition7: The place on the board where a processor sits. A processor fits only the socket its board names.

jsc.guide.assembly_screen.text1: A computer here is a case with parts inside it. Right-click the case to open the assembly screen. It shows the inside of the computer: a slot for each part, and the switches and lamps that run it. Sneak-click the side of the case, not one of its front parts, to take its left side panel off or put it back.
jsc.guide.assembly_screen.text10: If the build stops standing, the computer goes dark. When the build stands again with AUTO START on, the computer comes back on by itself.
jsc.guide.assembly_screen.text11: If you switch the power on with an invalid build, the switch goes on, but the computer does not run. The board then tests itself and beeps its failure.
jsc.guide.assembly_screen.text12: While the build is not valid, hovering POWER shows three lines: "Not a computer yet", then "Needs a board, a CPU, RAM, a disk and a PSU", then "Then press to switch on". The middle line is a general reminder, so it does not name the part that is wrong.
jsc.guide.assembly_screen.text13: The readouts and the POWER button show their tooltip only when the mouse rests on them and the cursor holds nothing.
jsc.guide.assembly_screen.text14: The screen of a Mainframe has AUTO START and FAILOVER. Read about failover in [Failover](jsc:failover) and about the Mainframe in [Mainframes](jsc:mainframes).
jsc.guide.assembly_screen.text15: The name field in the header names the computer. It takes up to 32 characters, and it saves each change as you type. An empty field shows a hint that invites you to name the computer.
jsc.guide.assembly_screen.text2: A computer runs only when its parts make a build that stands. You read the state of the build in the header of the window, and the window shows each part in its own slot.
jsc.guide.assembly_screen.text3: The POWER button's tooltip names the parts a computer needs. Without a graphics card the monitor stays dark, unless the processor has graphics built in.
jsc.guide.assembly_screen.text4: The title in the header tells you which computer you are looking at.
jsc.guide.assembly_screen.text5: The word in the top right tells you the state of the computer.
jsc.guide.assembly_screen.text6: Three lamps show what the computer is doing.
jsc.guide.assembly_screen.text7: A tower has readouts that show its numbers. Hover one to read its tooltip.
jsc.guide.assembly_screen.text8: The large button on the left of a tower's front panel is POWER. It switches the computer on and off. A tower has two switches.
jsc.guide.assembly_screen.text9: Switch AUTO START on while the build is valid, and the computer turns on at once. It stays on as long as the build stands. While AUTO START is on, POWER is locked, and its tooltip says: "Auto start keeps it on: switch auto start off to switch it off here".

jsc.guide.automation_engine.definition1: A saved IQL statement that the network runs by itself, at a set time or when a condition holds.
jsc.guide.automation_engine.definition2: The Mainframe's service that keeps the jobs and fires them. It has no window of its own.
jsc.guide.automation_engine.definition3: The part of a job that says when it fires: an interval after EVERY, or a condition after WHEN.
jsc.guide.automation_engine.definition4: The moment a condition turns from false to true. A WHEN job fires once for each such moment.
jsc.guide.automation_engine.fix1: Install the Automation Engine on the Mainframe, then type the job again.
jsc.guide.automation_engine.fix10: Restart it with the > control in the Automation Manager.
jsc.guide.automation_engine.fix11: The job runs as ordinary Operations. Look at the Operations it started ([](jsc:operations)), where each one shows its status.
jsc.guide.automation_engine.fix2: Use an engine that keeps saved objects, such as the Midsoft IQL Server ([](jsc:engines)).
jsc.guide.automation_engine.fix3: Add EVERY with a duration, or WHEN with a condition, at the end of the line.
jsc.guide.automation_engine.fix4: Write the statement between AS and EVERY or WHEN.
jsc.guide.automation_engine.fix5: Write the duration or the condition after EVERY or WHEN.
jsc.guide.automation_engine.fix6: Write VIEW, PROCEDURE or JOB after CREATE.
jsc.guide.automation_engine.fix7: Write CREATE JOB, the name, then AS and the statement.
jsc.guide.automation_engine.fix8: Choose a shorter name, of no more than 64 characters.
jsc.guide.automation_engine.fix9: IQL does not check an EVERY duration when you type the job, so a bad one never fires. Write a number with an optional unit: s, m, h or t, such as 30s or 100t.
jsc.guide.automation_engine.problem1: It says "jobs are kept by the Automation Engine; install it on the Mainframe first".

jsc.guide.automation_engine.step1: Install the Automation Engine on the Mainframe.
jsc.guide.automation_engine.step2: At the prompt of a computer on the network, type a CREATE JOB line, as the listing shows.
jsc.guide.automation_engine.step3: Press [[Enter]]. The answer ends with "created" and names the job.
jsc.guide.automation_engine.step4: Check the job on the Processes tab, or in the Automation Manager.
jsc.guide.automation_engine.table2_1_2: The Automation Engine is running, so the job can fire.
jsc.guide.automation_engine.table2_2_2: The Automation Engine is not running, so the job does not fire.
jsc.guide.automation_engine.table2_3_2: The job is paused, and it does not fire until it is restarted.
jsc.guide.automation_engine.text1: Some work should happen by itself, so you do not have to watch it: restock an item when the network runs short, or move items every hour. A job is a saved statement of IQL, the network's query language, with a trigger that says when the statement runs. The Automation Engine is the service that keeps the network's jobs and fires them on time, or when a condition holds.
jsc.guide.automation_engine.text10: The Processes tab of the Task Manager ([](jsc:system_monitor_and_task_manager)) lists the network's engine first, then each job with its state.
jsc.guide.automation_engine.text11: The detail beside a job shows its trigger, such as "every 5m" or "when qty(iron_ingot) < 64". On that tab, Start and Stop act on the network's engine, not on the jobs.
jsc.guide.automation_engine.text12: Pausing a job keeps it in the list and stops it from firing. Restarting a job resumes it, and an EVERY job counts its interval again from now. DROP JOB removes the job and its pause with it.
jsc.guide.automation_engine.text2: Install the Automation Engine on the Mainframe, as you install any service ([](jsc:mainframe_services)). It has no on or off switch of its own. It fires jobs while it is installed and the Mainframe is running, with a valid build and power on.
jsc.guide.automation_engine.text3: If the Mainframe is off, the jobs stay in the list and none of them fires. Turn the Mainframe back on, and they fire again.
jsc.guide.automation_engine.text4: You give a trigger after EVERY, with an interval, or after WHEN, with a condition. The Automation Engine checks the jobs every 10 ticks, which is half a second.
jsc.guide.automation_engine.text5: EVERY fires the job again after each interval. The first check only starts the count, so a new EVERY job waits one full interval before its first run.
jsc.guide.automation_engine.text6: WHEN fires the job on the rising edge of its condition: the moment the condition turns from false to true. It does not fire again while the condition stays true. A condition that is already true at the first check fires the job once, at that check.
jsc.guide.automation_engine.text7: A WHEN condition tests only the network's stock of an item, with qty(<item>), against a number. The operators are =, ==, !=, <, >, <=, and >=. An item name without a colon means minecraft:, so iron_ingot is minecraft:iron_ingot. A modded item needs its full name, with its mod's name before the colon.
jsc.guide.automation_engine.text8: The unit letters are s for seconds, m for minutes, h for hours and t for ticks. A number with no letter counts seconds. There are 20 ticks in a second.
jsc.guide.automation_engine.text9: Write the name, then AS and the statement the job runs, then EVERY with a duration or WHEN with a condition. Names are up to 64 characters long. DROP JOB followed by the name removes a job. The IQL book explains the job statements in full ([](jsc:iql_jobs)).
jsc.guide.automation_engine.title: The Automation Engine and jobs
jsc.guide.automation_manager.fix1: Install the Automation Engine on the Mainframe.

jsc.guide.automation_manager.fix4: Type an item and an interval such as 30s or 5m.

jsc.guide.automation_manager.fix6: Choose a script in the list, and type an interval such as 30s.
jsc.guide.automation_manager.fix7: Save the .iql file on the Mainframe's system disk, then choose it.
jsc.guide.automation_manager.fix8: The band shows the engine only while the Mainframe runs. Turn the Mainframe on.
jsc.guide.automation_manager.problem1: The chat says "jobs are kept by the Automation Engine; install it on the Mainframe first".
jsc.guide.automation_manager.problem2: The chat says "Give the job a name."
jsc.guide.automation_manager.problem3: The chat says "Restock below needs an item."
jsc.guide.automation_manager.problem4: The chat says "Batch Craft needs an item and a valid interval (e.g. 30s, 5m)."
jsc.guide.automation_manager.problem5: The chat says "Periodic Move needs FROM, TO, and a valid interval (e.g. 30s)."

jsc.guide.automation_manager.step1: Type a name in Name. Use one word, with no spaces.
jsc.guide.automation_manager.step2: Choose the type: Restock below, Batch Craft, Move or IQL.
jsc.guide.automation_manager.step3: Fill the fields that the type shows.
jsc.guide.automation_manager.step4: Click Create job. The fields clear, and the new job appears in the list.

jsc.guide.automation_manager.table1_2_2: How many jobs the network keeps, such as 3 jobs.
