jsc.guide.automation_manager.text1: The Automation Manager is the window where you write and watch the jobs, without typing IQL. It is a desktop program, so you open it from the desktop, like the other programs ([](jsc:programs)).
jsc.guide.automation_manager.text2: It runs on Frames, Linux and FreeBSD. It does not run on UNIX System V. It needs a Mainframe on the network: without one, the window says "no Mainframe".
jsc.guide.automation_manager.text3: The window works out the kind of a job from its statement and trigger, so a job you type in IQL is listed the same way. A statement that starts with CRAFT is Restock below when its trigger is WHEN, and Batch Craft otherwise. A statement that starts with neither CRAFT nor MOVE is Custom.
jsc.guide.automation_manager.text4: The Script field lists the .iql files on the Mainframe's system disk. If the disk has none, the field says "no .iql files on the Mainframe's system disk".
jsc.guide.automation_manager.text5: A Restock below job counts the stock that is in the network now. The window adds the note "Does not count what is already on its way." It also shows a tip that starts "Prophet YourIQL counts it: KEEP", with the item and the amount. Prophet is explained in ([](jsc:prophet_youriql)).
jsc.guide.automation_manager.text6: The amount takes digits only, and a blank amount counts as 1 item. An amount below 1 item becomes 1 item. The Every field takes an interval such as 30s or 5m, and it must be more than zero. The forms are the ones in ([](jsc:automation_engine)).
jsc.guide.automation_manager.text7: Creating a job with the name of an existing job replaces that job with the new one.
jsc.guide.automation_manager.title: The Automation Manager
jsc.guide.book_daemon_handbook.fix1: Take it from the creative tab J's Computers, among the programs, beside the Guide.
jsc.guide.book_daemon_handbook.problem1: You do not have this book.
jsc.guide.book_daemon_handbook.text1: The Daemon Handbook is a hardback for FreeBSD and UNIX System V: calm, complete and precise. Read a step before you take it, and you know what it will do.
jsc.guide.book_daemon_handbook.text2: Its chapters are FreeBSD, with the install, the services at boot, the packages and the ports tree; UNIX System V, with its install and the packages on its medium; and the four UNIX chapters it shares with the other books.
jsc.guide.book_daemon_handbook.text3: Its help opens first on FreeBSD and on UNIX. Start with [FreeBSD on this computer](jsc:freebsd_overview).
jsc.guide.book_daemon_handbook.title: The Daemon Handbook
jsc.guide.book_frames_resource_kit.fix1: Take it from the creative tab J's Computers, among the programs, beside the Guide.
jsc.guide.book_frames_resource_kit.probl: You do not have this book.
jsc.guide.book_frames_resource_kit.text1: The Frames Resource Kit is the reference for MC-DOS and the Frames editions, from Frames 95 to Frames 11. It is written the way a 1990s technical kit was: thorough and exact, with tables of settings and commands. You keep it open while you work on a Midsoft system.
jsc.guide.book_frames_resource_kit.text2: Its chapters are The Midsoft systems, MC-DOS, The desktop, The programs of Frames, Each edition, and The Command Prompt. If you have not chosen a system yet, start with [Which Frames goes on which machine](jsc:frames_which_machine).
jsc.guide.book_frames_resource_kit.text3: The help of MC-DOS and of every Frames opens this book first.
jsc.guide.book_frames_resource_kit.title: Frames Resource Kit
jsc.guide.book_learning_iql.fix1: Take it from the creative tab J's Computers, among the programs, beside the Guide.
jsc.guide.book_learning_iql.problem1: You do not have this book.
jsc.guide.book_learning_iql.text1: Learning IQL teaches the network's query language by example: a query, its answer, and why it works. You ask the network questions in IQL, and the network answers them by running Operations. Start with [What IQL and Operations are](jsc:what_iql_is) if you are new.
jsc.guide.book_learning_iql.text2: Its chapters are Getting started, The language (every verb and clause, and every error), The engines (the three engines and how to switch them), The tools, and Recipes, which are ready queries.
jsc.guide.book_learning_iql.text3: No system's help opens this book first. You reach it from [The library](jsc:library), or you take it from the creative tab.
jsc.guide.book_learning_iql.title: Learning IQL
jsc.guide.book_linux_by_hand.fix1: Take it from the creative tab J's Computers, among the programs, beside the Guide.
jsc.guide.book_linux_by_hand.problem1: You do not have this book.
jsc.guide.book_linux_by_hand.text1: Linux by Hand is a lab notebook. It takes you through one step at a time: what to type, what the machine answers, and what each step does and why. It covers the two systems you install by hand, Arch Linux from the live medium and Gentoo from source.
jsc.guide.book_linux_by_hand.text2: Its chapters are Before you begin, The disks, Arch, Gentoo, When the reboot refuses, and the four UNIX chapters it shares with the other books.
jsc.guide.book_linux_by_hand.text3: Its help opens first for Arch Linux and for Gentoo. Start with [Installing by hand](jsc:installing_by_hand).
jsc.guide.book_linux_by_hand.title: Linux by Hand
jsc.guide.book_linux_desk_reference.fix1: Take it from the creative tab J's Computers, among the programs, beside the Guide.
jsc.guide.book_linux_desk_reference.prob: You do not have this book.
jsc.guide.book_linux_desk_reference.text: The Linux Desk Reference lies open beside the machine. It is written for the command line first: you read what to type, what the system answers, and what each step does. It covers Fedora, Debian and Ubuntu, the three distributions you install with a guide.

Its chapters are Fedora, Debian and Ubuntu, with the installs, the first boot, apt and dnf, and the four UNIX chapters it shares with the other books: The shell, The desktops, Editors at the terminal and Finding help.
Its help opens first for Ubuntu, Debian and Fedora, when you installed them with a guide. Start with [Distributions](jsc:distributions).
jsc.guide.book_of_sigma.fix1: Take it from the creative tab J's Computers, among the programs, beside the Guide.
jsc.guide.book_of_sigma.problem1: You do not have this book.
jsc.guide.book_of_sigma.text1: The Book of Sigma is the classic language book: a definition, then a program that shows it, and the programs are the star. It teaches Sigma and Sigma#, the two languages the computers are programmed in, with their library and their tools.
jsc.guide.book_of_sigma.text2: Its chapters are Getting started, The language, The library (every class and every member), Programs running, Errors, Sharing and Examples.
jsc.guide.book_of_sigma.text3: No system's help opens this book first. You reach it from [The library](jsc:library), or you take it from the creative tab.
jsc.guide.book_of_sigma.title: The Book of Sigma
jsc.guide.boot_menu.definition1: The system's own start menu, shown before the system starts. It lets you choose one of the systems on a disk.
jsc.guide.boot_menu.fix1: The Boot Menu opens only when a disk or medium can start the computer ([](jsc:no_bootable_device)).
jsc.guide.boot_menu.fix2: Press Up or Down to highlight the system you want, then press Enter before the countdown ends.
jsc.guide.boot_menu.fix3: Turn off boot.show_boot_menu in the jscomputers-server config file.
jsc.guide.boot_menu.problem2: The boot manager starts the wrong system.
jsc.guide.boot_menu.problem3: The computer stops at the boot manager every time it starts.
jsc.guide.boot_menu.table1: The keys in the Boot Menu
jsc.guide.boot_menu.table1_1_2: Select an entry in the list.
jsc.guide.boot_menu.text1: The Boot Menu starts a disk or medium for one start only. Press [[F12]] while the computer starts ([](jsc:turning_on)). You choose with the keys below.
jsc.guide.boot_menu.text2: The screen is titled Boot Menu. On a blue BIOS machine it reads "Boot Menu  (this boot only)", and its list is headed "Boot Menu:".
jsc.guide.boot_menu.text3: The computer does not save the choice, so the next start follows the boot order ([](jsc:firmware)) again.
jsc.guide.boot_menu.text4: The boot manager is a different menu from the Boot Menu. Some systems show their own start menu before they start: GRUB does this on Linux, and the Midsoft Boot Manager on Frames, and FreeBSD has its own loader. The boot manager lets you choose between the systems of a disk ([](jsc:two_systems)).
jsc.guide.boot_menu.text5: If you do nothing, the boot manager counts down, and then it starts the highlighted entry by itself, after 5 seconds. Press Enter to start the highlighted entry at once.
jsc.guide.boot_menu.text6: Its help reads: "Use the Up and Down keys to select which entry is highlighted. Press Enter to boot the selected entry."
jsc.guide.boot_menu.text7: On a server, the setting boot.show_boot_menu decides whether a machine stops at its boot manager every time it starts. It is on by default. Turn it off, and the chosen system boots at once. The setting is in the jscomputers-server config file.
jsc.guide.boot_menu.title: The Boot Menu and the boot manager
jsc.guide.bsdinstall.definition1: FreeBSD's own installer, which asks its questions on pages in one fixed order.
jsc.guide.bsdinstall.definition2: The ports tree, the folder of recipes that builds programs from source.
jsc.guide.bsdinstall.definition3: The disk filesystem that bsdinstall lays down on the whole disk.
jsc.guide.bsdinstall.definition4: A compressed bundle of system files, such as base.txz or kernel.txz.
jsc.guide.bsdinstall.fix1: No Mirror answered, or this computer's era is older than the desktop's minimum. Connect to a network with a Mirror, or use a newer computer.
jsc.guide.bsdinstall.fix2: No Mainframe on this network runs the Mirror service. A Mainframe has to run it ([](jsc:mirror)).
jsc.guide.bsdinstall.fix3: Press Cancel, then start the installer again.
jsc.guide.bsdinstall.problem1: The Desktop page has no desktop in its list.
jsc.guide.bsdinstall.problem2: The Mirror Selection page has no mirror:// row.
jsc.guide.bsdinstall.problem3: You want to change an answer, and there is no Back button.
jsc.guide.bsdinstall.table1_2_2: Keep the name the field shows, or type another one.
jsc.guide.bsdinstall.table1_3_2: Tick ports to install the Ports Collection. It is ticked by default.
jsc.guide.bsdinstall.table1_4_2: Choose the disk and how it is used.
jsc.guide.bsdinstall.table1_5_2: Choose the Mirror to fetch from, or none to install from the CD only.
jsc.guide.bsdinstall.table1_6_2: Wait while the system is copied.
jsc.guide.bsdinstall.table1_7_2: Tick the services to start at boot. cron is ticked by default, and sshd is not.
jsc.guide.bsdinstall.table1_8_2: Only when a Mirror answers: choose a desktop, or None.
jsc.guide.bsdinstall.table2_1_1: Auto (UFS): use the whole of the disk
jsc.guide.bsdinstall.table2_2_1: Auto (UFS): use the whole of the disk, erasing what is on it
jsc.guide.bsdinstall.table2_2_2: The disk holds a system or files. Its files are erased.
jsc.guide.bsdinstall.table2_3_1: Beside: share the disk with its system
jsc.guide.bsdinstall.table2_3_2: The disk holds a system and has room left beside it.
jsc.guide.bsdinstall.text1: bsdinstall is FreeBSD's own installer. It asks its questions on pages, always in the same order, and then it copies the system onto the disk you choose. This page goes through each page, so you know what it asks before you answer.
jsc.guide.bsdinstall.text2: You need a computer with a disk and an install medium: the FreeBSD CD (compact disc), put in a CD Drive. A Mirror on the network is optional. With one, the installer also offers desktops and fetches packages from it.
jsc.guide.bsdinstall.text3: The Welcome page has the button Install, and every other page has OK. bsdinstall has no Back button: each page offers only Cancel and its own button, so to change an earlier answer, press Cancel and start the installer again.
jsc.guide.bsdinstall.text4: The Partitioning page lists one row per disk. The disks are named ada0, ada1 and so on, in the order of the drives. Each row offers a way to use that disk. Auto (UFS) puts the UNIX File System (UFS) on the whole disk.
jsc.guide.bsdinstall.text5: Before the installer erases a disk, it asks "Erase ada0?" and names what it erases. The dialog says "This cannot be undone." Press Y to erase, or N to cancel.
jsc.guide.bsdinstall.text6: The Mirror Selection page asks where pkg and ports fetch from. The row mirror://mainframe appears only when a Mirror answers ([](jsc:mirror)). Otherwise you install from the CD.
jsc.guide.bsdinstall.text7: When the copy is done, your answers become settings. Ticking cron turns cron on, and ticking sshd turns remote on. Both are the settings you can change later ([](jsc:rc_services)). With the ports box ticked and a Mirror in use, the whole ports tree is laid onto the disk now. Without a Mirror, the installer leaves an empty /usr/ports folder for portsnap to fill.
jsc.guide.bsdinstall.text8: At the end, the computer restarts into the new system once you take the CD out.
jsc.guide.bsdinstall.title: Installing FreeBSD, page by page
jsc.guide.bsdinstall.warning1: Erasing a disk deletes every file on it, and this cannot be undone.
jsc.guide.build_refusals.definition1: The watts the parts ask for in total. The processors, the memory, the disks and the expansion cards add up to it. The motherboard's own power is not counted.
jsc.guide.build_refusals.definition2: A slot on the board for an expansion card. The bus standards are ISA, PCI, AGP (Accelerated Graphics Port) and PCI-e (PCI Express), from the oldest to the newest.
jsc.guide.build_refusals.definition3: The family a bus belongs to: ISA, PCI, AGP or PCI-e. A card fits a board only when the bus families match, but for the PCI cards of the Workshop and the PCI Crafting Card, which fit any board but an ISA one. ISA is also the name of the oldest bus.
jsc.guide.build_refusals.fix1: Hold it over the slot to read the rule it breaks, and find that rule in the tables above.
jsc.guide.build_refusals.fix2: Put in a board the case takes, and a power supply.
jsc.guide.build_refusals.heading1: Parts that stay out of their slot
jsc.guide.build_refusals.problem1: A part does not go into its slot.
jsc.guide.build_refusals.problem2: The server says "Insert a motherboard and PSU to begin".
jsc.guide.build_refusals.table1: The lines of the CHECKS list
jsc.guide.build_refusals.table1_10_2: More memory modules than the board has slots.
jsc.guide.build_refusals.table1_10_3: Take modules out, or use a board with more RAM slots.
jsc.guide.build_refusals.table1_11_2: A module's generation is not on the board's list.
jsc.guide.build_refusals.table1_11_3: Use a module of a generation the board takes.
jsc.guide.build_refusals.table1_12_2: More disks in the board's disk slots than it has.
jsc.guide.build_refusals.table1_12_3: Move disks to the Hot-Swap Drive Bay, or use a board with more disk slots.
jsc.guide.build_refusals.table1_13_2: The power draw is more than the power supply gives.
jsc.guide.build_refusals.table1_13_3: Use a power supply with more watts. On a rack server, the DRAW readout shows the total.
jsc.guide.build_refusals.table1_1_3: Put a processor in the socket the board names.
jsc.guide.build_refusals.table1_2_2: The build has no memory module.
jsc.guide.build_refusals.table1_2_3: Put in a module of a generation the board takes, of its era.
jsc.guide.build_refusals.table1_3_2: More processors than the board has sockets for.
jsc.guide.build_refusals.table1_3_3: Take processors out, or use a board with more CPU slots.
jsc.guide.build_refusals.table1_4_2: A processor's socket is not the board's socket.
jsc.guide.build_refusals.table1_4_3: Use a processor with the board's socket.
jsc.guide.build_refusals.table1_5_2: Two processors understand different instruction sets.
jsc.guide.build_refusals.table1_5_3: Use processors of one instruction set.
jsc.guide.build_refusals.table1_6_2: More expansion cards than the board has expansion slots.
jsc.guide.build_refusals.table1_6_3: Take cards out, or use a board with more PCI-e slots.
jsc.guide.build_refusals.table1_7_2: A card's bus family is not the board's bus family.
jsc.guide.build_refusals.table1_7_3: Use a card of the board's bus family.
jsc.guide.build_refusals.table1_8_2: The sound card is of another era than the board.
jsc.guide.build_refusals.table1_8_3: Use a sound card of the board's era.
jsc.guide.build_refusals.table1_9_2: The computer has two sound cards.
jsc.guide.build_refusals.table2_1_1: A board of another form factor or era
jsc.guide.build_refusals.table2_1_2: The case takes only its own form factors, and boards of its own era.
jsc.guide.build_refusals.table2_2_1: A processor of another socket or era, while a board is in place
jsc.guide.build_refusals.table2_2_2: It must match the board's socket and era.
jsc.guide.build_refusals.table2_3_1: A memory module of another generation or era, while a board is in place
jsc.guide.build_refusals.table2_3_2: It must match a generation the board takes, and the board's era.
jsc.guide.build_refusals.table2_4_1: A disk of a newer era than the computer
jsc.guide.build_refusals.table2_4_2: A disk fits the computer's own era or an older one.
jsc.guide.build_refusals.table2_5_1: A part other than a drive in a bay
jsc.guide.build_refusals.table2_5_2: A bay takes only a drive.
jsc.guide.build_refusals.table2_6_2: A computer takes one sound card.
jsc.guide.build_refusals.table2_7_1: A second Cluster Interface Card in a Cluster Management Computer
jsc.guide.build_refusals.table2_7_2: A Cluster Management Computer takes only one of them.
jsc.guide.build_refusals.table2_8_1: A Workshop card in a computer other than a Personal Computer
jsc.guide.build_refusals.table2_8_2: Only a Personal Computer takes Workshop cards.
jsc.guide.build_refusals.table2_9_1: An Integra Phi coprocessor in a rack server other than a supercomputer node
jsc.guide.build_refusals.table2_9_2: Only a supercomputer node takes one, and only one per node.
jsc.guide.build_refusals.text1: When a build has problems, a rack server's assembly screen can tell you which ones. Its power area has a label, CHECKS. Hover it and every problem of the build shows as one line.
jsc.guide.build_refusals.text2: Towers and the Mainframe do not list the problems. Their POWER tooltip gives only the three generic lines of [The assembly screen](jsc:assembly_screen), so use the table below to find the cause.
jsc.guide.build_refusals.text3: When nothing is wrong, the list says "All checks passed" in green. With no board or power supply in place, it says "Insert a motherboard and PSU to begin".
jsc.guide.build_refusals.text4: The numbers in each line change to match your build.
jsc.guide.build_refusals.text5: Some parts never go into a slot. Hold one over the slot, and the window says which rule keeps it out, as the table below lists them.
jsc.guide.build_refusals.text6: A board the case refuses leaves the computer with no build at all. The same happens with no power supply in place.
jsc.guide.build_refusals.title: When the build is refused
jsc.guide.building_from_source.fix1: Check the spelling, or use the category and name, such as kde-plasma/plasma-meta.
jsc.guide.building_from_source.fix3: No Mainframe running the Mirror is on this network. Connect to one, then try again.
jsc.guide.building_from_source.heading1: emerge on the system you installed
jsc.guide.building_from_source.problem1: emerge says there are no ebuilds to satisfy the name you typed.
jsc.guide.building_from_source.problem2: emerge says "The portage tree is empty".
jsc.guide.building_from_source.table1: What the KDE Plasma desktop brings
jsc.guide.building_from_source.table2: What emerge does on the installed system
jsc.guide.building_from_source.table2_2_: Lists what it would build, and asks you before it starts.
jsc.guide.building_from_source.table2_3_: Searches the Mirror for packages whose names hold the term.
jsc.guide.building_from_source.table2_5_: Brings every installed package up to the version the Mirror serves.
jsc.guide.building_from_source.text1: Inside the new system, emerge installs programs the same way it did during the install. Portage compiles each program from its source on your machine, so every program takes time to build.
jsc.guide.building_from_source.text2: A compile is faster on a machine whose processor has a faster clock. The compiles at once are the smaller of two numbers: the count in MAKEOPTS ([](jsc:make_conf)), and the cores of your machine. There is always at least 1 compile at a time.
jsc.guide.building_from_source.text3: You name a program by its category and name, such as kde-plasma/plasma-meta, or by its name alone, in any letter case. The category follows the kind of program: applications go under app-misc, and desktops under x11-wm.
jsc.guide.building_from_source.text4: During the install, the Mirror installs by name only a program that runs on Linux, is not a background service, and fits the machine and its era.
jsc.guide.building_from_source.text5: To install a desktop, type emerge --ask kde-plasma/plasma-meta. It builds these packages in this order:
jsc.guide.building_from_source.text6: The GNOME, Cinnamon and CDE (Common Desktop Environment) desktops have their own chains. A package that is only listed, such as the desktop's meta package, takes no time to build.
jsc.guide.building_from_source.text7: Once Gentoo starts from your own disk, emerge stays as its package manager, and it still compiles what it installs. Each of its words reaches the Mirror over the network.
jsc.guide.building_from_source.title: Building programs from source
jsc.guide.bus_activity.fix1: The bus has not moved an item yet. Check what the bus needs before it moves ([](jsc:buses)), and what its filter lets through ([](jsc:bus_filters_and_tags)).
jsc.guide.bus_activity.fix2: The network or the chest has no room. Free space in the chest, or add storage to the network ([](jsc:storage)).
jsc.guide.bus_activity.fix3: A condition did not hold. Read the conditions of the bus in CONFIGURE ([](jsc:bus_conditions)).
jsc.guide.bus_activity.problem3: The reason says "a condition holds it".
jsc.guide.bus_activity.table1_2_2: Part of the move went through. The rest stays in the bus and is sent again.
jsc.guide.bus_activity.table1_3_2: The bus held back, because the chest kept its KEEP amount or a condition did not hold.
jsc.guide.bus_activity.table1_4_2: No room: the network is full for an Import Bus, or the chest is full for an Export Bus.
jsc.guide.bus_activity.table2_1_2: An Import Bus moved items into the network.
jsc.guide.bus_activity.table2_2_2: An Export Bus moved items into the chest.
jsc.guide.bus_activity.table2_3_2: The chest already holds its KEEP amount, so the Export Bus waits.
jsc.guide.bus_activity.table2_4_2: An Import Bus found no room in the network.
jsc.guide.bus_activity.table2_5_2: An Export Bus found the chest full.
jsc.guide.bus_activity.table2_6_2: A condition did not hold, so the bus waited.
jsc.guide.bus_activity.text1: The Activity tab is the log of one bus. Each line is a move the bus made, or a time it waited, with the reason. The bus keeps the latest 16 lines and shows 8 at a time, so you scroll to see the rest.
jsc.guide.bus_activity.text2: Each move is an Operation ([](jsc:what_operations_are)). The terminal and the Network Manager list the same log, so you can read these moves in the Network Manager ([](jsc:network_manager)).
jsc.guide.bus_activity.text3: A line shows the time, the item with its amount after an x, a status on the right, and the reason under the status.
jsc.guide.bus_activity.text4: A hold that repeats updates the time of the newest line, instead of adding a line. When the network takes only part of a move, the rest stays in the bus, and the bus sends it when there is room.
jsc.guide.bus_activity.title: What a bus did
jsc.guide.bus_conditions.definition1: How many of an item the whole network holds, not the count in one chest.
jsc.guide.bus_conditions.fix1: Open its Activity tab. A line that says "a condition holds it" means a condition is not met, so the bus waits. Read the sentence of each condition in CONFIGURE ([](jsc:bus_activity)).
jsc.guide.bus_conditions.fix2: A count below 1, an unknown item id or a bad tag is refused. The window shows nothing when it refuses.
jsc.guide.bus_conditions.fix3: A bus holds up to 4 conditions. Take one off first, then add the new one.
jsc.guide.bus_conditions.fix4: FROM and TO are the same hour. Set them to two different hours.
jsc.guide.bus_conditions.problem1: The bus waits and does not move.
jsc.guide.bus_conditions.problem2: The window refuses a STOCK condition.
jsc.guide.bus_conditions.problem3: The bus does not take a fifth condition.
jsc.guide.bus_conditions.problem4: The HOURS condition holds all day.
jsc.guide.bus_conditions.step1: Open the bus's window and go to CONFIGURE.
jsc.guide.bus_conditions.step2: Click + condition, and choose STOCK, HOURS or AFTER.
jsc.guide.bus_conditions.step3: Fill in the editor, with the - and + buttons for the numbers.
jsc.guide.bus_conditions.step4: To take a condition off, click the right end of its row.
jsc.guide.bus_conditions.table1_1_2: only while the network holds under 64 minecraft:iron_ore
jsc.guide.bus_conditions.table1_1_3: The network holds fewer than that number.
jsc.guide.bus_conditions.table1_2_3: The game's clock is between the two hours.
jsc.guide.bus_conditions.table1_3_2: after the bus Coal in finishes
jsc.guide.bus_conditions.table1_3_3: The named bus has made no move for 40 ticks.
jsc.guide.bus_conditions.text1: A condition is a rule that a bus checks before it moves. A Standard or later bus can have up to 4 conditions, and every one of them must hold for the bus to move. A bus whose condition does not hold waits, and its Activity tab says so.
jsc.guide.bus_conditions.text2: The bus checks its conditions every 20 ticks, which is a second, and keeps the answer until the next check. You can also write conditions in IQL ([](jsc:iql)) with WHEN.
jsc.guide.bus_conditions.text3: STOCK counts what the whole network holds. The condition holds while that total is below the number you set. The number starts at 64 items and changes by 1 item; with Shift held, it changes by 64 items.
jsc.guide.bus_conditions.text4: Write a tag after a # sign, such as #c:ores, and STOCK counts every held item that carries the tag. In the window, click the item field with an item in your hand to write that item's id into it.
jsc.guide.bus_conditions.text5: HOURS holds between two hours of the day. You set FROM and TO, and when TO comes before FROM, the window runs past midnight. The default is from 18:00 to 06:00, the night.
jsc.guide.bus_conditions.text6: The hours follow the game's clock, not the real one. 06:00 is the start of each game day. If FROM and TO are the same hour, the condition holds all day.
jsc.guide.bus_conditions.text7: A bus holds only one hours window. Adding a second one is refused, and the action bar says "A bus holds only one hours window. Remove it first to set another." From IQL, a new hours window replaces the old one.
jsc.guide.bus_conditions.text8: AFTER waits for another bus on the same network. It holds once the named bus has made no move for 40 ticks, which is 2 seconds. Finished here means no move for that long, not that the job is done.
jsc.guide.bus_conditions.text9: If no bus has that name, nothing holds this bus back, so the condition holds. Type the name in the window, up to 32 characters. The name is not case-sensitive.
jsc.guide.bus_conditions.title: Conditions
jsc.guide.bus_filters_and_tags.definitio: Matching an item as the plain item it is, whatever its damage and its components are.
jsc.guide.bus_filters_and_tags.fix1: Its filter is empty and set to ONLY THESE, so it lists no item. List the items, or choose ALL BUT THESE.
jsc.guide.bus_filters_and_tags.fix2: Its filter is empty, and an empty list takes everything. List the items you want, with ONLY THESE.

jsc.guide.bus_filters_and_tags.text1: A filter is the list of things a bus is told to move. It has five slots, and each slot holds one item, one fluid or one chemical. A filled fluid container selects its fluid.
jsc.guide.bus_filters_and_tags.text2: The two options for the list are ONLY THESE and ALL BUT THESE. ONLY THESE moves what the list names. ALL BUT THESE moves everything the list does not name.
jsc.guide.bus_filters_and_tags.text3: On a Transition bus, the + item button lists the item in the first free cell.
jsc.guide.bus_filters_and_tags.text4: Advanced buses also match tags. A tag names a group of items, such as c:ores, and a tag on the bus matches every item that carries it. The window takes up to 4 tags. Click + tag and type the tag, with or without the # sign.
jsc.guide.bus_filters_and_tags.text5: A tag counts as a listed entry for ONLY THESE and ALL BUT THESE, the same way an item does.
jsc.guide.bus_filters_and_tags.text6: A filter normally matches an item exactly. An Advanced bus can match loosely instead, which the window calls FUZZY.
jsc.guide.bus_filters_and_tags.text7: With FUZZY, a damaged or enchanted tool matches the plain tool. A fluid matches its fluid, not its bucket. The window's note reads "Fuzzy: an item matches whatever its damage and its components."

jsc.guide.bus_keep_max_and_priority.fix1: Check POWER: a bus set to OFF stops. Then check MODE: ON DEMAND needs a redstone signal on the cable's block.
jsc.guide.bus_keep_max_and_priority.fix2: A bus with a higher priority on the same network wanted the same thing a moment ago. Raise the priority of this bus, or lower the other one.
jsc.guide.bus_keep_max_and_priority.fix3: Only Standard and later buses have a priority. Vintage, Legacy and Transition buses do not.
jsc.guide.bus_keep_max_and_priority.fix4: The window keeps KEEP and MAX between 0 and 1,000,000, and PRIORITY between -99 and 99.

jsc.guide.bus_keep_max_and_priority.tabl: How many stay in the chest on an Import Bus, or how many the chest is filled to on an Export Bus, from 0 to 1,000,000.
The most one move takes, where zero means as much as the speed allows in one second.
Who goes first when two buses want the same thing, from -99 to 99 in the window, on Standard and later buses only.
CONTINUOUS moves at all times, and ON DEMAND moves only while the cable's block has a redstone signal.
ON lets the bus move, and OFF stops it.
jsc.guide.bus_keep_max_and_priority.text: Five settings decide how much your bus moves and when. KEEP and MAX set the amounts. PRIORITY decides who goes first when buses compete. MODE and POWER decide whether a bus moves at all.

KEEP works in opposite ways on the two buses. An Import Bus leaves that many items in the chest it faces, and takes only what is above that number. An Export Bus fills the chest up to that number, and then stops.

MAX is the most one move takes, not a total. Zero means no cap: the bus moves as much as its speed allows in one second, which is 20 ticks. The window shows "any" with the note "a time" when MAX is zero.

Each bus that wants something says so with its priority, every tick it wants it. A bus waits while a bus of a higher priority on the same network has wanted the same thing in the last 2 ticks. Equal priorities both go. Priority does not make a bus faster. It only decides who goes first ([](jsc:priorities)).
An Export Bus wants the item it sends. An Import Bus wants room in the network, and counts as wanting it while the network has had no room for its moves in the last 40 ticks.

A bus on ON DEMAND checks its cable's block for a redstone signal. A bus on CONTINUOUS does not check. A bus set to OFF does not move, whatever its mode. MODE and POWER are on every Import and Export Bus, and not on the External Storage Bus ([](jsc:external_storage_bus)).

A Transition bus has no keep or max for the whole bus. Each item in its filter has its own keep and max, shown as a row in the window. An item with a keep or a max of zero uses the bus-wide value, and there is none on a Transition bus, so zero means no keep and no cap.

jsc.guide.bus_window.text1: Right-click a placed bus to open its window. The title in capitals at the top says which bus it is, such as IMPORT BUS or EXTERNAL STORAGE BUS. A lamp at the top right shows the state of its cable, and your own inventory is on the same screen.
jsc.guide.bus_window.text2: The lamp is green when the bus's cable reaches a network. Hover it and it says LINKED. It is red when the cable reaches no network, and then it says OFFLINE.
jsc.guide.bus_window.text3: The NAME field comes first. Type a name, up to 32 characters, and the change reaches the server at once. Software finds the bus by this name, so give each bus one ([](jsc:programming_buses)).
jsc.guide.bus_window.text4: Below the name, the rows show the settings your bus's era has. Vintage shows the fewest, and Advanced shows the most. Each row has a label, its controls and sometimes a note.
jsc.guide.bus_window.text5: The SOFTWARE tab writes the bus's settings as IQL statements and as SIGMA calls, so you can copy them into a program. ADDRESS shows the name a program uses, such as bus://Ore in. The section SET BY PROGRAMS lists which program set which setting, with lines such as "Sigma: the keep".
jsc.guide.bus_window.text6: Hover a setting that a program set, and it says which program set it. Changing the setting in the window takes it back by hand.

jsc.guide.buses.definition2: A bus that takes items from the block it faces and puts them into the network.
jsc.guide.buses.definition3: A bus that takes items from the network and puts them into the block it faces.
jsc.guide.buses.definition4: A rule a bus checks before it moves, such as a stock count or an hour of the day.

jsc.guide.buses.text1: Buses are thin parts you put on the face of a data cable, against a chest or a machine, so the network can reach it without you.
jsc.guide.buses.text2: Every move a bus makes is an Operation ([](jsc:what_operations_are)) that the network's Mainframe runs. So no bus moves while its network has no Mainframe ([](jsc:mainframes)).
jsc.guide.buses.text3: There are three kinds of bus. Each one reaches one block, the chest, tank or machine it faces.
jsc.guide.buses.text4: Buses move fluids too ([](jsc:fluids)). The External Storage Bus has its own page ([](jsc:external_storage_bus)).
jsc.guide.buses.text5: If you point at the chest or the machine instead, the bus looks for a cable behind that face first, then for any cable next to it.
jsc.guide.buses.text6: A bus mounts only on an access or a backbone cable of its own era or of an earlier one ([](jsc:data_cables), [](jsc:eras)). On any other cable it does not fit. A face that already holds a part, or that a wire crosses, takes no bus, and nothing happens.
jsc.guide.buses.text7: A bus moves only when every requirement in this table holds. Check them in the bus's window when a bus stays still.
jsc.guide.buses.text8: A bus that has moved something in the last 60 ticks, which is 3 seconds, shows a busy model on its cable, and that model blinks.
jsc.guide.buses.title: Buses
jsc.guide.buses_by_era.definition1: The list of up to five items, fluids or chemicals that a bus is told to move.
jsc.guide.buses_by_era.definition2: A group of items with a shared name, such as c:ores. A bus can list a tag in place of single items.
jsc.guide.buses_by_era.definition3: How many items a bus leaves in the block it faces (Import), or fills that block up to (Export).
jsc.guide.buses_by_era.definition4: The most items one move takes. Zero means as many as the speed allows.
jsc.guide.buses_by_era.fix1: The cable is the limit. Use a cable of a newer era, or an access or backbone line ([](jsc:data_cables)).
jsc.guide.buses_by_era.problem1: The bus moves fewer items than the table says.
jsc.guide.buses_by_era.table2_1_3: No filter: an Export Bus sends the one item in its cell, and an Import Bus takes what it finds first.
jsc.guide.buses_by_era.table2_2_3: A filter of up to 5 items, ONLY THESE or ALL BUT THESE, and one keep and one max for the whole bus.
jsc.guide.buses_by_era.table2_3_3: A filter of up to 5 items, each with its own keep and max.
jsc.guide.buses_by_era.table2_4_3: A filter, a keep and a max for the whole bus, a priority and conditions.
jsc.guide.buses_by_era.table2_5_3: Everything Standard has, plus up to 4 tags and loose matching.
jsc.guide.buses_by_era.text1: Each era of hardware has its own buses, and the newer buses carry more. You get each bus from the creative tabs, as with everything in this mod. Exa and Singularity use the Advanced bus.
jsc.guide.buses_by_era.text2: The newer the era, the more you can set on the bus, and the faster it moves. The table shows the speed of each era's bus and what its window can set.
jsc.guide.buses_by_era.text3: A bus's speed is the lower of two numbers: what its era allows, and what its cable carries. A Standard Import Bus on a Standard access cable moves 32 items a tick. On a Legacy access cable it moves 16 items a tick, because that cable carries 16 items a tick. A Vintage bus moves 1 item a tick on any cable.
jsc.guide.buses_by_era.text4: Storage buses do not mount on long-distance or HPC lines. A cable of a newer era carries more, so a newer cable lifts the speed of a bus on it.
jsc.guide.buses_by_era.text5: The External Storage Bus has no speed of its own. The network reaches its inventory at one tenth of what the cable carries, and at least 1 item a tick. It has no POWER and no MODE setting. Its own page explains it ([](jsc:external_storage_bus)).

jsc.guide.buses_library.text1: A bus is a block that moves items between the network and a machine. Its settings say which items it handles, how many it keeps and moves, and when it works. The bus itself is explained in [](jsc:buses).
jsc.guide.buses_library.text2: If you want to set a bus, Bus.Named finds it by its name on the network. It gives null when no bus of that name is on the network. Bus came in version 2.
jsc.guide.buses_library.text3: Each setting gives the bus back, so settings can follow one another. For example, bus("Ore in").Keep(16).Max(64) keeps 16 of the item and moves at most 64 at once.
jsc.guide.buses_library.text4: Only and AllBut take the items separated by commas. Blank items are dropped. Between takes hours from 0 to 23.
jsc.guide.buses_library.text5: A setting goes through the network's own language. When the bus cannot take it, the program stops with the engine's answer. Each setting is marked with the program that made it: the class the program starts from, or Sigma when it has none.
jsc.guide.buses_library.text6: A BusItem is one item of a bus. Its fields are BusItem.Bus and BusItem.Item, the names of the bus and the item. Its settings are BusItem.Keep and BusItem.Max, and they work as the same settings on the bus do.

jsc.guide.calculator_paint_exceed.text1: Three programs of the desktop work with numbers and pictures: a Calculator for expressions, Paint for pictures, and Exceed for a sheet of cells that can ask the network what it holds.
jsc.guide.calculator_paint_exceed.text2: The Calculator works out the expression you type, with brackets, powers, roots, logarithms and the trigonometric functions. Type with the keys or the keyboard, and press = or [[Enter]] to get the answer. The expression holds at most 256 characters.
jsc.guide.calculator_paint_exceed.text3: Paint draws a picture on a canvas of up to 128 by 128 pixels, on one layer, in a palette of 256 colours. A saved picture is a .pix file of about a kilobyte.
jsc.guide.calculator_paint_exceed.text4: The buttons along the top are New, Open, Save, Undo, the zoom, Wallpaper and Print. Undo goes back through up to 24 steps. Wallpaper makes the picture the desktop background. Print sends the picture to a printer, one picture to a page ([](jsc:printers)).
jsc.guide.calculator_paint_exceed.text5: Exceed is a sheet of cells, as a spreadsheet is. It has 26 columns, from A to Z, and 99 rows. Each cell has a name made of its column letter and its row number, such as B7. Its files are plain comma-separated text (.csv).
jsc.guide.calculator_paint_exceed.text6: A formula uses the four arithmetic signs, brackets, the power sign, the names of other cells, and the functions below. A live cell is one that uses QTY, FREE or SERVERS. Exceed asks the network again after a wait of 3 seconds, so typing does not send a request for every key.
jsc.guide.calculator_paint_exceed.text7: The buttons of Exceed are Open, Save, Save As and Refresh.

jsc.guide.call_costs.text1: A program reaches the computer, the network and other computers through calls. Each call you make costs its one instruction, plus a price on top. The price depends on how much work the call does, so a call that reads a whole file costs more than one that reads a name.
jsc.guide.call_costs.text2: The price has three parts. The fixed part is always paid. A row is one entry of a list that the call brings back, such as one file name, and each row adds the second part. A block is 4,096 bytes, or 4 kilobytes (KB), of memory that the call reads or writes. Each block adds the third part, and a part of a block counts as a whole block.
jsc.guide.call_costs.text3: A call that only touches the program itself is free, so only its instruction is paid. Printing to the console and reading typed lines are free, and so are the calls that look at the program's own name and arguments.
jsc.guide.call_costs.text4: Every call is priced at one of these levels. The same levels apply on every computer.
jsc.guide.call_costs.text5: File calls use the same levels. Reading a file costs the read price, plus the price for each block it reads.
jsc.guide.call_costs.title: What each call costs

Cancels one, by the start of its ID
jsc.guide.cancelling_and_the_log.table2: What a row of the log shows
jsc.guide.cancelling_and_the_log.table2_: The kind of Operation, such as SELECT or MOVE.
The item that it worked on.
How much moved, out of how much was asked.
Its state, such as PENDING, COMPLETED or DISCARDED.
The line with the reason, when there is one.
How many ticks it waited for a queue, and how many it ran.
jsc.guide.cancelling_and_the_log.text1: You can stop an Operation while it runs or waits. The Processes tab of the Network Manager lists the Operations in flight. Click a row, and its popup shows the type, the item, the amount, the timing, the parts of its work and a Cancel button.
jsc.guide.cancelling_and_the_log.text2: Cancelling hands back what the Operation held. The Operation then settles as DISCARDED on the next tick, and the log records it.
jsc.guide.cancelling_and_the_log.text3: The Command Prompt has the same control through its interac command. The two forms in the next table work on the Operations in flight.
jsc.guide.cancelling_and_the_log.text4: The Mainframe keeps a log of the Operations that settled. It holds the last 32 Operations, newest first. The Log tab of the Network Manager shows it under the title "Network log".
jsc.guide.cancelling_and_the_log.text5: The Stats tab shows the Operations that settled in the last hour. It says "No Operations settled in the last hour." when none did.
jsc.guide.cancelling_and_the_log.text6: When the Mainframe is switched off, loses its operating system, or meets a network conflict, everything in flight ends. Each Operation is settled as DISCARDED and logged, and what it held is given back. A network conflict happens when two Mainframes claim the same network ([](jsc:network_identity)).
jsc.guide.cancelling_and_the_log.text7: A save keeps the Operations in flight, and they resume at the next start. A save older than 24 hours is discarded and logged instead, by default. The mod's configuration can change that time.
jsc.guide.cancelling_and_the_log.title: Cancelling and the log
jsc.guide.case_front.balloon1_detail: Click it to switch the computer on or off.
jsc.guide.case_front.balloon2_detail: The first is lit while the computer runs. The second blinks while it works its disk.
jsc.guide.case_front.balloon3_detail: Its eject button opens and closes the tray.
jsc.guide.case_front.balloon4_detail: Click with a disc in your hand to lay it on the open tray. Sneak-click to take it out.
jsc.guide.case_front.balloon5_detail: Sneak-click the port to pull the stick out.
jsc.guide.case_front.balloon6_detail: Click it with a USB flash drive in your hand to plug the stick in.
jsc.guide.case_front.definition1: A part that sticks out of the front and takes clicks of its own.
jsc.guide.case_front.definition2: A slot on the front of the case for a 5.25-inch drive.
jsc.guide.case_front.definition3: The drawer of an optical drive, which carries the disc.
jsc.guide.case_front.definition4: A part you can pull out and push back in while the computer is on.
jsc.guide.case_front.figure1: The front of a Standard Personal Computer: the power button and its two lamps, a DVD drive with its tray out, and a USB stick in a port. Drag it to look at the case from the side.
jsc.guide.case_front.fix1: Press the eject button on the drive's front to open the tray.
jsc.guide.case_front.fix2: The game names the drive, as in "This CD drive cannot read that disc." A CD drive reads CDs, a DVD drive DVDs and CDs, and a Blu-ray drive all three. Use a drive of the right kind.
jsc.guide.case_front.fix3: The drive is reading a disc. Wait for it to finish.
jsc.guide.case_front.fix4: Press the eject button to open the tray, then sneak-click the open tray to take the disc out.
jsc.guide.case_front.fix5: Sneak-click the port to pull its stick out.
jsc.guide.case_front.fix6: Click the bay with an empty hand to take its disk out.
jsc.guide.case_front.fix7: The disk is newer than the computer's era. Use a disk of the computer's era or of an older one.
jsc.guide.case_front.problem1: The disc will not go in, and the game says "The tray is closed - press the eject button to open it."
jsc.guide.case_front.problem2: The drive cannot read that disc.
jsc.guide.case_front.problem3: The tray will not come out, and the game says "The drive is reading - wait for it to finish."
jsc.guide.case_front.problem4: The drive already holds a disc.
jsc.guide.case_front.problem5: The port already holds a stick.
jsc.guide.case_front.problem6: The bay already holds a disk.
jsc.guide.case_front.problem7: The hot-swap bay refuses a disk, and the message says this computer does not take that disk.
jsc.guide.case_front.table1: The front of each era's case
jsc.guide.case_front.text1: The front of a Personal Computer, a Crafting Computer or a Cluster Management Computer has parts you can click. It has a power button, bays for drives and, from the Transition on, USB ports. Click one of those parts and it does its job. Click anywhere else on the case and the assembly screen opens, or, with a sneak-click, the side panel comes off or goes back on.
jsc.guide.case_front.text2: Look at a standing part, such as an open tray or a stick in a port, and your click goes to that part. The power button, at the top of the front, switches the computer on and off, whatever you hold. It does the same as POWER on the assembly screen.
jsc.guide.case_front.text3: Four parts go in a bay, one to a bay, and any of them goes in any bay the case has. You put one in on the assembly screen.
jsc.guide.case_front.text4: An internal drive works like the drive of its kind outside the case ([the drives](jsc:drives)). The eject button on its front opens or closes the tray. With the tray open, click with a disc in your hand to lay it on the tray. Sneak-click the open tray to take the disc out again.
jsc.guide.case_front.text5: A drive reads only the discs of its kind. A CD drive reads CDs, a DVD drive reads DVDs and CDs, and a Blu-ray drive reads all three.
jsc.guide.case_front.text6: The Hot-Swap Drive Bay takes a disk from the front. Click with a disk in your hand to slide it in, and click with an empty hand to take it out. It works with the computer on or off. It takes a disk of the computer's own era, or of an older one.
jsc.guide.case_front.text7: The disk in the bay is one of the computer's own. It gets a drive letter, a system can go on it, and the computer can boot from it. It adds to the computer's capacity and to the power it needs. It takes none of the board's disk slots, so a full board still takes one more disk here.
jsc.guide.case_front.text8: Click a port while you hold a USB flash drive to plug it in. Sneak-click a port to pull its stick out. A stick works as a drive of its own, and a system can be installed from it ([Installing a system](jsc:installing)).
jsc.guide.case_front.title: The front of the case
jsc.guide.cde.definition1: CDE's strip of controls at the bottom of the screen, with the workspace switch in its middle.
jsc.guide.cde.definition2: A tray that slides up out of a Front Panel control, and stays up until its arrow is pressed again.
jsc.guide.cde.definition3: One of four separate screens of the same desktop. A window lives on one, or on all of them.
jsc.guide.cde.definition4: The window style of CDE: a title bar, with a menu button at its left.
jsc.guide.cde.fix1: CDE has no Start menu. Open Applications on the Front Panel to find your programs.
jsc.guide.cde.fix2: The computer is a Vintage one. Use a Legacy computer or a newer one.
jsc.guide.cde.problem1: You look for a Start menu, and there is none.
jsc.guide.cde.problem2: The package manager says "cde needs Legacy hardware or later".
jsc.guide.cde.text1: CDE, the Common Desktop Environment, is the desktop of the Unix workstations, and the only desktop UNIX has. It runs on UNIX, FreeBSD and Linux. It is light: it needs Legacy hardware or later, 32 MB of disk and 16 MB of memory while it runs.
jsc.guide.cde.text2: CDE has no login and no logout. There is nobody to log in, so you never see a login. It starts straight away, with "Starting the desktop" on its splash screen.
jsc.guide.cde.text3: Where the other desktops have a start menu, a taskbar and an Action Center, CDE has one strip: the Front Panel, along the bottom centre of the screen. It has no start menu, no taskbar and no Action Center. It lists no open windows, because CDE never did: a window you put away becomes an icon on its workspace.
jsc.guide.cde.text4: The Front Panel holds its controls from left to right: Clock, Calendar, File Manager, Text Editor, Style Manager, Applications, Trash Can and Help Viewer. Most of them open something, as [](jsc:cde_front_panel) lists.
jsc.guide.cde.text5: A control with a small arrow at its head raises a subpanel: a tray that slides up out of the Front Panel. A subpanel stays up until you press its arrow again, and only one is up at a time.
jsc.guide.cde.text6: CDE has four workspaces, named One, Two, Three and Four. Each is a separate screen of the same desktop, and each can wear its own backdrop ([](jsc:cde_style_manager)).
jsc.guide.cde.text7: Each window has a title bar in the Motif style. The button at its left opens the window menu: Restore, Minimize, Maximize, Lower, Occupy Workspace..., Occupy All Workspaces and Close. A double click on that button closes the window with no menu.
jsc.guide.cde.text8: To install CDE, use the form for your system in [](jsc:install_a_desktop). On Debian and Ubuntu, that is apt install cde.
jsc.guide.cde.title: CDE
jsc.guide.cde_application_manager.fix1: A group with no program in it is not drawn. Install a program for it.
jsc.guide.cde_application_manager.fix2: A program named in no other group lands in Desktop_Tools. Look there.
jsc.guide.cde_application_manager.proble: A group you expect is not drawn.
A program is not in the group you expect.
jsc.guide.cde_application_manager.table1: Files, Editor, Command Prompt, Calculator and Settings
Every program named in no other group, such as one someone else wrote.

Network, Network Manager, ISMS, NextGre Studio, Prophet Console, Gateway Manager, Remote Control, Cluster Manager, Crafting Manager, Storage Insights, Craft Planner, Automation Manager and Pattern Studio
jsc.guide.cde_application_manager.text1: The Application Manager is CDE's program list. It groups the programs in folders, so you find a program by its group. Open it from the Applications control on the Front Panel, or from the first row of the Applications subpanel.
jsc.guide.cde_application_manager.text2: A group is drawn only when it holds a program. Its status line says how many programs it holds, such as "Games, 1 program". A double click on a group opens it in its own window, and a double click on a program starts it.
jsc.guide.cde_application_manager.text3: The window reads the desktop each time it draws, so a program you install while the window is open appears at once, without a refresh.
jsc.guide.cde_application_manager.title: The Application Manager
jsc.guide.cde_front_panel.fix1: Close that program first, so that nothing is lost, then press EXIT.
jsc.guide.cde_front_panel.problem1: The dialog says a program is still open.
jsc.guide.cde_front_panel.table1_1_2: Shows the time, with its hands
jsc.guide.cde_front_panel.table1_2_2: Shows the date, with the day on its page
jsc.guide.cde_front_panel.table1_3_2: Opens Files, with a subpanel of Home, Desktop and each medium in a drive
jsc.guide.cde_front_panel.table1_4_2: Opens a subpanel headed Personal Applications: Text Editor, Command Prompt and Calculator
jsc.guide.cde_front_panel.table1_6_2: Opens a subpanel headed Applications: the Application Manager, System Monitor and Workstation Info
jsc.guide.cde_front_panel.table1_7_2: Opens the Trash, and its picture shows whether it is empty or full
jsc.guide.cde_front_panel.table2_3_1: Two or more programs are still open
jsc.guide.cde_front_panel.table2_3_2: Two or more programs run, with the number spelled out
jsc.guide.cde_front_panel.text1: Each control of the Front Panel shows its name when you rest the pointer on it, such as "File Manager" or "Trash Can".
jsc.guide.cde_front_panel.text2: The EXIT button sits at the right end of the workspace switch, beside the four workspaces. It is not at the far right of the panel. Press it to open the Exit dialog, which has three buttons: Shut Down, Restart and Cancel.
jsc.guide.cde_front_panel.text3: The dialog says how many programs are open. The count is spelled out, so it reads, for example, "Three programs are still open", followed by "on this workstation." The last line warns that what is not saved will be lost.
jsc.guide.cde_front_panel.title: The Front Panel and EXIT
jsc.guide.cde_on_system_v.fix1: Use a Legacy computer or a newer one. A Vintage computer runs System V at a prompt only.
jsc.guide.cde_on_system_v.fix2: Free up disk space, or install on a bigger disk.
jsc.guide.cde_on_system_v.fix3: Put the CDE CD in a CD Drive linked to the computer, and try again.
jsc.guide.cde_on_system_v.fix4: The desktop shows only after a restart. Restart the computer.
jsc.guide.cde_on_system_v.problem1: The installation says "CDE needs Legacy hardware or newer. This computer is Vintage."
jsc.guide.cde_on_system_v.problem2: The installation says "CDE needs 32 MB free on the disk. There are <n> MB."
jsc.guide.cde_on_system_v.problem3: The installpkg line says "no package medium in a drive".
jsc.guide.cde_on_system_v.problem4: The computer starts at a prompt after CDE is installed.
jsc.guide.cde_on_system_v.step1: Put the CDE CD in a CD Drive linked to the computer.
jsc.guide.cde_on_system_v.step2: Type installpkg cde and press Enter.
jsc.guide.cde_on_system_v.step3: Wait for the setup to finish. Its line names the program and the CD.
jsc.guide.cde_on_system_v.step4: Restart the computer. The desktop starts at the next boot.
jsc.guide.cde_on_system_v.table1: CDE on System V at a glance
jsc.guide.cde_on_system_v.text1: CDE, the Common Desktop Environment, is the only desktop UNIX System V has. It is a desktop with windows and a panel, and it needs a Legacy computer or a newer one. A Vintage computer runs the system at a prompt only.
jsc.guide.cde_on_system_v.text2: CDE is a program, so you install it from its own medium, a CD. Once it is installed, the computer starts into it after a restart. The rest of CDE, its panel, its menus and its tools, is explained in [](jsc:cde).
jsc.guide.cde_on_system_v.text3: The desktop has a raised panel at the bottom centre of the screen, with four workspaces named One, Two, Three and Four. Its programs include a file manager, which the panel calls Files, a text editor, a terminal, a calculator, a performance meter, the Style Manager and the Help Viewer.
jsc.guide.cde_on_system_v.title: CDE on System V
jsc.guide.cde_on_system_v.value1_4: CD, read by a CD Drive
jsc.guide.cde_on_system_v.value1_6: UNIX System V, FreeBSD and Linux
jsc.guide.cde_style_manager.fix1: You left the Color page with Cancel, or by closing it. Open the page again and press OK.
jsc.guide.cde_style_manager.problem1: A colour change does not stay.
jsc.guide.cde_style_manager.problem2: A backdrop change does not stay.
jsc.guide.cde_style_manager.step2: Pick a palette. The desktop changes to show it.
jsc.guide.cde_style_manager.step3: Press OK to keep it with the machine.
jsc.guide.cde_style_manager.step5: Pick a pattern. Only the preview changes.
jsc.guide.cde_style_manager.step6: Press Apply. The pattern goes on the workspace named on the page.
jsc.guide.cde_style_manager.text1: The Style Manager is the settings window of CDE. Press its control on the Front Panel to open it. Its window is called Style Manager - Color, Style Manager - Backdrop or Style Manager - Audio, depending on the page.
jsc.guide.cde_style_manager.text2: It has three pages in a strip, and a click on one opens it. Color is the palette the whole desktop is drawn from. Backdrop is the pattern each workspace wears. Audio sets the system's volume and where its sound goes.
jsc.guide.cde_style_manager.text3: Everything else the machine keeps about itself is still set at its prompt, with the config command.
jsc.guide.cde_style_manager.text4: Color has eight palettes, under the names they have: Default, Alpine, Broica, Charcoal, Desert, Neptune, SeaFoam and Urchin. The whole desktop changes to a palette as soon as you pick it, so you see it before you keep it.
jsc.guide.cde_style_manager.text5: OK keeps the palette with the machine. Cancel, or closing the page any other way, puts back the palette the desktop had when the page opened. The buttons along the foot are Apply, OK and Cancel.
jsc.guide.cde_style_manager.text6: The backdrop is the pattern behind the windows. Each workspace wears its own, so the four workspaces can look different. The six patterns are Hatch, Pinstripe, Tiles, Weave, Dots and Plain.
jsc.guide.cde_style_manager.text7: The page stays open after Apply, so you can change the next workspace.
jsc.guide.cde_style_manager.text8: Audio has a volume scale with its value over the slider, and a Mute switch. It has two outputs, each a toggle, and both may be on. One output always stays on: the last one cannot be turned off.
jsc.guide.cde_style_manager.text9: Nothing is sent to the machine while you work the page, and only OK sends your choice to it.
jsc.guide.cde_style_manager.title: The Style Manager
jsc.guide.cde_trash_can.definition1: CDE's word for restoring an item to where it was. Other desktops call this Restore.
jsc.guide.cde_trash_can.definition2: CDE's word for deleting an item for good. Other desktops call this Delete.
jsc.guide.cde_trash_can.fix1: Shred deletes for good, and the item cannot be put back. Check the selection before you press Shred.
jsc.guide.cde_trash_can.fix2: Select everything in the Trash window, then press Shred.
jsc.guide.cde_trash_can.problem1: You shredded an item you wanted.
jsc.guide.cde_trash_can.problem2: There is no Empty Trash button.
jsc.guide.cde_trash_can.text1: On CDE the trash is the Trash Can, a control on the Front Panel. Other desktops keep it as an icon on the wallpaper. Its picture shows whether it is empty or full, so you see at a glance whether it holds anything. Click it to open the Trash window.
jsc.guide.cde_trash_can.text2: The Trash window has three menus: File, Selected and View. Put Back restores the selected items to where they were. Shred deletes them for good. The window also has Select All, Deselect All, By Name and By Size.
jsc.guide.cde_trash_can.text3: CDE has no Empty Trash button.
jsc.guide.cde_trash_can.text4: Before a delete, CDE asks Confirm File Delete. For one item it asks, for example, "Delete the item in the Home for good?" Its properties show the name, the original location and the size. The original location is Home or Desktop.
jsc.guide.cde_trash_can.title: The Trash Can
jsc.guide.cde_workstation_info.fix1: This workstation is not on a network. Connect it to one, as [](jsc:first_network) shows.
jsc.guide.cde_workstation_info.table1_1_: User Name, Host Name and Network, which reads "Not on a network" when there is none
jsc.guide.cde_workstation_info.table1_2_: Operating System, Architecture and Window System
jsc.guide.cde_workstation_info.table1_3_: Processor, with its clock, Physical Memory, Memory in Use with a meter, Video Memory and System Disk
jsc.guide.cde_workstation_info.text1: Workstation Info tells you about the workstation you sit at: who is using it, the system it runs and the hardware under it. It is the CDE answer to This PC, and only CDE bundles it. Open it from the Applications subpanel, or from the Applications control.
jsc.guide.cde_workstation_info.text2: Each figure is read when the window opens, and again every few seconds while the window stays open. So Memory in Use moves as the workstation works.
jsc.guide.cde_workstation_info.text3: The Devices... button opens the Devices dialog. It shows one row for each port of the workstation: Video, then Audio, then the other ports by name. Each row shows what is plugged in, or "free". Select a device to Disable or Enable it. A disabled device is shown crossed out, in a quieter ink.
jsc.guide.cde_workstation_info.title: Workstation Info

jsc.guide.cinnamon.fix1: The computer is older than Standard. Use a Standard computer or a newer one.
jsc.guide.cinnamon.fix2: On a Legacy computer, choose another desktop, because Cinnamon is offered only on Standard hardware or later.
jsc.guide.cinnamon.problem1: The package manager says "cinnamon needs Standard hardware or later".
jsc.guide.cinnamon.problem2: The installer does not offer Cinnamon on a Legacy computer.
jsc.guide.cinnamon.table1_1_2: Files, This PC, the System Monitor, the Command Prompt, the Network, Help and the other system tools
jsc.guide.cinnamon.table1_2_2: Everything else: the Calculator, the editors, the games
jsc.guide.cinnamon.table1_3_2: Exceed, the Workshop, the Crafting Manager, the Pattern Studio, the Craft Planner, the Storage Insights and the Automation Manager
jsc.guide.cinnamon.text1: Cinnamon is a desktop from Spearmint Linux, a software house of the mod's world. It runs on Linux and FreeBSD, and it needs Standard hardware or later. It is a later desktop, so no older computer can run it.
jsc.guide.cinnamon.text2: Cinnamon has one look, on every computer it runs on, so you never meet an older face. Its package is named cinnamon.
jsc.guide.cinnamon.text3: Its menu has three parts: a left rail of favourites, then the categories, then the list of programs in the chosen category. The categories are System, Accessories, Office and Preferences.
jsc.guide.cinnamon.text4: Cinnamon gives its programs its own names: Nemo for Files, xed for the Editor, Terminal for the Command Prompt, System Settings for Settings and System Info for This PC. The full list is in [](jsc:desktop_program_names).
jsc.guide.cinnamon.text5: To install it, use the form for your system in [](jsc:install_a_desktop). The boot lines show it as "Starting cinnamon Display Manager".
jsc.guide.cinnamon.title: Cinnamon

jsc.guide.clauses_priority_if_with.text1: The words after the item are clauses. Each verb accepts some of them. A clause that the verb does not accept is refused with a message, such as "FROM is not valid on a read". The table shows what each verb accepts.
jsc.guide.clauses_priority_if_with.text2: PRIORITY sets the level of each Operation a statement queues ([](jsc:priorities)). The default is MEDIUM, and you write the level after the word, such as PRIORITY HIGH.
jsc.guide.clauses_priority_if_with.text3: NORMAL means MEDIUM. A hyphen reads as an underscore, and capitals do not matter, so medium-high is MEDIUM_HIGH.
jsc.guide.clauses_priority_if_with.text4: IF runs the statement only when a condition holds. The condition uses the words of a WHERE condition ([](jsc:query_and_select)). The network checks it against its stock of the named item before the statement runs.
jsc.guide.clauses_priority_if_with.text5: When the condition does not hold, the statement does not run. The reply is not an error: "the IF did not hold, so the SELECT was not run", with the verb you typed. A file goes on to its next line.
jsc.guide.clauses_priority_if_with.text6: WITH gives UPDATE its second item: the material for REPAIR, or the item COMBINE adds. It comes after the action word, and no other statement takes it.
jsc.guide.clauses_priority_if_with.text7: OFFER takes one of the three enchantment offers, after ENCHANT. You type 1, 2 or 3 after the word. ([](jsc:update_cards)) shows what each offer means.

jsc.guide.cluster_command.text3: Names are matched without regard to capitals. jsc.guide.cluster_installs.text1: A bulk install writes one system or one program to every node of a cluster at once, or to the nodes you pick, instead of one machine at a time. You start it from the Cluster Manager ([](jsc:cluster_manager)) or with the cluster command ([](jsc:cluster_command)).
jsc.guide.cluster_installs.text2: The disc comes from a drive linked to the Cluster Management Computer. Cable the drive to the computer with a peripheral cable ([](jsc:peripheral_cables)), and put the disc in the drive ([](jsc:drives)).
jsc.guide.cluster_installs.text3: The card decides which machines a bulk install reaches, and how many nodes it writes at once.
jsc.guide.cluster_installs.text4: Each node that is written at once takes one lane. A card placed in a slot older than the card was made for runs fewer lanes, because that slot carries data more slowly.
jsc.guide.cluster_installs.text5: Writing one node takes 14 seconds on a machine with a clock speed of 2,000 megahertz (MHz). A faster machine takes less time, down to 3 seconds. A slower one takes more, up to 60 seconds.
jsc.guide.cluster_installs.text6: A node that cannot take the install is skipped, and the job goes on with the other nodes. The node's name is followed by the reason in brackets.
jsc.guide.cluster_installs.text7: A system lane installs the system and sets the node to restart into it. A program lane installs the program on the node. When the job is over, it leaves one summary line.
jsc.guide.cluster_installs.text8: Cancel stops the job after the nodes being written. The nodes still in the queue are left as they were. The ALL ON and ALL OFF buttons, and the power command, only switch power. They never start an install.
jsc.guide.cluster_installs.title: Installing on many machines

Cluster

When you have one rack, you walk up to each server. When you have ten, you will not want to. The Cluster Management Computer installs systems and programs on the machines of your racks, and switches their bays on and off, all from one desk.

Build it as you would a Personal Computer ([](jsc:personal_computers)), and give it a Cluster Interface Card. Without one, it is an ordinary computer ([](jsc:expansion_cards)). With one, it is the manager of its cluster: each card reaches a different set of machines, and installs on a set number of them at once.
The card decides what the manager reaches, not the era of the computer. The Serial Console Card of the Vintage era already reaches Server Racks, and every card reaches them.

A job installs on several nodes at once, as the card allows. Each node takes its own install time: 280 ticks at 2 GHz, which is 14 seconds. A faster processor takes less time, but never under 60 ticks, which is 3 seconds, or over 1,200 ticks, which is 60 seconds.
ALL ON and ALL OFF switch every bay of the cluster at once. Each node also has its own bay, which reads "Bay off" when it is switched off.
A system or a program comes from a disc in a reader that is linked to the manager by cable ([](jsc:drives)). The manager looks for a system disc and a program disc in those linked readers.
Cluster Management Computers

jsc.guide.cluster_manager.text1: The Cluster Manager is the window that lets you run many machines as one. It is a desktop program for a Cluster Management Computer ([](jsc:cluster_management_computers)). It needs a Cluster Interface Card in that computer ([](jsc:expansion_cards)).
jsc.guide.cluster_manager.text2: Each machine in a cluster is a node. Which clusters you reach depends on the card's reach.
jsc.guide.cluster_manager.text3: The window runs on Frames, Linux, FreeBSD and UNIX System V. Without a card, it says "A Cluster Interface Card is required."
jsc.guide.cluster_manager.text4: Each node row has its own buttons. SYSTEM and PROGRAM install on that node alone. POWER ON and POWER OFF only switch the node.
jsc.guide.cluster_manager.text5: A datacenter section is the set of servers behind one face of a Server Router ([](jsc:server_router)). The BALANCE button cycles the router's load-balance mode, from ROUND-ROBIN to LEAST-LOADED, then MANUAL, and back again. The modes are explained in ([](jsc:load_balancing)).
jsc.guide.cluster_manager.text6: Open INVENTORY to see what the section holds. The hint in the inventory says that you click an item to move it out, and drop a stack on the window to deposit it.
jsc.guide.cluster_manager.text7: Press RENAME and type a name. An empty name goes back to the default. Supercomputers are named SC-1, SC-2 and onward, in the order the network registered them. A section takes its router's name and the face it sits on, such as Router · NORTH.
jsc.guide.cluster_manager.text8: Each node row shows its state in capitals. NO SYSTEM means the node has no system installed. BAY OFF means the node is switched off. INSTALLING means a system or a program is being written to it now.

jsc.guide.computer_info.text1: A program can ask the machine it runs on what it is: its name, its processor, its system, its memory and its disks. The answers are pictures taken when you ask, not views that update by themselves.
jsc.guide.computer_info.text2: You read the machine through Computer, a built-in type whose members you read directly. Write Computer.Name, not the name of a variable that holds a computer.
jsc.guide.computer_info.text3: Name, RamMb and Online work in Sigma too. The rest are Sigma# only.
jsc.guide.computer_info.text4: A record is a value with fixed fields, and you read each field by its name. These are the records the Computer members give back.
jsc.guide.computer_info.text5: The era names are vintage, legacy, transition, standard, advanced, exa and singularity, written in lower case. A machine has seven eras to choose from, and an era is not the same thing as a hardware tier.

jsc.guide.computercraft_peripheral.text1: A ComputerCraft program reaches the Gateway through its peripheral, which has the type jsc_gateway. The program wraps it with peripheral.find("jsc_gateway") and calls its methods. Each call counts against the call cap ([](jsc:gateway_permissions)).
jsc.guide.computercraft_peripheral.text2: Names in the calls are the names the game uses. An item is an id such as iron_ingot, and the minecraft: namespace may be left out for vanilla items. A fluid is written fluid/ and its id, and a chemical chemical/ and its id.
jsc.guide.computercraft_peripheral.text3: The priority argument is optional. The quantity 0 means all ([](jsc:gateway_permissions)).
jsc.guide.computercraft_peripheral.text4: An operation has a long id. You may give only its first letters, as long as no other operation starts with the same letters.
jsc.guide.computercraft_peripheral.text5: A line written to the log is cut at 96 characters, and the log keeps 40 entries.

jsc.guide.computercraft_side.problem2: The error is the message of a CC: Tweaked method itself.
jsc.guide.computercraft_side.problem3: The program gets the text "there is no <name> on this Gateway's wire".
jsc.guide.computercraft_side.problem4: The program gets the text "no such method <name> on <peripheral>".
jsc.guide.computercraft_side.problem5: A ComputerCraft computer cannot see the Gateway.
jsc.guide.computercraft_side.table1_1_2: An operation the computer started settles. Only that computer hears it.
jsc.guide.computercraft_side.table1_2_2: The total of a watched name moves. The Gateway checks each watch every 20 ticks.
jsc.guide.computercraft_side.table1_3_2: You press Test event in the Gateway Manager, or send the test from the gateway command.
jsc.guide.computercraft_side.text1: On its front, the Gateway joins a ComputerCraft wired network. A ComputerCraft computer sees it as a peripheral of the type jsc_gateway. Its name is jsc_gateway_ followed by the Gateway's name, with each dash turned into an underscore: gateway-1 becomes jsc_gateway_gateway_1.
jsc.guide.computercraft_side.text2: A ComputerCraft computer finds the Gateway only when the Gateway is on its wire. Put a networking cable or a wired modem against the Gateway's front. Without CC: Tweaked there is no ComputerCraft side at all.
jsc.guide.computercraft_side.text3: A ComputerCraft program calls the Gateway's peripheral. The Gateway answers each call with the same service your own programs use, under the permissions you set on the host ([](jsc:gateway_permissions)). The cost of a call comes out of the host's budget.
jsc.guide.computercraft_side.text4: The Gateway shows the state of this side in its screen and with the gateway command. It says "reachable" when a ComputerCraft computer is attached or on its wire, and "nothing attached" when none is.
jsc.guide.computercraft_side.text5: The Gateway sends events to the ComputerCraft computers, so a program can wait for them instead of asking again and again.
jsc.guide.computercraft_side.text6: The status of an operation is one of done, partial, failed, running, waiting, locked, pending, discarded or unknown. The operation types are pull, push, delete, move, craft, analyze, reindex, vacuum, drop, update and operation.
jsc.guide.computercraft_side.text7: A ComputerCraft program can call send to say a line to the host. Only a program of J's Computers that is listening hears the line, and each line is written to the Gateway's log as said. With nobody listening, the line reaches no one.
jsc.guide.computercraft_side.text8: The advancement Talking to the Neighbours is earned when a program hears a ComputerCraft computer through a Network Gateway.
jsc.guide.computercraft_side.title: The Gateway and ComputerCraft

jsc.guide.craft_planner.text1: The Craft Planner is a program that shows you a craft before you make it. You pick an item from the network's craft catalogue. It then shows the whole plan: each step, each ingredient and the number of stages.
jsc.guide.craft_planner.text2: The network works out the catalogue and the plan, so they show what the network holds now. The Craft button sends the same request as the terminal and the Network Interactor ([](jsc:asking_for_a_craft)).
jsc.guide.craft_planner.text3: The planner works from what the network holds now, so "max" is the most the network can make at this moment. It looks only so deep: a recipe nested more than 16 levels down is not planned. A recipe that depends on itself is cut, so the plan does not loop.

jsc.guide.crafting_cards.definition2: One step of a pipeline: a bench pattern or a machine pattern.

jsc.guide.crafting_cards.table3_1_2: The kind of card: a crafting accelerator, built on a field-programmable gate array (FPGA).

jsc.guide.crafting_cards.text1: The Crafting Card is the part that lets a Crafting Computer craft. You put it in an expansion slot of the computer. Without a card the computer does not craft at all ([](jsc:crafting_computers)).
jsc.guide.crafting_cards.text2: A card sets how much its computer can do. It drives a number of Crafting Interfaces, and it keeps a number of bench recipes in its own memory. The recipes stay on the card, so they go with it to another computer.
jsc.guide.crafting_cards.text3: The two numbers are separate limits. Today they match in every era, but they measure different things: the interfaces a card drives, and the recipes it keeps.
jsc.guide.crafting_cards.text4: A computer with several cards adds them up: the interfaces it drives and the recipes it keeps are the totals over all its cards. A computer that is off drives no interfaces.
jsc.guide.crafting_cards.text5: A card also sets the speed. Each card adds its throughput, and the craft speed of the computer is its processor (CPU) capacity times the sum of those throughputs.
jsc.guide.crafting_cards.text6: Each card also adds its threads. The threads of a computer are the sum of the threads of its cards: the number of stages it runs in parallel for one craft.
jsc.guide.crafting_cards.text7: A card goes into a slot of its own bus. The PCI card also goes into an AGP or a PCI-e board, as the boards of its years had PCI slots beside the graphics slot: the Legacy boards are AGP or PCI-e.
jsc.guide.crafting_cards.text8: Hover over a card to read its tooltip. Each line of the tooltip tells you one thing.
jsc.guide.crafting_cards.text9: You load a bench recipe with the Load button of the Pattern Studio or in the Crafting Manager ([](jsc:crafting_manager)). It goes into the first card with room, counting from the first slot, and a card that already keeps the same recipe is not loaded twice.
jsc.guide.crafting_cards.title: Crafting Cards
jsc.guide.crafting_computers.fix1: It has no Crafting Card, or it is off. Put a card in it, and switch it on.
jsc.guide.crafting_computers.fix2: It lives on the card. It went with the card to another computer, so put the card back.
jsc.guide.crafting_computers.problem2: A crafting table pattern is gone.
jsc.guide.crafting_computers.text1: The Crafting Computer crafts for the network. It runs the crafting table recipes itself, and it drives the machines that make the rest through [Crafting Interfaces](jsc:crafting_interfaces).
jsc.guide.crafting_computers.text2: It crafts only with a Crafting Card in it: without one, it does not craft at all. The card decides how many Crafting Interfaces it drives, and it keeps the crafting table [patterns](jsc:patterns) in its own memory, so they move with the card ([](jsc:crafting_cards)).
jsc.guide.crafting_computers.text3: Build it as you would a Personal Computer ([](jsc:personal_computers)). It takes the same kinds of part, and it holds these:
jsc.guide.crafting_computers.text4: The era of the Crafting Card sets how many Crafting Interfaces it drives, and how many patterns its memory keeps:
jsc.guide.crafting_computers.text5: Open the Crafting Manager on it to load its patterns and watch the jobs ([](jsc:crafting_manager)).
jsc.guide.crafting_computers.title: Crafting Computers
jsc.guide.crafting_interfaces.definition: A cable part that sits on an interface's cable against one input face of a machine, and carries the inputs that face takes.
jsc.guide.crafting_interfaces.fix1: Put the interface on a cable that a Crafting Computer drives, switch the computer on, or give the computer another card.
jsc.guide.crafting_interfaces.fix2: Put a Crafting Receiving Bus against the machine's output.

jsc.guide.crafting_interfaces.step4: Put a Crafting Receiving Bus against the machine's output.
jsc.guide.crafting_interfaces.step5: Load the machine's pattern into the interface, from the Crafting Manager ([](jsc:crafting_manager)).
