jsc.guide.crafting_interfaces.text1: A machine line is how the network runs a machine. You build it on the Crafting Cable, and it has three parts: the Crafting Interface, the Crafting Input Routers and the Crafting Receiving Bus.
jsc.guide.crafting_interfaces.text2: The Crafting Interface sits on the cable against the machine. It holds that machine's patterns, and it feeds the machine directly when it sits against it. It can also feed the machine through a cable of its own, coloured apart from the main one.
jsc.guide.crafting_interfaces.text3: For a machine that takes inputs on more than one face, a Crafting Input Router goes against each input face, on the interface's own cable ([](jsc:input_routers_and_receiving_buses)). The Crafting Receiving Bus goes against the machine's output: it takes back what comes out, and it credits it to the craft that fed the machine.
jsc.guide.crafting_interfaces.text4: An interface works one recipe at a time, or several jobs at once. Its mode decides which.
jsc.guide.crafting_interfaces.text5: MAX JOBS sets how many jobs the interface runs at once, from 0 to 64 jobs. Auto (0) lets the interface take as many jobs as its machine accepts. A paused interface takes no new job. You name the interface too, with a name of up to 32 characters.
jsc.guide.crafting_interfaces.text6: An interface is driven when a Crafting Computer drives the cable it sits on. A card drives the interfaces of its cable in cable order.
jsc.guide.crafting_interfaces.text7: Interfaces beyond what the cards can drive wait, driven by no computer, until another card goes in. The screen reads "Driven by a Crafting Computer" or "Driven by no Crafting Computer".

jsc.guide.crafting_library.text1: A crafting interface holds patterns and asks the network for crafts. A crafting router, on the same crafting cable, decides which inputs it carries, by its filter. The machines themselves are explained in [](jsc:crafting_interfaces) and [](jsc:pattern_encoders).
jsc.guide.crafting_library.text2: The interface and the router are found on the machine's crafting network. The name your program finds them by is the name their windows give, and a window can rename them.
jsc.guide.crafting_library.text3: Each setting goes through the same engine as the bus settings. A refused setting stops the program with the engine's text. Each setting is recorded under the program's class name, or under Sigma when the program has none.

jsc.guide.crafting_manager.text1: The Crafting Manager is the program that loads recipes into the cards and the interfaces of a Crafting Computer, and that shows what its crafting parts are doing. It runs only on a Crafting Computer, and it does not come with any system. Install it from its CD, or on a Linux desktop from the Mirror, on a system with windows: Frames XP or newer, or a Linux, FreeBSD or UNIX desktop ([](jsc:programs)).
jsc.guide.crafting_manager.text2: You need a Crafting Card to manage recipes, and only a Crafting Computer loads them ([](jsc:crafting_computers)).
jsc.guide.crafting_manager.text3: The Crafting Manager has two tabs, "Recipes" and "Interfaces".
jsc.guide.crafting_manager.text4: The left pane lists the .craft files on a medium in a linked drive. With no medium in a linked drive, the pane reads "Removable media: none" and asks you to insert a disc into a linked drive. A medium with no pattern files reads "No .craft files".
jsc.guide.crafting_manager.text5: The right pane lists the places where the computer keeps recipes: each card's ROM, and each interface with its machine recipes. Bench recipes go into a card's ROM, and machine and pipeline recipes go into an interface.
jsc.guide.crafting_manager.text6: The Interfaces tab has one row for each Crafting Interface on the cable. The summary line above the rows gives the interfaces that the cards drive, out of the interfaces on the cable, and the number of Crafting Cards.
jsc.guide.crafting_manager.text7: Click the mode to switch it, and click the jobs to raise them by one. The jobs go up to 16 jobs, then wrap back to Auto, and a right-click lowers them. The interface's own screen allows up to 64 jobs. The Pause and Resume buttons pause and restart an interface.
jsc.guide.crafting_manager.text8: Each card is listed with the interfaces it drives and how full its ROM is. A line reads "N more on the crafting cable wait, driven by none, until another card goes in" when some interfaces have no card to drive them.
jsc.guide.crafting_manager.title: The Crafting Manager
jsc.guide.credits_per_tick.definition1: The number of instructions a computer's processors give its programs in one tick.
jsc.guide.credits_per_tick.fix1: The computer has no processor in its build, or its build is not valid. Put a processor in its build and make the build valid.
jsc.guide.credits_per_tick.fix2: Its processors have few cores or a slow clock, so it gets fewer credits. Install processors with more cores or a faster clock ([Processors](jsc:processors)).
jsc.guide.credits_per_tick.fix3: Many programs stopped in the same tick share the budget. Stop fewer programs at a time.
jsc.guide.credits_per_tick.problem1: The programs run nothing at all.
jsc.guide.credits_per_tick.problem2: A program is slow on an old computer.
jsc.guide.credits_per_tick.problem3: Some programs stop without their goodbye.
jsc.guide.credits_per_tick.table1_1_1: 0, with no processor in the build
jsc.guide.credits_per_tick.table2_1_2: Sits out every other round of the tick.
jsc.guide.credits_per_tick.table2_2_2: The default, which runs in every round.
jsc.guide.credits_per_tick.table2_3_2: Runs in every round, as medium does.
jsc.guide.credits_per_tick.text1: The central processing units (CPU) of a computer give its programs their work. Each tick, the computer turns its processors into credits: the number of instructions its programs may spend in that tick. More cores and a faster clock mean more credits.
jsc.guide.credits_per_tick.text10: A stopped program runs its goodbye out of a budget of 4,096 instructions per tick. All the programs stopped in that tick share the budget. A program that runs past its share stops before it can run its farewell code.
jsc.guide.credits_per_tick.text11: When a computer is switched off, or its build is no longer valid, the budget is split evenly among the programs that are stopped.
jsc.guide.credits_per_tick.text2: The computer adds up, for every processor in its build, the number of cores times the clock speed in megahertz (MHz). Cores are the parts of a processor that work at the same time. See [Processors](jsc:processors). If your programs run slowly, check the processors first.
jsc.guide.credits_per_tick.text3: Then it divides that sum by eight, dropping any fraction. A computer with a processor always gets at least 32 credits. A computer with no processor in its build gets no credits, so its programs run nothing. There is no upper limit: a faster processor gets more credits.
jsc.guide.credits_per_tick.text4: A processor's tooltip also shows a capacity in items a tick (it/t). That number measures the network's work, not the speed of a program. A program's speed is the credits above. See [Processors](jsc:processors).
jsc.guide.credits_per_tick.text5: On every tick the computer checks whether it runs. A computer that is switched on, with a valid build, runs its programs. A computer that is switched off, or whose parts no longer make a valid build, stops all of them. Each one is given its goodbye, within a budget.
jsc.guide.credits_per_tick.text6: The credits of a tick are shared among the programs in rounds. In each round, a program takes up to 64 credits, or an even share of what is left when that is less. A program that finishes or waits for something gives up its place for the rest of the tick.
jsc.guide.credits_per_tick.text7: Every program has a priority. Only the low priority changes anything: a low program sits out every other round. Give the priority as the third argument of Program.Start, after the file and the arguments.
jsc.guide.credits_per_tick.text8: A computer that does work for a [ComputerCraft](jsc:computercraft_side) computer, through a [Network Gateway](jsc:network_gateway), pays for that work out of its own credits. Its programs get fewer credits in the next ticks until the debt is paid.
jsc.guide.credits_per_tick.text9: A debt larger than one tick's credits carries over to the tick after. A computer with no programs still pays its debts, one tick at a time.
jsc.guide.credits_per_tick.title: How much a machine runs each tick
jsc.guide.data_cable_colours.definition1: The place a wire takes inside a cable block. The lanes let several lines share one block.
jsc.guide.data_cable_colours.fix1: They are of different lines or eras, or they are dyed in colours that do not agree. Check both: dye one to match the other, or leave both without dye.
jsc.guide.data_cable_colours.problem1: Two cables side by side do not join.
jsc.guide.data_cable_colours.text1: Every block of cable holds up to nine wires. Each wire sits in one of nine lanes, laid out three across and three up, so one block can carry several lines at once.
jsc.guide.data_cable_colours.text2: Each line has its own lane, so a data cable, a peripheral cable and a crafting cable can share one block without joining.
jsc.guide.data_cable_colours.text3: You can dye a wire. Use a dye on the wire you are looking at, and that wire takes its colour. The sixteen colours of the game are all there.
jsc.guide.data_cable_colours.text4: Two wires of one line and era join when their colours agree: the same colour, or either of them with no colour. So an uncoloured wire joins every colour, and two wires of different colours stop at each other. Wires of different lines or eras never join, whatever their colour.
jsc.guide.data_cable_colours.title: Colours and lanes of the cables
jsc.guide.data_cables.fix1: From the Standard on, fibre runs only straight. Turn it at an optical router.
jsc.guide.data_cables.fix2: The run is longer than its range. Add a repeater or a router inside it, so that the cable after it starts counting again ([](jsc:routers)).
jsc.guide.data_cables.problem1: Fibre will not turn a corner.
jsc.guide.data_cables.problem2: A run carries nothing beyond its range.

jsc.guide.data_cables.text1: The data cables are the network itself. They come in lines by the job they do, and each line has one cable for every era it exists in:
jsc.guide.data_cables.text2: The crafting line has one cable for all eras, the Crafting Cable. It is the only line that is not split by era.
jsc.guide.data_cables.text3: Every cable has a speed and a range, and both count. A run longer than its range carries nothing, so whatever lies only beyond it is off the network. A cable's tooltip says how far one run of it reaches, and what starts a new run.
jsc.guide.data_cables.text4: When you lay a run, count it against the range of its cable, and count the repeaters and routers you put in it. Those are the places where the range starts again.
jsc.guide.data_cables.text5: Two rules govern two of the lines. From the Standard on, the backbone's fibre runs only straight, so it turns at an optical router ([](jsc:routers)). And the long distance line runs between exactly two ends and holds its block alone.
jsc.guide.data_cables.text6: Fibre also goes into a Mainframe or a Cluster Management Computer only while that machine holds an Optical Network Card ([](jsc:expansion_cards)), and into a Server Rack only through a Fibre Optic Interface mounted in it ([](jsc:rack_equipment)).
jsc.guide.data_cables.title: Data cables
jsc.guide.data_cables.value1_2: Routers, the Mainframe and the racks
jsc.guide.data_cables.value1_4: A supercomputer's nodes to its HBW Interface
jsc.guide.data_cables.value1_5: A Crafting Computer to the parts that feed its machines
jsc.guide.datacenters.balloon1_detail: Each of its other faces leads to a section of racks.
jsc.guide.datacenters.balloon2_detail: The face that joins the router to the network.
jsc.guide.datacenters.definition1: The face of a Server Router that joins it to the network.
jsc.guide.datacenters.definition2: The Server Racks that one output face of a Server Router reaches.
jsc.guide.datacenters.figure1: A datacenter: a Server Router with a section of racks behind each of three faces, and its uplink to the network on the fourth. Drag it to look at each section.
jsc.guide.datacenters.fix1: The router manages 8 racks at most. Use a second Server Router for the others.
jsc.guide.datacenters.fix2: Take racks off that router, or put some on a second Server Router ([](jsc:server_router)).
jsc.guide.datacenters.problem1: The rack count shows in red.
jsc.guide.datacenters.problem2: A section has racks that are unmanaged.
jsc.guide.datacenters.text1: When you have many Server Racks, you group them into a datacenter. A Server Router does the grouping: it splits the racks into sections.
jsc.guide.datacenters.text2: A section is the racks that one output face of a Server Router reaches, without crossing back through the router. The face joining the router to the network is its uplink, and the router detects it. Up to five sections hang off one router, one for each other face.
jsc.guide.datacenters.text3: The label of a section shows its racks (R) and its servers (S). A section's default name is the router's name and its face.
jsc.guide.datacenters.text4: A Server Router has one budget for all its sections together. At its tier, T3, it manages 8 Server Racks in all, counted section by section. Racks past the eighth are counted as unmanaged, and the router shows its rack count in red when it goes over.
jsc.guide.datacenters.text5: More faces do not add budget. To manage more racks, use a second Server Router, which has a budget of its own.
jsc.guide.datacenters.title: Datacenters
jsc.guide.desktop_program_names.fix1: CDE does not bundle This PC. Use Workstation Info, which answers the same question.
jsc.guide.desktop_program_names.fix2: It shows only on a Mainframe. Look for it on a Mainframe.
jsc.guide.desktop_program_names.problem1: You look for This PC on CDE, and it is not there.
jsc.guide.desktop_program_names.problem2: You look for the Network Manager, and it is not in the menu.
jsc.guide.desktop_program_names.text1: Each desktop calls its programs by its own names. The program is the same one: the Editor on KDE Plasma is Kate, and it is the same text editor under any desktop. Find a program in the table under the name your desktop shows.
jsc.guide.desktop_program_names.text2: A product name, such as Dolphin, Kate or Nemo, reads the same in every language. A plain name, such as Text Editor or System Settings, is translated with the rest of the screen.
jsc.guide.desktop_program_names.text3: A program keeps its own window whatever its launcher is called. So a renamed launcher still opens the same program.
jsc.guide.desktop_program_names.text4: The Network Manager is bundled on every desktop, but it shows only on a Mainframe. On a computer that is not a Mainframe, you do not see it in any launcher.
jsc.guide.desktop_program_names.title: Program names under each desktop
jsc.guide.desktops.definition1: A piece of software that the system's package manager installs, updates and removes, by its name.
jsc.guide.desktops.definition2: The graphical shell a system starts into: its windows, its panel and the menu that lists the programs it shows.
jsc.guide.desktops.fix1: No desktop package is installed. Install one, as [](jsc:install_a_desktop) shows.
jsc.guide.desktops.fix2: The desktop starts at the next boot. Restart the computer.
jsc.guide.desktops.fix3: Every desktop on this page needs Legacy hardware or later, and Cinnamon needs Standard. Use a newer computer.
jsc.guide.desktops.problem1: The system starts at a shell, with no desktop.
jsc.guide.desktops.problem2: You installed a desktop, and the screen still shows the shell.
jsc.guide.desktops.problem3: The computer is a Vintage one, and the screen shows only the terminal.
jsc.guide.desktops.text1: A desktop is what a system shows when it starts with a graphical face: its windows, a panel or taskbar, and a menu that lists its programs. Without one, the system stops at its terminal, a prompt where you type commands. Each Frames edition brings its own desktop. Linux and FreeBSD do not, so you install one as a package. On UNIX, the one desktop is the Common Desktop Environment (CDE).
jsc.guide.desktops.text2: Four desktops are built in. Each has its own look, and its own names for the programs. The eras each one needs are explained at [](jsc:eras).
jsc.guide.desktops.text3: The disk and memory figures are the mod's own estimates of what each desktop takes. A Vintage computer has no graphical desktop at all: it lives at its terminal.
jsc.guide.desktops.text4: Each desktop wears the look of its era. On Legacy hardware KDE shows KDE 2 and GNOME shows GNOME 1. On Transition they show KDE 4 and GNOME 2. From the Standard on, KDE Plasma and GNOME have their own look. Cinnamon and CDE have one look each, on every era they run on.
jsc.guide.desktops.text5: A desktop shows as launchers only the programs it bundles, and only those your computer may run. KDE Plasma, GNOME and Cinnamon bundle the same ten: Network, This PC, Settings, Files, the Editor, the Command Prompt, the System Monitor, the Calculator, the Network Manager and Help. The Network Manager shows only on a Mainframe ([](jsc:mainframes)).
jsc.guide.desktops.text6: CDE bundles its own set. It has no This PC, so no CDE launcher shows it. Its answer to the question is Workstation Info ([](jsc:cde_workstation_info)).
jsc.guide.desktops.text7: A desktop you install starts at the next boot, not at the moment you install it. The computer checks what it has installed during its self-test, so restart it after an install ([](jsc:firmware)).
jsc.guide.desktops.title: Desktops
jsc.guide.device_listing.definition1: The name FreeBSD gives a device. The number counts the devices of that kind.
jsc.guide.device_listing.definition2: The name FreeBSD gives a USB device, such as ugen0.2.
jsc.guide.device_listing.fix1: Type the two letters together: pciconf -lv.
jsc.guide.device_listing.fix2: usbconfig takes no options. Type usbconfig alone.
jsc.guide.device_listing.fix3: The computer disabled the device, so it is not in use.
jsc.guide.device_listing.fix4: Run the command on the computer whose parts you want to list.
jsc.guide.device_listing.problem1: pciconf says usage: pciconf -l [-v] after you typed -l -v.
jsc.guide.device_listing.problem4: pciconf says no hardware to read.
jsc.guide.device_listing.table1_1_2: The device's driver name, then its slot as bus, device and function.
jsc.guide.device_listing.table1_2_2: The kind of device, as a code.
jsc.guide.device_listing.table1_4_2: With -lv: the kind of device in words.
jsc.guide.device_listing.table2_2_1: Serial and parallel ports, or a USB controller, in slot 00:14.0
jsc.guide.device_listing.table2_2_2: uart0 for serial and parallel, ehci0 for USB 2, xhci0 for USB 3
jsc.guide.device_listing.table2_3_1: Audio: the board's own audio, in slot 00:1b.0
jsc.guide.device_listing.table2_4_1: Network: the first one, in slot 00:19.0
jsc.guide.device_listing.text1: The board of your computer has two buses that carry its devices: the Peripheral Component Interconnect (PCI) bus, and the Universal Serial Bus (USB). The PCI bus holds the built-in parts and the expansion cards. The USB bus holds what you plug in. pciconf lists the PCI devices, and usbconfig lists the USB devices. Both commands are explained with the other hardware lists ([](jsc:devices_commands)); this page shows what FreeBSD prints.
jsc.guide.device_listing.text2: Type pciconf -lv with both letters together, to list the devices on the PCI bus with their details. Type usbconfig with no words, to list the USB devices.
jsc.guide.device_listing.text3: usbconfig takes no options. Its first line names the controller, USB 2 controller or USB 3 controller, with its number of ports.
jsc.guide.device_listing.text4: Each following line is a device, numbered as ugen0.2, ugen0.3 and so on, in the order the ports run. A hub is listed before the devices on it.
jsc.guide.device_listing.text5: A device the computer disabled shows cfg=255. Such a device is not in use.
jsc.guide.device_listing.title: pciconf and usbconfig: what is on the board
jsc.guide.device_manager.definition1: A socket on the machine, such as a card slot or a link port, that a device is plugged into.
jsc.guide.device_manager.definition2: A device that adds ports of its own. A device plugged into a hub is listed under it.
jsc.guide.device_manager.fix1: Only a device on one of this computer's linked ports can be disabled. Link it first ([](jsc:peripheral_cables)).
jsc.guide.device_manager.fix2: Enable the hub again. A device disabled by itself stays disabled, so enable it too.
jsc.guide.device_manager.fix3: Use Enable and Disable, which are the actions that work.
jsc.guide.device_manager.heading2: What a disabled device stops doing
jsc.guide.device_manager.problem1: The device you want to disable is missing from the list.
jsc.guide.device_manager.problem2: Every device under a hub is disabled.
jsc.guide.device_manager.problem3: Update Driver, Uninstall, Show hidden devices and Print do nothing when you choose them.
jsc.guide.device_manager.step1: Select the device in the list.
jsc.guide.device_manager.step2: Open the Action menu and choose Disable. A device that is already disabled offers Enable.
jsc.guide.device_manager.step3: Look at the list: a disabled device is drawn crossed out.
jsc.guide.device_manager.table1_3_2: The port each device is plugged into.
jsc.guide.device_manager.table2_2_2: Enable or Disable, Update Driver... (does nothing), Uninstall (does nothing), Properties
jsc.guide.device_manager.table2_3_2: The three views, and Show hidden devices (does nothing)
jsc.guide.device_manager.table3_1_2: It is not driven, and its video memory is not counted.
jsc.guide.device_manager.table3_3_2: It does nothing while its link is disabled.
jsc.guide.device_manager.table3_4_2: It is not active while its owner is disabled.
jsc.guide.device_manager.table3_5_2: It does not start a desktop.
jsc.guide.device_manager.text1: The Device Manager lists the hardware of the machine and the port each piece is plugged into. It lets you disable a device, which stops the computer from using it, and enable it again. It is on Frames only.
jsc.guide.device_manager.text2: Its look follows the edition. On Frames 95 it sits in System Properties, under the name System. On Frames XP it is a console window, with the views in its View menu. On Frames 11 the views are a switch in its menu row.
jsc.guide.device_manager.text3: A device you disable stays plugged in, and you can enable it again at any time. Only a device on one of this computer's own linked ports can be disabled.
jsc.guide.device_manager.text4: A hub is a device too, and disabling a hub disables every device under it. If you unlink a device, its disabled setting is removed, so a device you link again comes back enabled.
jsc.guide.device_manager.title: The Device Manager
jsc.guide.devices_commands.definition1: Peripheral Component Interconnect: the bus on the board that expansion cards and built-in parts sit on.
jsc.guide.devices_commands.definition2: Universal Serial Bus: the bus for plugged-in devices.
jsc.guide.devices_commands.fix1: Run it on the computer whose parts you want to list.
jsc.guide.devices_commands.fix2: Use pciconf on FreeBSD. The lspci command is a Linux command.
jsc.guide.devices_commands.problem1: The command says no hardware to read.
jsc.guide.devices_commands.problem2: The shell says lspci is not found on FreeBSD.
jsc.guide.devices_commands.text1: A computer has parts on its Peripheral Component Interconnect (PCI) bus, the bus that expansion cards and built-in parts sit on. It has devices on its Universal Serial Bus (USB), the bus for plugged-in devices.
jsc.guide.devices_commands.text2: Each place on a bus is a slot, and a slot is written as bus:device:function. The commands below list what sits in those slots. Linux has lspci and lsusb, and FreeBSD has pciconf and usbconfig.
jsc.guide.devices_commands.text3: The devices command is a different list. It shows the peripherals linked to your computer, and it is on the system commands page ([](jsc:system_commands)).
jsc.guide.devices_commands.title: Hardware lists: lspci, lsusb, pciconf and usbconfig
jsc.guide.dialogs_and_file_choice.defini: A small window that asks the player something, and opens over another window.
The window a dialog sits over.
jsc.guide.dialogs_and_file_choice.fix1: Show the owner window first, then open the dialog over it.
jsc.guide.dialogs_and_file_choice.fix2: Close the open dialog first, then open the next one.
jsc.guide.dialogs_and_file_choice.proble: The program stops and says "a dialog opens over a window that is open", because the owner window is not open.
The program stops and says this window already has a dialog open over it.
jsc.guide.dialogs_and_file_choice.table1: A window with a title and one line of text. Sigma# only.
Makes a dialog that asks the player to open a file. Version 2.
Makes a dialog that asks the player where to save a file. Version 2.
The filter text of the dialog.
Shows the dialog over the owner window.
The file name the dialog suggests.
The event that runs when the player chooses a file.
The event that runs when the player cancels.
jsc.guide.dialogs_and_file_choice.text1: A dialog is a small window that asks the player something. It opens over another window, its owner window, and it closes when the player answers it.
jsc.guide.dialogs_and_file_choice.text2: Your program makes the dialog, shows it over a window that is open, and reads the path the player picked.
jsc.guide.dialogs_and_file_choice.text3: A window holds one dialog at a time.
jsc.guide.dialogs_and_file_choice.title: Dialogs: picking a file to open or save
jsc.guide.disable_device.definition1: To stop a computer from using a device. The device keeps its port until it is enabled again.
jsc.guide.disable_device.fix1: Enable it again: Enable in the Device Manager or in Workstation Info, or E in the MSD list.
jsc.guide.disable_device.fix2: Look for it in another view of the list, because the Show hidden devices option does nothing.
jsc.guide.disable_device.heading3: On the Common Desktop Environment (CDE) and KDE
jsc.guide.disable_device.problem1: A device is dark, or not seen, after you disabled it.
jsc.guide.disable_device.problem2: The Device Manager does not list a device.
jsc.guide.disable_device.step3: Press Disable, or Enable if the device is already disabled.
jsc.guide.disable_device.table1: The LPT and COM Ports list
jsc.guide.disable_device.table1_2_2: What is plugged into the port.
jsc.guide.disable_device.text1: You can disable a device, so that its computer stops using it. The device keeps its port, and enabling it again brings it back. You disable a device when you want the computer to stop reading it, or writing to it.
jsc.guide.disable_device.text2: On Frames, the Device Manager ([](jsc:device_manager)) lists the devices by type, by connection or by port.
jsc.guide.disable_device.text3: The status line says that the device is disabled, and that the computer stops reading and writing it. If a device is missing from the list, look for it in another view, because the Show hidden devices option does nothing.
jsc.guide.disable_device.text4: MC-DOS and MC-NET have no Device Manager. Their Midsoft Diagnostics program, MSD ([](jsc:dos_msd)), takes the whole terminal. Press L for the LPT ports, or C for the COM ports. LPT and COM are the old names of the parallel and the serial ports.
jsc.guide.disable_device.text5: In the list, press E to enable the device on the port you picked, or D to disable it. Enter puts the list away, and F3 exits MSD.
jsc.guide.disable_device.text6: On CDE, the Workstation Info window has a Devices... button ([](jsc:cde_workstation_info)). In its Devices dialog, select a device, then press Disable or Enable.
jsc.guide.disable_device.text7: On KDE, the Info Center page Devices by port has a button for the selected device, which disables or enables it ([](jsc:kde_plasma)).
jsc.guide.disable_device.text8: A disabled device goes quiet. A monitor shows "No signal - the computer has disabled this monitor", and a Redstone Interface reads and emits nothing. The computer also stops reading a drive, or the disks of the Dock Station.
jsc.guide.disable_device.title: Disabling a device
jsc.guide.disks.definition1: The slowest kind of disk here.
jsc.guide.disks.definition2: A disk four times as fast as a hard disk.
jsc.guide.disks.definition3: A fast storage standard, short for Non-Volatile Memory Express. It is the quickest kind of disk here.
jsc.guide.disks.definition4: The ticks a disk waits before it starts a transfer. The table gives the defaults.
jsc.guide.disks.fix1: It is newer than the computer. Use a disk of the computer's era or of an older one.
jsc.guide.disks.fix2: Move disks to the Hot-Swap Drive Bay, or use a board with more disk slots ([the build refusals](jsc:build_refusals)).
jsc.guide.disks.problem1: The disk does not go into the disk slot.
jsc.guide.disks.problem2: The build says there are too many disks.
jsc.guide.disks.text1: A disk keeps what must survive turning the computer off: its system, its programs and your files. The size of a disk is counted in items, as [Items as data](jsc:items_as_data) explains.
jsc.guide.disks.text2: There are three kinds of disk, and they differ in speed. The hard disk is the slowest, the SSD is four times as fast, and the NVMe is sixteen times as fast.
jsc.guide.disks.text3: A disk's size is counted in items of its era. A 20 MB Vintage drive holds 20 items. A 1 TB disk of a later era holds 4,096 items ([Units and ticks](jsc:units_and_ticks)).
jsc.guide.disks.text4: The Vintage disks are Vaultis Trench HDD drives of 20M, 100M and 200M. The Legacy hard disks are Vaultis Link IDE-HDD drives of 4G, 20G and 40G, and the Transition SSD is a Vaultis Link SATA-SSD of 64G.
jsc.guide.disks.text5: A disk fits a computer of its own era or of a later one. A disk newer than the computer is refused, in a disk slot, in the hot-swap bay and in a rack's drive bay.
jsc.guide.disks.text6: The board's disk slots count the disks you put in them. A disk in the hot-swap bay takes none of those slots. Each disk also draws power, as the table shows.
jsc.guide.disks.title: Disks
jsc.guide.distributions.definition1: One Linux system, packaged with its own installer, its own package manager and its own sizes.
jsc.guide.distributions.definition2: The command that fetches and installs programs for a distribution, from the Mirror.
jsc.guide.distributions.definition3: The package server on the network's Mainframe. Installers and package managers fetch from it.
jsc.guide.distributions.definition4: The core of the system, the part that runs the programs and talks to the machine. Here it is named 6.8-jsc.
jsc.guide.distributions.fix1: No Mirror answers, so the computer is not on a network whose Mainframe runs the Mirror. Connect it, then install ([](jsc:mirror_and_packages)).
jsc.guide.distributions.fix2: The computer is a Legacy machine. Choose KDE Plasma or GNOME, or use a Standard computer.
jsc.guide.distributions.problem1: The installer shows no desktop page.
jsc.guide.distributions.problem2: Cinnamon is missing from the desktop list.
jsc.guide.distributions.text1: A Linux system comes in many versions, and each version is called a distribution. A distribution bundles the Linux kernel, the programs that run on it, its own installer and its own package manager. Here you can install three of them: Ubuntu, Debian and Fedora.
jsc.guide.distributions.text2: Each of the three is a Legacy system: it takes Legacy hardware or newer. All three boot the same kernel, named 6.8-jsc, and they differ in the disk they take, the random-access memory (RAM) they hold while they run, and the package manager they use. The numbers below are the game's own, not the exact requirements of a real machine.
jsc.guide.distributions.text3: The disk figure is the room the system takes for itself, before any program or desktop. A disk with less free room than that cannot take the system: see [](jsc:installing_linux_keys).
jsc.guide.distributions.text4: A distribution starts at its text console, the screen with a prompt. A desktop, the graphical screen with windows and menus, is a package you add afterwards. The three desktops are in the table below.
jsc.guide.distributions.text5: KDE Plasma and GNOME need Legacy hardware or newer. Cinnamon needs Standard hardware or newer, so a Legacy computer cannot take it. The installers offer a desktop only when a Mirror answers, as [](jsc:mirror_and_packages) explains.
jsc.guide.distributions.text6: The table gives the numbers to compare. Debian takes the least disk and holds the least memory, while Ubuntu and Fedora take the most. The package manager is the other difference: apt on Ubuntu and Debian, dnf on Fedora.
jsc.guide.distributions.title: What a distribution is, and which to choose
jsc.guide.dnf.fix1: This is Ubuntu or Debian, which use apt. Type apt in its place ([](jsc:apt)).
jsc.guide.dnf.fix2: The computer is not on a network whose Mainframe runs the Mirror. Connect it, as [](jsc:mirror_and_packages) explains.
jsc.guide.dnf.fix3: The name is wrong, or the program is not offered on Linux. Find the right name with dnf search.
jsc.guide.dnf.fix4: Nothing to do. dnf update brings every installed package up to date.
jsc.guide.dnf.problem2: E: could not resolve mirror:// - connect this computer to a network whose Mainframe runs the Mirror service
jsc.guide.dnf.table1_1_2: Installs the program from the Mirror.
jsc.guide.dnf.table1_2_2: Removes it. purge and erase do the same.
jsc.guide.dnf.table1_5_2: Brings the installed packages up to date.
jsc.guide.dnf.table1_6_2: Brings the installed packages up to date, as dnf update does; full-upgrade and dist-upgrade are the same.
jsc.guide.dnf.table2: What dnf prints for an install
jsc.guide.dnf.table2_1_2: When the package lists were last read.
jsc.guide.dnf.table2_2_2: The packages the program needs are worked out.
jsc.guide.dnf.table2_3_2: The program, its version and its size.
jsc.guide.dnf.table2_4_2: The download from the Mirror starts, with a line for its speed and progress.
jsc.guide.dnf.table2_5_2: The program is written to the computer.
jsc.guide.dnf.table2_6_2: Followed by the name of the installed program.
jsc.guide.dnf.text1: dnf is the package manager of Fedora. It works the way apt does: you type dnf, a verb, then the name of what it works on. On Ubuntu and Debian the word is not a command, and the shell answers "command not found: dnf".
jsc.guide.dnf.text2: The verbs are the same as apt's, with one difference. On dnf, update is the upgrade: it brings installed packages up to date. Upgrade does the same job, so either word works.
jsc.guide.dnf.text3: An install on Fedora prints its own lines, in this order.
jsc.guide.dnf.text4: A remove prints "Removing:  <package>" in place of the install lines. Every other refusal is the same as apt's, and begins with "E: ".
jsc.guide.dnf.title: dnf, verb by verb
jsc.guide.dock_station.balloon3_detail: It takes a Non-Volatile Memory Express (NVMe) disk.
jsc.guide.dock_station.balloon4_detail: It takes one USB flash drive.
jsc.guide.dock_station.definition1: A tray of the Dock Station that takes one disk of one size.
jsc.guide.dock_station.definition2: The short name a computer gives a drive or a docked disk, so that programs can find it.
jsc.guide.dock_station.figure1: A Dock Station joined to a Personal Computer, with a disk in each of its three bays and a USB flash drive in its port. Drag the scene to see the back.
jsc.guide.dock_station.fix1: Take the disk out in the window first.
jsc.guide.dock_station.fix2: Join the Dock to a computer with a peripheral cable ([](jsc:peripheral_cables)).
jsc.guide.dock_station.fix3: Only disks and USB flash drives go in the Dock. Anything else is refused, and the Dock says nothing.
jsc.guide.dock_station.problem1: That tray already holds a disk - sneak-click or use the window to take it out.
jsc.guide.dock_station.problem2: The Dock says "Not docked to a computer" or "No computer linked".
jsc.guide.dock_station.problem3: Nothing happens when you click the Dock.
jsc.guide.dock_station.step1: Click the Dock with a disk in your hand to put it in its bay.
jsc.guide.dock_station.step2: Click the Dock with a USB flash drive in your hand to plug it into the port.
jsc.guide.dock_station.step3: Sneak-click the Dock to take out the last thing you put in: the flash drive first, then the bays from the bottom.
jsc.guide.dock_station.step4: Click the Dock with an empty hand to open its window.
jsc.guide.dock_station.table2_1_2: "Linked to a computer" when a computer reaches the Dock, and "No computer linked" when none does.
jsc.guide.dock_station.table2_2_2: Each bay, empty, or with its disk and how much of it is used.
jsc.guide.dock_station.table2_3_2: The USB port, with the flash drive in it, or empty.
jsc.guide.dock_station.table2_4_2: The drive letter the computer gives each disk and the flash drive.
jsc.guide.dock_station.text1: The Dock Station reads storage disks and Universal Serial Bus (USB) flash drives for a computer. You join it to a computer like any device ([](jsc:peripheral_cables)), with a cable of any era. It has three bays for disks, and a USB port for one flash drive.
jsc.guide.dock_station.text2: A bay takes one disk, and only a disk of its own size. The Dock refuses anything that is not a disk or a flash drive.
jsc.guide.dock_station.text3: A system's installer can be on a USB flash drive in the Dock, so that you install from the Dock ([](jsc:installing)).
jsc.guide.dock_station.text4: The window shows each bay and the port, with what they hold. You can put disks in and take them out there too.
jsc.guide.dock_station.text5: The computer sees each disk in the Dock as an external drive, and it can open and copy to it. The Dock works only while a computer is linked to it.
jsc.guide.dock_station.title: The Dock Station
jsc.guide.dos_help.definition1: One page of the help: the page of a command, or an entry of a manual.
jsc.guide.dos_help.definition2: A word in a page that you pick with Tab and follow with Enter.
jsc.guide.dos_help.fix1: No command and no entry has every word you typed. Try fewer words, or the name of a command.
jsc.guide.dos_help.fix2: Esc first closes an open menu or the Find prompt. Press it again, or press [[Alt]]+[[F4]].
jsc.guide.dos_help.problem1: The bottom line says Match not found.
jsc.guide.dos_help.problem2: Esc does not leave the help.
jsc.guide.dos_help.step1: Type help at the prompt and press [[Enter]].
jsc.guide.dos_help.step2: Press [[Tab]] until a button or a link has the focus, then press [[Enter]] to follow it.
jsc.guide.dos_help.step3: Press [[Alt]]+[[N]] for the next topic, [[Alt]]+[[B]] for the one before, [[Alt]]+[[C]] for the Contents and [[Alt]]+[[I]] for the Index.
jsc.guide.dos_help.step4: Press [[Alt]]+[[S]] to open the Search menu, pick Find... and press [[Enter]].
jsc.guide.dos_help.step5: Type the words to find, then press [[Enter]].
jsc.guide.dos_help.step6: Press [[Esc]] to leave the help, or press [[Alt]]+[[F4]].
jsc.guide.dos_help.table1: The parts of the help screen
jsc.guide.dos_help.table1_2_2: Four buttons: Next, Back, Contents and Index.
jsc.guide.dos_help.table1_4_2: The keys, a message or the Find prompt.
jsc.guide.dos_help.table2_13_2: Closes an open menu or the Find prompt, or leaves the help when nothing is open.
jsc.guide.dos_help.table2_1_2: Picks the next button or link, and Shift with Tab picks the previous one.
jsc.guide.dos_help.table2_2_2: Follows the link or button picked.
jsc.guide.dos_help.table2_5_2: Go to the top and the bottom of the topic.
jsc.guide.dos_help.table2_6_2: Opens the File menu, with Exit.
jsc.guide.dos_help.table2_7_2: Opens the Search menu, with Find... and Repeat Last Find.
jsc.guide.dos_help.text1: Type help at the prompt to open the help of MC-DOS. It takes the whole screen, in place of the prompt, and it shows the topics of the manual. Its topics come from the Frames Resource Kit, the book you are reading.
jsc.guide.dos_help.text2: Type help and a command's name, such as help dir, to open the page of that command. The same page opens when you type the command's name, a space and /?.
jsc.guide.dos_help.text3: The help screen has four parts, from the top down, as the table shows.
jsc.guide.dos_help.text4: The bottom line shows only Alt+C=Contents, Alt+N=Next and Alt+B=Back. Alt+I and Alt+S work too.
jsc.guide.dos_help.text5: Find first looks for a command with exactly that name. Then it looks for the next entry of the manual you are reading whose title or text has every word you typed. It goes round from the topic on the screen. Repeat Last Find, or [[F3]], looks for the same words again.
jsc.guide.dos_help.title: The help, full screen
jsc.guide.dos_install.definition1: The program on the motherboard that starts the computer. It runs before any system does.
jsc.guide.dos_install.fix1: The Floppy Drive is not joined to the computer, or the firmware does not find it. Join the drive, then check the firmware ([](jsc:firmware)).
jsc.guide.dos_install.fix2: The disk you picked has less than 4 megabytes (MB) free. Pick another disk that has room ([](jsc:disks)).
jsc.guide.dos_install.fix3: No disk is picked yet, or the picked disk has no room. Pick a disk with room first.
jsc.guide.dos_install.fix4: The copy has begun, and [[F3]] works only before it. Wait for the last page.
jsc.guide.dos_install.problem2: The screen says "No room here. Erase this disk, or choose another."
jsc.guide.dos_install.problem3: Continue does nothing on the settings page.
jsc.guide.dos_install.step1: Put the MC-DOS floppy disk in the Floppy Drive.
jsc.guide.dos_install.step2: Start the computer with the floppy in its drive, as the installing page explains ([](jsc:installing)).
jsc.guide.dos_install.step3: Read the page "Welcome to Setup." and press [[Enter]].
jsc.guide.dos_install.step4: Move the cursor to a disk with the arrow keys. Type a name in "Computer name:" if you want one, then press [[Enter]].
jsc.guide.dos_install.step5: Wait while the bar fills. The page says "Setup is copying MC-DOS to the disk."
jsc.guide.dos_install.step6: Read "MC-DOS Setup is complete." and press [[Enter]] to restart.
jsc.guide.dos_install.table2_2_2: Setup will use the following settings:
jsc.guide.dos_install.table2_3_2: Setup is copying MC-DOS to the disk.
jsc.guide.dos_install.text1: MC-DOS is the Vintage system that works at the prompt ([](jsc:the_systems)). You install it from a medium only: a floppy disk, put in a Floppy Drive. The installer copies the system to a disk you choose, and then the computer starts from that disk.
jsc.guide.dos_install.text2: The firmware is the program on the motherboard that starts the computer ([](jsc:firmware)).
jsc.guide.dos_install.text3: The settings page lists the disks of the computer. Continue stays off until you pick a disk that has at least 4 megabytes (MB) free. Setup copies the system onto the disk you picked. When the copy is done, the computer restarts from that disk.
jsc.guide.dos_install.text4: As the computer starts, the screen prints a line for each drive, such as Drive C:, and then the version line, MC-DOS Version 1.0. You are then at the prompt ([](jsc:dos_prompt)).
jsc.guide.dos_install.title: Installing MC-DOS
jsc.guide.dos_install.value1_1: The MC-DOS floppy disk, from the creative tabs.
jsc.guide.dos_install.value1_2: A Floppy Drive joined to the computer ([](jsc:drives)).
jsc.guide.dos_install.value1_3: 4 megabytes (MB) free on the disk you install on.
jsc.guide.dos_msd.definition1: The program that reads the hardware of the computer and reports what it finds.
jsc.guide.dos_msd.definition2: A parallel port, where a printer is usually plugged in.
jsc.guide.dos_msd.definition3: A serial port, where a modem or a mouse of the era could be plugged in.
jsc.guide.dos_msd.fix1: msd has no computer to read. Type msd at the prompt of a computer.
jsc.guide.dos_msd.fix2: Nothing is plugged into that port, so there is no device to enable or disable.
jsc.guide.dos_msd.fix3: You disabled its device. Pick the port and press [[E]] to enable the device again.
jsc.guide.dos_msd.problem1: The screen says msd: there is no machine to read.
jsc.guide.dos_msd.problem3: A port says Off (disabled) under Status.
jsc.guide.dos_msd.step1: Type msd at the prompt and press [[Enter]].
jsc.guide.dos_msd.step2: Move the pick with the arrow keys. Press [[Enter]] on LPT Ports or COM Ports to open a list.
jsc.guide.dos_msd.step3: In the list, pick a port with the arrows, then press [[E]] to enable its device or [[D]] to disable it.
jsc.guide.dos_msd.step4: Press [[Enter]] or [[Esc]] to put the list away. Press [[F3]] on the main screen to give the terminal back.
jsc.guide.dos_msd.table1: The buttons of the main screen
jsc.guide.dos_msd.table1_1_2: The name of the first processor.
jsc.guide.dos_msd.table1_2_2: The conventional memory, 640K, then the memory above 1 MB, counted in K.
jsc.guide.dos_msd.table1_3_2: The name of the first video card, or (none).
jsc.guide.dos_msd.table1_4_2: The cable of the first network adapter, or (none).
jsc.guide.dos_msd.table1_6_2: The drive letters the machine sees, such as C: D:.
jsc.guide.dos_msd.table1_7_2: The number of parallel ports. Zero when there are none. Opens a list.
jsc.guide.dos_msd.table1_8_2: The number of serial ports. Opens a list.
jsc.guide.dos_msd.table2: The columns of a ports list
jsc.guide.dos_msd.table2_1_2: The name of the port, such as COM1 or LPT1.
jsc.guide.dos_msd.table2_2_2: The device on the port, or (none) when nothing is attached.
jsc.guide.dos_msd.table2_3_2: On, or Off (disabled) for a device you have disabled.
jsc.guide.dos_msd.table3_1_3: Move the pick between the buttons.
jsc.guide.dos_msd.table3_7_3: Enables the device of the port picked.
jsc.guide.dos_msd.table3_8_3: Disables the device of the port picked, which keeps its port while the computer neither reads nor writes it.
jsc.guide.dos_msd.text1: Midsoft Diagnostics (MSD) reads the hardware of the computer and shows what it is made of. Type msd at the prompt to open it. The program takes the whole screen, and it works on MC-DOS and on [MC-NET](jsc:mc_net).
jsc.guide.dos_msd.text2: Only LPT Ports and COM Ports open a list. The other buttons show what they found, and Enter does nothing on them.
jsc.guide.dos_msd.text3: A mouse click works too: on a button, on a port, and on the Enable and Disable buttons under the list.
jsc.guide.dos_msd.title: MSD and its keys
jsc.guide.dos_printing.fix1: The printer is not linked, or it is off. Check the printer, then print again ([](jsc:printers)).
jsc.guide.dos_printing.problem1: print says Errors on list device indicate that it may be off-line.
jsc.guide.dos_printing.text1: print sends text files to the printer in the background, so the prompt is free while the files print. You need a printer linked to the computer ([](jsc:printers)).
jsc.guide.dos_printing.text2: The first time you use print, it says "Resident part of PRINT installed". Each file that you name joins the queue. The queue lists the file being printed, then the files waiting in the queue. When the queue is empty, it says "PRINT queue is empty".
jsc.guide.dos_printing.title: Printing from the prompt
jsc.guide.dos_prompt.definition1: The line where MC-DOS waits for a command. It shows the current folder and a greater-than sign.
jsc.guide.dos_prompt.definition2: The name a disk or a drive has on MC-DOS: a letter and a colon, such as C:.
jsc.guide.dos_prompt.definition3: The full address of a file or a folder: its drive, its folders and its name.
jsc.guide.dos_prompt.definition4: The list of folders MC-DOS searches for a program when you type only the program's name.
jsc.guide.dos_prompt.fix1: No command or program of that name is in the folder you are in or on the search path. Check the spelling, or type the full path, such as C:\DOS\HELLO. [Finding a command](jsc:finding_a_command) explains the rest.
jsc.guide.dos_prompt.fix2: The machine has no drive with that letter. Type one of the letters in the table above.
jsc.guide.dos_prompt.fix3: The drive has no disk in it. Put a disk or a medium in the drive ([](jsc:drives)).
jsc.guide.dos_prompt.fix4: The computer has no system disk to start from. Put a disk in a disk slot, or install MC-DOS on one ([](jsc:dos_install)).
jsc.guide.dos_prompt.fix5: The folder does not exist. List the folder with dir, then type the name again.
jsc.guide.dos_prompt.fix6: Delete the files in the folder first, then remove the folder with rmdir.
jsc.guide.dos_prompt.problem1: The prompt says "command not found: HELLO".
jsc.guide.dos_prompt.problem2: The prompt says E:\ The system cannot find the drive specified.
jsc.guide.dos_prompt.problem3: The prompt says "D:\ The device is not ready."
jsc.guide.dos_prompt.problem4: The prompt says no system disk or OS installed.
jsc.guide.dos_prompt.problem5: The prompt says The system cannot find the path specified.
jsc.guide.dos_prompt.problem6: The prompt says The directory is not empty.
jsc.guide.dos_prompt.table1_1_2: The system disk, or the first data disk when there is no system disk.
jsc.guide.dos_prompt.table1_2_2: The data disks in the disk slots, in slot order; the first one is D: when there is a system disk.
jsc.guide.dos_prompt.table1_3_2: The readers, the Dock Station bays and the case-front drives, each keeping its letter.
jsc.guide.dos_prompt.table1_4_2: Never. The machine has no drive A: and no drive B:.
jsc.guide.dos_prompt.table2_1_2: Changes to drive D: and its top folder.
jsc.guide.dos_prompt.table2_2_2: The folder DIR at the top of drive D:.
jsc.guide.dos_prompt.table2_3_2: The top folder of the current drive.
jsc.guide.dos_prompt.table2_4_2: The folder DIR at the top of the current drive.
jsc.guide.dos_prompt.table2_5_2: The folder above; at the top folder it stays put, with no error.
jsc.guide.dos_prompt.text1: MC-DOS waits for you at the prompt, the line where you type a command and press [[Enter]]. The prompt shows where you are: the folder you are in, then a greater-than sign. At the top of the system disk it reads C:\>, and in a folder called SYSTEM it reads C:\SYSTEM>. A command works on the folder the prompt shows, unless you name another place.
jsc.guide.dos_prompt.text2: Every disk and drive has a drive letter: a letter and a colon, such as C:. Type the letter and the colon to change drive, for example D:. You then stand at the top folder of that drive. MC-DOS keeps no current folder for each drive, so a drive does not remember where you were.
jsc.guide.dos_prompt.text3: Removable drives are the ones you join to the computer ([](jsc:drives)). Data disks are the disks in its slots ([](jsc:disks)).
jsc.guide.dos_prompt.text4: A path is the full address of a file or a folder: its drive, its folders and its name. A path can join the folders with a backslash or a slash, so C:\DOS\README.TXT and C:/DOS/README.TXT name the same file.
jsc.guide.dos_prompt.text5: When you type only a word, MC-DOS takes it for a built-in command first, and then for a program. It looks for the program in the folder you are in, then in the folders of the search path, the list kept in the PATH setting.
jsc.guide.dos_prompt.text6: To run a program that is in another folder, type its full path, such as C:\DOS\HELLO.
jsc.guide.dos_prompt.text7: The commands for folders are dir, cd, mkdir and rmdir. dir lists a folder, cd shows the current folder or changes it, mkdir makes a folder and rmdir removes an empty one. [Working with files and folders](jsc:working_with_files) explains them all.
jsc.guide.dos_prompt.text8: Type a command's name, a space and /? to read its page. Typing help dir opens the same page ([](jsc:dos_help)).
jsc.guide.dos_prompt.title: The prompt, the drives and the paths
jsc.guide.dos_shell.definition1: The menu program of MC-DOS for its files and programs, opened with the command dosshell.
jsc.guide.dos_shell.definition2: A program or a Command Prompt that runs from the shell and is kept in the Active Task List.
jsc.guide.dos_shell.fix1: Only the files that end in .EXE, .COM and .BAT start from the shell. Press [[F9]] to read a text file.
jsc.guide.dos_shell.fix2: Finish each task, then press [[F3]]. The tasks are the programs listed in the Active Task List.
jsc.guide.dos_shell.fix3: The pattern in File Display Options shows no file. Change it, for example to *.* to see every file.
jsc.guide.dos_shell.fix4: The drive has no disk. Put a disk in it, or pick another drive.
jsc.guide.dos_shell.fix5: The shell does not offer that item. Use the commands at the prompt for the same job.
jsc.guide.dos_shell.problem1: Enter on a file does nothing.
jsc.guide.dos_shell.problem2: The screen says You cannot quit MC-DOS Shell with programs in the Active Task List; quit those programs first.
jsc.guide.dos_shell.problem3: The screen says No files match file specifier.
jsc.guide.dos_shell.problem4: The screen says Drive not ready.
jsc.guide.dos_shell.problem5: The screen says Not available on this machine.
jsc.guide.dos_shell.step1: Type dosshell at the prompt and press [[Enter]].
jsc.guide.dos_shell.step2: Press [[Tab]] to move from one area to the next, and the arrow keys to move within one.
jsc.guide.dos_shell.step3: Press [[Enter]] on a program to start it as a task.
jsc.guide.dos_shell.step4: Hold [[Alt]] and press [[Tab]] to pick the next task, and let go of [[Alt]] to switch to it.
jsc.guide.dos_shell.step5: Press [[F3]] to leave the shell, once no task is listed.
jsc.guide.dos_shell.table1_1_2: The folders of the disk you are on.
jsc.guide.dos_shell.table1_2_2: The drives the machine has, shown only when it has some.
jsc.guide.dos_shell.table1_3_2: The files of the folder you picked.
jsc.guide.dos_shell.table1_4_2: The tasks you started, shown while the Task Swapper is on.
jsc.guide.dos_shell.table2_1_2: The tree and the files, over the programs and the tasks, the way the shell opens.
jsc.guide.dos_shell.table2_2_2: The tree and the list of files, down to the bottom of the screen.
jsc.guide.dos_shell.table2_3_2: The programs and the tasks only.
jsc.guide.dos_shell.table3_14_2: Leaves the shell, which is refused while a task is listed.
jsc.guide.dos_shell.table3_15_2: Leaves the shell, as F3 does.
jsc.guide.dos_shell.table3_1_2: Moves to the next area, and Shift with Tab goes back.
jsc.guide.dos_shell.table3_20_2: Shows the contents of the selected file, which Escape closes.
jsc.guide.dos_shell.table3_21_2: Opens a Command Prompt as a task.
jsc.guide.dos_shell.table3_22_2: Deletes the selected file, or the selected empty folder in the tree.
jsc.guide.dos_shell.table3_23_2: Switches to the next task, and Shift+Alt+Tab goes back.
jsc.guide.dos_shell.table3_24_2: Leaves a group of the program list, or closes a menu.
jsc.guide.dos_shell.table3_25_2: In the tree: shows the folders in the selected folder.
jsc.guide.dos_shell.table3_26_2: In the tree: shows every folder under the selected folder.
jsc.guide.dos_shell.table3_27_2: In the tree: puts away the folders under the selected folder.
jsc.guide.dos_shell.table3_3_2: Moves a page up the list.
jsc.guide.dos_shell.table3_4_2: Moves a page down the list.
jsc.guide.dos_shell.table3_7_2: Opens the item picked, or starts a program as a task.
jsc.guide.dos_shell.table4_1_3: Starts a program, or opens the folder picked.
jsc.guide.dos_shell.table4_2_3: Shows the file, as the TYPE command does.
jsc.guide.dos_shell.table4_3_3: Moves a file, as MOVE does.
jsc.guide.dos_shell.table4_4_3: Copies a file, as COPY does.
jsc.guide.dos_shell.table4_5_1: Delete..., with a question when Confirmation is on
jsc.guide.dos_shell.table4_5_3: Deletes the file, as DEL does, or the folder, as RMDIR does.
jsc.guide.dos_shell.table4_6_3: Gives the file another name, as REN does.
jsc.guide.dos_shell.table4_7_1: Create Directory..., with the parent and a name
jsc.guide.dos_shell.table4_7_3: Makes a folder, as MKDIR does.
jsc.guide.dos_shell.table4_8_3: Leaves the shell for the prompt.
jsc.guide.dos_shell.text1: The MC-DOS Shell is a menu program for the files of the system. You see the folders and the files, copy, move or delete them, and start programs with the keys, without typing each command yourself. Every action of its File menu runs one of MC-DOS's own commands.
jsc.guide.dos_shell.text2: Type dosshell at the prompt to open it. It runs on MC-DOS only, takes the whole screen and opens on the top folder of C:.
jsc.guide.dos_shell.text3: Dual File Lists and All Files answer "Not available on this machine." Select Across Directories does the same.
jsc.guide.dos_shell.text4: The program list has a group called Main. It holds Command Prompt, which starts a command prompt as a task, and Sigma when Sigma is installed. It holds the groups [Programs] and [Disk Utilities]. [Programs] lists the programs you installed, except the Command Prompt.
jsc.guide.dos_shell.text5: The Options menu holds Confirmation, which asks before deleting, and Enable Task Swapper. The Task Swapper keeps each program you start as a task, so that you can switch between them. Show Information shows the selected file, its folder and its disk.
jsc.guide.dos_shell.text6: Disk Utilities holds Format. Its dialog has a field that starts with the text "a:". Replace the text with the drive you mean and add /y, as in D: /y. Without /y, Format prints its warning and erases nothing.
jsc.guide.dos_shell.text7: Print sends the selected file to a printer ([](jsc:printers)). It is greyed out when no printer is linked.
jsc.guide.dos_shell.text8: The bottom line shows the keys: F10=Actions, Shift+F9=Command Prompt and, while the Task Swapper is on, Alt+Tab=Next Task.
jsc.guide.dos_shell.title: DOSSHELL and its keys
jsc.guide.dos_system_files.fix1: Type the full path of the program's .EXE file: C:\ followed by its folder and its file name. Programs typed by name are found in the folder you are in and in the folders of the PATH line.
jsc.guide.dos_system_files.fix2: The prompt always shows the folder and a greater-than sign. No line of AUTOEXEC.BAT changes it ([](jsc:dos_prompt)).
jsc.guide.dos_system_files.problem1: You type the name of a program you installed, and the prompt says command not found.
jsc.guide.dos_system_files.problem2: You expect the PROMPT line to change the prompt, and it does not.
jsc.guide.dos_system_files.table1: The files of the system disk
jsc.guide.dos_system_files.table1_1_2: The folder of the system's own files.
jsc.guide.dos_system_files.table1_2_2: The startup file, with the PATH line.
jsc.guide.dos_system_files.table1_3_2: The configuration file, whose lines have no effect on this system.
jsc.guide.dos_system_files.table1_4_2: The command interpreter: the program that reads what you type and runs it.
jsc.guide.dos_system_files.table1_6_2: The memory driver of the system.
jsc.guide.dos_system_files.table1_7_2: The notes of the system, which tell you to type HELP for the commands.
jsc.guide.dos_system_files.table1_8_2: The folder of an installed program, named with up to eight capital letters.
jsc.guide.dos_system_files.text1: When MC-DOS is installed, the system disk, C:, shows you some files that were never copied onto it. The system builds them from what is installed each time the disk is read, so they are not stored on the disk. They sit at the top of C: and in its DOS folder.
jsc.guide.dos_system_files.text2: AUTOEXEC.BAT holds three lines: @ECHO OFF, PROMPT $P$G and a PATH line. The PATH line lists the DOS folder first, then the folder of each installed program in the order they were installed. When you type only a program's name, MC-DOS searches the folders on that line. If AUTOEXEC.BAT or its PATH line is missing, it searches the DOS folder only.
jsc.guide.dos_system_files.text3: The PROMPT line does not set your prompt. The prompt always shows the folder you are in and a greater-than sign ([](jsc:dos_prompt)).
jsc.guide.dos_system_files.text4: CONFIG.SYS holds the lines DEVICE=C:\DOS\HIMEM.SYS, DOS=HIGH, FILES=30 and BUFFERS=20. The file is there for you to read, but its lines have no effect on this system.
jsc.guide.dos_system_files.title: The system's own files
jsc.guide.dos_text_tools.definition1: A line of two or more commands joined by a bar symbol, so that the output of the first command becomes the input of the next.
jsc.guide.dos_text_tools.definition2: Sending the output of a command to a file, or reading its input from a file, with an arrow symbol.
jsc.guide.dos_text_tools.definition3: A viewer that shows one screen of a file at a time and waits for you to go on.
jsc.guide.dos_text_tools.fix1: find is case-sensitive unless you add /I. Check the capital letters too, and keep the text in double quotes.
jsc.guide.dos_text_tools.fix2: sort compares lines as text, so a line "10" comes before a line "9". The DOS sort has no numeric option.
jsc.guide.dos_text_tools.fix3: A pipe needs a command on each side of the bar.
jsc.guide.dos_text_tools.fix4: Type the file name after the arrow, such as > RESULT.TXT.
jsc.guide.dos_text_tools.problem2: sort does not put the numbers in order as numbers.
jsc.guide.dos_text_tools.problem3: The line says syntax error near unexpected token, and names the bar.
jsc.guide.dos_text_tools.problem4: An arrow has no file name after it, and the line stops with a syntax error.
jsc.guide.dos_text_tools.table1_1_2: Sends the output of the left command to the right command.
jsc.guide.dos_text_tools.table1_2_2: Writes the output to a file, replacing what the file had.
jsc.guide.dos_text_tools.table1_3_2: Adds the output to the end of a file.
jsc.guide.dos_text_tools.table1_4_2: Reads the input from a file.
jsc.guide.dos_text_tools.table2_1_2: Goes on to the next screen.
jsc.guide.dos_text_tools.table2_2_2: Goes on to the next screen.
jsc.guide.dos_text_tools.table2_6_2: Looks for the text you type.
jsc.guide.dos_text_tools.table2_7_2: Finds the next match of the search.
jsc.guide.dos_text_tools.text1: The DOS family has three verbs for text. find prints the lines that hold some text, sort puts lines in order, and more shows a file one screen at a time.
jsc.guide.dos_text_tools.text2: find and sort take their text from a file that you name, or from a pipe. more reads only the file that you name.
jsc.guide.dos_text_tools.text3: The pipe sends the output of one command to the next command as its input. Each bar needs a command on each side of it. A stage hands at most 4,096 lines to the next one.
jsc.guide.dos_text_tools.text4: The DOS text tools take a file name or a pipe. The Unix systems have tools of the same names that work separately, with their own rules ([](jsc:text_tools)).
jsc.guide.dos_text_tools.text5: find prints the lines that hold the text in double quotes. It is case-sensitive unless you add /I, which ignores capital letters. /V prints the lines that do not hold the text.
jsc.guide.dos_text_tools.text6: sort puts the lines in order, comparing them as text. /R reverses the order. It reads a pipe or the file that you name.
jsc.guide.dos_text_tools.text7: more shows a file one screen at a time. It is a pager: a viewer that waits for you between screens. Its keys are these.
jsc.guide.dos_text_tools.title: Text: find, sort, more and the pipe
jsc.guide.drives.definition1: A drive joined to the computer, into which you put a disc or a stick, such as a CD Drive or a Dock Station.
jsc.guide.drives.definition2: The physical kind of medium: floppy, CD, DVD, USB or Blu-ray. It decides which drives read the medium.
jsc.guide.drives.definition3: The sliding part that a disc sits on. The eject button beside the drive moves it out and back in.
jsc.guide.drives.fix1: Each medium goes in a drive of its own kind: a CD goes in a CD Drive, and a DVD in a DVD Drive or a Blu-ray Drive.
jsc.guide.drives.fix2: Press the eject button beside the drive.
jsc.guide.drives.fix3: The computer is installing from the disc. Wait until the installation has finished.
jsc.guide.drives.fix4: Sneak-click the drive while its tray is open.
jsc.guide.drives.problem1: This CD drive cannot read that disc.
jsc.guide.drives.problem2: The tray is closed - press the eject button to open it.
jsc.guide.drives.problem3: The drive is reading - wait for it to finish.
jsc.guide.drives.problem4: The drive already holds a disc - sneak-click to eject it.
jsc.guide.drives.step1: Press the eject button beside the drive to bring the tray out.
jsc.guide.drives.step2: Click the drive with the disc in your hand, so that it lies on the tray.
jsc.guide.drives.step3: Press the eject button again, or push the tray in with an empty hand.

jsc.guide.drives.text1: A drive reads removable media: a disk or a disc that you put in, and take out again. You need drives to install systems and programs, and to carry files from one computer to another. Each drive is a peripheral, joined to its computer like any other device ([](jsc:peripheral_cables)).
jsc.guide.drives.text2: Media are named after their formats. CD stands for compact disc, DVD for digital versatile disc, and USB for Universal Serial Bus. A read-only memory (ROM) medium can only be read; a rewritable one (RW or RE) can also be written to.
jsc.guide.drives.text3: Each drive reads only some formats. The table shows what each drive reads.
jsc.guide.drives.text4: The Dock Station is a drive of its own for storage disks. The USB port on the front of a case takes a flash drive ([](jsc:case_front)).
jsc.guide.drives.text5: Writable means that the computer can write to the medium as well as read it.
jsc.guide.drives.text6: A floppy disk goes into the slot of its Floppy Drive, and a USB flash drive goes into its port with no tray in the way. A disc needs its tray open first.
jsc.guide.drives.text7: A computer sees a drive with its tray out as empty. The tray also stays shut while the computer reads the disc, that is, while it installs from the disc. To take a disc out, sneak-click the drive while its tray is open.
jsc.guide.drives.title: Drives and media
jsc.guide.editions_compared.definition1: A generation of hardware, such as Legacy or Standard.
jsc.guide.editions_compared.definition2: An edition's place in its family's order, counted from one.
jsc.guide.editions_compared.definition3: The room a system takes on a disk once it is installed, counted in the disk's items.
jsc.guide.editions_compared.fix1: The computer is older than the edition. Use a computer of the era the message names, or install an older edition ([](jsc:installing)).
jsc.guide.editions_compared.fix2: Use a larger disk. A Legacy disk holds Frames 95 in 3 items, and Frames 11 needs 80 items of an Advanced disk.
jsc.guide.editions_compared.fix3: Install a disk in the computer first ([](jsc:disks)).
jsc.guide.editions_compared.fix4: Each install medium belongs to one system. Use the medium made for the edition you want ([](jsc:installing)).
jsc.guide.editions_compared.problem1: The installer says "Frames 10 needs Standard era hardware or newer; this machine is Legacy era."
jsc.guide.editions_compared.problem2: The installer says the target disk has no room for the edition, and gives the megabytes it needs.
jsc.guide.editions_compared.problem3: The installer says "No disk is installed to put Frames 11 on."
jsc.guide.editions_compared.problem4: The installer says "The system on the medium is not known to this machine."
jsc.guide.editions_compared.table1_4_4: USB stick, in the Dock Station
jsc.guide.editions_compared.table1_5_4: USB stick, in the Dock Station
jsc.guide.editions_compared.text1: Frames is one family of five editions. An edition is one version of Frames, with its own installer, its own desktop and its own built-in programs. The editions have an order, from Frames 95, the oldest, to Frames 11, the newest.
jsc.guide.editions_compared.text2: Each edition has a family rank: its place in the family's order, counted from one. A program can ask for a version by its rank. A program that needs "Frames XP or newer" runs on XP, 7, 10 and 11, and it refuses Frames 95.
jsc.guide.editions_compared.text3: Every edition needs a computer of its own era or newer. Frames 95 and XP need Legacy, Frames 7 needs Transition, Frames 10 needs Standard and Frames 11 needs Advanced. Each edition also runs on every computer of a newer era. A newer edition does not go on an older computer, and the installer tells you so ([](jsc:the_systems)).
jsc.guide.editions_compared.text4: The install medium is the item you put in a drive to install an edition. Frames 95 and XP install from a compact disc (CD), Frames 7 from a digital versatile disc (DVD), and Frames 10 and 11 from a universal serial bus (USB) stick, which goes in the [Dock Station](jsc:dock_station).
jsc.guide.editions_compared.text5: The footprint is the room a system takes on a disk once it is installed. A disk counts its room in items, and an item is 1 MB on a Vintage disk, 16 MB on a Legacy disk and 256 MB from the Transition on. So Frames 95 takes 3 items of a Legacy disk.
jsc.guide.editions_compared.text6: The RAM held column is the memory that each system keeps for itself before any program opens.
jsc.guide.editions_compared.title: The editions side by side
jsc.guide.editor.definition1: One open file in the Editor. The Editor keeps up to 8 tabs at once.
jsc.guide.editor.definition2: The way a long line continues on the next row of the screen. You can turn it off.
jsc.guide.editor.definition3: The strip where you type what to find. It also does the Go to line action.
jsc.guide.editor.fix1: The file has no name yet, so [[Ctrl]]+[[S]] cannot save it. Give it a name first.
jsc.guide.editor.fix2: A .dat file is read-only: you can read it, but the Editor cannot save it.
jsc.guide.editor.fix3: Shorten the text. A file holds up to 32,767 characters.
jsc.guide.editor.fix4: Use a shorter name or fewer folders. A path holds up to 160 characters.
jsc.guide.editor.fix6: Save with [[Ctrl]]+[[S]], or close the tab again to discard the changes.
jsc.guide.editor.fix7: The Editor leaves the file as it is, so nothing is lost.
jsc.guide.editor.problem2: The Editor says "Cannot save a .dat file".
jsc.guide.editor.problem3: The Editor reports that the file is too long to save, with its length and the limit in characters.
jsc.guide.editor.problem4: The Editor reports that the path is too long to save to, with its length and the limit in characters.
jsc.guide.editor.problem5: The Editor says "Only 8 files at once".
jsc.guide.editor.problem6: The Editor warns about unsaved changes when you close a tab, and asks you to close again to discard them.
jsc.guide.editor.problem7: The Editor says a file "is too large to open here".
jsc.guide.editor.step1: Press [[Ctrl]]+[[S]] to save the file under its name.
jsc.guide.editor.step2: If the file has no name, the Editor says "Save As first". Use Save As to give it a name, then save.
jsc.guide.editor.step3: To close a tab with changes you have not saved, press [[Ctrl]]+[[W]] and read the message.
jsc.guide.editor.step4: Save with [[Ctrl]]+[[S]], or press [[Ctrl]]+[[W]] again to discard the changes.
jsc.guide.editor.table1_10_2: While the find bar is open, closes it and returns to the text.
jsc.guide.editor.table1_1_2: Saves the file. A file with no name asks for one first.
jsc.guide.editor.table1_2_2: Opens a file through the system's file window.
jsc.guide.editor.table1_5_2: Opens the find bar in Go to line mode.
jsc.guide.editor.table1_6_2: Opens a new tab with a new file.
jsc.guide.editor.table1_9_2: While the find bar has focus, runs its action.
jsc.guide.editor.text1: The Editor writes and changes text files. Each file you open gets a tab of its own, and you can have up to 8 files open at once. It shows line numbers, so you can find your place, and the line and column of the cursor in the status bar.
jsc.guide.editor.text2: Long lines can wrap onto the next row of the screen. You can turn wrap off, so that each line stays on one row.
jsc.guide.editor.text3: Press [[Ctrl]]+[[F]] to open the find bar, which offers Replace, Next and Replace all. Press [[Ctrl]]+[[G]] to use the same bar to go to a line: the bar then offers Go to and Go.
jsc.guide.editor.title: The Editor
jsc.guide.editors_overview.definition1: The cursor in the text: the place where the next letter goes.
jsc.guide.editors_overview.fix1: The editor is not installed on this computer. Install it ([](jsc:programs)), then type its name again.
jsc.guide.editors_overview.fix2: The cause and the cure are the same.
jsc.guide.editors_overview.fix3: ee comes only with FreeBSD ([](jsc:the_systems)). On other systems, use another editor.
jsc.guide.editors_overview.fix4: Type the name of a file after the editor's name, with a space between them.
jsc.guide.editors_overview.problem1: The prompt says "command not found: vim" and "type 'help' to list commands".
jsc.guide.editors_overview.problem2: On FreeBSD the same problem looks like "vim: not found. Try: apropos <word>, or man intro".
jsc.guide.editors_overview.problem3: You type ee on Linux or MC-DOS, and the prompt says the command is not found.
jsc.guide.editors_overview.problem4: You type the name of an editor and nothing else, and the prompt says "usage: vim <file>".
jsc.guide.editors_overview.step1: Type the name of the editor, a space and the name of the file, then press [[Enter]].
jsc.guide.editors_overview.step2: Write or change the text, with the keys of that editor.
jsc.guide.editors_overview.step3: Save the file, then leave the editor with that editor's keys.

jsc.guide.editors_overview.text1: A file holds text: a note, a setting or a program. To change the text you need an editor. At the prompt, the editor takes over the whole screen while you work, and gives the screen back when you leave. The prompt is where you type commands ([](jsc:shell_prompt)).
jsc.guide.editors_overview.text2: Four editors take the screen: [vim](jsc:vim), [emacs](jsc:emacs), [vi](jsc:vi) and [ee](jsc:ee). Each one has its own keys, and its entry lists them.
jsc.guide.editors_overview.text3: The arrow keys move the caret.
jsc.guide.editors_overview.text4: You start an editor by typing its name, a space, and the name of the file. The file does not have to exist. The editor opens an empty file under that name, and the file is made when you first save it.
jsc.guide.editors_overview.text5: To install vim or emacs, see [](jsc:programs). Until an editor is installed, the prompt does not know its name, so install it before you type the name.
jsc.guide.editors_overview.title: Editors at the prompt
jsc.guide.ee.definition1: The five rows of shortcuts on the screen, which you can hide in the settings.
jsc.guide.ee.fix1: The command line knows only write, quit and exit. Type one of those words.
jsc.guide.ee.fix2: The text is not in the file, or it is spelled differently. Check it and search again.
jsc.guide.ee.fix3: No search text has been typed yet. Search with ^y first, then ^x searches again.
jsc.guide.ee.fix4: The file does not exist, or its name is wrong. Type the name again, exactly as the file has it.
jsc.guide.ee.fix5: ee does not ask first when you leave with no save or with quit. Choose save changes in the main menu, or type write at the command prompt (^c), before you leave.
jsc.guide.ee.fix6: The info window is off. Open the main menu, choose settings, then info window: on.

jsc.guide.ee.problem2: The bottom row says Not found, followed by your text.
jsc.guide.ee.problem4: You choose read a file, and the bottom row says "name": No such file or directory.
jsc.guide.ee.problem5: You leave with no save or with quit, and your changes are gone.

jsc.guide.ee.text1: ee is a small editor, and it comes only with FreeBSD. It has no modes. Every key you press types a letter, except the keys held with Control and the Escape key.
jsc.guide.ee.text10: Any prompt on the bottom row waits for you. Press [[Enter]] to answer it, [[Esc]] to cancel it, and Backspace to correct what you typed.
jsc.guide.ee.text2: While the info window is on, five rows of shortcuts sit on the screen. Each row shows a key and the name of what it does. The ^ in front of a letter means Control: ^k is Control with K.
jsc.guide.ee.text3: The fifth row ends with the tip ESC-Enter: exit. Names such as prev li and next li are short, because the screen is narrow.
jsc.guide.ee.text4: Press [[Esc]] to open the main menu, titled ee main menu. Move with the Up and Down keys, choose with [[Enter]], or close the menu with [[Esc]].
jsc.guide.ee.text5: Choose no save instead to leave without writing the file. ee does not ask again before it leaves.
jsc.guide.ee.text6: When you open a file, the bottom row says "hello.txt" [New file] for a new file. For an existing file it says the name, the lines and the characters, as in "hello.txt" 3 lines, 42 characters. Saving says the same thing.
jsc.guide.ee.text7: Under the shortcut rows, a row shows where the caret is: its line, its column and how many lines it is from the top of the screen.
jsc.guide.ee.text8: Press ^c. The bottom row shows the label "Command" and waits for a word. Type the word and press [[Enter]].
jsc.guide.ee.text9: Press ^y, or choose search in the main menu, and type the text. Press [[Enter]]. The caret moves to the text. ^x searches again for the last text you typed.
