jsc.guide.effects.definition1: The opaque look that Frames 7 falls back to, when its graphics cannot run the glass.
jsc.guide.effects.fix1: The graphics are too weak for the glass, so Frames 7 uses the Basic look. Install a stronger graphics card, with more video memory, and check the System page.
jsc.guide.effects.fix2: Play animations in Frames is off. Switch it on, on the Effects page.
jsc.guide.effects.fix3: The Ease of Access switch Turn off all unnecessary animations is on. Switch it off.
jsc.guide.effects.problem1: The glass is opaque, and the effects are gone on Frames 7.
jsc.guide.effects.table2: The switches of each Effects page
jsc.guide.effects.table2_1_2: One box: "Animate windows when minimizing and restoring". The footer has OK, Cancel and Apply.
jsc.guide.effects.table2_2_2: Four presets, from "Let Frames choose what's best for my computer" to "Custom:". Four boxes: animating windows, fading or sliding menus, fading or sliding ToolTips, and drop shadows for icon labels; the footer has OK, Cancel and Apply.
jsc.guide.effects.table2_3_2: The same presets, plus "Enable transparent glass", and boxes for the animations, the menus, the ToolTips and the icon shadows. Under Ease of Access, a switch: "Turn off all unnecessary animations (when possible)".
jsc.guide.effects.table2_4_2: Two switches: "Transparency effects" and "Play animations in Frames". There are no buttons: a change takes effect at once.
jsc.guide.effects.table2_5_2: One switch: "Animation effects". There are no buttons: a change takes effect at once.
jsc.guide.effects.table3: The highest score by video memory
jsc.guide.effects.text1: Effects are the animations and visual extras of a Frames desktop: the glass of Frames 7, the fades, the shadows and the motion when a window opens. You can switch them on or off. Each edition has its own Effects page, reached from another page of Settings.
jsc.guide.effects.text2: On Frames 10, with Play animations in Frames off, windows open, close and minimise at once, and the live tiles stop turning.
jsc.guide.effects.text3: Frames 7 draws its glass only when the graphics can run it. Your computer checks its graphics first. If they are too weak, Frames 7 falls back to the Basic look: the same frames and buttons, but opaque, with no glass. The check applies only to a computer built of parts.
jsc.guide.effects.text4: The check uses the graphics score of the computer. The score comes from the best graphics card, or from the integrated graphics when there is no card. Video memory (VRAM), the memory of the graphics card, sets the highest score a card can reach:
jsc.guide.effects.text5: The Basic look applies when the score is under 3.0. A card with under 128 MB of video memory therefore always gets the Basic look on Frames 7, and so does a computer with integrated graphics and no card.
jsc.guide.effects.text6: Frames 10 and Frames 11 check the graphics too. They keep their look, and only their effects go off.
jsc.guide.effects.text7: When the Basic look is on, every effect is off. The Effects page then shows this note: "The graphics are too weak for these effects, so all are off. A stronger card brings back what is chosen here." Your choices stay saved.
jsc.guide.effects.text8: When Frames 7 falls back to the Basic look, a balloon titled "Frames 7 Basic" appears, once.
jsc.guide.effects.text9: The System page of Frames 7 shows an experience rating. It has five scores: the processor, the memory, the graphics, the gaming and the disk. The lowest of the five is the base score.
jsc.guide.effects.title: Visual effects and the basic look

jsc.guide.emacs.text1: Emacs has no modes. Every key you press types a letter, unless you hold Control or Alt with it. A command is one of those held keys, sometimes followed by a second key. The keys with Control are written C-, and the keys with Alt are written M-.
jsc.guide.emacs.text2: While a command waits for its next key, the bottom row shows the keys you pressed so far, such as C-x-. Otherwise it shows the file's name. For a file without changes it reads -UUU:----F1 and then the name. For a file with changes that are not saved, the two dashes after -UUU: are two asterisks.
jsc.guide.emacs.text3: Letters, digits and symbols type into the file. [[Enter]] starts a new line with the same indent as the line above, and [[Tab]] types four spaces. The arrow keys, Home and End move the caret, and PageUp and PageDown move it ten lines.
jsc.guide.emacs.text4: Emacs does not know the other chords that you may know from Emacs, such as C-s for search. It says so: C-s is undefined, and the keys you typed are thrown away.
jsc.guide.emacs.text5: When the text has changes that are not saved, C-x C-c asks: Modified buffers exist; exit anyway? (y or n). Press y to leave without saving. Press n to stay in the file, then save with C-x C-s.
jsc.guide.emacs.text6: While the question is open, Ctrl+G or Esc cancels it, and the bottom row says Quit. Any other key asks again: Please answer y or n.
jsc.guide.emacs.text7: M-x compile compiles the text as it is in the buffer, the way the compiler of its language reads a file. It does not save the file first. The result opens in a second area under the text, so the mistakes can be read while the text stays on the screen.
jsc.guide.emacs.text8: The ending of the file's name decides which language the file is in. Which languages can compile depends on the compilers installed on the machine.

jsc.guide.engine_services.text1: You start, stop and replace engines in the Services tab of the Network Manager. The tab's header card shows the state of the engine in one word: Running, Stopped or Replacing. The buttons under it depend on that word.
jsc.guide.engine_services.text10: A replacement takes 40 ticks, plus one tick for every four item types the network stores, up to 2,400 ticks. A tick is the game's basic time step: 20 ticks make a second.
jsc.guide.engine_services.text11: The progress window moves through the steps of the replacement in turn. N in the Keep step is the number of Operations still running.
jsc.guide.engine_services.text12: Building indexes takes the most time, because the network indexes each item type it stores. The window then says Ready.
jsc.guide.engine_services.text13: While a replacement runs, no engine plans. The Operations already in flight carry on, but a new request that needs planning is refused until the new engine is ready. When the time ends, the new engine becomes the active one and starts.
jsc.guide.engine_services.text14: An engine comes from its disc, like every program. You put the disc in a drive linked to the Mainframe, then install the program as you install any other ([](jsc:programs)).
jsc.guide.engine_services.text15: The install puts the engine in the Mainframe's list, at the version for the Mainframe's age. If no engine is chosen yet, the new one becomes the active engine and starts at once.
jsc.guide.engine_services.text16: An install is refused when the engine is already installed, or when it was not made for the Mainframe's age.
jsc.guide.engine_services.text17: Removing the engine that runs leaves the network with no engine, as a stop does.
jsc.guide.engine_services.text18: The Midsoft IQL Server also has a command of its own, typed at a prompt: iqlengine. It takes one of four verbs.
jsc.guide.engine_services.text19: On a network that runs NextgreIQL, iqlengine stop answers that the Midsoft IQL Server is already stopped, because the Midsoft is not the active engine.
jsc.guide.engine_services.text2: A button does what it says or nothing at all. If the server refuses a press, nothing happens and the tab shows the true state again.
jsc.guide.engine_services.text3: Stop asks nothing. It stops the active engine, which stays installed and chosen. Until you start an engine again, the network has no engine running.
jsc.guide.engine_services.text4: The tab then says "No Network Operations Engine is running". Storage stays, and the Operations in flight carry on. Transfers still work, but crafts and IQL queries are refused until an engine runs.
jsc.guide.engine_services.text5: An engine runs only while its Mainframe is on. When the Mainframe is turned off, the engine stops with it.
jsc.guide.engine_services.text6: The list starts with the first stopped engine selected. Its note says "The engine starts at once and plans every new request."
jsc.guide.engine_services.text7: If you choose an installed engine that is not the active one, the network switches to it at once. The timed steps of a replacement do not run then.
jsc.guide.engine_services.text8: A replacement switches the network from the running engine to another installed one. It takes time, and the tab shows Replacing until it ends. The new engine starts at the end.
jsc.guide.engine_services.text9: In the dialog, the Replace button is greyed out when the engine you chose is the one already active.
jsc.guide.engine_services.title: Starting, stopping and replacing an engine

jsc.guide.engines.fix2: An engine is being replaced. Wait until the replacement ends. The work already running carries on.

jsc.guide.engines.problem3: A program says it needs an engine that offers a feature the network does not have.
jsc.guide.engines.table1_2_2: Shows the plan it made and how it ran, takes hints that change the plan, and takes extras from other mods.
jsc.guide.engines.table1_3_2: You declare the state the network keeps; it works out the Operations to hold it, and answers subscriptions.
jsc.guide.engines.text1: What reads IQL and plans the network's work is the engine. Every new Mainframe comes with the Midsoft IQL Server, installed and running. Other engines can be installed on the Mainframe too, and each one speaks its own version of IQL with its own extras.
jsc.guide.engines.text2: NextgreIQL and Prophet YourIQL come from the Legacy era on. Prophet works differently from the others: you say what state the network must keep, and it does the work to keep it. The book Learning IQL explains each engine ([](jsc:iql_engines_overview)).
jsc.guide.engines.text3: A program names the engine it needs. The IQL Server Management Studio needs the Midsoft IQL Server, version 2000 or newer. The Nextgre Planner Studio needs NextgreIQL, and the Prophet Reactive Console needs Prophet YourIQL, version 3.23 or newer.
jsc.guide.engines.text4: Replacing an engine takes at least 2 seconds, and up to 2 minutes. A network with more kinds of item takes longer. While the engine is replaced, the work already running carries on, and new plans are refused.
jsc.guide.engines.text5: Without a working engine, only the transfers still work, such as moving items with SELECT, INSERT, MOVE and DELETE. CRAFT, QUERY and UPDATE are refused.
jsc.guide.engines.text6: When a program says it needs an engine, you install that engine on the Mainframe, or start it if it is stopped ([](jsc:engine_services)).
jsc.guide.engines.title: Engines
jsc.guide.eras.definition1: The language a processor understands. A program built for one runs on it and on every newer one, never on an older one: x86-64 runs x86 and IA-16 programs.
jsc.guide.eras.fix1: The processor, the memory module or the sound card must have the era of its board ([](jsc:motherboards)).
jsc.guide.eras.problem1: A part does not go into the slot of a board from another era.

jsc.guide.eras.text1: Computers and parts of J's Computers belong to an era, a generation of hardware. The eras run from Vintage to Advanced, and each has its own word size, instruction set, firmware and media.
jsc.guide.eras.text2: The word size is how much data a processor handles at once. Older computers had smaller words, so the room an item takes on a disk depends on the era ([](jsc:items_as_data)).
jsc.guide.eras.text3: A disk's room is measured in megabytes (MB). The room per item is how many megabytes one item takes on a disk of that era.
jsc.guide.eras.text4: Parts do not mix freely across eras, so check the era of each part before you put it in. A Personal Computer takes only a motherboard of its own era. A processor, a memory module and a sound card must also match the era of the board. A graphics card is checked only for the bus it plugs into.
jsc.guide.eras.text5: A newer era is faster: its parts have more cores, higher clocks, more memory and faster disks. Its start-up also finishes sooner ([](jsc:turning_on)).
jsc.guide.eras.text6: Every era has its own creative tab, from J's Computers - Vintage to J's Computers - Advanced.
jsc.guide.eras.title: The eras
jsc.guide.expansion_cards.definition1: The kinds of machine a card can reach, from the rack servers of a datacenter up to every kind of rack.
jsc.guide.expansion_cards.definition2: The number of nodes a bulk install writes at once. In an older slot the lanes fall, but never below one.
jsc.guide.expansion_cards.fix1: Give smelting its fuel, or give enchanting its lapis.
jsc.guide.expansion_cards.fix2: Only a Personal Computer takes Workshop cards. Put it in one.
jsc.guide.expansion_cards.fix3: A Cluster Management Computer takes only one. Take the other one out.
jsc.guide.expansion_cards.fix4: Only a Cluster Management Computer uses it. Put it in one.
jsc.guide.expansion_cards.fix5: Take cards out, or use a board with more PCI-e slots.
jsc.guide.expansion_cards.problem1: The Workshop shows "No fuel" or "No lapis".
jsc.guide.expansion_cards.problem2: A Workshop card does not go into a computer.
jsc.guide.expansion_cards.problem3: A second Cluster Interface Card does not go in.
jsc.guide.expansion_cards.problem4: A Cluster Interface Card does nothing.
jsc.guide.expansion_cards.problem5: The build says there are too many PCI-e cards.
jsc.guide.expansion_cards.text1: Besides graphics and sound, the expansion slots of a board take cards that give a computer a job it could not do before. Each card goes in a slot of its own bus family ([the bus family](jsc:build_refusals)).
jsc.guide.expansion_cards.text10: Vaultis makes a RAID controller and a read cache for each era's slot. In a server they join its drives into one volume and answer their reads faster; in another computer they sit in their slot and do nothing ([RAID modes](jsc:raid_arrays)).
jsc.guide.expansion_cards.text2: The Crafting Table Card, the Furnace Card, the Enchanting Card and the Anvil Card each give a Personal Computer one job in the Workshop program. Only a Personal Computer takes them, and each one draws 15 W.
jsc.guide.expansion_cards.text3: The Workshop shows "No fuel" when smelting has no fuel, and "No lapis" when enchanting has no lapis.
jsc.guide.expansion_cards.text4: Four cards let a Cluster Management Computer reach the machines of your racks: the Serial Console Card, the Management NIC, the Fabric Host Adapter and the Fabric DPU. Each newer one reaches more. A Cluster Management Computer takes one of them ([Cluster Management Computers](jsc:cluster_management_computers)).
jsc.guide.expansion_cards.text5: Only a Cluster Management Computer uses these cards.
jsc.guide.expansion_cards.text6: A network card with a fibre port. A Mainframe or a Cluster Management Computer with one shows its fibre port as connected, so it can join the fibre backbone of the network ([Data cables](jsc:data_cables)). A server never takes it: a rack joins the fibre through a Fibre Optic Interface ([](jsc:rack_equipment)). It is a Standard card, on PCI-e 3.0, and it draws 15 W.
jsc.guide.expansion_cards.text7: Four Integra Phi coprocessors add computing power to the nodes of a supercomputer. Only a supercomputer node takes one, and only one per node. A rack server of another kind refuses it ([Server racks and servers](jsc:server_racks)).
jsc.guide.expansion_cards.text8: The last column is the range of supercomputer slots that the tooltip gives, as in "Supercomputer slots 1-2".
jsc.guide.expansion_cards.text9: The Crafting Cards give a Crafting Computer its crafting. There are six, from the Vintage to the Advanced, and autocrafting explains them ([Crafting Cards](jsc:crafting_cards)).
jsc.guide.expansion_cards.title: Expansion cards
jsc.guide.external_storage_bus.definitio: Any chest, tank or machine that holds items or fluid, and that a bus can face.
jsc.guide.external_storage_bus.fix1: The bus faces nothing. Put it on a data cable beside an inventory.
jsc.guide.external_storage_bus.fix2: Join the bus's cable to a network ([](jsc:data_cables)).
jsc.guide.external_storage_bus.fix3: The inventory has no free room. Take items out of it.
jsc.guide.external_storage_bus.fix4: The bus is READ ONLY. Set it to READ AND WRITE.
jsc.guide.external_storage_bus.fix5: The bus is WRITE ONLY. Set it to READ AND WRITE or READ ONLY.
jsc.guide.external_storage_bus.fix6: Access starts at the Legacy era. Use a Legacy or newer External Storage Bus.
jsc.guide.external_storage_bus.problem1: The window says "no inventory before it".
jsc.guide.external_storage_bus.problem3: The window says "the chest is full".
jsc.guide.external_storage_bus.problem4: The network never puts items into the bus.
jsc.guide.external_storage_bus.problem5: The network never takes items from the bus, and never sees them.
jsc.guide.external_storage_bus.problem6: The bus has no READ ONLY setting.
jsc.guide.external_storage_bus.table1: The External Storage Bus by era
jsc.guide.external_storage_bus.table2_1_: Takes items out of the inventory and puts items into it (the default).
jsc.guide.external_storage_bus.table2_2_: Only takes items out, and never fills the inventory.
jsc.guide.external_storage_bus.table2_3_: Only puts items in; what is in the inventory is never taken or seen.
jsc.guide.external_storage_bus.text1: An External Storage Bus lets the network use a chest, a tank or a machine as storage, with no disk in it. You put the bus on a data cable beside the inventory, and the network counts what the inventory holds as its own storage.
jsc.guide.external_storage_bus.text10: The bus window says "10x slower than the network's own storage." That holds against a hard disk only. A server of solid-state or NVMe disks is faster still.
jsc.guide.external_storage_bus.text11: The network looks at the inventory again every 10 ticks. So a change in the inventory can reach the network's list of items up to 10 ticks late.
jsc.guide.external_storage_bus.text12: The room the bus offers is the inventory's free room. A READ ONLY bus offers none. An INSERT skips the bus when it is READ ONLY, or when its filter does not let the item through.
jsc.guide.external_storage_bus.text2: Its tooltip reads "Right-click a data cable beside an inventory; the network uses the inventory as its storage". A bus mounts on cables of its own era or an earlier one.
jsc.guide.external_storage_bus.text3: Its storage is much slower than the network's own disks. The speed below shows by how much.
jsc.guide.external_storage_bus.text4: The Vintage, Legacy, Transition and Advanced versions carry their era in their names, such as "Vintage External Storage Bus". The Standard version has the plain name.
jsc.guide.external_storage_bus.text5: The External Storage Bus has no conditions in any era. Conditions belong to the Import Bus and the Export Bus ([](jsc:bus_conditions)).
jsc.guide.external_storage_bus.text6: Access sets what the network may do with the inventory. It starts at the Legacy era, and a Vintage bus always reads and writes.
jsc.guide.external_storage_bus.text7: The filter decides which items the bus lets through. With no item listed, the bus lets everything through. With items listed, only those pass, or with "ALL BUT THESE" everything except them.
jsc.guide.external_storage_bus.text8: The bus window shows what the inventory holds under "HOLDS", as slots and how many are used, with the note "shown to the network as its storage".
jsc.guide.external_storage_bus.text9: The bus moves a tenth of what its cable carries each tick, and at least one item. Its read latency is 100 ticks, which is 5 seconds: ten times the 10 ticks of a hard disk (HDD). A solid-state drive (SSD) answers about 33 times faster than the bus, and an NVMe disk 100 times faster.
jsc.guide.external_storage_bus.title: The External Storage Bus
jsc.guide.failover.balloon1: The Mainframe that runs the network
jsc.guide.failover.balloon2_detail: Wire both Mainframes to the same segment.
jsc.guide.failover.balloon3_detail: Turn on its FAILOVER switch. Its screen reads STANDBY.
jsc.guide.failover.figure1: Two Mainframes on one network: one runs it and the other stands by to take over. Drag it to see them from behind.
jsc.guide.failover.fix1: Another standby with a lower position is waiting first, or the standby is not on the owner's segment. A standby has nothing to back if it is not on that segment.
jsc.guide.failover.fix2: Two running owners share a segment. A standby does not cause a conflict. Separate the owners ([](jsc:network_identity)).
jsc.guide.failover.step1: Open the Mainframe's screen and turn on the FAILOVER switch.
jsc.guide.failover.step2: Wire the failover Mainframe to the same segment as its owner.
jsc.guide.failover.step3: Check that the screen reads STANDBY.
jsc.guide.failover.table1_1_2: Runs the network on its segment.
jsc.guide.failover.table1_2_2: Powered and synced, but not running the network.
jsc.guide.failover.table1_3_2: Took over the network, and runs it now.
jsc.guide.failover.text1: A Mainframe can be a failover member. A failover member does not run the network while its owner is there. It waits, powered and ready, and takes over when the owner is gone.
jsc.guide.failover.text2: Turning failover on removes the network this Mainframe owned, instead of leaving it orphaned. A machine that is about to back somebody else's network cannot keep one of its own, or the two would be in conflict the moment they were wired together.
jsc.guide.failover.text3: You make a failover member in three steps, and the screen tells you which role the Mainframe has.
jsc.guide.failover.text4: A standby takes over only when no owner is running on its segment. It then waits 60 ticks, which is 3 seconds of game time, before it decides that its owner is really gone. The wait gives the owner time to come back first.
jsc.guide.failover.text5: When several standbys wait, only the one placed lowest in the world, by its block position, takes over. The others stay on standby.
jsc.guide.failover.text6: A standby does not hold a conflict. Only a running owner can put a network into conflict. The wait is kept when the world reloads, so a takeover in progress does not start its wait again.
jsc.guide.failover.title: Failover
jsc.guide.file_commands.fix1: Give the name of one file after cat.
jsc.guide.file_commands.fix2: Run df and choose one of the devices it lists.
jsc.guide.file_commands.fix3: No disk is in the system or in a drive. Put one in, then run df again.
jsc.guide.file_commands.problem1: The shell says usage: cat <file>, because you gave no file name.
jsc.guide.file_commands.problem2: The mkfs.ext4 command says it cannot open a device, and that there is no such device.
jsc.guide.file_commands.problem3: The df command says there are no filesystems mounted.
jsc.guide.file_commands.step1: Type write notes.txt followed by the text you want in the file.
jsc.guide.file_commands.step2: Type cat notes.txt to read the file back.
jsc.guide.file_commands.step3: Type ls to see the file in the folder.
jsc.guide.file_commands.text1: Most of your work on a Unix system is with files and folders: you list them, move between them, copy, rename and delete them. These commands need a disk, the system disk or one in a drive.
jsc.guide.file_commands.text2: Here is a short session. It shows how the shell answers when a command gets no file name.
jsc.guide.file_commands.text3: Folder names end with a slash in the ls listing, so you can tell files and folders apart at a glance. The commands below are the commonest first.
jsc.guide.file_commands.text4: The df command lists every disk the computer has, with its device name. The mkfs.ext4 command makes a new, empty file system on one device.
jsc.guide.file_commands.title: Working with files and folders
jsc.guide.file_commands.warning1: mkfs.ext4 erases the whole device. Everything on it is lost, and the erase cannot be undone.
jsc.guide.file_explorer.definition1: Dragging a box over several rows to select all of them at once.
jsc.guide.file_explorer.definition2: A read-only file that lists the items stored on a disk. You can read it, but you cannot change it by hand.
jsc.guide.file_explorer.fix1: Delete on a medium is permanent. Copy the file to the system disk first if you may need it.
jsc.guide.file_explorer.fix2: Run the setup program to install it, as the message says.
jsc.guide.file_explorer.fix3: Read the file. To change its items, use the network interactor ([](jsc:interactor_screen)).
jsc.guide.file_explorer.fix4: Copy the file with [[Ctrl]]+[[C]] and paste it onto a disk you can change.
jsc.guide.file_explorer.fix5: Read the message in the dialog: it says what was refused.
jsc.guide.file_explorer.problem1: A file on a medium is gone, and there is no Recycle Bin to bring it back.
jsc.guide.file_explorer.problem2: The window says "This file is part of the installer and cannot be changed, copied or deleted."
jsc.guide.file_explorer.problem3: The window says "This file is impossible to modify, create, delete or change manually, use the network interactor for it."
jsc.guide.file_explorer.problem4: Cut and Delete are refused on a read-only medium.
jsc.guide.file_explorer.problem5: A dialog titled "Could not do that" opens.
jsc.guide.file_explorer.step1: Click the file to select it.
jsc.guide.file_explorer.step2: Press [[Ctrl]]+[[X]] to cut it, or [[Ctrl]]+[[C]] to copy it.
jsc.guide.file_explorer.step3: Open the folder you want, and press [[Ctrl]]+[[V]].
jsc.guide.file_explorer.table1_10_2: Closes the ribbon, if one is open.
jsc.guide.file_explorer.table1_4_2: Deletes the selected row, or every row you swept.
jsc.guide.file_explorer.table1_7_2: Cuts the selected row, unless it is on a read-only medium.
jsc.guide.file_explorer.table1_8_2: Pastes what you copied or cut.
jsc.guide.file_explorer.table1_9_2: Selects every file and folder in the listing.
jsc.guide.file_explorer.text1: The Files window is where you look at the files on your disks, and open, copy, move, rename and delete them. On Frames 10 the same window is called File Explorer. On the other editions it is called Files.
jsc.guide.file_explorer.text2: The tree on the left groups the places: Quick access, Storage, Network and Shares. Quick access holds the shortcuts. Shares are the network folders you can reach from this window. The Recycle Bin is a place too: a file dropped on it is deleted.
jsc.guide.file_explorer.text3: Frames 7 shows a command bar above the list. Frames 10 shows a ribbon with the tabs File, Home and View. The Layout group on the ribbon chooses between Details and Large icons. The other editions show no bar. Press [[Esc]] to close an open ribbon.
jsc.guide.file_explorer.text4: Right-click a row to see its menu: Open, Run, Open with, Choose another program, Cut, Copy, Paste, Rename, Delete, New, Eject, Refresh, Extract here and Compress to, with the name of the archive.
jsc.guide.file_explorer.text5: On the system disk, Delete moves the file into the Recycle Bin. On a medium or a network share, Delete removes the file for good, once you say yes. A read-only medium refuses Cut and Delete, and the bar says "read-only medium".
jsc.guide.file_explorer.text6: A .dat file is different: it is a read-only list of the items stored on a disk. You can read it, but no one can change it by hand. The window says that to change those items you use the network interactor ([](jsc:interactor_screen)).
jsc.guide.file_explorer.title: Files and the File Explorer
jsc.guide.file_tree.definition1: The address of a file or folder: its folder names, with a slash between them.
jsc.guide.file_tree.fix1: Run pwd to see the folder you are in. A path that starts with a slash begins at the top folder, not at your folder.
jsc.guide.file_tree.fix2: Put a disk in that drive, then run df again ([](jsc:file_commands)).
jsc.guide.file_tree.problem2: The df command shows the device with "(no medium)" after it.
jsc.guide.file_tree.table1_2_1: Your Desktop, whose files the desktop shows as icons
jsc.guide.file_tree.table1_4_1: The other drives, one folder each
jsc.guide.file_tree.table2_1_2: An absolute path: it starts at the top folder and names the whole address.
jsc.guide.file_tree.table2_2_2: A relative path: it starts at the folder you are in.
jsc.guide.file_tree.table2_3_2: Your home folder. The form ~/x is a folder inside it.
jsc.guide.file_tree.table2_4_2: The folder above the one you are in.
jsc.guide.file_tree.table2_5_2: The file x on drive D:, on Linux and FreeBSD. On UNIX System V the same file is /mnt/d/x.
jsc.guide.file_tree.text1: Unix shows all of a computer's storage as one tree of folders. The tree starts at the top folder, written /, and every file sits somewhere inside it.
jsc.guide.file_tree.text2: Under the hood the storage keeps the DOS (Disk Operating System) model of drive letters, and the shell translates it. The system disk is C: and it is the top folder. Another disk appears as a folder inside /media on Linux and FreeBSD, or inside /mnt on UNIX System V.
jsc.guide.file_tree.text3: You name a folder or file with a path. The first character tells the shell where to start.
jsc.guide.file_tree.text4: Commands that name a disk use its device name. The system disk is sda1, drive D: is sdb, drive E: is sdc, and each drive after that goes on by one letter.
jsc.guide.file_tree.title: The tree of folders and paths
jsc.guide.files_and_file_handles.definit: The way a file is opened: reading, writing, adding at the end, or both with a plus sign.
jsc.guide.files_and_file_handles.fix1: Check the path, or use File.TryRead to ask first without stopping.
jsc.guide.files_and_file_handles.fix10: Open the file in a mode that writes, such as w, a or r+.
jsc.guide.files_and_file_handles.fix11: Open the file in a mode that reads, such as r, r+ or a+.
jsc.guide.files_and_file_handles.fix12: Open the file again with File.Open before you use it.
jsc.guide.files_and_file_handles.fix2: Free some space on the disk, or write less text.
jsc.guide.files_and_file_handles.fix3: Choose another path. A file ending in .dat is read-only, and the message names the Network Interactor for items.
jsc.guide.files_and_file_handles.fix4: Use a name that this drive accepts.
jsc.guide.files_and_file_handles.fix5: Use the Network Interactor, as the message says. .dat files cannot be deleted from here.
jsc.guide.files_and_file_handles.fix6: Choose a new name, or delete the file that is there first.
jsc.guide.files_and_file_handles.fix7: Read the file with File.Read, write it with File.Write, then delete the original with File.Delete.
jsc.guide.files_and_file_handles.fix8: Make the folder on a drive that supports folders.
jsc.guide.files_and_file_handles.fix9: Check that the mode is one listed above, that the path is not blank, and that a file read in mode r exists. A program may also hold only so many files at once: 8 on a Vintage machine, 20 on a Legacy machine and 64 on every other era. Close a file you no longer need.
jsc.guide.files_and_file_handles.heading: Whole files
A missing file
Files you open: FILE
