jsc.guide.frames_which_machine.text1: Midsoft made five editions of Frames. Each edition is built for one era of computer, the generation a machine belongs to ([](jsc:eras)). A system runs on the era it was made for and on every newer era, but never on an older machine.
jsc.guide.frames_which_machine.text2: Choose the edition by the machine you have. The editions also have a rank, from 1 for Frames 95 to 5 for Frames 11. Programs use the rank when they ask for a Frames edition, such as XP or newer. The installer does not use it.
jsc.guide.frames_which_machine.text3: The install medium is the compact disc (CD), digital versatile disc (DVD) or Universal Serial Bus (USB) stick that a system is installed from. You read a medium in a drive joined to the computer: a CD goes in a CD Drive, a DVD in a DVD Drive, and a USB stick in a Dock Station ([](jsc:dock_station)).
jsc.guide.frames_which_machine.text4: Own RAM is the random-access memory (RAM) that the running system keeps for itself before any program opens. Footprint is the space the system takes on its disk. Both are counted in megabytes (MB), and the table below gives them for each edition ([](jsc:frames_memory)).
jsc.guide.frames_which_machine.text5: A disk measures its room in items, and an item takes 1 MB on a Vintage disk, 16 MB on a Legacy disk and 256 MB on a disk of the Transition era or newer. So the same system takes fewer items on a newer disk. The footprint counts whole items, rounded up ([](jsc:disks)).
jsc.guide.frames_which_machine.text6: A Legacy disk of 4 gigabytes (GB), such as the Vaultis Link IDE-HDD 4G, holds 4,096 MB. That is room for Frames XP, which needs 1,536 MB, but not for Frames 7, which needs 16,384 MB. The disks you can buy are listed in [Disks](jsc:disks).
jsc.guide.frames_which_machine.text7: The era also sets the firmware, the program that starts the machine. Frames 95, XP and 7 start in the blue basic input/output system (BIOS), and Frames 10 and 11 in the Unified Extensible Firmware Interface (UEFI) ([](jsc:firmware)).
jsc.guide.frames_which_machine.text8: The memory of a machine comes from its memory modules. The smallest module of the Legacy era is the Stratix Layer SDRAM-128, with 128 MB. A Legacy machine with that module runs Frames XP without tight RAM, which the memory page explains ([](jsc:frames_memory)).
jsc.guide.frames_which_machine.title: Which Frames goes on which machine
jsc.guide.frames_windows.definition1: The strip along the top of a window, with its name and its three boxes.
jsc.guide.frames_windows.definition2: The small corner at the bottom right of a window, which you drag to change its size.
jsc.guide.frames_windows.definition3: To let a window go at a screen edge, so that it fills half or all of the work area.
jsc.guide.frames_windows.definition4: The desktop minus the taskbar: the part of the screen a maximised window fills.
jsc.guide.frames_windows.fix1: Snap works on Frames 11 only. On the other editions, use the maximise box.
jsc.guide.frames_windows.fix2: Only Frames 10 has the Task View button. Frames 95, Frames XP, Frames 7 and Frames 11 have none.
jsc.guide.frames_windows.problem1: A window will not snap to the top edge of the screen.
jsc.guide.frames_windows.problem2: You look for the Task View button, and it is not on the taskbar.
jsc.guide.frames_windows.step1: Drag the title bar to move the window.
jsc.guide.frames_windows.step2: Drag the resize grip to change the size of the window.
jsc.guide.frames_windows.table1_1_2: The window goes down to its button on the taskbar. Click that button to bring the window back.
jsc.guide.frames_windows.table1_2_2: A maximised window fills the work area. The same box returns the window to its old size.
jsc.guide.frames_windows.table1_3_2: The window closes. The program may ask you first.
jsc.guide.frames_windows.text1: A window is the box that holds one open program. Its title bar runs along the top, with the program's name and three boxes. The corner at the bottom right is the resize grip.
jsc.guide.frames_windows.text2: The window stays on the screen: its title bar cannot be dragged off the desktop. A program sets the smallest size its windows can take, so the window stops shrinking at that size.
jsc.guide.frames_windows.text3: On Frames 11, you can snap a window by letting it go at an edge of the screen. Let go with the mouse pointer at the top edge of the work area, and the window maximises. Let go at the left edge, and it takes the left half of the work area. Let go at the right edge, and it takes the right half.
jsc.guide.frames_windows.text4: Windows do not snap on Frames 95, Frames XP, Frames 7 or Frames 10.
jsc.guide.frames_windows.text5: On Frames 10, the Task View button on the taskbar shows every open window at once. The desktop dims, and each window becomes a card: its program's icon and its title, over a live picture of the window.
jsc.guide.frames_windows.text6: A click on a card brings that window to the front. A click anywhere else, or on the Task View button again, puts the view away.
jsc.guide.frames_windows.text7: Frames 7 has a narrow corner at the far right of the taskbar. Click it to show the desktop. Every edition has the same row in the taskbar's menu, Show the Desktop, and both minimise every window.
jsc.guide.frames_windows.text8: Cascade Windows, in the same menu, arranges the windows in a cascade.
jsc.guide.frames_windows.title: Windows: move, resize, minimise, maximise, snap and Task View
jsc.guide.frames_xp.definition1: A way of running programs in which the system takes the processor from a program when its turn is over.
jsc.guide.frames_xp.fix1: A Vintage computer cannot run Frames XP. Use a Legacy computer or newer ([](jsc:eras)).
jsc.guide.frames_xp.fix2: Use a Legacy disk with room for 96 items, which is what Frames XP takes.
jsc.guide.frames_xp.problem1: The installer says "Frames XP needs Legacy era hardware or newer; this machine is Vintage era."
jsc.guide.frames_xp.problem2: The installer says that the target disk has no room for Frames XP, and gives the megabytes it needs.
jsc.guide.frames_xp.step1: Put the Frames XP CD in the CD Drive, and start the computer from it. If the computer does not start from it, open the Boot Menu ([](jsc:boot_menu)).
jsc.guide.frames_xp.step2: On the page "The following list shows the disks on this computer.", choose the disk.
jsc.guide.frames_xp.step3: Wait on the copying page, which says "Please wait while Setup copies files to the disk."
jsc.guide.frames_xp.step4: Give the computer a name on the page "Computer Name", where the side panel shows "Collecting information".
jsc.guide.frames_xp.step5: Wait while the side panel shows "Installing Frames" and then "Finalizing installation".
jsc.guide.frames_xp.text1: Frames XP is the second edition. It keeps the Legacy era, so a Legacy computer runs it, but it asks for far more room: its footprint is 1,536 MB, which is 96 items on a Legacy disk.
jsc.guide.frames_xp.text10: Its splash screen is black, with the logo above the middle and three blocks in a trough.
jsc.guide.frames_xp.text2: Frames XP is preemptive. The system takes the processor from a program when that program's turn is over, so one program does not hold the processor from the others.
jsc.guide.frames_xp.text3: Its look is the Luna look: a taskbar along the bottom of the screen and a Start menu in two columns.
jsc.guide.frames_xp.text4: The copy happens in two stages: the first before the name, and the second after it. The installer changes shape between them, and the second stage shows its steps in a side panel.
jsc.guide.frames_xp.text5: Frames XP calls its help program Help and Support. Its window is the Help and Support Center, with one pane called "Technical Reference".
jsc.guide.frames_xp.text6: Its Task Manager has four tabs: Applications, Processes, Performance and Networking, with a menu bar and a status bar. Its Device Manager is a console window: the views are in the View menu, and a right-click opens its actions.
jsc.guide.frames_xp.text7: The visual effects settings are in Performance Options, which you reach from System. The page has the heading "Visual effects", four presets, and four checks. The presets are "Let Frames choose what's best for my computer", "Adjust for best appearance", "Adjust for best performance" and "Custom:".
jsc.guide.frames_xp.text8: The checks are "Animate windows when minimizing and maximizing", "Fade or slide menus into view", "Fade or slide ToolTips into view" and "Use drop shadows for icon labels on the desktop".
jsc.guide.frames_xp.text9: On a new computer, Frames XP greets you with a balloon notice, a small pop-up from the taskbar area, instead of a window. It plays "Frames XP chimes" when it starts and "Frames XP error" when something goes wrong.
jsc.guide.frames_xp.title: Frames XP
jsc.guide.freebsd_editors.fix1: The command prompt takes write, quit and exit. Type one of them.
jsc.guide.freebsd_editors.fix2: Type :w to write first, or :q! to leave without writing.
jsc.guide.freebsd_editors.fix3: Type a command from the vi page ([](jsc:vi)).
jsc.guide.freebsd_editors.fix4: Press i to start inserting text, and Esc to stop inserting.
jsc.guide.freebsd_editors.problem1: ee says Unknown command at its command prompt.
jsc.guide.freebsd_editors.problem2: vi says E37: no write since last change (add ! to override).
jsc.guide.freebsd_editors.problem3: vi says E492: not an editor command.
jsc.guide.freebsd_editors.problem4: Your typing does not appear as text in vi.
jsc.guide.freebsd_editors.table1_1_2: FreeBSD's own editor. It shows its shortcuts on the top rows of the screen.
jsc.guide.freebsd_editors.table1_2_2: The vi of FreeBSD is nvi. It has no colour and no ruler.
jsc.guide.freebsd_editors.text1: FreeBSD comes with two editors for text files: ee, the small one, and vi, the editor of UNIX. Both are already on the system, so you never install them.
jsc.guide.freebsd_editors.text2: Each editor has its own pages with its keys and its steps: [ee](jsc:ee) and [vi](jsc:vi), and both are in [Editors at the prompt](jsc:editors_overview). This page only says what is particular to FreeBSD.
jsc.guide.freebsd_editors.text3: ee shows "<name>" [New file] when the file you named is new. After a save, it shows "<name>" with the number of lines and the number of characters.
jsc.guide.freebsd_editors.text4: vi shows <name>: new file: line 1 for a new file, and <name>: unmodified: line 1 for a file that exists. After a write, it shows the number of lines and characters.
jsc.guide.freebsd_editors.text5: To leave ee, press [[Esc]] to open its menu, then press [[Enter]] to choose leave editor. The screen shows the same tip: ESC-Enter: exit. In vi, press [[Esc]] to return to normal mode, then type :wq to write and quit.
jsc.guide.freebsd_editors.title: Editors on FreeBSD
jsc.guide.freebsd_help.definition1: A command name that Tab could fill in.
jsc.guide.freebsd_help.fix1: Type apropos and a word for what you want to do, or type man intro.
jsc.guide.freebsd_help.fix2: Try a shorter word, or a different one.
jsc.guide.freebsd_help.fix3: Type the whole name, such as man graphics-cards.
jsc.guide.freebsd_help.problem1: The computer says help: not found.
jsc.guide.freebsd_help.problem3: man says No manual entry for graphics.
jsc.guide.freebsd_help.step1: Type apropos and a word for what you want to do, such as apropos network.
jsc.guide.freebsd_help.step2: Read the lines it prints. Each line is a command name and its one line.
jsc.guide.freebsd_help.step3: Type man and the command name to read its manual page.
jsc.guide.freebsd_help.table1_1_2: Searches the name and the summary of every command here, and every topic, for the word.
jsc.guide.freebsd_help.table1_2_2: Opens the manual page of a command. A manual entry such as graphics-cards opens the same way.
jsc.guide.freebsd_help.table1_3_2: Opens the one topic FreeBSD has: the introduction to the commands.
jsc.guide.freebsd_help.table1_4_2: Shows the one line that a manual page opens with.
jsc.guide.freebsd_help.table2_1_2: FreeBSD has no help command. Use one of the two ways it names.
jsc.guide.freebsd_help.table2_2_2: No command or topic matches the word you searched.
jsc.guide.freebsd_help.table2_3_2: There is no manual page with that name. Check the spelling.
jsc.guide.freebsd_help.text1: FreeBSD has no help command. Typing help gets a line that points to two other ways. You use those ways, and the Tab key, to find any command.
jsc.guide.freebsd_help.text2: At the prompt, type help and press [[Enter]]. FreeBSD answers with one line:
jsc.guide.freebsd_help.text3: The introduction is short, so read it first. It says that a command is a small program that does one thing, and that a shell runs the one you type at its prompt.
jsc.guide.freebsd_help.text4: Press [[Tab]] once to fill in a command name, when only one name fits. Press it twice in a row, with nothing left to fill, to list every candidate. The candidates show on the line above the prompt, with two spaces between them.
jsc.guide.freebsd_help.title: Finding your way without help
jsc.guide.freebsd_overview.definition1: A system that starts at a text prompt. A desktop is an optional package.
jsc.guide.freebsd_overview.definition2: The generation of a computer's hardware, from Vintage to Singularity. Legacy is the first one FreeBSD runs on.
jsc.guide.freebsd_overview.definition3: The package server of the network, run by a Mainframe that runs the Mirror service.
jsc.guide.freebsd_overview.fix1: Install FreeBSD on a Legacy computer, or on a newer one.
jsc.guide.freebsd_overview.fix2: Put a disk in one of the computer's slots.
jsc.guide.freebsd_overview.fix3: Use a bigger disk, or erase a disk on the Partitioning page ([](jsc:bsdinstall)).
jsc.guide.freebsd_overview.heading1: What you see when it starts
jsc.guide.freebsd_overview.problem1: The installer says "FreeBSD needs Legacy era hardware or newer; this machine is Vintage era."
jsc.guide.freebsd_overview.problem2: The installer says "No disk is installed to put FreeBSD on."
jsc.guide.freebsd_overview.problem3: The installer says "No disk in this machine has room for it."
jsc.guide.freebsd_overview.table1_2: Disk space of the installed system
jsc.guide.freebsd_overview.table2_1_3: Legacy era, 256 MB of disk, 224 MB of memory
jsc.guide.freebsd_overview.table2_2_3: Legacy era, 192 MB of disk, 256 MB of memory
jsc.guide.freebsd_overview.table2_3_3: Legacy era, 32 MB of disk, 16 MB of memory
jsc.guide.freebsd_overview.table2_4_3: Standard era, 160 MB of disk, 160 MB of memory
jsc.guide.freebsd_overview.text1: FreeBSD is a UNIX-like system, and the Daemon Handbook is about it and about UNIX System V. On your computer it works the way the other systems do: you install it from a medium, you start it, and you work at its prompt. It starts at a text prompt, and a desktop is an extra package you may add later.
jsc.guide.freebsd_overview.text2: FreeBSD needs Legacy hardware or newer, the first hardware era it runs on. A computer of the Vintage era cannot install it. The installed system takes 2,048 MB of disk space, and 16 MB of memory while it runs.
jsc.guide.freebsd_overview.text3: When a prompt opens, FreeBSD greets you with the lines below. The first line names the architecture: IA-32, the 32-bit Intel architecture, on a 32-bit computer, and vel64 on a 64-bit one.
jsc.guide.freebsd_overview.text4: The greeting names three ways to find your way. The last section of this chapter explains each one ([](jsc:freebsd_help)).
jsc.guide.freebsd_overview.text5: You add a desktop later, or choose one during the installation. A desktop is offered only when the network's Mirror answers and your computer's hardware is new enough for it.
jsc.guide.freebsd_overview.text6: The desktops of every system are described in [Desktops](jsc:desktops).
jsc.guide.freebsd_overview.title: FreeBSD on this computer
jsc.guide.fstab_by_hand.fix1: No line in the file mounts /. Write the root line as shown above, then reboot again ([](jsc:gentoo_reboot)).
jsc.guide.fstab_by_hand.problem1: The reboot says "no root filesystem in /etc/fstab".
jsc.guide.fstab_by_hand.step3: Find the line of the root partition, and cut it down to UUID=<its uuid>  /  ext4  noatime  0 1.
jsc.guide.fstab_by_hand.step4: Save the file and close nano.
jsc.guide.fstab_by_hand.table1: The fields of the root line
jsc.guide.fstab_by_hand.table1_1_3: The root partition, by its identifier.
jsc.guide.fstab_by_hand.table1_2_3: The root folder of the system.
jsc.guide.fstab_by_hand.table1_3_3: The file system the partition is formatted with.
jsc.guide.fstab_by_hand.table1_4_3: Do not record when each file was last read.
jsc.guide.fstab_by_hand.table1_5_3: Not backed up by the dump tool.
jsc.guide.fstab_by_hand.text1: The file system table, /etc/fstab, tells the system which partitions to mount at boot ([](jsc:arch_fstab)). The base starts with only a header in it, so you write the root line yourself.
jsc.guide.fstab_by_hand.text2: The root line names the root partition by its universally unique identifier (UUID). The UUID belongs to one partition, and it stays the same when the disks are reordered ([](jsc:filesystems_and_mkfs)).
jsc.guide.fstab_by_hand.text3: At reboot, the machine looks for a line whose mount point is /. It needs that line to find the root, so the reboot checks for it before it starts.
jsc.guide.fstab_by_hand.title: The fstab by hand
jsc.guide.games.definition1: A mark you place on a cell that you think holds a mine.
jsc.guide.games.definition2: The seven columns of cards in Solitaire, where the cards are laid out in a row.
jsc.guide.games.definition3: One of the four piles in Solitaire, where a suit is built from ace up to king.
jsc.guide.games.table2_4_1: From a foundation back to the tableau
jsc.guide.games.text1: Three games run on the desktop systems. Each one is installed like any other program ([](jsc:programs)), and needs 1 megabyte (MB) of memory.
jsc.guide.games.text2: Reveal a cell to see how many mines touch it. A number shows that count, in its own colour. An empty cell opens the cells around it. You flag a cell you think holds a mine.
jsc.guide.games.text4: Solitaire is Klondike. You draw one card at a time from the stock, the face-down pile, into the waste, which holds the cards you drew. The seven columns of cards are the tableau, and the four piles, one for each suit, are the foundations, built from ace up to king.
jsc.guide.games.text5: The window shows the score and the moves, and it says "You win" when the game is done. The New button starts another game.
jsc.guide.games.text6: Snake runs on a grid of 20 by 12 cells. You eat the food to grow, and each food is worth 10 points. The snake starts at a length of 4. Press an arrow key to start.
jsc.guide.games.text7: The speed sets how many ticks pass between two steps. A tick is the game's beat, and 20 ticks make a second ([](jsc:units_and_ticks)).
jsc.guide.games.text8: With walls on, running into a wall ends the game. With walls off, the grid wraps round, and only running into yourself ends the game. The window shows the score, the best score and the length, and it says "Game over" when you lose.
jsc.guide.games.title: Minesweeper, Solitaire and Snake
jsc.guide.gateway_command.fix1: No Gateway is linked to a port of this computer. Plug the cable in the back of the Gateway ([](jsc:network_gateway)).
jsc.guide.gateway_command.fix2: Install CC: Tweaked to use the ComputerCraft side. The rest of the Gateway still works.
jsc.guide.gateway_command.fix3: Check the name with gateway list. Names are not case-sensitive, but the spelling must match.
jsc.guide.gateway_command.fix4: Run the command from the command line of a computer.
jsc.guide.gateway_command.problem1: The command says no gateways on this computer's ports.
jsc.guide.gateway_command.problem2: The command says CC: Tweaked is not installed.
jsc.guide.gateway_command.problem3: The command says no gateway named <name> on this computer.
jsc.guide.gateway_command.problem4: The command says this terminal is not on a computer.
jsc.guide.gateway_command.step1: Type gateway list to see the Gateways on this computer's ports.
jsc.guide.gateway_command.step2: Type the Gateway's name, then status, perms, computers or log, to see its details.
jsc.guide.gateway_command.table1_10_2: Turns the read switch on or off.
jsc.guide.gateway_command.table1_11_2: Turns the operations switch on or off.
jsc.guide.gateway_command.table1_1_2: Lists the Gateways on this computer's ports, with NAME, LINK, CC and WHERE.
jsc.guide.gateway_command.table1_2_2: Shows the link, the network, the budget, the buffer and the latest log lines.
jsc.guide.gateway_command.table1_3_2: Shows the read and operations switches, the priority ceiling and the calls a tick.
jsc.guide.gateway_command.table1_4_2: Lists the ComputerCraft computers attached, with ID, LABEL, STATE, AGENT and LAST SEEN.
jsc.guide.gateway_command.table1_5_2: Shows what the Gateway did, oldest first at the bottom.
jsc.guide.gateway_command.table1_6_2: Gives the Gateway a new name, under the same rules as the Gateway Manager.
jsc.guide.gateway_command.table1_8_2: Sends the items in the buffer to the network.
jsc.guide.gateway_command.table1_9_2: Sends the jsc_test event to the computers that listen for it.
jsc.guide.gateway_command.text1: The gateway command manages the Gateways from the command line of a computer. It works on any computer with peripheral ports, even one with no Gateway, so it can tell you what is missing.
jsc.guide.gateway_command.text2: Names are matched without regard to capitals, so Gateway-1 and gateway-1 name the same Gateway.
jsc.guide.gateway_command.title: The gateway command
jsc.guide.gateway_library.fix1: Use a machine that has a Gateway.
jsc.guide.gateway_library.fix3: Install ComputerCraft, then start the game again.
jsc.guide.gateway_library.fix4: The peripheral refused the call. Check the method name and the arguments in Gateway.Peripherals.
jsc.guide.gateway_library.problem1: The program stops and says this computer has no Gateway.
jsc.guide.gateway_library.problem2: The program stops and says this computer has no Gateway with that name.
jsc.guide.gateway_library.problem3: The program stops and says the machine has no ComputerCraft side, and asks whether ComputerCraft is installed.
jsc.guide.gateway_library.problem4: Gateway.Call stops the program with the error text from ComputerCraft.
jsc.guide.gateway_library.table1_10_2: Reboots the computer with that number.
jsc.guide.gateway_library.table1_11_2: Sends a message to that computer.
jsc.guide.gateway_library.table1_12_2: Sets the handler that runs for each message from a ComputerCraft computer.
jsc.guide.gateway_library.table1_1_2: Yes when this machine has a Gateway that is online.
jsc.guide.gateway_library.table1_2_2: The name of the Gateway the program chose.
jsc.guide.gateway_library.table1_3_2: The names of the Gateways, as a list of text.
jsc.guide.gateway_library.table1_4_2: Chooses the Gateway that later calls use, by name, in any case.
jsc.guide.gateway_library.table1_5_2: The ComputerCraft computers, as a list of CcComputer.
jsc.guide.gateway_library.table1_6_2: The peripherals, as a list of CcPeripheral.
jsc.guide.gateway_library.table1_7_2: Asks a peripheral to run a method, with up to three arguments after the two names, and gives back what it returns.
jsc.guide.gateway_library.table1_8_2: Switches on the computer with that number.
jsc.guide.gateway_library.table1_9_2: Switches off the computer with that number.
jsc.guide.gateway_library.table2_1_3: The number, name and label of the computer, and whether it is on.
jsc.guide.gateway_library.table2_2_3: The name and type of the peripheral, and the names of its methods.

jsc.guide.gateway_library.text1: A Gateway links the network to ComputerCraft computers on the wire. A program can list those computers and their peripherals, call a method of a peripheral, switch a computer on, off or reboot it, and send it a message. The block is explained in [](jsc:network_gateway).
jsc.guide.gateway_library.text2: The Gateway a call uses is the one the program chose with Select. If the program chose none, the first Gateway the machine lists is used.
jsc.guide.gateway_library.text3: Send gives your message the event name jsc_message on the ComputerCraft side. A call across a Gateway costs more than most things a program does, and each argument adds to its cost.
jsc.guide.gateway_library.text4: Every call is written in the Gateway's log: called when it went through, and the refusal text when it did not.
jsc.guide.gateway_library.title: Gateways: talking to ComputerCraft computers
jsc.guide.gateway_manager.definition1: The highest priority that any request from a ComputerCraft program may carry.
jsc.guide.gateway_manager.definition2: The number of calls per game tick that the Gateway answers for a ComputerCraft program.
jsc.guide.gateway_manager.fix1: No Gateway is selected. Click one in the list on the left, then press the button again.
jsc.guide.gateway_manager.fix2: The ComputerCraft side is missing. Install CC: Tweaked to use it.
jsc.guide.gateway_manager.fix3: The action needs a program on that ComputerCraft computer, and none is there. Try an action that does not need one.
jsc.guide.gateway_manager.fix4: Operations need a running Mainframe. Put one on the network ([](jsc:mainframes)).
jsc.guide.gateway_manager.fix5: Nothing is in the buffer to send. Put items in it yourself, or have a ComputerCraft program pull them in.

jsc.guide.gateway_manager.step1: Open the Gateway Manager on the computer that has the Gateway on its port.
jsc.guide.gateway_manager.step2: Select the Gateway in the list on the left.
jsc.guide.gateway_manager.step3: Open the Permissions tab, and turn on the switches you need.
jsc.guide.gateway_manager.step4: Choose the priority ceiling and the calls a tick.
jsc.guide.gateway_manager.step5: Open the Status tab to check the link and the Mainframe.
jsc.guide.gateway_manager.table1_1_2: The link, the Mainframe, the budget, the calls served and the latest log lines.
jsc.guide.gateway_manager.table1_2_2: The four settings: reading, operations, the priority ceiling and the calls a tick.
jsc.guide.gateway_manager.table1_3_2: The ComputerCraft computers attached to the Gateway, with ID, LABEL, STATE, AGENT and LAST SEEN.
jsc.guide.gateway_manager.table1_4_2: What the Gateway did, with WHEN, WHO and RESULT columns.

jsc.guide.gateway_manager.table2_3_2: Sends the items in the buffer to the network.
jsc.guide.gateway_manager.text1: The Gateway Manager is a desktop program. It lists the Network Gateways on this computer's ports, and it is where you set what ComputerCraft may do through each one. It is a Legacy-era program ([](jsc:eras)).
jsc.guide.gateway_manager.text2: Select a Gateway in the list on the left, then use the tabs and the buttons on the right. Until a Gateway is linked to one of this computer's ports, the list says none linked yet.
jsc.guide.gateway_manager.text3: The Status tab has two cards. THIS SIDE says "Linked to" and the host's name, or "Not linked", and it says whether the Mainframe is online or offline. COMPUTERCRAFT SIDE says CC: Tweaked with its version, or that CC: Tweaked is not installed.
jsc.guide.gateway_manager.text4: The budget line shows the share of each tick that the Gateway's calls take from the host's programs, such as "Budget: 12% of a tick".
jsc.guide.gateway_manager.text5: On the Computers tab, Turn on, Reboot, Shutdown and Test event act on the ComputerCraft computers attached to the Gateway.
jsc.guide.gateway_manager.title: The Gateway Manager
jsc.guide.gateway_permissions.fix1: Turn the read switch on in the Permissions tab, or type gateway <name> set read on in the command line.
jsc.guide.gateway_permissions.fix2: Turn the operations switch on in the Permissions tab, or type gateway <name> set operations on in the command line.
jsc.guide.gateway_permissions.fix3: The program called more than the cap in one tick. Raise the cap to 16, or slow the program down.
jsc.guide.gateway_permissions.fix4: The priority ceiling is lower than the request, so the request is lowered to it. Raise the ceiling in the Permissions tab.
jsc.guide.gateway_permissions.problem1: The message "denied: reading the network is off" appears.
jsc.guide.gateway_permissions.problem2: The message "denied: operations are off" appears.
jsc.guide.gateway_permissions.problem3: The message "busy: 8 calls a tick" appears.
jsc.guide.gateway_permissions.problem4: A program asks for a priority and gets a lower one.
jsc.guide.gateway_permissions.table1_1_2: The reading calls: capacity, used, types, total, find, servers, computers, operation, operations and watch.
jsc.guide.gateway_permissions.table1_2_2: The calls pull, push, craft, cancel and run.
jsc.guide.gateway_permissions.table1_3_2: The highest priority a request may carry. A higher request is lowered to it.
jsc.guide.gateway_permissions.table1_4_2: How many calls the Gateway answers in one game tick, which is a twentieth of a second.
jsc.guide.gateway_permissions.table2_10_: No pattern makes that item, so no craft can start.
jsc.guide.gateway_permissions.table2_11_: The id you gave matches two operations.
jsc.guide.gateway_permissions.table2_12_: The computer you named is not on this network.
jsc.guide.gateway_permissions.table2_13_: The computer you asked to run a program is off.
jsc.guide.gateway_permissions.table2_14_: The computer refuses programs that come from another computer.
jsc.guide.gateway_permissions.table2_15_: The computer has nothing that can run that program.
jsc.guide.gateway_permissions.table2_16_: The computer has too little free memory for the program.
jsc.guide.gateway_permissions.table2_3_2: The program called more often than the call cap in one tick. The number is the cap.
jsc.guide.gateway_permissions.table2_5_2: The game knows no item by that name, and fluids and chemicals say unknown fluid or unknown chemical.
jsc.guide.gateway_permissions.table2_6_2: The host has no network to serve the request from.
jsc.guide.gateway_permissions.table2_7_2: A running Mainframe must be on the network.
jsc.guide.gateway_permissions.table2_8_2: The network refused to start the operation, such as a SELECT or an INSERT.
jsc.guide.gateway_permissions.table2_9_2: A push asked for an item that the buffer does not hold.
jsc.guide.gateway_permissions.text1: A ComputerCraft program can ask the Gateway for two kinds of things: reading what the network holds, and starting operations that move or make items. You decide which kinds it may ask for, with four settings on the host.
jsc.guide.gateway_permissions.text2: The switches do not cover unwatch, log, send, online, name or host. Unwatch and log still count against the call cap, and send does not.
jsc.guide.gateway_permissions.text3: A request names its priority with one word: low, medium or high. A request with no word, or with a word the Gateway does not know, runs at medium. A ceiling lower than that priority then lowers it. [Priorities](jsc:priorities) explain the order in which the network serves them.
jsc.guide.gateway_permissions.text4: A quantity of 0 or less means all: pull all of a name, or push everything in the buffer of that name. The Gateway Manager shows it as pull all. What a push cannot move goes back into the buffer.
jsc.guide.gateway_permissions.text5: The run call starts a compiled program on another computer of the network. You give it the computer's name, the program's name and any arguments, and it returns a process number. It takes no priority.
jsc.guide.gateway_permissions.text6: A refused request goes back to the program as text, and the Gateway's log writes it as DENIED.
jsc.guide.gateway_permissions.title: What ComputerCraft may do
jsc.guide.gentoo_bootloader.fix1: GRUB is not compiled yet. Type emerge --ask sys-boot/grub first.
jsc.guide.gentoo_bootloader.fix2: Step into the new system first: chroot /mnt/gentoo /bin/bash, then run the command there.
jsc.guide.gentoo_bootloader.fix3: Build the kernel first: genkernel all, or make in /usr/src/linux ([](jsc:kernel_gentoo)).
jsc.guide.gentoo_bootloader.fix4: The EFI system partition is not mounted where grub-install looks. Mount it, then name its place with --efi-directory=/efi, as the walkthrough does.
jsc.guide.gentoo_bootloader.fix5: BIOS firmware needs the disk named. Type grub-install /dev/sda.
jsc.guide.gentoo_bootloader.fix6: GRUB goes on the disk, not in a partition. Type grub-install /dev/sda.
jsc.guide.gentoo_bootloader.fix7: GRUB is not installed yet. Run grub-install first.
jsc.guide.gentoo_bootloader.problem2: grub-install says "command not found". The program belongs to the new system and is not built there yet.
jsc.guide.gentoo_bootloader.problem3: grub-install says "warning: no kernel image found in /boot."
jsc.guide.gentoo_bootloader.problem4: grub-install says "error: /boot/efi doesn't look like an EFI partition."
jsc.guide.gentoo_bootloader.problem5: grub-install says "error: install device isn't specified."
jsc.guide.gentoo_bootloader.problem6: grub-install says "error: cannot find a device for /dev/<dev>."
jsc.guide.gentoo_bootloader.problem7: grub-mkconfig says "/boot/grub: No such file or directory".
jsc.guide.gentoo_bootloader.step1: Type emerge --ask sys-boot/grub and press [[Enter]]. Answer the question with Enter.
jsc.guide.gentoo_bootloader.step2: Type the install command for your firmware, from the table below, and press [[Enter]].
jsc.guide.gentoo_bootloader.table1: The install command for each firmware
jsc.guide.gentoo_bootloader.text1: The bootloader starts the kernel you built, and it shows the menu of the systems on the disk. On Gentoo the bootloader is GRUB ([](jsc:arch_bootloader)). GRUB is a package like any other, so you compile it from source too.
jsc.guide.gentoo_bootloader.text2: The firmware decides where GRUB goes. UEFI (Unified Extensible Firmware Interface) reads it from the EFI system partition. BIOS (basic input/output system) finds it on the disk itself.
jsc.guide.gentoo_bootloader.text3: The --efi-directory=/efi part must name the place where the EFI system partition is mounted in the new system. The mount step put it at /mnt/gentoo/efi, which is /efi inside the new system.
jsc.guide.gentoo_bootloader.text4: The menu that grub-mkconfig writes has one entry, named Gentoo Linux. The entry starts the kernel you built, and it gives the kernel your root partition by its UUID.
jsc.guide.gentoo_bootloader.title: GRUB on Gentoo
jsc.guide.gentoo_overview.definition1: Turning source code, the text a programmer writes, into a program the computer can run.
jsc.guide.gentoo_overview.definition2: The core program of the operating system. It drives the hardware and runs the other programs.
jsc.guide.gentoo_overview.definition3: Gentoo's package manager. It reads build recipes and compiles each program from its source.
jsc.guide.gentoo_overview.fix1: Only /mnt/gentoo lives on your disk. Write the new system there, not in /root.
jsc.guide.gentoo_overview.fix2: Each refusal names the step it is missing. Do that step, then try again.
jsc.guide.gentoo_overview.problem1: A file you wrote is gone after a restart.
jsc.guide.gentoo_overview.problem2: The steps stop, and you cannot tell what to do next.
jsc.guide.gentoo_overview.table1_1_2: Only the steps marked with an asterisk (the default).
jsc.guide.gentoo_overview.table1_2_2: Every step of the handbook, the optional ones too.
jsc.guide.gentoo_overview.text1: Gentoo has no installer that does the work for you. Its installation medium gives you a shell and a walkthrough, and you type every step yourself. Each tool you run is the real one. The general steps for every system are in [Installing a system](jsc:installing).
jsc.guide.gentoo_overview.text2: The system you end up with is built on your machine from source code. The kernel and every program you add are compiled from their source first, so the install takes a long time. You decide how many compiles run at once.
jsc.guide.gentoo_overview.text3: Gentoo is a Linux system of the Legacy era, and it takes 4,096 MB of disk once installed. Its package manager is Portage, which installs programs by compiling them.
jsc.guide.gentoo_overview.text4: The walkthrough is a file on the medium, /root/install.txt. Read it at any time: type less /root/install.txt and press [[Enter]]. The file is always in English.
jsc.guide.gentoo_overview.text5: Long steps keep the terminal busy until they finish. Press [[Ctrl]]+[[C]] to stop a step that runs too long ([](jsc:medium_shell)).
jsc.guide.gentoo_overview.text6: The walkthrough marks the steps a system cannot boot without with an asterisk. The setting install_by_hand.gentoo_every_step decides which steps you are asked, and it is off by default.
jsc.guide.gentoo_overview.text7: Every download and every package comes from the [Mirror](jsc:mirror). A [Mainframe](jsc:mainframes) on the same network must run the Mirror, or the fetch steps fail.
jsc.guide.gentoo_overview.text8: The new system is built in /mnt/gentoo, on your disk. The live medium runs in memory, and it forgets every file written outside /mnt/gentoo when it restarts.
jsc.guide.gentoo_overview.title: How Gentoo is installed
jsc.guide.gentoo_reboot.fix1: Type exit to leave the new system, then type reboot again.
jsc.guide.gentoo_reboot.fix2: Each item names its fix in brackets. Do that step, then type reboot again.
jsc.guide.gentoo_reboot.fix3: Use up to 15 letters, digits and hyphens, and start with a letter or digit.
jsc.guide.gentoo_reboot.fix4: Step into the new system first with chroot /mnt/gentoo /bin/bash, then set the name.
jsc.guide.gentoo_reboot.problem1: reboot says "you are inside the new system. exit first."
jsc.guide.gentoo_reboot.problem2: The machine says "The new system will not boot" and lists items.
jsc.guide.gentoo_reboot.problem3: hostname says "the specified hostname is invalid".
jsc.guide.gentoo_reboot.problem4: hostname says "you cannot change the host name of the live medium".
jsc.guide.gentoo_reboot.step3: Type umount -R /mnt/gentoo and press [[Enter]]. The command prints nothing.
jsc.guide.gentoo_reboot.table1_1_2: no base system installed (wget the stage 3, then tar)
jsc.guide.gentoo_reboot.table1_2_2: no root filesystem in /etc/fstab (blkid, then write the line)
jsc.guide.gentoo_reboot.table1_3_2: no kernel (genkernel all, or make in /usr/src/linux)
jsc.guide.gentoo_reboot.table1_5_2: nothing for the bootloader to start (grub-mkconfig -o /boot/grub/grub.cfg)
jsc.guide.gentoo_reboot.table2: Checked when every step is asked
jsc.guide.gentoo_reboot.table2_1_2: /proc, /sys, /dev and /run were not bound into the new system (mount --rbind, --types proc)
jsc.guide.gentoo_reboot.table2_2_2: no profile chosen (eselect profile list, then set)
jsc.guide.gentoo_reboot.table2_3_2: the system was not brought up to date (emerge --ask --verbose --update --deep --newuse @world)
jsc.guide.gentoo_reboot.text1: The reboot is the last step. Before it starts the new system, the machine checks that the system has everything it needs to boot. If you missed something, it lists the missing items and refuses to start ([](jsc:reboot_checklist)).
jsc.guide.gentoo_reboot.text2: The machine always checks the items in the first table. Each missing item prints with its fix in brackets.
jsc.guide.gentoo_reboot.text3: With install_by_hand.gentoo_every_step set to true, the machine also checks the items in the second table.
jsc.guide.gentoo_reboot.text4: The name is set inside the new system, with echo <name> > /etc/hostname or with hostname <name>. A name starts with a letter or digit, holds up to 15 characters, and may contain hyphens.
jsc.guide.gentoo_reboot.text5: When every item is in place, the reboot makes the disk you chose boot first. The machine answers "Rebooting into the new system".
jsc.guide.gentoo_reboot.title: Rebooting into Gentoo
jsc.guide.gnome.definition1: GNOME's full-screen view of the desktop, with a search field, the workspaces and a grid of every program.
jsc.guide.gnome.fix1: The computer is a Vintage one. Use a Legacy computer or a newer one.
jsc.guide.gnome.fix2: It is installed already. A desktop that is installed starts at the next boot, so restart the computer.
jsc.guide.gnome.problem1: The package manager says "gnome needs Legacy hardware or later".
jsc.guide.gnome.problem2: The package manager says "gnome is already the newest version".
jsc.guide.gnome.text1: GNOME is a desktop that runs on Linux and FreeBSD, from Legacy hardware on. Its package is named gnome. Its house is the GNOME Trust, a software house of the mod's world.
jsc.guide.gnome.text2: GNOME changes its face with the era too. On Legacy hardware you see GNOME 1: a thick frame in relief, a centred title in muted purple, warm greys and chunky bevelled studs. On Transition you see GNOME 2. From the Standard on you see GNOME itself.
jsc.guide.gnome.text3: GNOME has no start menu as such. Its panel is a bar along the top of the screen, with the Activities overview. Open it, and the overview covers the desktop with a search field, the workspace strip and a grid of every program.
jsc.guide.gnome.text4: On Transition, GNOME 2 has its own menu, with sections named Places, System, Preferences, Accessories, Games, Internet and System Tools.
jsc.guide.gnome.text5: GNOME gives its programs its own names, as the table shows. This PC is called About.
jsc.guide.gnome.text6: To install it, use the form for your system in [](jsc:install_a_desktop). On Fedora, that is dnf install gnome. The boot lines show it as "Starting gnome Display Manager".
jsc.guide.gnome.title: GNOME
jsc.guide.graphics_cards.definition1: The graphics card's own memory. Monitors and the windows that draw pictures use it.
jsc.guide.graphics_cards.fix1: Switch the computer on. Monitors light only while the computer runs.
jsc.guide.graphics_cards.fix2: No graphics card is in the computer, and its processor has no graphics. Put in a card, or use a processor with graphics built in.
jsc.guide.graphics_cards.fix3: Use a card with more video memory, or fewer or smaller monitors.
jsc.guide.graphics_cards.fix4: It sits in an older slot. Move it to a newer slot.
jsc.guide.graphics_cards.problem1: The monitor stays dark while the computer is off.
jsc.guide.graphics_cards.problem3: The monitor says "Not enough video memory: this monitor needs <a>, and <b> are free".
jsc.guide.graphics_cards.problem4: A card does less than its tooltip says.
jsc.guide.graphics_cards.table1: A card in an older slot
jsc.guide.graphics_cards.table1_4_2: An eighth, which is the least it keeps
jsc.guide.graphics_cards.table2: Video memory for one block of a monitor
jsc.guide.graphics_cards.text1: The graphics card draws the picture: it lights the monitors and draws the windows on them. A computer with no graphics card has nothing to show, unless its processor has graphics built in.
jsc.guide.graphics_cards.text10: A window that draws a picture costs a quarter of a colour block of its era, or a whole block while it is maximised. Only graphical programs take that memory, and a minimised window takes none.
jsc.guide.graphics_cards.text2: A card has a memory of its own, the video memory (VRAM). Every monitor uses some of it, a bigger monitor more, and every window that draws a picture of its own uses some too.
jsc.guide.graphics_cards.text3: A processor with graphics built in has no video memory of its own. It takes a quarter of the computer's RAM for its picture, up to 1,792 MB. A computer with a graphics card of its own does not share its RAM this way.
jsc.guide.graphics_cards.text4: In a Mainframe, each card adds one parallel queue: a line of work the Mainframe runs at the same time as the others. A Mainframe with three cards runs four queues, one from its processors and one for each card ([States, priorities and queues](jsc:states_and_queues)).
jsc.guide.graphics_cards.text5: A card's queue never runs faster than the processors of the Mainframe. A card whose queue runs slower than that is shown in amber.
jsc.guide.graphics_cards.text6: Cards go in the board's expansion slots ([Expansion cards](jsc:expansion_cards)). A card in an older slot runs slower than its tooltip says. The table shows how much of its speed it keeps.
jsc.guide.graphics_cards.text7: The same share cuts the video memory the computer counts for the card, and the card's queue.
jsc.guide.graphics_cards.text8: There are 76 cards, from the VGA-256 to the Envya Vertex RTX 5090. Hover a card and its tooltip shows you its cores, its video memory and its power.
jsc.guide.graphics_cards.text9: A monitor is counted in blocks of its big screen. Its video memory cost is its number of blocks, times the cost of one block in its era.
jsc.guide.graphics_cards.title: Graphics cards
jsc.guide.hbw_interface.fix1: Its racks are not all on the high compute cable that reaches the interface. Join every rack to that same high compute run.
jsc.guide.hbw_interface.step1: Join the supercomputer racks to the interface with high compute cable.
jsc.guide.hbw_interface.step2: Join the interface to the network's backbone.
jsc.guide.hbw_interface.text1: A supercomputer is not one block. It is every Supercomputer Rack tied together by a fabric cable, and you meet it at the HBW Interface, the one point where it meets the rest of the network through the backbone.
jsc.guide.hbw_interface.text2: The Standard has one, and the Advanced has another that takes the OSFP cable.
jsc.guide.hbw_interface.text3: The interface looks along the high compute cable from it, through up to 256 cable steps, and counts each Supercomputer Rack on that run. Racks on any other run do not count.
jsc.guide.hbw_interface.title: HBW Interface
jsc.guide.help_command.definition1: A subject the full-screen help opens on, such as a command's name or a title in its contents.
jsc.guide.help_command.definition2: A word in the help text that you pick with Tab and follow with Enter.
jsc.guide.help_command.fix1: The name is not a command of this computer. Type help on its own to list the commands it has.
jsc.guide.help_command.fix2: FreeBSD has no help command. Type apropos and a word, or man intro for the introduction.
jsc.guide.help_command.fix3: Press Escape once for each open menu or search, then once more to leave the help.
jsc.guide.help_command.fix4: Check the spelling of the word, or try a shorter word.
jsc.guide.help_command.problem1: The reply is "no such command:" and the name you typed.
jsc.guide.help_command.problem2: The reply is "help: not found. Try: apropos <word>, or man intro".
jsc.guide.help_command.problem3: The full screen does not close.
jsc.guide.help_command.step1: Type help and press [[Enter]] to list the commands this computer has.
jsc.guide.help_command.step2: Type help, a space and a name, such as help ls on Linux, to read that command's page.
jsc.guide.help_command.step3: On MC-DOS or MC-NET, press [[Esc]] when you are done, to return to the prompt.
jsc.guide.help_command.table1_10_2: Show the contents, the next topic, the topic before, and the index.
jsc.guide.help_command.table1_11_2: Closes an open menu or search, or leaves the help when none is open.
jsc.guide.help_command.table1_1_2: Picks the next button or link.
jsc.guide.help_command.table1_2_2: Picks the button or link before.
jsc.guide.help_command.table1_3_2: Follows the picked link, or picks a menu item.
jsc.guide.help_command.table1_6_2: Go to the start or the end of the topic.
jsc.guide.help_command.text1: help is the command that tells you what the other commands do. Type help on its own, and it lists the commands this computer has. Type help and a command's name, and it prints that command's page: its form, what it does and its options.
jsc.guide.help_command.text2: On MC-DOS and MC-NET, help takes the whole screen, and you move through the page with the keys below. On Frames, Linux and UNIX System V it prints the page as text. The Help windows of the desktop are a different thing ([](jsc:help_on_a_computer)).
jsc.guide.help_command.text3: On MC-DOS and MC-NET, the top line of the full screen reads, for example, "MC-DOS Help: dir". The keys are the ones below.
jsc.guide.help_command.text4: To search, press [[Alt]]+[[S]], then press [[Enter]] on the first item of the Search menu, the one named Find with three dots after it. The screen asks "Find what:". Type the word and press [[Enter]].
jsc.guide.help_command.text5: The second item, "Repeat Last Find", searches again. When the word is not in the text, the screen says "Match not found."
jsc.guide.help_command.title: The help command
jsc.guide.help_on_a_computer.fix1: Check the name. For the entry on graphics cards, type man graphics-cards, not man graphics.
jsc.guide.help_on_a_computer.fix3: info is for Linux only. Use man instead ([](jsc:man_pages)).
jsc.guide.help_on_a_computer.problem1: man says No manual entry for a name.
jsc.guide.help_on_a_computer.problem2: help does not work on FreeBSD.
jsc.guide.help_on_a_computer.problem3: info does not work on your system.
jsc.guide.help_on_a_computer.table2_3_2: Goes up to the node above.
jsc.guide.help_on_a_computer.table2_4_2: Goes back to the node you were at.
jsc.guide.help_on_a_computer.table2_7_2: Goes to a menu item, by its name.
jsc.guide.help_on_a_computer.text1: Every desktop has a Help program, under a name of its own. It ships with the desktop, so you do not install it. It reads the manuals of the series, and beside them the manual pages of the machine's own commands. This manual is not only in your hands: every computer can read it too.
jsc.guide.help_on_a_computer.text2: At a prompt, several commands give you help. Each one works on a different set of systems.
jsc.guide.help_on_a_computer.text3: The help command lists the commands, or shows how one of them is used. Type help alone to list them, or help and a command's name to see its use. It works on every system except FreeBSD. On MC-DOS and MC-NET it takes the whole screen. On the other systems it prints its text ([](jsc:help_command)).
jsc.guide.help_on_a_computer.text4: The man command opens the manual page of a command, on Linux, UNIX System V and FreeBSD. A topic such as graphics-cards opens as a page of section 7 ([](jsc:man_pages)). The whatis and apropos commands search the manual ([](jsc:whatis_and_apropos)).
jsc.guide.help_on_a_computer.text5: On Linux the info command reads the manuals as a tree of nodes. Its keys are these:
jsc.guide.help_on_a_computer.text6: With no name, info opens the directory of every manual.

jsc.guide.how_autocrafting_works.table1_: The Mainframe starts a craft only while it is running and has an operating system.
The network works out the plan, and the craft waits until the plan is ready.
The plan goes to a Crafting Computer that is switched on and holds a Crafting Card.

jsc.guide.how_autocrafting_works.text1: You ask for 512 pistons. The network works out every step from what it has: how many planks, how much cobblestone, iron and redstone it needs, and what it must make first. It also decides on which machines and in which order. Then it runs the crafting table recipes and the machines, and puts the pistons in storage. That is autocrafting.
jsc.guide.how_autocrafting_works.text2: To do it, the network must know the recipes. A recipe it knows is a pattern, and there are three kinds: a bench pattern, a 3x3 grid like a crafting table's with its result; a machine pattern, what goes into a machine and what comes back; and a multi-stage pattern, steps of both kinds in order.
jsc.guide.how_autocrafting_works.text3: The parts are a Crafting Computer that runs the crafts ([](jsc:crafting_computers)), the Crafting Cable that joins it to the machines, and on that cable the parts that feed each machine. A Crafting Card in the computer is what lets it craft at all ([](jsc:crafting_cards)). Two programs you install yourself write the patterns and load them: the Pattern Studio and the Crafting Manager ([](jsc:pattern_studio), [](jsc:crafting_manager)).
jsc.guide.how_autocrafting_works.text4: Patterns are written in the Pattern Studio and carried to the Crafting Computer on media ([](jsc:pattern_encoders)). A craft then goes through the steps below.
jsc.guide.how_autocrafting_works.text5: The network needs two things before any of it works: a running Mainframe with an operating system, and the recipes held in a card or in an interface. A machine works with the network when it offers item, fluid and chemical access, whatever mod it comes from.

A Crafting Input Router sits on the cable that leaves a Crafting Interface, against one input face of a machine that has several. Its tooltip reads "On the cable that leaves a Crafting Interface, against one input face of a machine with several".

The interface sends each input of a pattern through the router chosen for it. A router moves nothing on its own: the interface feeds through it, and the interface measures and accounts for every item.
Each router has a filter, set the same way as the filters of the buses ([](jsc:buses)). The filter takes an item, or a tag, and the screen asks for "item, or #tag". A tag looks like "c:ores".
The default router for an input is the one whose filter takes it. The screen says "Chosen in the interface", so you can choose a different router in the interface.

A Crafting Receiving Bus sits on the crafting cable against a machine's output. Its tooltip reads "On the crafting cable, against a machine's output; takes back what its interface's jobs made". It takes back what comes out of the machine and credits it to the craft that fed the machine.

The bus ties itself to the Crafting Interface that feeds its machine, either against it or through the routers of its own cable. You can also tie it by hand to one interface, or to several. Tying it by hand is how an output that goes into a chest beside the machine is handled, and by hand the bus takes up to 8 ties.

While a job of its interfaces runs, what comes out of the machine is credited to that job, up to what the job fed in. What was in the machine before the job began stays there. A fluid or a chemical that no pattern lists stays in the machine as its buffer.

The routers and the buses are cable parts, so they mount on the crafting cable. An interface's own cable is coloured apart from the main crafting cable, which keeps the two runs apart ([](jsc:data_cables)).
Input routers and Receiving Buses
jsc.guide.insert_delete_move_drop.fix1: Add TO and the name of a bus.
jsc.guide.insert_delete_move_drop.fix2: Name the place to take from after FROM, and the place to put the items in after TO.
jsc.guide.insert_delete_move_drop.fix3: Remove the TO. DROP only destroys items.
jsc.guide.insert_delete_move_drop.fix4: Type the name as one word, with no space.
jsc.guide.insert_delete_move_drop.proble: DELETE exports out of the network and needs a TO destination
MOVE is internal and needs both FROM and TO
expected a location after FROM, got: <text>
jsc.guide.insert_delete_move_drop.table1: INSERT [quantity] item [FROM bus]. Brings the items this computer holds into the network, or imports them from a bus.
DELETE [quantity] item TO bus. Sends the items the network holds out to a bus.
MOVE [quantity] item FROM source TO destination. Carries items between two servers, or to and from a bus.
DROP [quantity] item. Destroys the items the network holds.
jsc.guide.insert_delete_move_drop.table2: The items are on their way into the network.
There is nothing for INSERT to push.
This computer has none of the item. Put it into this computer first.
The import has started. The reply says MOVE, although you typed INSERT: that is the network's own wording.
The bus holds nothing to import.
The bus has no chest or machine beside it to take from.
jsc.guide.insert_delete_move_drop.table3: The items are on their way out to the bus.
The network holds none of the item.
No bus has that name on the network. Check the name in the bus's window.
jsc.guide.insert_delete_move_drop.table4: The items are on their way to that bus.
The source holds none of the item.
The source holds nothing to send to that bus.
Neither a server nor a bus has that name.
The destination cannot take items now.
The network did not start the move.
jsc.guide.insert_delete_move_drop.table5: The network holds none of the item.
jsc.guide.insert_delete_move_drop.text1: These four verbs move items or destroy them. INSERT brings items into the network. DELETE sends them out of the network. MOVE carries them from one place to another. DROP destroys them. Where you type a quantity, it is a number, ALL, or nothing.
jsc.guide.insert_delete_move_drop.text2: A bus is a block that moves items between the network and a chest or machine beside it. That chest or machine is the bus's external inventory ([](jsc:buses)).
jsc.guide.insert_delete_move_drop.text3: Without FROM, INSERT pushes what this computer holds into the network. With FROM and the name of a bus, it imports from that bus instead. Whatever the network cannot keep goes back to the bus.
jsc.guide.insert_delete_move_drop.text4: DELETE sends items out of the network. It needs TO and the name of a bus, and a server name is not valid there. Only items the network holds are sent, so a second DELETE does nothing once the stock runs out. DELETE accepts FROM but ignores it.
jsc.guide.insert_delete_move_drop.text5: MOVE needs both FROM and TO. Between two servers, it moves items inside the network. A bus after TO sends items out, and a bus after FROM brings them in.
jsc.guide.insert_delete_move_drop.text6: DROP takes no TO. It destroys only the items the network holds, so you cannot drop what you do not have on the network. The Management Studio asks you to confirm a DROP, and a DELETE with ALL, before it runs them.
jsc.guide.insert_delete_move_drop.title: INSERT, DELETE, MOVE and DROP
jsc.guide.insert_delete_move_drop.warnin: A DROP destroys the items for good. They leave the network and are not kept.

jsc.guide.install_a_desktop.text1: On Linux and FreeBSD you have two ways to get a desktop. You can choose one while the system installs, or add one afterwards from the terminal. Both ways read the Mirror, the network's package shelf ([](jsc:mirror)).
jsc.guide.install_a_desktop.text2: A Mirror answers when your computer reaches a Mainframe that runs it, through a data cable. The Mirror is a service, so it stops answering when the cable is cut.
jsc.guide.install_a_desktop.text3: The installer of Ubuntu, Debian, Fedora and FreeBSD has a Desktop page. Gentoo, Arch Linux, UNIX System V and MC-DOS have none. The Desktop page appears only when a Mirror answers.
jsc.guide.install_a_desktop.text4: Once the system runs, you add a desktop from its terminal. Use the install form of the system's package manager, and give the desktop's name ([](jsc:software_commands)).
jsc.guide.install_a_desktop.text5: The name is the desktop's command name: kde-plasma, gnome, cinnamon or cde. The id works too, as kde_plasma. Capitals do not matter.
jsc.guide.install_a_desktop.text6: Gentoo builds a desktop from source in the terminal, and the terminal waits until the build is done.
jsc.guide.install_a_desktop.text7: Which desktops the installer offers depends on the system and on your computer's era.
jsc.guide.install_a_desktop.text8: On a Legacy computer it offers KDE Plasma, GNOME and CDE, where the system runs them. A Standard computer is also offered Cinnamon. A Vintage computer is offered none.
jsc.guide.install_a_desktop.text9: UNIX System V installs its programs from its install media, and has no package manager. A desktop is not added from the Mirror on UNIX.
jsc.guide.install_a_desktop.title: Installing a desktop

jsc.guide.install_debian.text1: Debian has its own installer, titled "Debian installer". You start it from the install medium, as you do for Ubuntu. It is a grey window with a tab on its top edge that carries the page's heading.
jsc.guide.install_debian.text2: The line at the bottom shows the keys to use. Read that line with care: some of the keys it names do nothing here.
jsc.guide.install_debian.text3: The installer goes through its pages in order, and ENTER goes on from each page. The software page appears only when a Mirror answers.
jsc.guide.install_debian.text4: The name page has the heading "Configure the network", which is the installer's own text. The field on that page is the computer's name, and the name becomes the host name.
jsc.guide.install_debian.text5: The line at the bottom reads "<Tab> moves; <Space> selects; <Enter> activates buttons". On Debian, Tab and Space do nothing. Use UP and DOWN to move, and ENTER to choose.

You start it from its install medium, the disc or stick a system is installed from, after you boot the computer from that drive ([](jsc:firmware)). The installer opens in a window titled "Ubuntu installer", with a band across the top that holds the page's heading and the words "[ Help ]".

jsc.guide.installing.text1: A computer without a system is a box that shows its firmware. The system is what you actually use: its files and its programs. To install one, you start the computer from the system's install medium, and follow its installer.
jsc.guide.installing.text2: Every era has its own install medium. It goes in a drive that reads it. The drive has to be joined to the computer, like any other device ([](jsc:drives)).
jsc.guide.installing.text3: Programs come on media of their own. The Standard uses DVD-ROM for programs, the Advanced uses Blu-ray for them, and both use the USB Flash Drive for background services.
jsc.guide.installing.text4: Not every system holds your hand. Arch Linux and Gentoo boot like a live medium, and you put their system on the disk by hand. Gentoo also builds its programs from source.
jsc.guide.installing.text5: A server setting can make both ask for every step. In the jscomputers-server config file, install_by_hand.arch_every_step and install_by_hand.gentoo_every_step are off by default. With the Arch setting on, Arch asks for the whole guide, plus the hardware clock and a name for the machine. With the Gentoo setting on, Gentoo asks for the whole handbook.
jsc.guide.installing.text6: A system needs hardware of its era or newer, so Frames 10 will not go on a Legacy computer, and the installer says so ([](jsc:the_systems)).
jsc.guide.installing.title: Installing a system
jsc.guide.installing.value1_1: Floppy Disk, in a Floppy Drive
jsc.guide.installing.value1_4: USB Flash Drive, in a Dock Station or a case's USB port
jsc.guide.installing_by_hand.definition1: The floppy disk, compact disc (CD), digital versatile disc (DVD) or universal serial bus (USB) stick a system is installed from.
jsc.guide.installing_by_hand.definition2: An install medium that is running with its own shell. The shell comes from the medium, not from your disk, and nothing is installed until you type the steps.
jsc.guide.installing_by_hand.definition3: A Linux system you install by hand from its live medium, taking its base system from the network's package repository.
jsc.guide.installing_by_hand.definition4: A Linux system you install by hand from its live medium, compiling its base system and its kernel from source.
jsc.guide.installing_by_hand.fix1: That shell is the live medium. Nothing is installed yet: read the walkthrough and type its steps, starting with help ([](jsc:the_walkthrough)).
jsc.guide.installing_by_hand.problem1: You expect an installer to start on its own, and a shell opens instead.
jsc.guide.installing_by_hand.table1: The two systems installed by hand
jsc.guide.installing_by_hand.table1_1_3: The base system is installed from the network's package repository.
jsc.guide.installing_by_hand.table1_2_3: The base system and the kernel are compiled from source first, which takes time.
jsc.guide.installing_by_hand.text1: Most systems install themselves. You put their medium in a drive, boot from it, and the installer does the work while it asks you a few questions. Arch Linux and Gentoo do not work that way. You type each step of their installation yourself, in order, and the system answers the way the real tool would.
jsc.guide.installing_by_hand.text2: The install medium is the floppy disk, compact disc (CD), digital versatile disc (DVD) or universal serial bus (USB) stick that a system is installed from. For these two systems it is a CD. When you boot it, the CD runs its own shell, a line where you type commands, and that running CD is the live medium.
jsc.guide.installing_by_hand.text3: The shell answers with the real tools' words, and it refuses what a real machine would refuse at that step. A mistake looks like a mistake on a real computer, so you learn the same reasons the real systems give.
jsc.guide.installing_by_hand.text4: The install ends when you type reboot. The shell refuses the reboot until the new system has everything it needs to start, and it lists what is missing. How long the steps take depends on your machine: a slow machine takes longer to compile (Gentoo) and to unpack (Arch Linux).
jsc.guide.installing_by_hand.text5: Before you boot the medium, check what you need ([](jsc:what_you_need)).
jsc.guide.installing_by_hand.title: Installing by hand

jsc.guide.installing_linux_keys.text2: The disk page lists the disks of the machine in four columns: "Disk", "Size", "Free" and "Holds". A disk can take the system only when its free room covers what the system takes. A disk marked for erasing counts as empty, so its whole size counts.
jsc.guide.installing_linux_keys.text3: To erase a disk, press E on the disk page. The prompt reads "Erase Disk N?", where N is the disk's number. It says every file on the disk will be deleted and that "This cannot be undone." Below it, "Y = erase" and "N = cancel" show the keys.
jsc.guide.installing_linux_keys.text4: The name page says "This name identifies the computer at the prompt and on the network." The name becomes the host name and the name shown in the prompt.
jsc.guide.installing_linux_keys.text5: The desktop page appears only when a Mirror answers. Its list holds the desktops this machine can run: a Legacy computer sees KDE Plasma and GNOME, and a Standard computer also sees Cinnamon. Choosing "None, the terminal only" leaves the system at its terminal.
jsc.guide.installing_linux_keys.text6: The copy page shows the progress as "<n>% complete" and "About <n> seconds left". When the copy ends, the installer says "INSTALLATION COMPLETE" and asks you to "Take the installation medium out before rebooting, or the machine boots the installer again."

jsc.guide.installpkg.text1: Programs on UNIX System V come on their own medium, and you install them with installpkg. There is no package manager and no Mirror. The program is on the medium, and the medium must be in a drive linked to the computer ([](jsc:drives)).
jsc.guide.installpkg.text2: With nothing said, installpkg takes the program on the medium in the drive, which is how the real system worked: the medium is the question and the answer. With more than one medium in, it lists the programs and asks you to say which one, by name.
jsc.guide.installpkg.text3: The setup line names the medium: the floppy, the compact disc (CD), the digital versatile disc (DVD), the USB drive (Universal Serial Bus) or the Blu-ray disc.
jsc.guide.installpkg.text4: A program written for a newer era than your computer is refused, with the line about its hardware. A program written for the Vintage era, on a floppy, has no era rule.
jsc.guide.installpkg.text5: Installed programs go to /usr/bin. While a program's medium is in a drive, its files appear under /mnt with the letter of the drive.
jsc.guide.installpkg.title: Installing a package from the medium

jsc.guide.interactor_screen.text1: The Interactor is the network's full-screen window on MC-NET. On its own it takes the whole terminal. Its headings are the network, the servers, what is held back, the work in flight and what you have starred, and a list sits under them.
jsc.guide.interactor_screen.text2: Arrows move through the list. Tab goes to the next heading, and typing looks for something. Along the foot of the screen are ten keys, labelled 1 to 10. Each key is the function key of the same number: press [[F1]] for key 1, up to [[F10]] for key 10.
jsc.guide.interactor_screen.text3: The same words work at the prompt, and they do the same things. Each one is shown here with what it does.
jsc.guide.interactor_screen.text4: The option --to local leaves what is taken in this computer, and not in your hands. The option --sort count orders a listing by how much there is, and --sort name orders it by name.
jsc.guide.interactor_screen.text5: You can name an item the way you would say it: cobblestone, minecraft:cobblestone, or "oak log". A name that fits more than one thing is answered with the things it fits, so that your next line can name the one you meant.
jsc.guide.interactor_screen.text6: With words, the Interactor does the one thing you asked and gives the prompt back. An operation that takes time prints its number, and its result appears before the next prompt.
jsc.guide.interactor_screen.title: The Interactor

jsc.guide.iql.fix2: Add TO, and the name of a bus ([](jsc:buses)).

jsc.guide.iql.problem3: The result says MOVE is internal and needs both FROM and TO.
jsc.guide.iql.problem4: The result says nothing to select.

jsc.guide.iql.step1: Open the Command Prompt on a computer that is on the network.
jsc.guide.iql.step2: Type iql, a space, and the statement, such as iql SELECT 64 Cobblestone.
jsc.guide.iql.text1: Clicking in the Network program is fine for taking a stack of iron. But what if you want to ask which items the network holds more than 100 of, or to craft 64 torches from a script? That is what IQL is for: asking the network for anything, in words, at a command prompt, in a program or in a script.
jsc.guide.iql.text2: IQL reads like the language of databases. A few lines show the idea:
jsc.guide.iql.text3: A statement starts with a verb. An action needs a quantity and an item, and it may add other clauses. A question starts with QUERY or SHOW. The quantity is a number, or ALL for everything the network holds of that item. Percentages such as 50% are not supported.
jsc.guide.iql.text4: The words operation, op and sql do the same as iql. Outside the network, the command refuses to run, and it says that the computer is not on a network.
jsc.guide.iql.text5: The IQL Server Management Studio is the full console: you query the network, trace its work, look after its index and locks, and run its jobs from one place. It needs the Midsoft IQL Server, version 2000 or newer ([](jsc:studio_overview)).
jsc.guide.iql.text6: A script is statements separated by semicolons. Two dashes start a comment that runs to the end of the line. A script can also have parameters, written like <name, type, default>, and the Studio asks you for their values when you run it.
jsc.guide.iql.text7: On an engine that keeps them, you can save a query as a view or a procedure. A job runs statements on a timer, or when a condition is met. A job needs the Automation Engine installed on the Mainframe ([](jsc:automation_engine)).
jsc.guide.iql.text8: The book Learning IQL explains every verb, clause and error, each in its own entry ([](jsc:what_iql_is)).
jsc.guide.iql.title: IQL, the network's language
jsc.guide.iql.warning1: DROP destroys items for good. DELETE with ALL sends out everything the network holds of an item. The Studio asks before it runs either one, unless you have turned that question off.
jsc.guide.iql_count.fix1: COUNT needs an object or an item after it, such as COUNT items.
jsc.guide.iql_count.fix2: A file that runs at the prompt refuses QUERY and COUNT. Type the read at the prompt, one statement at a time.
jsc.guide.iql_count.problem2: <file>: QUERY/COUNT are not supported by 'run', use 'operation' instead
jsc.guide.iql_count.text1: COUNT is written like a query, but it does not add up the quantities. It reads the same rows as QUERY, and the reply tells you how many rows there are.
jsc.guide.iql_count.text2: So the reply is a row count, such as "12 rows". To see each row's quantity, read the qty column of a QUERY items, or open the table view in the Management Studio ([](jsc:studio_queries)).
jsc.guide.iql_count.text3: COUNT reads an IF clause, but it ignores it. Your rows are listed whatever the IF says.
jsc.guide.iql_count.title: COUNT

jsc.guide.iql_craft.step1: Type CRAFT, a quantity and the item, such as CRAFT 64 torch.

jsc.guide.iql_craft.text1: CRAFT asks the network to make items from its recipes. You do not make the items by hand. The network uses the patterns it has learned ([](jsc:patterns)) and the machines that carry them out.
jsc.guide.iql_craft.text2: CRAFT needs an engine running on the Mainframe, because an engine works out how to make the craft. Without one, the network refuses the statement. What an [engine](jsc:iql_engines_overview) is, and how you start one, is explained there.
jsc.guide.iql_craft.text3: With no quantity, the reply shows "all" in place of the number. PRIORITY works on a CRAFT as it does on the other actions ([](jsc:clauses_priority_if_with)). FROM and TO are read, but CRAFT does not use them. The recipes are the patterns the network has learned, such as those a Crafting Interface holds ([](jsc:crafting_interfaces)).
jsc.guide.iql_craft.title: CRAFT
jsc.guide.iql_engines_overview.definitio: A program on the Mainframe that reads IQL, plans how the network does the work, and hands the plan on. Only one installed program of this kind plans at a time.
The one computer of a network that runs the network's own software, such as the engine that plans its work.
The flavour of IQL an engine speaks. Every dialect accepts the core language, so the same core statements work on every engine.
jsc.guide.iql_engines_overview.fix1: No engine runs. Start one in the Services tab ([](jsc:engine_services)).
jsc.guide.iql_engines_overview.problem1: A craft or a query says the Network Operations Service is unavailable.
jsc.guide.iql_engines_overview.text1: When you type an IQL statement, something has to read it and decide how the network does the work. On the network, that something is an engine. It runs as a program on the Mainframe ([](jsc:mainframes)), reads the statement, plans the steps, and hands the plan to the part of the network that carries the work out.
jsc.guide.iql_engines_overview.text2: A new Mainframe comes with the Midsoft IQL Server installed and running, in the version of its age. Two more engines exist: NextgreIQL and Prophet YourIQL. Each speaks its own dialect of the language, and each offers extras beyond the core.
jsc.guide.iql_engines_overview.text3: You manage an engine in the Services tab of the Network Manager ([](jsc:network_manager)), and a program that needs a particular engine says so when you open it. Every engine answers the same core: transfers, crafts and the statements of the core language.
jsc.guide.iql_engines_overview.text4: Only one engine plans at a time, the active engine. When you stop or replace it, the Operations already running keep going on the plans they started with. You can still browse, deposit and withdraw items with no engine running.
jsc.guide.iql_engines_overview.text5: With no engine running, transfers keep working, but crafts and IQL queries are refused. You start an engine to plan again.
jsc.guide.iql_engines_overview.title: What an engine is

jsc.guide.iql_errors.text1: A refusal is an error message that stops a statement before it runs. You read it from the start: the first words say what went wrong, and the words in angle brackets show where your own text goes. Find the message below, and read the fix beside it.
jsc.guide.iql_errors.text2: A file runs one statement per line. Blank lines and lines that start with -- are left out. A semicolon does not split a line in a file, so put one statement on each line. The file stops at the first statement that fails, and the statements above it have already run. The whole file is read first, so a syntax error on any line means nothing runs.
jsc.guide.iql_errors.title: Error messages and their fixes

jsc.guide.iql_jobs.text1: A job is a statement that the network runs on its own. You give it a trigger: a time interval with EVERY, or a condition with WHEN. Each time the trigger fires, the statement runs again.
jsc.guide.iql_jobs.text2: Jobs are kept by the [Automation Engine](jsc:automation_engine), which must be installed on the Mainframe. Jobs also need the [Midsoft IQL Server](jsc:midsoft_iql_server).
jsc.guide.iql_jobs.text3: The trigger word is the last EVERY or WHEN that stands outside quotes and braces. Jobs run only while the Automation Engine is installed and running. A paused job stays idle until you restart it from the Processes tab. A job is credited to the player who created it.
jsc.guide.iql_jobs.text4: The network checks the jobs every 10 ticks, so an interval is exact to about 10 ticks. The first check starts the clock, so a job does not fire at once.
jsc.guide.iql_jobs.text5: WHEN fires the job once, when its condition turns from false to true. It does not fire again while the condition stays true. A condition that is already true fires at the first check.
jsc.guide.iql_jobs.text6: The only field a WHEN can read is qty(item), which is the network's total of that item. A WHEN with any other field never fires.
jsc.guide.iql_jobs.text7: A CREATE JOB whose statement is SET BUS with WHEN TIME does not make a job. It sets the hours of the bus instead ([](jsc:set_bus)).
jsc.guide.iql_jobs.title: Jobs, EVERY and WHEN
jsc.guide.iql_library.definition1: One line of a result, given as a map of name, quantity and detail.
jsc.guide.iql_library.fix1: Build a network with a Mainframe, and check Mainframe.Online before you call Iql.
jsc.guide.iql_library.fix2: Use Run or Exec instead. They give Ok false and the message, and the program goes on.
jsc.guide.iql_library.fix3: Read the message. It is the network's answer, and the verbs are explained in [](jsc:iql).
jsc.guide.iql_library.fix4: Check the path with File.Exists before you call RunFile.
jsc.guide.iql_library.problem1: The program stops and says this computer is not on a network with a Mainframe.

jsc.guide.iql_library.table1_1_2: Runs one statement and gives an IqlResult. A refused statement does not stop the program.
jsc.guide.iql_library.table1_2_2: Runs a statement and gives its rows as a list of maps. A refused statement stops the program.
jsc.guide.iql_library.table1_3_2: Runs a statement and gives an IqlResult.
jsc.guide.iql_library.table1_4_2: The same, with the values passed to a stored statement.
jsc.guide.iql_library.table1_5_2: Runs each statement in the file and gives an IqlResult.
jsc.guide.iql_library.table2_1_3: Ok: yes when the network took the statement. Message: the network's answer. Rows: the result lines.
jsc.guide.iql_library.text1: IQL is the network's query language. One IQL statement asks for something, or changes what the network holds and does. The language itself is in [](jsc:iql), and the book Learning IQL teaches it from zero in [](jsc:what_iql_is).
jsc.guide.iql_library.text2: Iql lets a program send those statements itself, instead of you typing them at a prompt. Every Iql call needs a network with a Mainframe. Only Sigma# programs can use it.
jsc.guide.iql_library.text3: Exec puts EXEC in front of your statement, and adds each value after the statement, one after another. Use it to pass values to a stored statement.
jsc.guide.iql_library.text4: RunFile reads the file first. When the file cannot be read, the program stops with the file's message.
jsc.guide.iql_library.text5: Each row is a map with three keys: name, quantity and detail. The name is the item or thing the row is about, quantity is its count, and detail says more about it.
jsc.guide.iql_library.title: Iql: the network's language from a program
