jsc.guide.iql_limits.text1: The network sets limits on what one statement can take. Some limits cut a result short.
jsc.guide.iql_limits.text2: Others refuse the statement, or stop it part way, and show a message.
jsc.guide.iql_limits.text3: The table gives each limit and what happens when you pass it.
jsc.guide.iql_limits.text4: Some limits protect the network, not your statement. If a QUERY reaches 4,096 rows, use a WHERE to narrow the rows you read, so the rows you need are not cut short.

jsc.guide.iql_names_quotes_columns.text1: Every statement starts with a verb: the word for what the statement does, such as SELECT or QUERY. The verb is followed by the item or the object the statement works on. Clause words come after that. Each one adds a part: WHERE picks rows, ORDER BY sorts them and LIMIT cuts them short.
jsc.guide.iql_names_quotes_columns.text2: Verbs and clause words do not care about capitals, so query items and QUERY Items mean the same thing. A name with no colon is a vanilla item: cobblestone means minecraft:cobblestone. Read the three kinds of text below, because IQL reads each kind in its own way.
jsc.guide.iql_names_quotes_columns.text3: A sign such as = or < joins to a word that has no space around it. So qty<100 reads as three parts: qty, < and 100. Put a space on each side of a sign, and you avoid the problem.
jsc.guide.iql_names_quotes_columns.text4: Item names have no spaces, so an item is always a plain word. A bus name can have spaces, so you put it in quotes after SET: SET BUS 'Ore in' ON.

jsc.guide.iql_names_quotes_columns.text6: An item has more fields than its table shows. A WHERE clause can compare any of these:
jsc.guide.iql_names_quotes_columns.text7: A comment starts with two dashes, --, and runs to the end of the line. A line that starts with the dashes does nothing when a file runs. The Management Studio can also ask you for a value when a script runs: its templates are in ([](jsc:studio_templates)).

jsc.guide.iql_procedures.definition1: A list of statements saved under one name. EXEC runs the statements in order.

jsc.guide.iql_procedures.fix2: Fix the statement that failed, then run EXEC again.
jsc.guide.iql_procedures.fix3: A procedure runs itself, directly or through another. Remove the loop.
jsc.guide.iql_procedures.fix4: Give the procedures fewer statements to run, or split the work into several requests.
jsc.guide.iql_procedures.fix6: Run one procedure at a time, with one EXEC for each name.
jsc.guide.iql_procedures.fix7: Check the name, or create the procedure first.
jsc.guide.iql_procedures.fix8: Type the name after DROP PROCEDURE.
jsc.guide.iql_procedures.problem1: CREATE PROCEDURE needs a name and an AS body
jsc.guide.iql_procedures.problem3: IQL recursion too deep (a procedure or view referencing itself?)

jsc.guide.iql_procedures.step1: Type CREATE PROCEDURE, a name, AS, and the statements in braces, with a semicolon after each statement but the last.
jsc.guide.iql_procedures.step3: Type EXEC and the name to run it, such as EXEC restock.
jsc.guide.iql_procedures.table1_1_2: Every statement ran, and the reply counts them.
jsc.guide.iql_procedures.table1_2_2: The statement with that number failed. The message after it says why.
jsc.guide.iql_procedures.text1: A procedure is a list of statements saved under one name. When you run it with EXEC, the statements run one after another, so one name does several things for you.
jsc.guide.iql_procedures.text2: A procedure can also hold a single statement, without braces. PROC means the same as PROCEDURE, and CALL means the same as EXEC.
jsc.guide.iql_procedures.text3: The statements run in order. If one fails, the procedure stops there, and the statements before it have already run. Procedures need the same engine as views ([](jsc:iql_views)).
jsc.guide.iql_procedures.text4: A procedure can run another procedure or a view, up to 32 levels deep. One request may run at most 4,096 statements. Past either limit, the network stops and shows the message.
jsc.guide.iql_procedures.title: Procedures and EXEC
jsc.guide.iql_views.definition1: A saved statement with a name. Each time you type the name, the network runs the saved statement again.
jsc.guide.iql_views.fix1: Type VIEW, PROCEDURE or JOB after CREATE.
jsc.guide.iql_views.fix2: Type a name after VIEW, then AS and the statement. The same holds for PROCEDURE and JOB.
jsc.guide.iql_views.fix3: Type the word AS after the name.
jsc.guide.iql_views.fix5: Shorten the name to 64 characters or fewer.
jsc.guide.iql_views.fix6: Use an engine that keeps them: the Midsoft IQL Server ([](jsc:midsoft_iql_server)).
jsc.guide.iql_views.problem1: CREATE expects VIEW, PROCEDURE, or JOB

jsc.guide.iql_views.step1: Type CREATE VIEW, a name, AS and the statement, all on one line.
jsc.guide.iql_views.step3: Type QUERY and the name to run it, such as QUERY low_iron.
jsc.guide.iql_views.table1_3_2: Type the name after DROP VIEW.
jsc.guide.iql_views.text1: A view is a statement that you save under a name. You write it once, with CREATE VIEW. Then each time you type the name, the network runs the saved statement again, so the answer is what it is now.
jsc.guide.iql_views.text2: The saved statement is kept exactly as you typed it. It can be any statement, though it is usually a QUERY.
jsc.guide.iql_views.text3: Saved statements are kept on the Mainframe. A name is unique for each kind of saved statement, and capitals do not matter.
jsc.guide.iql_views.text4: Views need the [Midsoft IQL Server](jsc:midsoft_iql_server) on the Mainframe. Other engines refuse them.
jsc.guide.iql_views.text5: To remove a view, type DROP VIEW and its name, such as DROP VIEW low_iron.
jsc.guide.iql_views.title: Views
jsc.guide.items_as_data.definition1: The room an item takes on a disk: 1 MB in the Vintage, 16 MB in the Legacy, 256 MB from the Transition on.
jsc.guide.items_as_data.table1: Disk sizes in items, from the Transition on
jsc.guide.items_as_data.text1: The network keeps your items on the disks of its computers, as data. Its disks count items, not raw space. A bucket of fluid takes as much room as one item.
jsc.guide.items_as_data.text2: How much room an item takes depends on the era of the disk, because older computers had smaller words: 1 MB in the Vintage, 16 MB in the Legacy, and 256 MB from the Transition on. So a 20 MB Vintage drive holds 20 items, and a 1 terabyte (TB) disk holds 4,096 items from the Transition on.
jsc.guide.items_as_data.text3: Above 8 TB, only hard disks are made, up to 24 TB, which holds 98,304 items.
jsc.guide.items_as_data.text4: Memory works in items too, in its own way. Each memory module keeps a buffer of items for the Mainframe, one item for every 4 MB of the module's size ([](jsc:memory)). A buffer too small for the processor leaves the processor waiting for memory.
jsc.guide.items_as_data.text5: Disks differ in speed. A solid-state drive (SSD) is 4 times as fast as a hard disk, and an NVMe disk is 16 times as fast ([](jsc:disks)).
jsc.guide.items_as_data.title: Items as data
jsc.guide.jade.fix1: That is expected for now. Read the block's own page in this guide, which explains its window and its parts.
jsc.guide.jade.problem1: Jade shows only a name on a Computers block.
jsc.guide.jade.text1: Jade is a mod that tells you what you are looking at. Point at a block, and a small box shows its name and a few lines about it. Jade is optional.
jsc.guide.jade.text2: When Jade is installed, the plugin of this series for it switches on. A machine that describes its state to Jade adds a line to the box, such as "Working: 40%" or "Idle", as the processing machines of J's Industrial do.
jsc.guide.jade.text3: The blocks of J's Computers do not describe themselves to Jade. For them, the box shows the block's name and nothing more.
jsc.guide.jade.title: Jade
jsc.guide.jei_and_emi.definition1: A screen in a mod that lists recipes: which ingredients make which result.
jsc.guide.jei_and_emi.definition2: The button of a recipe viewer that sends a recipe's ingredients to the Pattern Studio.
jsc.guide.jei_and_emi.definition3: The side panel of a recipe viewer that lists the items you can use as ingredients.
jsc.guide.jei_and_emi.definition4: The unit of volume for fluids on the network: one thousandth of a bucket.
jsc.guide.jei_and_emi.fix1: Open the Studio on the desktop, bring it to the front, and press the button again.
jsc.guide.jei_and_emi.fix2: The Bench tab fills the grid in the viewer's order. Rearrange the cells in the Bench tab.
jsc.guide.jei_and_emi.fix3: A recipe with no items or fluids that could be mapped leaves the draft incomplete. Add the missing input or output in the Machine tab.
jsc.guide.jei_and_emi.fix4: Only recipes that machines make fit the Machine tab. Choose a recipe that a machine makes.

jsc.guide.jei_and_emi.problem2: The recipe lands on the wrong cells.
jsc.guide.jei_and_emi.problem3: The Machine tab says "The machine draft needs an input and an output."
jsc.guide.jei_and_emi.problem4: The Studio says "Not a machine recipe: <name>".
jsc.guide.jei_and_emi.table1_1_3: Its ingredients fill the grid in the viewer's order.
jsc.guide.jei_and_emi.table1_2_3: One data cell for each input and each output.
jsc.guide.jei_and_emi.text1: A recipe viewer is a screen that lists how things are made. JEI and EMI are two of them, and each one is optional. With JEI installed, you can send a recipe from the viewer to the Pattern Studio, which writes the patterns for autocrafting ([](jsc:pattern_studio)).
jsc.guide.jei_and_emi.text2: In JEI, each recipe you can send has a transfer button. Pressing it moves the recipe's ingredients into the Pattern Studio. The Studio has two tabs for this, and the recipe goes to the one it fits.
jsc.guide.jei_and_emi.text3: The Bench tab has a grid of nine cells, three by three. The ingredients fill it row by row, in the order the viewer shows them. Any ingredient beyond the ninth is left out.
jsc.guide.jei_and_emi.text4: The Machine tab takes the other recipes, such as the ones of J's Industrial machines. Each input and output becomes a data cell there: an item with its count, or a fluid in millibuckets (mB).
jsc.guide.jei_and_emi.text5: The Pattern Studio must be the front window of its desktop, or the transfer button refuses and the viewer shows an error.
jsc.guide.jei_and_emi.text6: You can also drag an item from the ingredient list onto a cell of the Studio. The cell takes that item, as if you had clicked it with the item on your cursor.
jsc.guide.jei_and_emi.text7: EMI lists the same recipes and can show one of its categories. A recipe does not move from EMI into the Pattern Studio, so use JEI when you want a transfer.
jsc.guide.jei_and_emi.text8: When J's Industrial is installed, its macerating and compressing recipes also appear in JEI and EMI, each in its own category.
jsc.guide.jei_and_emi.title: Recipe viewers: JEI and EMI
jsc.guide.kde_plasma.definition1: KDE's start menu: a launcher you open from the panel, with a list of programs beside its places.
jsc.guide.kde_plasma.definition2: The boot step that starts a graphical desktop. The boot lines name the desktop it starts.
jsc.guide.kde_plasma.fix1: The computer is a Vintage one. Use a Legacy computer or a newer one.
jsc.guide.kde_plasma.fix2: Plasma takes 256 MB of disk. Free some disk space, then try again.
jsc.guide.kde_plasma.problem1: The package manager says "kde-plasma needs Legacy hardware or later".
jsc.guide.kde_plasma.problem2: The package manager says "unmet requirements (hardware or free disk space)".
jsc.guide.kde_plasma.text1: KDE Plasma is the desktop of the KDE project. It runs on Linux and FreeBSD, on Legacy hardware or later, and its package is named kde-plasma. Its house is the KDE Guild, a software house of the mod's world.
jsc.guide.kde_plasma.text2: KDE changes its face with the era. On Legacy hardware you see KDE 2. On Transition you see KDE 4, with its Kickoff 4 menu. From the Standard on you see KDE Plasma.
jsc.guide.kde_plasma.text3: The panel sits along the bottom of the screen. On KDE Plasma, Kickoff is a two-pane launcher: a column of places beside the list of programs. Type in it, and the search looks through every program. KDE 4 shows the tabs Favorites, Applications, Computer, Recently Used and Leave.
jsc.guide.kde_plasma.text4: KDE gives seven programs their own names, as the table shows. The rest keep the names they have on every desktop ([](jsc:desktop_program_names)).
jsc.guide.kde_plasma.text5: To install it, use the form for your system in [](jsc:install_a_desktop). On Debian and Ubuntu, that is apt install kde-plasma. The boot lines call it kde plasma, as in "Starting kde plasma Display Manager".
jsc.guide.kde_plasma.title: KDE Plasma
jsc.guide.kernel_gentoo.definition1: A script that builds the kernel and its modules with one command.
jsc.guide.kernel_gentoo.definition2: A piece of the kernel that loads when something needs it, kept as its own file.
jsc.guide.kernel_gentoo.fix1: Step into the new system first: chroot /mnt/gentoo /bin/bash. make needs the same step.
jsc.guide.kernel_gentoo.fix2: Download the sources first: emerge sys-kernel/gentoo-sources.
jsc.guide.kernel_gentoo.fix3: Download the sources first: emerge sys-kernel/gentoo-sources.
jsc.guide.kernel_gentoo.fix4: The kernel is built in its sources. Type cd /usr/src/linux first.
jsc.guide.kernel_gentoo.fix5: The kernel is not built yet. Type make first, then the install.
jsc.guide.kernel_gentoo.problem1: genkernel says "command not found", because the command is on the new system and you are still in the live medium.
jsc.guide.kernel_gentoo.problem2: genkernel says "* ERROR: no kernel sources found in /usr/src".
jsc.guide.kernel_gentoo.problem3: eselect says "!!! Error: No kernel sources found in /usr/src".
jsc.guide.kernel_gentoo.problem4: make says it has no targets and no makefile.
jsc.guide.kernel_gentoo.problem5: make says it has no rule for the target vmlinux.
jsc.guide.kernel_gentoo.step2: Type eselect kernel list and press [[Enter]] to see the kernels.
jsc.guide.kernel_gentoo.step3: Type eselect kernel set 1 and press [[Enter]]. The command prints nothing.
jsc.guide.kernel_gentoo.step4: Build and install the kernel by one of the two routes in the table below.
jsc.guide.kernel_gentoo.table1_1_3: Builds the kernel and its modules, and copies the kernel into /boot.
jsc.guide.kernel_gentoo.table1_2_3: Builds in /usr/src/linux, installs the modules, and copies the kernel into /boot.
jsc.guide.kernel_gentoo.text1: The kernel is the part of the system that drives the hardware. Every program reaches the processor, the memory and the disks through it. Gentoo builds your kernel from its sources, so the install downloads the sources first.
jsc.guide.kernel_gentoo.text2: This install uses kernel version 6.11.5. Its files carry the name 6.11.5-gentoo, and the compressed kernel goes into /boot.
jsc.guide.kernel_gentoo.text3: genkernel is a script that builds the whole kernel with one command. The by-hand route runs in /usr/src/linux, the folder that the kernel choice makes.
jsc.guide.kernel_gentoo.text4: The modules live under /lib/modules, in a folder named for the kernel version.
jsc.guide.kernel_gentoo.title: The kernel
jsc.guide.knot.definition1: The desktop program that saves the revisions of a file and shows what changed between them.
jsc.guide.knot.definition2: The store of every file and every revision that one KnotHub keeps.
jsc.guide.knot.definition3: One saved state of one file in the repository, with its author, its message and the time it was saved.
jsc.guide.knot.definition4: The list of lines that changed between a revision and the revision before it.
jsc.guide.knot.fix1: Put a system disk in the computer. Knot reads files from it.
jsc.guide.knot.fix2: Check the path in the File field. Knot reads the file from the system disk, by its full path.
jsc.guide.knot.fix3: The file has the same text as its newest revision, so nothing new was saved. Change the file and push again. A new file is also refused once the repository holds 64 files, and the window shows the same message for that case.
jsc.guide.knot.fix4: The system disk is full. Free some space on it, then pull again.
jsc.guide.knot.fix5: The revision was dropped, or the KnotHub was reset. Pick another revision from the history.
jsc.guide.knot.fix6: No Server with KnotHub is running. See the KnotHub entry ([](jsc:knothub_service)).
jsc.guide.knot.problem2: Push says No <file> on this machine.
jsc.guide.knot.problem3: Push says Nothing changed since the last revision.
jsc.guide.knot.problem4: Pull says Not enough free space.
jsc.guide.knot.problem6: The window says No KnotHub on this network.
jsc.guide.knot.step1: Type the file's full path in the File field.
jsc.guide.knot.step2: Type a message in the message box, if you want one.
jsc.guide.knot.step4: Read the answer on the status bar, such as Pushed plant.sgs.
jsc.guide.knot.step5: Click the revision in the history.
jsc.guide.knot.step7: Read the answer, such as Wrote r3 to plant.sgs.
jsc.guide.knot.table1_1_2: Push saves a new revision, Pull writes the picked revision back to disk, and Refresh asks the KnotHub for the state again.
jsc.guide.knot.table1_2_2: The full path of the file a Push reads. A Pull does not use it.
jsc.guide.knot.table1_3_2: The note a push carries, up to 128 characters.
jsc.guide.knot.table1_4_2: The newest revisions, each with its number, author and message. It shows 4 rows and scrolls.
jsc.guide.knot.table1_5_2: The changes of the picked revision against the one before it: a plus sign for an added line, a minus sign for a removed line, and plain lines that did not change.
jsc.guide.knot.table1_6_2: On the left, the last answer, or the KnotHub's host name. On the right, the number of revisions and the size of the repository.
jsc.guide.knot.table2_1_2: The window is not on a computer.
jsc.guide.knot.table2_2_2: The computer has no system disk.
jsc.guide.knot.table2_3_2: Push cannot find the file on the system disk.
jsc.guide.knot.table2_4_2: The file has the same text as its newest revision, or it is a new file and the repository already holds 64 files.
jsc.guide.knot.table2_6_2: The picked revision is gone from the history, or the KnotHub was reset.
jsc.guide.knot.table2_7_2: Pull could not write: the disk is full.
jsc.guide.knot.text1: Knot is a desktop program that keeps the source of a file you are still writing. Each time you push the file, Knot saves a copy as a revision in the network's repository. A revision holds one saved state of the file, with its author, its message and the time it was saved.
jsc.guide.knot.text2: Knot then shows you who changed what, line by line. It works only where a KnotHub is running on the network ([](jsc:knothub_service)). Knot is not a package manager: a package is a finished program handed to others, and Knot keeps the source before that.
jsc.guide.knot.text3: Click a row of the history to pick that revision. The File field then shows the revision's file, and the comparison shows its changes. The newest revision is picked when the window opens.
jsc.guide.knot.text4: Knot reads the file from the system disk of the computer you are at, not from the text in the window. A push with an empty message is saved as "no message". A push of the same text as the newest revision of that file changes nothing, so Knot refuses it.
jsc.guide.knot.text5: A Pull writes the revision back to the file it belongs to, on the system disk. It does not write to the path in the File field.
jsc.guide.knot.text6: A revision's number counts up across the whole repository, not file by file, and a number is never reused while the repository lives. The first revision of a file is compared with empty text, so every line of it shows as added.
jsc.guide.knot.text7: The comparison runs line by line, in reading order. A line that both versions share is shown as it is. A line only in the older version is removed, and a line only in the newer version is added. It does not search for the smallest set of changes, so it can show more lines than that.
jsc.guide.knot.title: Knot
jsc.guide.knot.warning1: When a file already has 64 revisions, its next push drops the oldest one, and nothing tells you so.
jsc.guide.knot_and_knothub.definition1: One saved state of a file in Knot, numbered r1, r2 and so on.
jsc.guide.knot_and_knothub.definition2: To send the file's current state to the repository as a new revision.
jsc.guide.knot_and_knothub.definition3: To fetch the network's copy of a file.
jsc.guide.knot_and_knothub.fix1: Install KnotHub on a server in a rack of this network, and let it run.
jsc.guide.knot_and_knothub.fix2: The file has not changed since its last revision. Change the file on your disk, then push again.
jsc.guide.knot_and_knothub.problem1: The window says No KnotHub on this network.
jsc.guide.knot_and_knothub.problem2: Push answers No change in r, followed by a number.
jsc.guide.knot_and_knothub.text1: Knot keeps the history of a file that the players of a network are still working on. You send the file to the network's repository, and Knot keeps it as a revision: one saved state of the file, numbered r1, r2 and so on.
jsc.guide.knot_and_knothub.text2: Knot holds the source that is still being worked on, before it becomes a finished package ([](jsc:programs)). Push reads the file from this computer's own disk, not from text typed in the window, so the network keeps what the machine really holds. The history runs along the top of the window, and the changes sit underneath.
jsc.guide.knot_and_knothub.text3: A file keeps at most 64 revisions, and the oldest go first. A repository keeps at most 64 files. Each revision is kept whole, not as a difference from the last one, so the computer that holds the repository needs the disk space for all of them.
jsc.guide.knot_and_knothub.text4: KnotHub keeps the repository for the network, and it runs on a server in a rack of the network ([](jsc:server_racks)). The [Book of Sigma](jsc:knot) explains Knot for programs.
jsc.guide.knot_and_knothub.title: Knot and KnotHub
jsc.guide.knothub_service.fix1: Put a Server with KnotHub installed in a Server Rack, and switch the Server on ([](jsc:server_racks)).
jsc.guide.knothub_service.fix2: The same fix applies: a running KnotHub must answer on the network.
jsc.guide.knothub_service.fix3: Put a system disk in the computer ([](jsc:knot)).
jsc.guide.knothub_service.fix4: The revision was dropped, or the KnotHub was reset. Pick another revision from the history.
jsc.guide.knothub_service.problem1: The window says No KnotHub on this network, and it shows no revisions.
jsc.guide.knothub_service.problem2: The status bar reads no service.
jsc.guide.knothub_service.problem3: Push or Pull says No System Disk.
jsc.guide.knothub_service.text1: KnotHub is the service that keeps the repository: every file you pushed with Knot and every revision of each one. It is installed on a Server, one of the computers in a Server Rack ([](jsc:server_racks)). It does not run on the Mainframe or on a desktop.
jsc.guide.knothub_service.text2: Each Server keeps its own repository, and the source is saved with that Server item. If you take the Server out of the rack, its history goes with it. Knot reads the repository of the first running KnotHub it finds on the network, in the order the network lists its Servers.
jsc.guide.knothub_service.text3: A KnotHub on a Server that is switched off does not answer. The window then shows no revisions, and its status bar reads no service.
jsc.guide.knothub_service.title: KnotHub
jsc.guide.knothub_service.warning1: Uninstalling KnotHub deletes all its source: every file and every revision. Its numbering starts again at revision 1.
jsc.guide.kvm_switch.definition1: One slot of height in a rack, counted in U. A KVM Switch takes one.
jsc.guide.kvm_switch.definition2: One computer of a rack, chosen on the bar of a KVM Switch.
jsc.guide.kvm_switch.fix1: Mount a KVM Switch in a free unit slot of the rack ([](jsc:server_racks)).
jsc.guide.kvm_switch.fix2: Put a computer in the rack.
jsc.guide.kvm_switch.fix3: That machine is not running: switch it on at its case.
jsc.guide.kvm_switch.problem1: This rack holds several computers - mount a KVM Switch to pick one
jsc.guide.kvm_switch.problem2: The rack holds no computer to show
jsc.guide.kvm_switch.table1_2_2: How many machines the rack holds, for example "2 machines".
jsc.guide.kvm_switch.table1_3_2: The label of each channel, one row for each computer.
jsc.guide.kvm_switch.table1_4_2: The name of the machine. A machine with no name shows its place in the rack, such as "bay 3U".
jsc.guide.kvm_switch.table1_5_2: ONLINE when the machine runs, and OFF when it does not.
jsc.guide.kvm_switch.text1: A KVM Switch lets one monitor reach every computer of a rack. It is a rack unit that you mount in a Server Rack ([](jsc:server_racks)).
jsc.guide.kvm_switch.text2: Each computer of the rack is a channel. A rack with one computer needs no KVM Switch: the monitor shows that computer. With two or more, the monitor first shows the channel bar, and you pick the machine you want.
jsc.guide.kvm_switch.text3: Pick a channel with a click on its row, or with the number keys 1 to 8. The machine's own screen then opens on top. The bar holds 8 channels at most.
jsc.guide.kvm_switch.title: The KVM Switch
jsc.guide.library.definition1: One of the seven books of J's Computers, read as pages in the game.
jsc.guide.library.fix1: The system and its install choose the first book, and you cannot change that. The other books still follow in their order.
jsc.guide.library.fix2: Open the creative tab J's Computers and look among the programs, beside the Guide.
jsc.guide.library.problem1: The help opened a book you did not expect.
jsc.guide.library.table1: The first book of each system
jsc.guide.library.table1_4_3: Installing by hand from the live medium
jsc.guide.library.table2_1_2: MC-DOS and the Frames editions, from Frames 95 to Frames 11.
jsc.guide.library.table2_2_2: Fedora, Debian and Ubuntu, and the shell, desktops, editors and help they share with the other UNIX books.
jsc.guide.library.table2_3_2: Installing Arch Linux and Gentoo by hand, one step at a time.
jsc.guide.library.table2_5_2: The network's query language, its engines and its tools.
jsc.guide.library.table2_6_2: Sigma and Sigma#, their library and their tools.
jsc.guide.library.text1: A book is an item you can hold. The Guide to Operations is the first, and six more sit beside it: the Frames Resource Kit, The Linux Desk Reference, Linux by Hand, The Daemon Handbook, Learning IQL and The Book of Sigma. Each book opens its own manual when you use it, and each is written for one family of systems or one language.
jsc.guide.library.text2: A manual is one of these seven books, read as pages in the game. You turn its pages and find its chapters the same way you read this Guide.
jsc.guide.library.text3: You get the books from the creative tab J's Computers, among the programs, beside this Guide. J's Computers has no crafting recipes of its own, so the creative tab is where you take one, unless your modpack gave the books a recipe; the recipe viewer shows it if so.
jsc.guide.library.text4: When you open a computer's help, the system opens its own book first, and the other books follow in their order. The help of MC-NET opens the Guide to Operations.
jsc.guide.library.text5: Every Linux install that is not guided opens Linux by Hand, which means Arch Linux and Gentoo.
jsc.guide.library.title: The library
jsc.guide.library_overview.definition1: A group of types with a dotted name, such as System.IO. A using line brings it in, so its types can be written by bare name.
jsc.guide.library_overview.definition2: The set of types and their members that a program can call, such as Console, File and Network.
jsc.guide.library_overview.definition3: A method, value or event that belongs to a type.
jsc.guide.library_overview.definition4: The level of the language a build is held to: 1 is the first level, and 2 is the newest.
jsc.guide.library_overview.definition5: The smaller language, Sigma, which offers fewer names than Sigma#.
jsc.guide.library_overview.fix1: Add the using line it names at the top of the file: using System.IO.*; for everything in the namespace, or using System.IO.<name>; for one type.
jsc.guide.library_overview.fix2: Write .* after the namespace to bring in everything in it.
jsc.guide.library_overview.fix3: Write using Standard.*; and use the names it holds, or write the program in Sigma#.
jsc.guide.library_overview.fix4: Use the replacement in the table of names Sigma refuses, or write the program in Sigma#, which has all of them. Threads have their own page ([](jsc:threads_and_locks)).
jsc.guide.library_overview.fix5: Use one of the members the compiler lists in its message.
jsc.guide.library_overview.fix6: Use the newest version of the compiler, or write the program without that name.
jsc.guide.library_overview.problem1: The compiler says a name is in a namespace you did not bring in, and it asks for a using line.
jsc.guide.library_overview.problem2: The compiler says a name is a namespace and refuses it alone.
jsc.guide.library_overview.problem3: The compiler says Sigma has no System library, and that everything Sigma has is in Standard.
jsc.guide.library_overview.problem4: The compiler refuses List, Map or Thread.
jsc.guide.library_overview.problem5: The compiler refuses a member that Sigma does not offer.
jsc.guide.library_overview.problem6: A version 1 build refuses a name that came in version 2.
jsc.guide.library_overview.step1: Write using Standard.*; at the top of the file, to bring in everything in Standard.
jsc.guide.library_overview.step2: Below the using line, write namespace, then a name of your own and a semicolon, such as namespace MyProgram;.
jsc.guide.library_overview.step3: Write the entry point of your kind of program, as the table below shows.
jsc.guide.library_overview.table1_2_2: A class that extends Script, with OnInit, OnTick or OnDestroy written in it.
jsc.guide.library_overview.table2_2_2: Every System namespace, such as System.IO
jsc.guide.library_overview.table3_1_2: An array, and a count of your own beside it.
jsc.guide.library_overview.table3_2_2: Two arrays, or one array you search for the key.
jsc.guide.library_overview.table3_3_2: Nothing: these machines run one thing at a time.
jsc.guide.library_overview.text1: A program reaches the machine through the library. The library is a set of named types, and each type has members you call, such as the terminal, files, the clock and the network.
jsc.guide.library_overview.text2: Sigma and Sigma# both use the library, but they do not reach the same part of it. Sigma is the smaller language, and it reaches only the library's Standard namespace. Sigma# is the whole language, and it reaches every System namespace, such as System.IO and System.Sound.
jsc.guide.library_overview.text3: Every name in Standard is a type Sigma# also has, under the namespace it has always had. A using line, explained in [](jsc:sigma_namespaces_using), brings a namespace in.
jsc.guide.library_overview.text4: Script is a base class in Standard. Its three methods do nothing until your class writes its own.
jsc.guide.library_overview.text5: A version is the level of the language a build is held to. There are two versions, 1 and 2, and version 2 is the newest. A build that asks for no version is held to the newest one.
jsc.guide.library_overview.text6: This book marks each name that came in version 2. A version 1 build refuses those names, so a program that uses them needs the newest version.
jsc.guide.library_overview.text7: Sigma refuses some names that Sigma# has. The compiler names the replacement it expects you to use.
jsc.guide.library_overview.text8: A member that Sigma does not offer is refused too. The compiler lists the members the type does have, in alphabetical order, so you can pick one of them.
jsc.guide.library_overview.title: The library, and the two languages
jsc.guide.listcmd.fix1: The switch is off on this server, so the command does not exist. Ask the server owner to set prompt.list_commands to true.
jsc.guide.listcmd.fix2: Each computer lists only what it has. A program appears under PROGRAMS once it is installed on that computer.
jsc.guide.listcmd.problem1: The reply is "command not found: listcmd".
jsc.guide.listcmd.problem2: The list is shorter on one computer than on another.
jsc.guide.listcmd.step1: Open jscomputers-server.toml in the serverconfig folder of the world.
jsc.guide.listcmd.table2: The two parts of the list
jsc.guide.listcmd.table2_1_2: One row per command this computer has, with its one-line summary.
jsc.guide.listcmd.table2_2_2: One row per installed program, with its name and its id.
jsc.guide.listcmd.text1: listcmd lists everything this computer can run: its commands, whichever system they belong to, and the programs installed on it. It prints one list, and nothing is hidden from it.
jsc.guide.listcmd.text2: Normally listcmd does not exist, because each system teaches its own commands in its own way. The server owner can switch it on for every computer, if you would rather read one list.
jsc.guide.listcmd.text3: In single-player, it is the same file, in the serverconfig folder of your world.
jsc.guide.listcmd.text4: The commands depend on the computer's system, and the programs depend on what is installed on it. When the switch is on, listcmd also appears in the list that help prints, like any other command.
jsc.guide.listcmd.title: The listcmd command
jsc.guide.load_balancing.definition1: Sharing new items among the servers, so that no single server fills first.
jsc.guide.load_balancing.fix1: If the section is in MANUAL, it fills the first server in the list. Press the button until it reads ROUND-ROBIN or LEAST-LOADED.
jsc.guide.load_balancing.fix2: Run the Load Balancer service on that server.
jsc.guide.load_balancing.problem1: All the items go to one server.
jsc.guide.load_balancing.problem2: The bay's drives fill one after another.
jsc.guide.load_balancing.table1_1_3: The next server in turn. The start rotates for each face.
jsc.guide.load_balancing.table1_2_3: Sorts the servers by free space, most free first, and fills in that order.
jsc.guide.load_balancing.table1_3_3: Fills the servers in the order of the list.
jsc.guide.load_balancing.text1: Load balancing decides where a new item goes when several servers could take it. Each section of a Server Router has its own balancing mode, and the button on the router moves a section to the next mode.
jsc.guide.load_balancing.text2: Every section starts in ROUND-ROBIN, and you see each section's mode on the router. The router keeps its place per face, so in ROUND-ROBIN each new write takes the next server in turn.
jsc.guide.load_balancing.text3: A server can also run the Load Balancer service: a program that spreads writes over the bay's drives, instead of filling them one after another ([](jsc:programs)).
jsc.guide.load_balancing.title: Load balancing
jsc.guide.loader.definition1: The program at the start of the disk that loads the kernel.
jsc.guide.loader.definition2: The core of the system, and the first thing the boot lines name.
jsc.guide.loader.definition3: The text the system prints on its way up, when it starts, and on its way down, when it stops.
jsc.guide.loader.fix1: Press Enter to start Boot, or wait 5 seconds for it to start on its own.
jsc.guide.loader.fix2: The loader starts only FreeBSD. Change the firmware's boot order, or use its Boot Menu ([](jsc:firmware)).
jsc.guide.loader.fix3: The server setting boot.show_boot_menu is off. Turn it on to show the menu again.
jsc.guide.loader.fix4: Boot an installation medium and install over it to repair.
jsc.guide.loader.heading2: The boot lines on the way up
jsc.guide.loader.heading3: The boot lines on the way down
jsc.guide.loader.heading4: When the system's file is missing
jsc.guide.loader.problem1: The computer waits at the loader's menu, and nothing starts.
jsc.guide.loader.problem2: The computer starts a system other than FreeBSD.
jsc.guide.loader.problem3: The loader's menu does not appear.
jsc.guide.loader.problem4: The system's file boot/kernel is missing from the system disk.
jsc.guide.loader.table1: The entries of the loader's menu
jsc.guide.loader.table1_1_2: Starts the running system. It is the default: Enter starts it.
jsc.guide.loader.table1_3_2: Opens the firmware's settings, shown only on Standard and later hardware, which uses UEFI (the Unified Extensible Firmware Interface).
jsc.guide.loader.table2: The boot lines on the way up
jsc.guide.loader.table2_14_2: Only when a desktop is installed.
jsc.guide.loader.table2_3_2: Always: the processor of the computer.
jsc.guide.loader.table2_4_2: Always: the memory the computer has.
jsc.guide.loader.table2_5_2: One line for each disk, then ada1 and so on.
jsc.guide.loader.table2_8_2: Only when a data cable reaches the computer.
jsc.guide.loader.text1: After the firmware, the computer runs the loader. The loader is the program at the start of the disk that loads the kernel, which is the core of the system. It is the boot manager of FreeBSD, and it can show a short menu for five seconds before it starts the system.
jsc.guide.loader.text2: The loader does not choose between systems. It starts FreeBSD from the system disk and lists no other system. If you want another system on the same computer, use the firmware's boot order or its Boot Menu ([](jsc:firmware), [](jsc:boot_menu)).
jsc.guide.loader.text3: The menu counts down from 5 seconds. Its top line says "Welcome to FreeBSD", and the line under it says "Autoboot in 5 seconds. [Space] to pause".
jsc.guide.loader.text4: Any key stops the count, although the line names the space bar. Once the count stops, press [[Enter]] to start the default entry, or a number from 1 to 9 to start that entry at once. Keys beyond the entries do nothing.
jsc.guide.loader.text5: The server setting boot.show_boot_menu turns the menu on or off. It is on by default. When it is off, the computer starts the system at once.
jsc.guide.loader.text6: On its way up, FreeBSD prints a fixed set of lines. Each line appears only when its condition holds, as the last column says.
jsc.guide.loader.text7: When you stop or restart the computer, FreeBSD prints its way down. It stops each service that is running, and it syncs the disks. The last line says "Rebooting..." when the computer restarts, and "The operating system has halted." when it stops.
jsc.guide.loader.text8: The loader starts the file boot/kernel, in the folder boot on the system disk. Without that file, FreeBSD cannot start. To repair it, install over it from a medium.
jsc.guide.loader.title: The loader and the boot lines
jsc.guide.local_storage.definition1: A unit the game uses to show a computer's room, 64 items each. It is not a limit on what a disk holds.
jsc.guide.local_storage.definition2: Parts of a thousand: 1,000 is the whole disk, 100 is a tenth of it.
jsc.guide.local_storage.fix1: Its system disk shares nothing. Raise the public share of the system disk in Settings, under Network.
jsc.guide.local_storage.problem1: The Network Manager says "Private 100%" for your computer.
jsc.guide.local_storage.table2_1_2: Reads nothing from this disk. This is the default.
jsc.guide.local_storage.table2_2_2: Reads half the disk. The other half stays private.
jsc.guide.local_storage.text1: A disk does not carry its contents inside the item. The network keeps what the disks hold in one store for the whole save, and each disk item carries only a number that finds its part of that store. So what a disk holds travels with the disk: pull it from a computer and carry it to another machine, a rack or another dimension.
jsc.guide.local_storage.text2: What a disk holds is counted in the same units as everything on the network: items, fluids and chemicals ([](jsc:items_as_data)). Once a disk holds something, its tooltip shows a line that starts with "Used".
jsc.guide.local_storage.text3: Each computer keeps its own disks as local storage, and that storage works without any network. The computer shows its room in storage slots.
jsc.guide.local_storage.text4: Pulling a disk out of a computer does not erase it. The disk keeps its data for the next machine it goes into. In a server's bay, the array's RAID mode decides what happens to that data ([](jsc:raid_arrays)).
jsc.guide.local_storage.text5: The network does not read a computer's disks unless you let it. Each disk has a public share: the part of it that the network may read, counted in per-mille (parts of a thousand). A new disk is fully private, so its public share starts at 0 per-mille.
jsc.guide.local_storage.text6: On a computer, you set the public share of its system disk in the Settings program, under Network, as "System disk public share" ([](jsc:this_pc_and_desktop_tools)). Each step moves it by 5%, which is 50 per-mille.
jsc.guide.local_storage.text7: The network can take items out of a computer's public part, but it never puts items into it. The disks of a server are always fully public.
jsc.guide.local_storage.text8: In the Network Manager ([](jsc:network_manager)), each computer's line shows its share as "Private". So "Private 90%" means a tenth of that disk is public.
jsc.guide.local_storage.title: Local storage
jsc.guide.local_storage.warning1: Formatting a disk erases everything on it: the items the network keeps there, and its files and installed systems. Take out what you need first.

jsc.guide.lock_unlock.text1: LOCK holds items where they are. Another Operation that asks for the same items then waits, instead of taking them. UNLOCK lets them go again. Use LOCK to keep stock in place while you need it.
jsc.guide.lock_unlock.text2: With no quantity, or with ALL, LOCK holds every free item of that kind. UNLOCK uses only the item, so a quantity you type after UNLOCK has no effect.
jsc.guide.lock_unlock.text3: LOCK and UNLOCK work with no engine. PRIORITY is accepted on them, but it changes nothing. The Task Manager shows what is locked ([](jsc:system_monitor_and_task_manager)).

jsc.guide.machine_verbs.text1: These verbs ask the machine about itself. status shows its power, its rate and its link. config shows and changes its settings. devices lists the linked devices, reboot restarts the computer, date tells the day and the time, and mem shows the memory.
jsc.guide.machine_verbs.text2: status shows whether the computer is online, its processing rate, its memory buffer and its network link. The first line reads ONLINE in green, or OFFLINE in red. Then come three rows.
jsc.guide.machine_verbs.text3: config with no words lists this computer's settings under the heading settings, and tells you how to change one. With a key and a value after it, config key value changes one setting.
jsc.guide.machine_verbs.text4: Other keys go to the machine's settings store. A machine without one says that it has no settings store. For example, config netshare 500 sets how much of the disk the network may read to half of it.
jsc.guide.machine_verbs.text5: devices lists the peripherals linked to this computer. Only a computer with ports for peripherals has this verb.
jsc.guide.machine_verbs.text6: reboot restarts the computer at once. reboot --firmware restarts it into the firmware setup instead, the program that runs before the system ([](jsc:firmware)). The prompt says "The system is going down for reboot NOW!" and then restarts.
jsc.guide.machine_verbs.text7: date prints the day and the time by the world's clock. The first day is day 1. A day starts at 06:00 by that clock, so the hours of a day run from six in the morning.
jsc.guide.machine_verbs.text8: mem shows how much memory the computer has, how much is held right now, and how much is promised to what runs. Free is what is left once the promised memory is taken away, so it tells you whether one more program fits.
jsc.guide.machine_verbs.title: The machine: status, config, devices, reboot, date and mem
jsc.guide.machine_verbs.warning1: reboot starts at once, with no question first. Save your work before you type it.

jsc.guide.mainframe_commands.text1: A few commands work on the network itself, so the prompt offers them only on the computer that keeps that part of the network. Type one anywhere else, and the prompt says it does not know the command.
jsc.guide.mainframe_commands.text2: The Mainframe is the computer that coordinates a network ([](jsc:mainframes)). Its commands are there only while it is on a network.
jsc.guide.mainframe_commands.text3: iqlengine starts and stops the Midsoft IQL Server, the engine that plans the network's work ([](jsc:midsoft_iql_server)). Type iqlengine start, iqlengine stop or iqlengine status. services lists the network's services, each with its state. The prompt offers both only while the Midsoft IQL Server is installed on the Mainframe.
jsc.guide.mainframe_commands.text4: The Mainframe keeps the storage index: its list of which disks hold which items, so the network finds an item without reading every disk. Three commands look after it.
jsc.guide.mainframe_commands.text5: When you pull a drive out of a running bay that has no Integrity Monitor, the index stops trusting that bay until you type reindex ([](jsc:network_services)). Learning IQL explains the same three jobs as statements ([](jsc:maintenance_analyze_vacuum_reindex)).
jsc.guide.mainframe_commands.text6: mirror install puts the Mirror on the Mainframe: the service your package manager fetches packages from ([](jsc:mirror)). mirror status says whether it serves. It answers serving, installed (Mainframe off) or not installed.
jsc.guide.mainframe_commands.text7: cluster does at the prompt what the Cluster Manager does in its window ([](jsc:cluster_management_computers)). It lists the network's supercomputers and datacenters, shows the nodes of one, turns them on or off, and installs a system or a program on them.
jsc.guide.mainframe_commands.text8: gateway does what the Gateway Manager does for the Network Gateways on this computer's ports, the bridge to ComputerCraft ([](jsc:network_gateway)). It lists them, shows the status, permissions, computers and log of one, and changes its settings.
jsc.guide.mainframe_commands.title: Looking after the network from the prompt

jsc.guide.mainframe_services.table1_1_2: Plans the network's work and answers it in IQL. The ISMS is its studio. ([](jsc:engines))
jsc.guide.mainframe_services.table1_2_2: Shows how it plans the network's work, and lets you take part in the planning.
jsc.guide.mainframe_services.table1_3_2: You tell it which state the network is to keep, and it works out how to get there and stay there.
jsc.guide.mainframe_services.text1: The Mainframe carries three kinds of software: an engine that decides the network's work, the Automation Engine that runs saved jobs, and the Mirror ([](jsc:mirror)). A new Mainframe ships with the Midsoft IQL Server installed and running, in the version of its age.
jsc.guide.mainframe_services.text2: The services of a Mainframe are on or off. They serve only while the Mainframe is powered, and they are removed when its disk is formatted.
jsc.guide.mainframe_services.text3: Only one engine plans the network's work at a time. An engine that you install becomes the active one when the network has none. Activating an installed engine makes it the one that plans, and the work the previous engine planned carries on, since an Operation belongs to the network once it is made.
jsc.guide.mainframe_services.text4: Replacing an engine takes a while, and the network has no engine until the replacement is over. The replacement goes through these steps, in order:
jsc.guide.mainframe_services.text5: The Automation Engine keeps the network's jobs and fires them on time. You write and supervise those jobs in the Automation Manager ([](jsc:automation_engine)).
jsc.guide.mainframe_services.title: Services on the Mainframe

jsc.guide.mainframes.text1: Every network has exactly one Mainframe, and it is the network's control room. Only the Mainframe runs the Network Manager. Two Mainframes on one network are a conflict, so give each network its own.
jsc.guide.mainframes.text10: With the [FAILOVER](jsc:failover) switch off, the Mainframe is an owner: it takes the network segment it stands on, or lays down a network of its own. With FAILOVER on, it is a standby: when an owner is on its network, it attaches to that network and does not run it.
jsc.guide.mainframes.text11: A standby takes over a network that has no owner. After 3 seconds, which is 60 ticks, one standby runs the network itself. The countdown is saved with the world, so reloading does not restart it. If two owners sit on one segment of a network, the network goes into conflict, and the screen shows CONFLICT.
jsc.guide.mainframes.text12: If you break a Mainframe, it drops the Mainframe of its own era, and the items in its inventory spill out. If it was the last Mainframe of its network, the network is orphaned, not deleted, so its storage survives ([](jsc:network_identity)).
jsc.guide.mainframes.text2: A Mainframe is big: three blocks wide, two tall and two deep. Place a Mainframe block in the middle of the ground floor, on the front row. If the whole 3 by 2 by 2 space is clear, the cabinet forms. If not, the item stays in your hand, and particles outline the blocked spaces so you can see what is in the way.
jsc.guide.mainframes.text3: The Mainframe takes an MTX motherboard of its own era. There is one Mainframe for each era: the Mainframe (Standard), and the Vintage, Legacy, Transition and Advanced Mainframes.
jsc.guide.mainframes.text4: A Mainframe runs the network only with a system on one of its disks, such as MC-NET ([](jsc:mc_net)). Install it as on any computer ([](jsc:installing)); until then the Mainframe holds every Operation it is given. From the Standard on, the backbone is fibre, and the Mainframe takes fibre only while an Optical Network Card sits in one of its card slots ([](jsc:expansion_cards)).
jsc.guide.mainframes.text5: Its hardware sets how fast the network works. Its processors add up to its capacity, and the Subframes that work for it add to that ([](jsc:subframes)). Its memory sets a RAM buffer, counted in items: a Vintage memory module gives 1 to 16 items, and an Advanced module gives 2,048 to 32,768. The Mainframe works at the lower of its capacity and its RAM buffer, so a small buffer holds back fast processors.
jsc.guide.mainframes.text6: The processors run one queue, and each graphics card runs one more. The queues do not share capacity. A weak card can hold its queue down, and the assembly screen then says "A card's queue runs at most at the CPU's speed, and no faster than the card".
jsc.guide.mainframes.text7: The assembly screen shows these parts of the Mainframe:
jsc.guide.mainframes.text8: Its power button sits on the sill, the ledge at the bottom of the front, in the middle. A click on it switches the Mainframe on or off, whatever you hold. A click anywhere else on the cabinet opens its assembly screen. Sneak-click the cabinet to open or close the service panel. Its processors, memory and cards are seen only through that opening.
jsc.guide.mainframes.text9: AUTO START keeps the Mainframe ready. With it on and a valid build, the Mainframe starts at once, as a cold start that runs its self-test. If a change breaks the build, the Mainframe turns off. When the build stands again, it turns on by itself.
jsc.guide.mainframes.title: Mainframes
jsc.guide.maintenance_analyze_vacuum_rei: The network's record of what its disks hold. The maintenance verbs keep it up to date.
Type the command at the Mainframe itself.
Put a Mainframe on the network and let it run ([](jsc:mainframes)).
A maintenance verb takes one word at most. Remove the extra word.
maintenance runs on the Mainframe only
the network has no running Mainframe
Reconciles the index. The reply is "ANALYZE complete - <n> types reconciled", with the number of item types it holds.
Frees the ghost entries. The reply is "VACUUM freed <n> ghost entries", with the number freed.
Rebuilds the index from the disks. The reply is "REINDEX started - rebuilding the catalog from disks", and the new index replaces the old one a short time later.
What it does, and its reply

The network keeps an index: its record of what its disks hold. ANALYZE, VACUUM and REINDEX look after that index. Each one may take one word after it, such as an object's name, and the network then ignores that word.
You run maintenance on the Mainframe. Typed on any other computer, it is refused. It needs no engine.
jsc.guide.make_conf.definition1: One of the processing units inside a processor, each able to run its own work at the same time.

jsc.guide.make_conf.table1_1_2: The compiler flags for every program. -O2 asks for faster programs, and -pipe makes the compiler itself faster.
jsc.guide.make_conf.table1_2_2: Writes the build messages in English.
jsc.guide.make_conf.table2: How many compiles run at once
jsc.guide.make_conf.text1: Portage reads a settings file before it builds any program: /etc/portage/make.conf, in the new system. The base system comes with one. It holds the compiler flags, the language of the build messages, and the setting that decides how many compiles run at once.
jsc.guide.make_conf.text2: Your central processing unit (CPU) has several cores. A core is one of its processing units, and each one can run its own work at the same time.
jsc.guide.make_conf.text3: The base file has no MAKEOPTS line. Without one, every build runs a single compile at a time, which is slow on a machine with several cores. Add the line yourself.
jsc.guide.make_conf.text4: You can also add the line in one command, from inside the new system: type echo 'MAKEOPTS="-j4"' >> /etc/portage/make.conf and press [[Enter]].
jsc.guide.make_conf.text5: The number follows -j. The count comes from the MAKEOPTS line that is not commented out, and a line that begins with # sets nothing. More compiles at once than cores buys nothing, so the build uses the smaller of the two numbers.
jsc.guide.make_conf.text6: A -j with no number counts as no setting, and a count below 1 becomes 1 compile. If you write several MAKEOPTS lines, the last one counts.
jsc.guide.make_conf.title: make.conf and MAKEOPTS
