jsc.guide.nextgre_planner_studio.text1: The Nextgre Planner Studio shows how NextgreIQL plans a craft, and how long each step of the plan takes. Use it when a craft takes longer than you expect, or when you want to tune the planner.
jsc.guide.nextgre_planner_studio.text10: A hint goes after a CRAFT and changes its plan. The built-in hints are these. The hints are explained in full in [the NextgreIQL hints](jsc:nextgre_hints).
jsc.guide.nextgre_planner_studio.text11: Every plan NextgreIQL made lately is kept on the Mainframe. Click a plan to show it on the Explain tab. The State column reads "planned", "running", "done" or "fell short". Until a craft is planned, the History tab says "No plans yet. Every craft NextgreIQL plans is kept here."
jsc.guide.nextgre_planner_studio.text2: The studio needs the NextgreIQL engine, version 7.0, running on the Mainframe. The engine is explained in [the NextgreIQL engine](jsc:nextgre_iql).
jsc.guide.nextgre_planner_studio.text3: Type a CRAFT or a SELECT, then press [[F7]] for Explain, or [[Shift]]+[[F7]] for Explain Analyze. Explain plans the statement without running it. Explain Analyze runs it too, and the boxes fill in as the craft goes.
jsc.guide.nextgre_planner_studio.text4: The plan is a tree of boxes. Each box is one step, with its name and its time. Before the craft runs, a box reads "est <n> s", the estimate in seconds (20 ticks make one second). After Explain Analyze, it reads "est <n> s, actual <n> s".
jsc.guide.nextgre_planner_studio.text5: Under the name, a box says where its step runs: "at a bench, <item> runs" or "on a machine, <item> runs". It also says "from <server>" for the server that gives the items, and "<n> steps, <n> at once" when steps run side by side. The hints of the statement are marked on the boxes they changed.
jsc.guide.nextgre_planner_studio.text6: The header shows "Planning <n> ms" and "Execution <n>". Beside the tree, PLANS WEIGHED lists each plan the planner weighed, with its cost in ticks. The chosen plan reads "chosen". A plan that was set aside reads "set aside by", and the reason.
jsc.guide.nextgre_planner_studio.text7: A partial plan reads "makes <n> of the <n> asked for". A plan that cannot be made reads "cannot be made: <n> <item> missing".
jsc.guide.nextgre_planner_studio.text8: The Statistics tab shows what the planner has measured on this network. Press Gather Statistics to measure again. The reply reads "statistics gathered: <n> item types on <n> servers, <n> recipes timed".
jsc.guide.nextgre_planner_studio.text9: A rule is a choice the planner makes when it weighs plans. You can switch each rule on or off for this Mainframe. Rules that other mods add are listed under RULES FROM OTHER MODS.
jsc.guide.nextgre_planner_studio.title: Nextgre Planner Studio
jsc.guide.no_bootable_device.fix1: No disk has a system yet, and no install medium is in a drive. Put one in ([](jsc:installing)).
jsc.guide.no_bootable_device.fix2: The medium is in the wrong kind of drive, or the drive is not joined to the computer. See the table above ([](jsc:drives)).
jsc.guide.no_bootable_device.fix3: Join a drive, or a disk, to the computer ([](jsc:drives)).
jsc.guide.no_bootable_device.problem1: The screen says that no bootable device was found.
jsc.guide.no_bootable_device.problem2: A medium is in a drive, but the screen does not list it.
jsc.guide.no_bootable_device.problem3: The screen says "No disk and no drive is attached to this computer."
jsc.guide.no_bootable_device.step1: Put an install medium into a drive that is joined to the computer.
jsc.guide.no_bootable_device.step2: Press Enter on this screen to start from it, or press DEL to go to the Setup.
jsc.guide.no_bootable_device.table1_1_2: "Non-system disk or disk error", then "Replace and press any key when ready".
jsc.guide.no_bootable_device.table1_2_2: "DISK BOOT FAILURE, INSERT SYSTEM DISK AND PRESS ENTER".
jsc.guide.no_bootable_device.table1_3_2: "No bootable device found", then "Press any key to enter Setup".
jsc.guide.no_bootable_device.table2_2_2: CD Drive, DVD Drive or Blu-ray Drive.
jsc.guide.no_bootable_device.table2_4_2: Dock Station, or the USB port on the front of a case from the Transition on.
jsc.guide.no_bootable_device.text1: Sometimes the firmware finds nothing it can start. Then it says so on the screen and waits for you. The words depend on the era of the motherboard.
jsc.guide.no_bootable_device.text2: When a disk holds a system whose boot loader was deleted, that system's own complaint replaces the firmware's text. The screen then adds "Put in an installation medium and install over it to repair."
jsc.guide.no_bootable_device.text3: The screen lists each disk and drive it knows. When there are more than it can show, the last line says how many more there are. An empty list says "No disk and no drive is attached to this computer."
jsc.guide.no_bootable_device.text4: The hint reads "Insert installation media and press Enter, or DEL for Setup". Press any other key, and the screen says Entering Setup and opens the Setup ([](jsc:setup_utility)).
jsc.guide.no_bootable_device.title: When nothing will boot
jsc.guide.notices.definition1: A box in the middle of the screen that waits until you answer it.
jsc.guide.notices.definition2: A small box over the status area of the taskbar, which goes away by itself after 9 seconds.
jsc.guide.notices.definition3: The Frames 10 form of the balloon, shown in a corner of the screen.
jsc.guide.notices.definition4: A switch that keeps notices from popping up. The notices still go to the list.
jsc.guide.notices.fix1: On Frames 10, Quiet hours may be on. Open the Action Center: a lit Quiet hours button means it is on. Click it to turn it off.
jsc.guide.notices.fix2: The list lasts only while the desktop is open, so it clears when the desktop closes.
jsc.guide.notices.problem1: No notice appears on the screen.
jsc.guide.notices.problem2: The list of notices is empty after you open the desktop again.
jsc.guide.notices.table1_1_2: Waits until you answer it: an error, a question, or the Open with chooser.
jsc.guide.notices.table1_1_3: In the middle of the screen, over everything else.
jsc.guide.notices.table1_2_2: Says one thing, then goes away by itself after 9 seconds.
jsc.guide.notices.table1_2_3: Over the status area of the taskbar, on Frames 95, Frames XP, Frames 7 and Frames 11.
jsc.guide.notices.table1_3_2: The Frames 10 form of the balloon.
jsc.guide.notices.table1_3_3: In a corner of the screen, on Frames 10 only.
jsc.guide.notices.table2_1_2: The memory has passed nine tenths. It names the three programs that hold the most, and what each holds. A program that does not fit after that brings the system down ([](jsc:frames_memory)).
jsc.guide.notices.table2_2_2: A program needs more video memory than the graphics card has free.
jsc.guide.notices.table2_3_2: No program on this computer opens the item you chose.
jsc.guide.notices.table3_1_2: Closes the pane, and opens Settings on its first page, Personalize.
jsc.guide.notices.table3_2_2: Opens the Network Manager. If it cannot open, Settings opens instead.
jsc.guide.notices.table3_3_2: Turns Quiet hours on or off. The button is lit while it is on.
jsc.guide.notices.table3_4_2: Opens Settings on the Sound page.
jsc.guide.notices.text1: A notice is a message that the desktop or a program sends you. Frames has three kinds of notice, and each one asks something different of you. A dialog waits for your answer. A balloon says one thing and goes away by itself. A toast is the Frames 10 form of the balloon.
jsc.guide.notices.text2: An error dialog has the title "Error". A question offers the buttons "OK", "Yes" and "No", and you choose one of them. A click beside a dialog makes the computer beep, and the dialog stays on the screen. The Escape key closes a dialog.
jsc.guide.notices.text3: A balloon plays the notify sound when it appears, unless Quiet hours is on. These are some of the balloons you may see:
jsc.guide.notices.text4: Each notice goes into a list, with the newest first. The list keeps up to 12 notices. It lasts while the desktop is open, and the list clears when the desktop closes.
jsc.guide.notices.text5: The Action Center is a dark pane down the right edge of the screen. Open it with the Action Center button at the far right of the taskbar, and close it with the same button. Opening it marks the notices as read.
jsc.guide.notices.text6: The list is headed "Notifications", with "Clear all" beside it, and each notice opens its program when you click it. If there are no notices, the pane says "No new notifications". Four quick actions sit along its foot.
jsc.guide.notices.text7: Quiet hours keeps notices from popping up. While it is on, a notice goes to the list only: no balloon appears, and no notify sound plays. The switch does not mute dialogs, so an error or a question still appears.
jsc.guide.notices.title: Notices and the Action Center
jsc.guide.numbers_and_time.definition1: The number a whole-number draw stays below. Random.Next(6) gives 0 to 5.
jsc.guide.numbers_and_time.fix1: Give a fallback as the second value of Convert.ToInt, or check the text first with Convert.TryInt.
jsc.guide.numbers_and_time.fix2: Use a base from 2 to 36, such as 10 or 16.
jsc.guide.numbers_and_time.fix3: Give a bound of 1 or more. A bound of 6 gives numbers from 0 to 5.
jsc.guide.numbers_and_time.problem1: The program stops and says that the text is not a number.
jsc.guide.numbers_and_time.problem2: The program stops and says there is no base in that number.
jsc.guide.numbers_and_time.table1_1_2: The size of a number, without its sign.
jsc.guide.numbers_and_time.table1_4_2: The whole number at or below a decimal number.
jsc.guide.numbers_and_time.table1_5_2: The whole number at or above a decimal number. Sigma# only.
jsc.guide.numbers_and_time.table1_6_2: The nearest whole number. Sigma# only.
jsc.guide.numbers_and_time.table1_7_2: The square root of a decimal number.
jsc.guide.numbers_and_time.table1_8_2: A number raised to a power.
jsc.guide.numbers_and_time.table1_9_2: The value, kept between low and high. Sigma# only.
jsc.guide.numbers_and_time.table2_10_2: The same as TryInt, for the other kinds. Sigma# only.
jsc.guide.numbers_and_time.table2_1_2: The whole number in the text. Stops the program when the text is not a number.
jsc.guide.numbers_and_time.table2_2_2: The whole number in the text, or the fallback when the text is not a number. Version 2.
jsc.guide.numbers_and_time.table2_3_2: A long whole number. Sigma# only.
jsc.guide.numbers_and_time.table2_4_2: A short decimal number. Sigma# only.
jsc.guide.numbers_and_time.table2_5_2: The decimal number in the text.
jsc.guide.numbers_and_time.table2_6_2: True or false, from the text.
jsc.guide.numbers_and_time.table2_8_2: The number as text in a base from 2 to 36. Version 2.
jsc.guide.numbers_and_time.table2_9_2: True and the number when the text is a number, false otherwise. Sigma# only.
jsc.guide.numbers_and_time.table3_1_2: A whole number from 0 up to the bound, not including the bound.
jsc.guide.numbers_and_time.table3_2_2: A decimal number from 0 up to 1, not including 1. Sigma# only.
jsc.guide.numbers_and_time.table3_3_2: Starts the sequence again from that number.
jsc.guide.numbers_and_time.table4_1_2: The world's tick count, as a long whole number.
jsc.guide.numbers_and_time.table4_2_2: The time of day in ticks, from 0 up to 23,999. Sigma# only.
jsc.guide.numbers_and_time.table4_3_2: The day number of the world's clock.
jsc.guide.numbers_and_time.table4_4_2: The number of ticks in that many seconds. Sigma# only.
jsc.guide.numbers_and_time.text1: Programs compute with numbers, and the library gives you the common sums and conversions in Math and Convert. Random gives you numbers you cannot predict, and Time tells the program what the world's clock says. Calls to these cost nothing.
jsc.guide.numbers_and_time.text2: Sigma offers Abs, Min, Max, Floor, Sqrt and Pow. The other members here are Sigma# only.
jsc.guide.numbers_and_time.text3: A base is how many different digits a number is written with. Base 10 is the ordinary way, and base 16 is hexadecimal. Base 10 keeps the minus sign. Every other base writes the 32 bits of the number, so -1 in base 16 is ffffffff.
jsc.guide.numbers_and_time.text4: Convert.ToBool takes true, yes, y, on or 1 for true, and false, no, n, off or 0 for false, in any case.
jsc.guide.numbers_and_time.text5: Random is in Sigma# from version 1, and in Sigma from version 2. Each program has its own sequence, and seeding it with the same number gives the same sequence again.
jsc.guide.numbers_and_time.text6: A tick is one step of the world's clock, and the game runs 20 ticks each second. Time.Ticks is the one place the library turns seconds into ticks. The credits a program gets each tick are explained in [](jsc:credits_per_tick).
jsc.guide.numbers_and_time.title: Math, Convert, Random and Time
jsc.guide.operation_states.definition1: The Mainframe's list of the last 32 Operations that settled, newest first.
jsc.guide.operation_states.definition2: A reservation on items. Other Operations that need those items wait until the reservation ends.
jsc.guide.operation_states.fix1: All the queues are busy. A Mainframe with more graphics cards has more queues ([](jsc:expansion_cards)), and a faster processor finishes each one sooner ([](jsc:mainframes)).
jsc.guide.operation_states.fix2: The items were held for longer than the waiting time, which is 60 seconds by default. Wait, or UNLOCK the item ([](jsc:lock_unlock)).
jsc.guide.operation_states.fix3: The network held less than you asked for. Store more of the item ([](jsc:storage_servers)), or ask for less.
jsc.guide.operation_states.fix4: The network held none of the item, or a step was refused. Check the item's name, and that the item is stored.
jsc.guide.operation_states.table1_1_3: Ready, and waiting for a free queue.
jsc.guide.operation_states.table1_2_3: Holds a queue and moves items.
jsc.guide.operation_states.table1_3_3: Blocked by another Operation's hold. It takes no queue while it waits.
jsc.guide.operation_states.table1_5_3: Moved some of it, less than was asked.
jsc.guide.operation_states.table1_6_3: Moved nothing, and was not done.
jsc.guide.operation_states.table1_7_3: Gave up waiting for a hold, after the waiting time ran out.
jsc.guide.operation_states.table1_8_3: Stopped before it finished, on purpose or by the machine.
jsc.guide.operation_states.table2_1_2: It moved some of what was asked. The two numbers are what moved and what was asked.
jsc.guide.operation_states.table2_2_2: A hold on the items lasted too long.
jsc.guide.operation_states.table2_3_2: Nothing was moved, and the Operation was not done.
jsc.guide.operation_states.table2_4_2: A SELECT asked for more than the network holds.
jsc.guide.operation_states.table2_5_2: An INSERT found no room left in the network's storage.
jsc.guide.operation_states.text1: Every Operation is in one of eight states at any time. The Processes tab of the [Network Manager](jsc:network_manager) shows you each one, in the words of the table below.
jsc.guide.operation_states.text2: Three states mean that the Operation is still going: queued, running and waiting. The other five are final. The Operation is then done, and it is kept in the log ([](jsc:cancelling_and_the_log)).
jsc.guide.operation_states.text3: The list colours each row by its state: going or done, held up, or stopped. A row can also show a line that gives the reason, such as the ones below.
jsc.guide.operation_states.title: The eight states of an Operation
jsc.guide.operations_catalogue.definitio: Item Query Language: the network's own language, in which you type the work that you want done, such as SELECT 64 iron_ingot.
One IQL instruction: an action, a question or a maintenance command.
The word that starts an IQL instruction, such as SELECT or QUERY.
A workshop card in the computer that asks for an UPDATE. The card does the work for that computer.
jsc.guide.operations_catalogue.fix1: The network does not hold that item. Store it first ([](jsc:storage_servers)), or check its name.
jsc.guide.operations_catalogue.fix2: Check the item. A card needs something to change, and the player who asked needs enough levels for the work.
jsc.guide.operations_catalogue.fix3: The player who asked has to be there to pay the experience. Ask again with them present.
jsc.guide.operations_catalogue.problem1: The result says "the network was not holding the", followed by an item.
jsc.guide.operations_catalogue.problem2: The result says the card could not do it: nothing to change, too expensive or too few levels.
jsc.guide.operations_catalogue.problem3: The result says whoever asked for it was not here to pay.
jsc.guide.operations_catalogue.table1_10: Removes the index entries that hold nothing, or point at a server that is no longer on the network.
jsc.guide.operations_catalogue.table1_11: Reserves items, so that other Operations wait for them.
jsc.guide.operations_catalogue.table1_1_: Takes items out of storage and brings them to the computer that asked.
jsc.guide.operations_catalogue.table1_2_: Puts items that the computer holds into the network's storage.
jsc.guide.operations_catalogue.table1_3_: Moves items between two servers, or between a server and a named bus.
jsc.guide.operations_catalogue.table1_4_: Sends items out of the network, through the bus named after TO. Destroys nothing.
jsc.guide.operations_catalogue.table1_6_: Makes items the network crafts, in machines or in steps.
jsc.guide.operations_catalogue.table1_7_: Changes an item the network holds, with a personal-use card.
jsc.guide.operations_catalogue.table1_8_: Keeps the index up to date. It looks only at the servers that changed, and drops the entries of servers that left.
jsc.guide.operations_catalogue.table1_9_: Rebuilds the whole index from every disk.
jsc.guide.operations_catalogue.text1: Here is every Operation the network knows, and what it does. Most of their names come from the commands of databases, so if you know a little SQL, you already know many of them.
jsc.guide.operations_catalogue.text2: Each name in the first column is an IQL verb ([](jsc:query_and_select)). QUERY and COUNT only read the network, so they are not Operations. The Learning IQL book explains each verb in its own entry: UPDATE in [](jsc:update_cards), and LOCK in [](jsc:lock_unlock).
jsc.guide.operations_catalogue.text3: The Network program sends most of them for you when you click, so you do not have to type them. In IQL you can say exactly what you want ([](jsc:iql)).
jsc.guide.operations_catalogue.text4: UPDATE works in three stages. The item is taken out of the network with a SELECT, the card works on it, and the result is put back with an INSERT. The card is a workshop card in the computer that asked ([](jsc:workshop)).
jsc.guide.operations_catalogue.text5: Whoever asked pays the card's experience price, except for smelting. A name with no prefix, such as iron_ingot, means the Minecraft item of that name.
jsc.guide.operations_catalogue.title: The catalogue of Operations
jsc.guide.operations_catalogue.warning1: DROP destroys items for good, and nothing brings them back.
jsc.guide.operations_library.fix2: Add a pattern for the item in the Pattern Studio ([](jsc:pattern_studio)).
jsc.guide.operations_library.fix3: Start a Mainframe on the network, then ask again.
jsc.guide.operations_library.fix4: Add storage to the network, such as a storage server ([](jsc:storage_servers)).
jsc.guide.operations_library.fix5: The Operation has finished or was cancelled. Use Operations.List to see what is running.
jsc.guide.operations_library.problem1: The program stops and says this computer is not on a network.
jsc.guide.operations_library.problem2: AskResult says no pattern crafts the item.
jsc.guide.operations_library.problem3: AskResult says the network has no running Mainframe.
jsc.guide.operations_library.problem4: AskResult says the network has no room for the item.
jsc.guide.operations_library.table1_1_2: Asks the network to bring the item to this machine's storage (SELECT).
jsc.guide.operations_library.table1_2_2: Sends items from this machine's storage to the network (INSERT).
jsc.guide.operations_library.table1_3_2: Asks the network to make the item (CRAFT).
jsc.guide.operations_library.table1_4_2: Cancels the Operation with that id.
jsc.guide.operations_library.table1_5_2: Changes how urgently the Operation runs.
jsc.guide.operations_library.table1_6_2: Asks for an UPDATE with the action, such as SMELT. Added in version 2.
jsc.guide.operations_library.table1_7_2: The OperationInfo of the Operation with that id, or nothing when it is no longer in flight.
jsc.guide.operations_library.table1_8_2: Every Operation in flight, as a list of OperationInfo.
jsc.guide.operations_library.table2_1_3: Ok: yes when the network took the request. Message: the network's answer, in English.
jsc.guide.operations_library.table2_2_3: Id: the id to use. Type and Status: lower-case text. Item: the item. Moved and Requested: how much has moved, and how much was asked for.
jsc.guide.operations_library.table4_1_2: The network does not know the item.
jsc.guide.operations_library.table4_2_1: the network has no running Mainframe
jsc.guide.operations_library.table4_2_2: No Mainframe runs on the network.
jsc.guide.operations_library.table4_3_2: A push of an item this machine does not hold.
jsc.guide.operations_library.table4_4_2: The push has no items to send.
jsc.guide.operations_library.table4_6_1: the network has no room for <item>
jsc.guide.operations_library.table4_6_2: The network's storage has no room for the item.
jsc.guide.operations_library.table4_7_2: No Operation with that id is running.
jsc.guide.operations_library.table4_8_2: The priority name is not one of the levels above.
jsc.guide.operations_library.text1: An Operation ([](jsc:what_operations_are)) is one job the network does. A SELECT brings an item from the network to this machine, an INSERT sends items the other way, and a CRAFT asks the network to make an item. Operations is the type a program uses to ask for these jobs, and to look at the jobs in flight.
jsc.guide.operations_library.text2: Every Operations call needs a network, so check Network.Online first when you are not sure. A request the network cannot take does not stop the program: Ok is false, and the message says why. The kinds of Operation are in [](jsc:operations_catalogue).
jsc.guide.operations_library.text3: Pull, Push, Craft, Cancel, Reprioritise and Update give an AskResult. Get and List give OperationInfo. Cancel accepts the start of an id, provided that start is at least as long as the short form of the id. Get needs the whole id, and ignores case.
jsc.guide.operations_library.text4: The five Operation levels in the table are not the same scale as a program's priority, which is written as low, medium or high.
jsc.guide.operations_library.title: Operations from a program
jsc.guide.other_mods_intro.definition1: A block that links one of your computers to ComputerCraft computers.
jsc.guide.other_mods_intro.definition2: The mod CC: Tweaked, which adds programmable computers to Minecraft.
jsc.guide.other_mods_intro.definition3: The programming language in which the programs of ComputerCraft computers are written.
jsc.guide.other_mods_intro.text1: Some of the mods you play with can add to J's Computers. Five of them each add a feature when they are installed: ComputerCraft, JEI, EMI, Mekanism and Jade.
jsc.guide.other_mods_intro.text2: Each of them is optional. Without one of these mods, its feature is missing, and the rest of J's Computers works as before.
jsc.guide.other_mods_intro.text3: ComputerCraft computers run programs written in Lua. The Network Gateway is the bridge between those computers and yours ([](jsc:network_gateway)). The section after this one explains the Gateway in detail.
jsc.guide.other_mods_intro.title: Other mods
jsc.guide.pace.definition1: One window of menus in PACE. A new frame opens over the last one, and the keys move between them.
jsc.guide.pace.fix1: Nothing can be set on this system. The frame says "Nothing to set on this machine."
jsc.guide.pace.fix2: Your home folder is /usr/player, and PACE does not list bin, lib or player under /usr, so no other user shows up.
jsc.guide.pace.fix3: Press F6 on a Sigma listing, a file ending in .sg, to run it.
jsc.guide.pace.problem2: The Other Users frame says "(no other users)".
jsc.guide.pace.problem3: ENTER on a Sigma file opens it in vi, and it does not run.
jsc.guide.pace.step2: Choose Office of player and press Enter.
jsc.guide.pace.step4: Move to a file with the arrow keys, and press Enter. A standard file opens in vi.
jsc.guide.pace.table1_1_2: The Office: the Filecabinet, your home, and the other folders.
jsc.guide.pace.table1_2_2: The programs that are installed. ENTER runs one.
jsc.guide.pace.table1_3_2: Machine Information, File Systems and Software Installation.
jsc.guide.pace.table1_4_2: A shell of its own. Type exit at it to come back to PACE.
jsc.guide.pace.table1_5_2: Leaves PACE and gives the terminal back.
jsc.guide.pace.table2_4_2: PREV-FRM: goes to the frame before this one.
jsc.guide.pace.table2_5_2: NEXT-FRM: goes to the frame after this one.
jsc.guide.pace.table2_6_2: CANCEL: closes the frame on top. On the last frame it leaves PACE.
jsc.guide.pace.table2_8_2: Moves to the next item that starts with that letter.
jsc.guide.pace.table3: What ENTER does on each kind of entry
jsc.guide.pace.table3_2_1: Sigma listing, a file ending in .sg
jsc.guide.pace.table3_2_2: Opens the file in vi. F6 runs it.
jsc.guide.pace.table3_3_1: Sigma# listing, a file ending in .sgs
jsc.guide.pace.table3_3_2: Opens the file in vi. It does not run.
jsc.guide.pace.text1: PACE is the menu system of UNIX System V, and only that system has it. It opens a frame of menus over the screen, and each choice you make opens a frame of its own over the last one. The name stands for the Panelled Access Command Environment of Bellwether Labs' UNIX System V.
jsc.guide.pace.text2: Type pace to start it. It takes the whole terminal, and its first frame is the main one, titled PACE. Choose Exit PACE, or press F5 on the last frame, and the terminal comes back.
jsc.guide.pace.text3: Inside a frame, these keys work. The labels on the bottom line of the screen name the function keys.
jsc.guide.pace.text4: A mouse click brings a frame to the front and picks its item. A second click on the same item opens it.
jsc.guide.pace.text5: The Filecabinet opens your home folder, /usr/player. Other Users lists the folders under /usr, except bin, lib and player, and says "(no other users)" when there are none. Preferences is greyed out, and it says "Nothing to set on this machine."
jsc.guide.pace.text6: A folder frame is titled with its name and its path, and it lists what is in the folder. The vi editor is explained in [](jsc:vi). A Sigma listing is a program in the Sigma language, explained in [](jsc:sigma_two_languages).
jsc.guide.pace.text7: Press F6 to open the command menu, except on a Sigma listing, where F6 runs the file. The menu's items are cancel, exit, help, next-frm, prev-frm, refresh, run and unix-system. Refresh reads the folder again.
jsc.guide.pace.text8: Run opens a command line. Type a UNIX command, press Enter, and read its output. Escape or F5 cancels the line.
jsc.guide.pace.text9: A command run from PACE shows its output, then says "Press ENTER to return to PACE." The UNIX System item has no such line: type exit in its shell to come back.
jsc.guide.pace.title: PACE, the menus in frames
jsc.guide.package_tree_and_world.definit: The build recipe of one program: where to fetch its source, and how to build it.
A named set of default build choices. It says how programs are built, and it installs nothing.
The set of packages the system wants. Updating it brings each one up to date.
A switch that turns an optional feature of a program on or off when it is built.
jsc.guide.package_tree_and_world.fix1: Run emerge-webrsync, or emerge --sync, before you merge anything.
jsc.guide.package_tree_and_world.fix2: No Mainframe running the [Mirror](jsc:mirror) is on this network. Connect to one, then try again.
jsc.guide.package_tree_and_world.fix3: Step into the new system first: chroot /mnt/gentoo /bin/bash.
jsc.guide.package_tree_and_world.fix4: Type the name of at least one package after emerge.
jsc.guide.package_tree_and_world.fix5: Check the spelling. The name must be a program the Mirror has ([](jsc:building_from_source)).
jsc.guide.package_tree_and_world.fix6: Type a number from the list that eselect profile list shows.
jsc.guide.package_tree_and_world.problem: emerge says "The portage tree is empty".
emerge says "command not found" when run outside the new system, since the package manager is the new system's.
emerge says there are no ebuilds to satisfy the name you typed.
eselect says that the target does not appear to be valid.
jsc.guide.package_tree_and_world.step1: Inside the new system, type emerge-webrsync and press [[Enter]].
jsc.guide.package_tree_and_world.step2: Type eselect profile list and press [[Enter]] to see the profiles.
jsc.guide.package_tree_and_world.step3: Type eselect profile set, then the number you want, and press [[Enter]].
jsc.guide.package_tree_and_world.table2_: On: cxx, tinfo. Off: debug, doc.

jsc.guide.package_tree_and_world.text1: Portage installs programs from recipes. The package tree is the collection of those recipes, one for each program.
jsc.guide.package_tree_and_world.text2: The tree comes from a dated snapshot of the repository. Portage checks the snapshot against its checksum and its GNU Privacy Guard (GPG) signature. You get the tree with emerge-webrsync, which downloads the snapshot, or with emerge --sync, which copies it over rsync. Either one works with no tree yet.
jsc.guide.package_tree_and_world.text3: The profile sets the defaults that every build follows. Choose one from this table.
jsc.guide.package_tree_and_world.text4: Choose a profile with eselect profile set, even when profile 1 suits you.
jsc.guide.package_tree_and_world.text5: The update command compiles every package of the world that is out of date. Each package has USE flags, which are switches that turn its optional features on or off.
jsc.guide.package_tree_and_world.text6: With --ask, Portage stops and asks: Would you like to merge these packages? [Yes/No]. An answer that starts with n quits, and the screen says Quitting. Any other answer carries on, Enter included.
jsc.guide.package_tree_and_world.text7: Each package then goes through its phases. It downloads its archive from the Mirror, unpacks the source, prepares it, configures it, compiles it, installs it and merges it into the system.
jsc.guide.package_tree_and_world.title: The package tree, the profile and @world
jsc.guide.partitioning_with_fdisk.defini: The modern kind of partition table, which UEFI machines read.
A globally unique identifier: a long code, which looks random, that a partition table or a partition is given so that it can be told apart from others.
The smallest piece of a disk that the table counts in: 512 bytes.
A small partition that the firmware reads to find the boot loader. Only UEFI machines need one.

jsc.guide.partitioning_with_fdisk.fix10: Both leave without writing. Only w keeps the changes, so type w before you leave.
jsc.guide.partitioning_with_fdisk.fix2: fdisk opens a whole disk only, not a partition. Use the disk's name, such as sda.
jsc.guide.partitioning_with_fdisk.fix3: This is information, not a refusal: the disk has no partitions yet. Type g to make a GPT, then n.
jsc.guide.partitioning_with_fdisk.fix4: t and d need a partition to act on. Make one with n first.

jsc.guide.partitioning_with_fdisk.fix6: The disk is full, or an earlier partition took the rest of it, or there are 128 partitions. Delete the last partition with d. A partition that took the rest has to be deleted and made again with a size.
jsc.guide.partitioning_with_fdisk.fix7: Type 1 or uefi for an EFI system partition, 20 or linux for a Linux filesystem, or L to see the list.
jsc.guide.partitioning_with_fdisk.fix8: The letter x is not a command of the editor. Type m to see the commands it has.

jsc.guide.partitioning_with_fdisk.table2: The words that set a type
jsc.guide.partitioning_with_fdisk.text1: fdisk is the editor that writes a disk's partition table: the list of where each partition begins and ends. You open it on a whole disk, and it asks you what to do next.
jsc.guide.partitioning_with_fdisk.text10: Type L to see the types the editor knows. It prints two rows, EFI System and Linux filesystem, and then asks again. With one partition on the disk, t selects it and asks for the type. With several, it asks which partition first, and Enter picks the last one.
jsc.guide.partitioning_with_fdisk.text11: When the change works, the editor prints the old and new type, exactly as it writes them: "Changed type of partition 'Linux filesystem' to 'EFI System'."
jsc.guide.partitioning_with_fdisk.text12: p prints the table as the editor sees it, before anything is written. It starts with the disk's size, and then one row for each partition. The rows show Device, Start, End, Sectors, Size and Type, in that order.
jsc.guide.partitioning_with_fdisk.text13: d deletes a partition and renumbers the rest from partition 1. Then the editor prints "Partition 2 has been deleted.", with the number of the one you chose.
jsc.guide.partitioning_with_fdisk.text14: w stores the table on the disk. The editor then says that the partition table has been altered, and that it is syncing the disks. After that the partitions show in lsblk, and mkfs can use them.
jsc.guide.partitioning_with_fdisk.text2: The editor works in memory. Nothing reaches the disk until you type w, so you can try things and throw them away. Leaving with q, or with [[Ctrl]]+[[C]], drops everything you typed since the editor opened.
jsc.guide.partitioning_with_fdisk.text3: A new disk has no partition table, and fdisk says so when you open it. Type g to make a GPT, the modern kind that UEFI (Unified Extensible Firmware Interface) machines read. The old kind, which p prints as dos, is not one this editor can make.
jsc.guide.partitioning_with_fdisk.text4: The line that g prints shows the disk's GUID, a long identifier that stays the same for that disk. Only g makes a new GPT, although a disk that already has partitions may be GPT as well.
jsc.guide.partitioning_with_fdisk.text5: With a size on the line, n makes the partition at once. Type n +512M for 512 megabytes, or n +1G for a gigabyte. A plain number, such as "n 1024", also means megabytes.
jsc.guide.partitioning_with_fdisk.text6: Typed alone, n asks three questions in turn. For the first two, press [[Enter]]: the editor picks the number and the starting sector for you. The third asks where the partition ends, and the question shows the range. On a 1G disk it reads:
jsc.guide.partitioning_with_fdisk.text8: Press [[Enter]] to take the rest of the disk, or type a size such as +512M. A sector is 512 bytes, and a megabyte is 2,048 sectors, so the question also takes a sector number.
jsc.guide.partitioning_with_fdisk.text9: When the partition is made, the editor says so: "Created a new partition 1 of type 'Linux filesystem' and of size 512 MiB." Every new partition starts as a Linux filesystem. You change it with t, when it is to be the EFI (Extensible Firmware Interface) system partition.
jsc.guide.partitioning_with_fdisk.title: Dividing a disk (fdisk)
jsc.guide.partitioning_with_fdisk.warnin: Writing with w replaces the disk's partition table, and the partitions it held before are gone.

jsc.guide.paths_and_drives.text1: A path is the address of a file or a folder: the folder names, with a backslash between them, starting from a drive letter. C:\DOS is the folder that MC-DOS searches for its programs by default. The rules for paths are in [the prompt, the drives and the paths](jsc:dos_prompt); this page gives the forms the prompt reads.
jsc.guide.paths_and_drives.text10: A star (*) in a name is passed to the command as it is. The command decides what the star matches.
jsc.guide.paths_and_drives.text11: If the word you type is not a command, the shell searches for a program of that name in the PATH. The PATH is the list of folders it searches. On MC-DOS it comes from the PATH line of C:\AUTOEXEC.BAT, and C:\DOS is the default.
jsc.guide.paths_and_drives.text2: Read a path from left to right. The forms below are the ones the prompt understands.
jsc.guide.paths_and_drives.text3: The prompt shows where you are: the current folder, then a greater-than sign. At the top of drive C: it reads C:\>. After you type cd C:\DOS, it reads C:\DOS>.
jsc.guide.paths_and_drives.text4: Type a drive letter and a colon, and nothing else, and the prompt moves to that drive. Type D: to move to drive D:. The drives you can use are the ones linked to the computer.
jsc.guide.paths_and_drives.text5: With no words after it, cd prints the folder you are in, such as C:\DOS.
jsc.guide.paths_and_drives.text6: A switch changes what the command does. You write it the way that command takes it, such as /y. Each command reads only the switches it declares; the shell itself knows none of them.
jsc.guide.paths_and_drives.text7: Both forms print the command's page, the same text that help <command> prints. You can read the same page here, in the command pages of this book.
jsc.guide.paths_and_drives.text8: Words in double quotes stay together as one word. The find command takes its text that way, so find "oak log" looks for the whole phrase.
jsc.guide.paths_and_drives.text9: On the DOS family, a name between percent signs, such as %USERNAME%, is replaced by its value before the command runs. The built-in names are HOSTNAME, COMPUTERNAME, USER, USERNAME, OS, CD (the prompt) and PATH. You give a name a value with set ([](jsc:shell_verbs)).

jsc.guide.pattern_encoders.text1: A pattern on one computer is no use to another, so a pattern must travel. The Pattern Encoder is the device that burns patterns onto media, such as floppy disks, discs and USB sticks, and you carry the medium from one computer to another. The encoder joins to a computer with a Peripheral Cable ([](jsc:peripheral_cables)).
jsc.guide.pattern_encoders.text2: A bench pattern goes into a card, and a machine pattern goes into the interface of its machine. The plain Pattern Encoder is the Standard one, and each era has its own encoder.
jsc.guide.pattern_encoders.text3: A read-only medium, marked no, is refused, because a pattern needs a medium the encoder can write.
jsc.guide.pattern_encoders.text4: From the Legacy on, the encoder burns discs, and the discs lie on a tray. Press the eject button to bring it out, put the disc on it, and press the button again, or push the tray in with an empty hand. Nothing is burned while the tray is out, and the tray stays shut while a pattern is written. A floppy disk or a USB stick does not use the tray: it goes into its slot whatever the tray does.
jsc.guide.pattern_encoders.text5: A burn runs in three phases: seeking, writing and verifying. The display shows "Seeking", then "Writing" and the file's name, then "Verifying" and the name, and last "Done:" and the name.
jsc.guide.pattern_encoders.text6: Seek is the time to find the place on the medium, and verify is the read-back check. A tick is a twentieth of a second, so 20 ticks make one second.
jsc.guide.pattern_encoders.text7: The queue holds up to 8 burns. A burn is refused when the queue is full. The file is named after the pattern, with .craft at its end, and its name is made unique on the medium. When the write ends, the encoder reads the medium back and compares it. A mismatch shows "Verify failed" and the file's name.
jsc.guide.pattern_encoders.text8: The bay is locked while a burn runs, so you cannot take the disc out until the burn has finished. The panel reads "Not linked" when no computer is joined, and "Linked to" with the computer's name when one is.

jsc.guide.pattern_studio.text1: The Pattern Studio is the desktop program in which you write patterns. It keeps three drafts on the computer, one for each tab: "Bench", "Machine" and "Multi-stage". A draft is not a recipe until it is complete, so you can leave one half written and come back to it.
jsc.guide.pattern_studio.text10: The Studio answers "Recipe placed on the bench" or "Recipe placed in the machine draft". If the Studio is not open, the message is "Open the Pattern Studio to transfer recipes".
jsc.guide.pattern_studio.text2: The Studio does not come with any system. Install it from its CD, or on a Linux desktop from the Mirror, on a system with windows: Frames XP or newer, or a Linux, FreeBSD or UNIX desktop ([](jsc:programs)).
jsc.guide.pattern_studio.text3: Nothing is used up in the Studio. A click on a cell of the editor records a copy of what your cursor holds, and your inventory sits in a band under the editor.
jsc.guide.pattern_studio.text4: The Load button works only on a Crafting Computer, because only that computer loads recipes ([](jsc:crafting_computers)).
jsc.guide.pattern_studio.text5: On the right, the rail lists the files on the drives of the computer and the linked Pattern Encoder, under the tabs "Files" and "Encoder". The hints of the rail read "Click adds a stage" and "Click opens the file".
jsc.guide.pattern_studio.text6: The Name and Note fields name the pattern, up to 64 and 256 characters. The Timeout field sets how many ticks a machine pattern waits, and it is at least 1 tick.
jsc.guide.pattern_studio.text7: The preview shows what the network would use for the draft. Its lines read "Network would use:" and "In stock:". A cell that takes a tag shows "Any #" and the tag.
jsc.guide.pattern_studio.text8: Until you add a stage, the multi-stage tab reads "No stages yet". Each stage then shows its number, its kind in brackets, "[bench]" or "[machine]", and its name.
jsc.guide.pattern_studio.text9: If Just Enough Items (JEI), the recipe viewer, is installed, the transfer button of a recipe sends it into the open Studio. A bench recipe goes to the bench draft, and any recipe with inputs and outputs goes to the machine draft.
jsc.guide.pattern_studio.title: The Pattern Studio
jsc.guide.patterns.definition1: A multi-stage pattern: an ordered list of stages that the network runs in turn.
jsc.guide.patterns.fix1: Add a bench or a machine pattern as a stage.
jsc.guide.patterns.fix2: Put the stages of the inner pipeline in directly, one bench or machine pattern each.
jsc.guide.patterns.fix3: Remove a stage before you add one: a pipeline holds 16 stages at most.
jsc.guide.patterns.problem2: The screen says "A pipeline cannot hold another pipeline".
jsc.guide.patterns.problem3: A pipeline with 16 stages refuses another.
jsc.guide.patterns.table1_1_2: An item, a fluid or a chemical, with the amount it takes per run (at least 1).
jsc.guide.patterns.table1_2_2: An item, a fluid or a chemical, with the amount it gives per run and a chance in percent.
jsc.guide.patterns.table1_3_2: How long the craft waits while nothing moves on the interface, in ticks (the default is 200, which is 10 seconds).
jsc.guide.patterns.text1: A pattern is a recipe the network can use, and there are three kinds. Each kind fits a different job, and you write each one in its own tab of the Pattern Studio ([](jsc:pattern_studio)).
jsc.guide.patterns.text10: A multi-stage pattern is a pipeline: an ordered list of stages, and each stage is exactly one bench pattern or one machine pattern. Stage 1 takes its inputs from the network. Each later stage takes the output of the stage before it, and it starts only when that stage has made its result.
jsc.guide.patterns.text11: Fluids work only inside machine stages. A pipeline cannot hold another pipeline, and it holds up to 16 stages.
jsc.guide.patterns.text12: The network works out how much each stage must make, starting from the last stage and going back. For example, a stage that makes one iron block needs nine ingots from the stage before it, and a stage that makes one ingot needs nine nuggets from the stage before it.
jsc.guide.patterns.text2: A bench pattern is a 3x3 grid of nine cells and a result. A cell that the recipe leaves empty stays empty. You can give the pattern a name of up to 64 characters and a note of up to 256 characters, or leave both out: an unnamed pattern goes by the name of its result.
jsc.guide.patterns.text3: A cell can accept an item tag, such as any kind of planks, instead of one exact item. When a craft is planned, the network uses whatever of that tag it holds in stock. The hint "Right-click a cell: the tag it accepts" tells you what a cell takes.
jsc.guide.patterns.text4: A bench pattern holds items only. You put fluids and chemicals into machine patterns.
jsc.guide.patterns.text5: A machine pattern says what goes into a machine and what comes out. You write its inputs and its outputs, and each one has an amount per run: an input of 1 means one of that item each time the machine runs.
jsc.guide.patterns.text6: The chance of an output is between 1 and 100 percent. An output of 100 always comes out. A smaller chance makes a byproduct that may or may not come out. The network counts a byproduct at its expected amount when it plans the craft, but a byproduct never blocks a craft: the real amount is counted when the machine runs.
jsc.guide.patterns.text7: Anything else that comes out of the machine is an unexpected output. It goes to the network, and it never fails a craft.
jsc.guide.patterns.text8: An input can be marked as estimated when its amount came from a meter that measures per tick, and not from the author of the pattern. The Pattern Studio then shows "per run (estimated)" after the amount, and the recipe still runs.
jsc.guide.patterns.text9: A machine pattern works only from a Crafting Interface that holds it. The interface is described in [](jsc:crafting_interfaces).

jsc.guide.peripheral_cables.balloon2_det: It joins the computer to its devices and carries no network.

jsc.guide.peripheral_cables.definition1: A socket on a computer, a hub or a device. Each socket has a kind: device, video or audio.
jsc.guide.peripheral_cables.definition2: A device that takes one port and offers more ports of its kind, so that more devices can join one computer.
jsc.guide.peripheral_cables.figure1: A Personal Computer with its devices on a Peripheral Cable: two speakers, a Hub, a Floppy Drive, a CD Drive and a Printer. Drag the scene to see the back.
jsc.guide.peripheral_cables.fix1: Check that the cable is within the reach of its era, and that it is not newer than the port.
jsc.guide.peripheral_cables.fix2: Screens and speakers do not pass through a hub. Join them to the computer.
jsc.guide.peripheral_cables.problem2: A monitor joined through a hub stays dark.

jsc.guide.peripheral_cables.table4: Hubs and the ports they offer
jsc.guide.peripheral_cables.text1: A peripheral cable joins a computer to its devices: monitors, speakers, drives, printers and Redstone Interfaces. It is not a data cable, and it carries no network. A device placed right against its computer needs no cable at all.
jsc.guide.peripheral_cables.text2: Each era has its own peripheral cable, and each one reaches a fixed number of cables from its computer. A device further away than that is not seen. A port takes the cable of its own era and of every earlier era, never a newer one.
jsc.guide.peripheral_cables.text3: Each kind of port takes its own kind of device. A drive, a printer, a Redstone Interface or a hub takes a device port. A monitor takes a video output of a graphics card. A speaker takes an audio output, and each audio output drives two speakers. The number of ports depends on the era of the board and of the card.
jsc.guide.peripheral_cables.text4: A server board adds one console output of its own. A processor with built-in graphics adds one output to the board. The audio outputs come from the sound card, and from the board itself from the Transition on ([](jsc:sound_cards)).
jsc.guide.peripheral_cables.text5: When the board runs out of device ports, a hub takes one port and offers ports of its own. A hub is a device, and each device cabled to it takes one of the hub's ports.
jsc.guide.peripheral_cables.text6: A cable after a hub reaches as far again as the cable before it, and a hub can hang from another hub. Only device links pass through a hub. Screens and speakers do not, so join them to the computer. If you break a hub, the devices behind it lose their link.
jsc.guide.peripheral_cables.text7: The Device Manager, the Frames tool that lists the hardware, shows what is on every port ([](jsc:device_manager)).
jsc.guide.peripheral_cables.title: Peripheral cables and hubs
jsc.guide.personal_computers.fix1: A computer needs a motherboard, a processor, memory, a disk and a power supply.
jsc.guide.personal_computers.fix2: Choose a processor with the socket the motherboard takes ([](jsc:motherboards)).
jsc.guide.personal_computers.fix3: Take a card out, or use a motherboard with more PCI Express slots.
jsc.guide.personal_computers.fix4: Use a power supply that gives more watts than the parts draw ([](jsc:power_supplies)).
jsc.guide.personal_computers.fix5: Use memory of a kind the board takes ([](jsc:memory)).

jsc.guide.personal_computers.text1: The Personal Computer (PC) is your own computer, the one you sit at. You install a system on it and run programs, and from it you reach the network: you store and take items, watch the machines work, and ask the network to craft.
jsc.guide.personal_computers.text2: Inside, it takes one motherboard, one processor (CPU), four memory modules (random-access memory, or RAM), four graphics cards (graphics processing units, or GPUs), two disks and one power supply.
jsc.guide.personal_computers.text3: Its storage is the space of its own disks, counted in storage slots: up to 18 slots.
jsc.guide.personal_computers.text4: Every era has its own Personal Computer. From the Standard on, you can choose a plain case, a High Performance case or an Aesthetic case. The Vintage, Legacy and Transition eras have one case each.
jsc.guide.personal_computers.text5: Some cards serve the Workshop program, which gives you a crafting table, a furnace, an enchanting table and an anvil in one window. Each card works on a Personal Computer from the Legacy on, and each draws 15 W of power.
jsc.guide.personal_computers.text6: The Workshop keeps what you put in its window in the computer: the crafting grid, the furnace's input and output, the item to enchant and the items on the anvil. It is lost when the computer breaks.
jsc.guide.personal_computers.title: Personal Computers

jsc.guide.personalize.text1: Personalize is the page where you change how the desktop looks. You choose a wallpaper and the clock format. On the richer editions you also choose an accent and a theme. Frames 10 and Frames 11 add a light or dark look, and Frames 11 lets you align the taskbar.
jsc.guide.personalize.text2: The [Effects](jsc:effects) entry sits at the top of this page. It leads to the effects of your edition.
jsc.guide.personalize.text3: The grid shows the desktop's own wallpaper first, and then every wallpaper that you can choose. Each edition starts with its own.
jsc.guide.personalize.text4: The backdrop of the Common Desktop Environment (CDE) cannot be chosen on a Frames.
jsc.guide.personalize.text5: The accent is the highlight colour of your desktop. You choose one of six accents: blue, green, orange, violet, pink or amber. A theme sets the accent and the wallpaper for you. Frames has three themes:
jsc.guide.personalize.text6: The theme you chose appears as the highlighted button.
jsc.guide.personalize.text7: Frames 10 and Frames 11 have a Light and a Dark look. The other editions have no such row: Frames 7 and Frames XP have no dark look.
jsc.guide.personalize.text8: Frames 11 offers Center and Left for the taskbar. Center puts the Start button and the program icons together in the middle, and it is the default. Left moves them to the left edge.
jsc.guide.personalize.text9: The clock shows 24-hour time by default. Choose 12-hour to change it on any edition.
jsc.guide.personalize.title: Personalising: themes, wallpapers and colours
jsc.guide.pipes_and_variables.definition: A connection that gives what one command prints to the next command as its input.
Sending a command's answer to a file with the arrows > and >>, or reading its input from a file with <.
A command you started with the ampersand and left to run in the background. It has a number, which you use to list it or stop it.
A name that stands for a text value, such as USER for the login name.
A symbol, such as the star, that stands for other text in names. The shell replaces it with the matching names.
jsc.guide.pipes_and_variables.fix1: A pipe needs a command on each side, and an arrow needs a file name. Put a space around the bar.
jsc.guide.pipes_and_variables.fix2: Run the command alone. To read a long answer, pipe the command into grep or head to keep only the lines you need, or write the answer to a file and read it with less.
jsc.guide.pipes_and_variables.fix3: Stop a finished or unwanted job with kill %<id> ([](jsc:processes_and_jobs)).
jsc.guide.pipes_and_variables.fix4: The ls command prints every name on one line unless you give -l. Use ls -l, which prints one line for each name.
jsc.guide.pipes_and_variables.fix5: Choose a variable name with only letters, digits and underscores, and do not start it with a digit.
jsc.guide.pipes_and_variables.problem1: The shell says syntax error near unexpected token, followed by a bar or an arrow.
jsc.guide.pipes_and_variables.problem2: The shell says the command takes the whole terminal, so it cannot be piped or redirected.
jsc.guide.pipes_and_variables.problem3: The shell says the machine has no memory left for another job.
jsc.guide.pipes_and_variables.problem5: The shell says a name is letters, digits and underscores, and does not start with a digit.
jsc.guide.pipes_and_variables.table1_1_2: Sends the answer of the left command to the right one.
jsc.guide.pipes_and_variables.table1_2_2: Writes the answer to a file, and replaces what the file held.
jsc.guide.pipes_and_variables.table1_3_2: Adds the answer to the end of a file.
jsc.guide.pipes_and_variables.table1_4_2: Reads a file as the input of the command.
jsc.guide.pipes_and_variables.table1_5_2: Runs the command in the background, as the last word of the line.
jsc.guide.pipes_and_variables.table2_2_2: The login name, which is always player.
jsc.guide.pipes_and_variables.table2_3_2: The system: Linux, FreeBSD or UNIX.
jsc.guide.pipes_and_variables.table2_5_2: Set by default only on UNIX System V; on Linux and FreeBSD it is empty until you set it.
jsc.guide.pipes_and_variables.table3_1_2: The semicolon, && and || are plain words that the command receives as text.
jsc.guide.pipes_and_variables.table3_2_2: There is no way to send errors to a file; only the arrows above exist.
jsc.guide.pipes_and_variables.table3_3_2: A command cannot take the place of its own answer.
jsc.guide.pipes_and_variables.table3_4_2: There is no alias command, and no ! history form, on any of these systems.
jsc.guide.pipes_and_variables.table3_5_2: Not on Unix, where find is a DOS command; grep searches the lines of a file instead.
jsc.guide.pipes_and_variables.table3_6_2: Not on Unix, where the command for reading by the page is less.
jsc.guide.pipes_and_variables.text1: A few small signs change what a command reads and where its answer goes. They work on Linux, FreeBSD and UNIX System V, and this entry says where the three differ.
jsc.guide.pipes_and_variables.text10: A name holds only letters, digits and underscores, and it does not start with a digit. The set command gives a value on every machine. The export command makes a value visible to the programs the shell runs, and unset forgets a name.
jsc.guide.pipes_and_variables.text11: A variable belongs to the computer, not to one window, so a name you set stays set for the whole computer.
jsc.guide.pipes_and_variables.text12: A star stands for any text in a file name. An unquoted word with a star opens into the names of the matching files in its folder, before the command runs.
jsc.guide.pipes_and_variables.text13: Put the word in quotes, as in "notes*", and the shell keeps the star as you wrote it. On MC-DOS and the Frames systems the command gets the star itself.
jsc.guide.pipes_and_variables.text14: Press Tab to complete a word you have started. On the first word, Tab completes a command name. After a command such as mkfs.ext4 or mount, it completes a device name. Tab does not complete file or folder names.
jsc.guide.pipes_and_variables.text15: Press Tab twice in a row, and the shell prints every possible completion above the prompt.
jsc.guide.pipes_and_variables.text16: Some shell features of other systems are missing from these three. The table says what each one does here.
jsc.guide.pipes_and_variables.text2: A pipe, written with a bar, takes what the command on its left prints and gives it to the command on its right. Two commands joined this way work as one.
jsc.guide.pipes_and_variables.text3: The shell reads a bar or an ampersand only as a word of its own. Written as ls|grep x, the whole thing is one word, and no pipe is made.
jsc.guide.pipes_and_variables.text4: The file name may stick to the arrow, as in >notes.txt, or follow it as its own word, as in > notes.txt. An arrow with no file name is a syntax error. A quoted operator is plain text, so a quoted bar is a plain character.
jsc.guide.pipes_and_variables.text5: A pipe carries at most 4,096 lines from one command to the next.
jsc.guide.pipes_and_variables.text6: Some commands take the whole terminal, so they cannot be piped or redirected: less, vim, emacs, vi and ee, info on Linux, and man when it opens a manual entry.
jsc.guide.pipes_and_variables.text7: Put an ampersand as the last word of a line, and the command runs in the background. You get the prompt back at once, and you can go on typing while the command works.
jsc.guide.pipes_and_variables.text8: Each background job takes 1 MB of the machine's memory. When no room is left, the shell refuses the new job.
jsc.guide.pipes_and_variables.text9: A variable is a name that stands for a text value. You give it a value with NAME=value on a line of its own, and you use it with a dollar sign: $NAME, or ${NAME} when letters follow the name directly.
jsc.guide.pipes_and_variables.title: Pipes, redirection, background jobs, variables, wildcards and Tab
jsc.guide.pkg.definition1: A package another player published to the Mirror.
jsc.guide.pkg.definition2: An installed package whose version differs from the one the Mirror serves now.
jsc.guide.pkg.fix1: Connect this computer to a network whose Mainframe runs the Mirror service.
jsc.guide.pkg.fix2: Type pkg search and a word to find the real name, then use that name.
jsc.guide.pkg.fix3: Free some disk space, or use a computer with better hardware.
jsc.guide.pkg.fix4: Type pkg info to find the exact name.
jsc.guide.pkg.fix5: Nothing to do: it is already on the computer.
jsc.guide.pkg.problem1: pkg says it could not resolve mirror://.
jsc.guide.pkg.problem2: pkg says it cannot locate the package by its name.
jsc.guide.pkg.problem3: pkg says the requirements are unmet.
jsc.guide.pkg.problem4: pkg says the package is not installed when you delete it.
jsc.guide.pkg.problem5: pkg says the program comes with every system.
jsc.guide.pkg.step1: Type pkg install and the name of the package.
jsc.guide.pkg.step2: Read the lines that name the packages and the download size.
jsc.guide.pkg.step3: Wait while the package is set up. The setup runs as a job you can watch.
jsc.guide.pkg.table1_1_2: Fetches a package from the Mirror and installs it.
jsc.guide.pkg.table1_3_2: Lists the packages that match the term, one row each.
jsc.guide.pkg.table1_4_2: Lists every installed package, with its description.
jsc.guide.pkg.table1_5_2: Refreshes the Mirror's list of packages without changing any installed package.
jsc.guide.pkg.table1_6_2: Installs newer versions of the packages you have installed.
jsc.guide.pkg.table2_10_2: pkg info has nothing to list.
jsc.guide.pkg.table2_11_2: pkg search found no package with that word.
jsc.guide.pkg.table2_1_2: This computer is not on a network whose Mainframe runs the Mirror service.
jsc.guide.pkg.table2_2_2: The Mirror does not offer a package with that name.
jsc.guide.pkg.table2_3_2: The computer lacks the hardware or the free disk space the package needs.
jsc.guide.pkg.table2_4_2: You tried to delete a package that is not installed.
jsc.guide.pkg.table2_5_2: The program is already there, so there is nothing to install.
jsc.guide.pkg.table2_6_2: The package is on the computer already.
jsc.guide.pkg.table2_7_2: The computer is of an older era than the package needs.
jsc.guide.pkg.table2_8_2: The package runs only on that kind of computer: the Mainframe, a server in a rack, a Cluster Management Computer or a Personal Computer.
jsc.guide.pkg.table2_9_2: The computer has no disk to keep programs on.
jsc.guide.pkg.text1: pkg is the package manager of FreeBSD. A package is a program built by someone else and fetched ready to install, so you do not build it yourself. The packages come from the network's Mirror, and you type pkg, a verb, and the name it works on.
jsc.guide.pkg.text2: Three shorter words also work: add means install, remove means delete, and query means info.
jsc.guide.pkg.text3: pkg search marks a package [installed] when it is on your computer, and [community] when another player published it. pkg upgrade installs the newer version of each Outdated package.
jsc.guide.pkg.text4: A delete lists the packages it removes, then says how much space it frees, such as "The operation will free <n> MiB."
jsc.guide.pkg.title: pkg, verb by verb
jsc.guide.ports_build.definition1: Compiling the program's source on this computer.
jsc.guide.ports_build.definition2: The source archive that a build fetches from the Mirror.
jsc.guide.ports_build.fix1: Go into the port's folder first, such as /usr/ports/sysutils/screenfetch.
jsc.guide.ports_build.fix2: Type make reinstall, or make deinstall and then make install.
jsc.guide.ports_build.fix3: The Mirror cannot be reached. Connect the network to a Mirror, then try again.
jsc.guide.ports_build.fix4: Use a computer with a faster processor, or free some disk space.
jsc.guide.ports_build.problem1: make says there is no target to make.
jsc.guide.ports_build.problem2: make says the program is already installed.
jsc.guide.ports_build.problem3: fetch says there is no address record for the Mirror.
jsc.guide.ports_build.problem4: make says the computer is short of the processor or the free disk space.
jsc.guide.ports_build.step1: Type cd and the port's folder, such as /usr/ports/sysutils/screenfetch.
jsc.guide.ports_build.step2: Type make install clean to build, install and clean the port.
jsc.guide.ports_build.step3: Type make deinstall to take the program off the computer again.
jsc.guide.ports_build.table1_1_2: Builds the port on this computer, which is what make does when you give no target.
jsc.guide.ports_build.table1_2_2: Builds the port if it is not built, then installs it.
jsc.guide.ports_build.table1_3_2: Builds and installs the port over the one installed.
jsc.guide.ports_build.table1_4_2: Takes the installed port off the computer; with clean, it cleans first.
jsc.guide.ports_build.table1_5_2: Deletes the work folder that the build left.
jsc.guide.ports_build.table3_1_2: The folder is not a port's folder. make then stops in that folder.
jsc.guide.ports_build.table3_2_2: make does not know that target.
jsc.guide.ports_build.table3_3_2: The port is on the computer already; the message suggests make deinstall and make install, or make reinstall.
jsc.guide.ports_build.table3_4_2: A gate of the install blocks the port, such as its era or the kind of computer.
jsc.guide.ports_build.table3_5_2: The port is a Mainframe service, so install it with pkg instead.
jsc.guide.ports_build.table3_6_2: The computer has no disk to keep programs on.
jsc.guide.ports_build.table3_7_2: The computer is too small for the port.
jsc.guide.ports_build.table3_8_2: The build needs its source, and no Mirror answers.
jsc.guide.ports_build.text1: You build a port in its own folder, with the make command, which reads the port's recipe. The build compiles the program's source on this computer. It takes a while, and the result is made for this computer.
jsc.guide.ports_build.text2: The usage line of make is: usage: make [build] [install | reinstall | deinstall] [clean].
jsc.guide.ports_build.text3: You combine targets in one line, such as make install clean. A build takes between 5 seconds and 30 minutes. It runs one job per processor core, and a faster processor shortens it.
jsc.guide.ports_build.text4: A program you build on this computer needs 10% less than the package of the same program. When a build ends, it prints Built for this machine:, then a line such as 10% less memory, disk and processor than the package.
jsc.guide.ports_build.title: Building ports: make, and the 10% lighter build
jsc.guide.ports_tree.definition1: The folder of recipes, one per program, that builds programs on this computer.
jsc.guide.ports_tree.definition2: The recipe for one program in the ports tree.
jsc.guide.ports_tree.definition3: The copy of the ports tree that the Mirror serves, fetched as one unit.
jsc.guide.ports_tree.fix1: Connect the network to a Mainframe that runs the Mirror service.
jsc.guide.ports_tree.fix2: Type portsnap fetch first, then extract or update.
jsc.guide.ports_tree.fix3: Type portsnap extract once. Afterwards, update works.
jsc.guide.ports_tree.problem1: portsnap says none found for the Mirror.
jsc.guide.ports_tree.problem2: portsnap says there is no snapshot available.
jsc.guide.ports_tree.problem3: portsnap says /usr/ports was not created by portsnap.
jsc.guide.ports_tree.problem4: portsnap says there is no space left on the device.
jsc.guide.ports_tree.step1: The first time, type portsnap fetch extract.
jsc.guide.ports_tree.table1_1_2: Brings the snapshot from the Mirror without laying out a tree.
jsc.guide.ports_tree.table1_2_2: Lays out the tree afresh from the snapshot, replacing any tree there.
jsc.guide.ports_tree.table1_3_2: Brings a tree that is laid out already up to date.
jsc.guide.ports_tree.table1_4_2: Fetches, then extracts or updates, whichever the computer needs.
jsc.guide.ports_tree.table2: Where some programs sit in the tree
jsc.guide.ports_tree.table3_1_2: The computer has no disk to hold the tree.
jsc.guide.ports_tree.table3_2_2: fetch found no Mirror, so no snapshot comes; it then prints No mirrors remaining, giving up.
jsc.guide.ports_tree.table3_3_2: extract and update need a snapshot first.
jsc.guide.ports_tree.table3_4_2: update works only on a tree that portsnap laid out, so run portsnap extract once.
jsc.guide.ports_tree.text1: FreeBSD also builds programs from source, on your own computer. The recipes for them sit in the ports tree, a folder on the system disk. You fetch the tree with portsnap, and the Mirror serves it as one copy.
jsc.guide.ports_tree.text2: The tree is real files. Each port has a folder at /usr/ports/<category>/<name>/ with three files. Makefile holds the recipe, distinfo holds the checksum and size of its source, and pkg-descr holds the one-line description.
jsc.guide.ports_tree.text3: The words combine in the order you type them. While it runs, portsnap prints its progress, and its last line gives the number of ports and the disk they take.
jsc.guide.ports_tree.title: The ports tree: portsnap
jsc.guide.ports_tree.warning1: portsnap extract replaces the whole ports tree, and the build folders inside it go too.
jsc.guide.power_supplies.definition1: The share of the power a supply takes in that reaches the parts. The build check does not use it.
jsc.guide.power_supplies.fix1: Its parts draw more than its supply gives. Use a supply with more watts.
jsc.guide.power_supplies.problem1: The computer does not start, or the build says "PSU insufficient".
jsc.guide.power_supplies.text1: Most parts draw power, and the power supply gives it. The processors, the memory, the graphics cards, the disks and the expansion cards each draw watts. The supply has to give at least their total.
jsc.guide.power_supplies.text2: There are twelve supplies, from 200 W to 3,000 W, each with its own efficiency.
jsc.guide.power_supplies.text3: The build adds up the draw of the processors, the memory, the disks and the expansion cards. If the sum is more than the supply gives, the build fails with PSU insufficient ([When the build is refused](jsc:build_refusals)).
jsc.guide.power_supplies.text4: On a rack server, the DRAW readout shows the draw and the supply's watts, and it turns red when the draw is over. A tower has no draw readout, so keep the sum in mind when you choose.
jsc.guide.power_supplies.text5: A computer whose supply gives less than its parts draw does not start. It stays off, and a server says why.
jsc.guide.power_supplies.title: Power supplies
jsc.guide.printers.fix1: Read the status. "no paper" means the tray is empty, so add plain paper. "take the sheets" means the output is full, so take the sheets out.
jsc.guide.printers.fix2: Join the printer to the computer with a peripheral cable ([](jsc:peripheral_cables)).
jsc.guide.printers.fix3: Wait for the queue to empty, or cancel the job with CANCEL JOB.
jsc.guide.printers.fix4: Print it on a printer that prints in colour: the Legacy, Transition or Advanced printer.
jsc.guide.printers.fix5: Use the name of a printer joined to the computer. lpstat shows them.
jsc.guide.printers.problem2: No printer is connected to this computer.
jsc.guide.printers.problem3: The printer says it cannot take more documents: its queue is full.
jsc.guide.printers.problem4: A picture in colour came out in black and white.
jsc.guide.printers.problem5: The lp command says the destination is "non-existent".

jsc.guide.printers.text1: A printer puts a document on paper. Each era has its own printer, and each one draws the picture on paper its own way, as the real printers of that time did. Join a printer to a computer, put plain paper in its tray, and print from a program.
jsc.guide.printers.text10: On the command line, a file goes to a printer with a command. The MC-DOS prompt uses PRINT, and the shells of Linux, FreeBSD and UNIX System V use lp. The commands are explained in full in the MC-DOS book ([](jsc:dos_printing)) and in the Linux books ([](jsc:printing)).
jsc.guide.printers.text11: For lp, each printer has a name. Give it with -d. The name is also the start of the request id that lp answers with: the name, a dash and a number.
jsc.guide.printers.text2: A picture can come out on paper too. A sheet with a picture can hang in an item frame, where it fills the face of the frame. Right-click a Printed Paper sheet to read it.
jsc.guide.printers.text3: The printer's tooltip, and the print dialog, say which printers print in black and white: "Prints in black and white", or "Prints in color". The dialog also shows the word Mono or Color beside the printer's name.
jsc.guide.printers.text4: The FX-80 draws in black dots, one pass for every eight rows. The DeskJot leaves bands of colour, and the FotoSmart prints the same inks in finer dots. The LaserJot uses toner, and the EcoTonk prints the picture as it is.
jsc.guide.printers.text5: A tick is a twentieth of a second, so 20 ticks make a second. The fewer ticks a page takes, the faster the printer.
jsc.guide.printers.text6: The tray takes plain paper only. Right-click the printer with paper to fill its tray. Each page takes one sheet from the tray. When the tray is empty, the job waits with the status "no paper".
jsc.guide.printers.text7: The printer puts finished pages in its three output places. When they are full, the status says "take the sheets". Take the sheets from the printer's window: shift-click a sheet to move it into your inventory.
jsc.guide.printers.text8: The queue is the list of jobs waiting to print, and the first job is the one printing. The printer keeps 16 jobs, and a job can ask for 1 to 99 copies. A job sent to a full queue is refused. In the printer's window, PAUSE stops the printing, RESUME starts it again, and CANCEL JOB cancels the job.
jsc.guide.printers.text9: The print dialog names the printer's state: "Ready", "Printing", "Paused", "Out of paper" or "Output tray full".
jsc.guide.printers.title: Printers
jsc.guide.printing.definition1: The printer that a print job goes to.
jsc.guide.printing.definition2: How many prints of each file one job makes.

jsc.guide.printing.fix2: Type the name exactly as lpstat shows it.
jsc.guide.printing.fix3: Give at least one file name after the command.
