jsc.guide.printing.text1: You print from the terminal with two commands. The lp command sends files to a printer, and the lpstat command shows the print requests and the printers.
jsc.guide.printing.text2: Name the destination with -d, or leave it out to use the default one. The number of copies comes with -n.
jsc.guide.printing.title: Printing from the terminal
jsc.guide.priorities.definition1: The level, from LOW to HIGH, that decides which waiting Operation gets a free queue first.
jsc.guide.priorities.definition2: The rise of a waiting Operation's level: one step for each period it waits for a queue.
jsc.guide.priorities.fix1: A waiting Operation waits for a hold on items, not for a queue. Wait until the hold ends, or UNLOCK the item ([](jsc:lock_unlock)).
jsc.guide.priorities.fix2: Take PRIORITY off the QUERY. It sets the level of an Operation, and a QUERY only reads ([](jsc:clauses_priority_if_with)).
jsc.guide.priorities.fix3: Write one of the five names from the table, such as HIGH.
jsc.guide.priorities.problem1: An Operation is WAITING, and raising its level changes nothing.
jsc.guide.priorities.problem2: The result says PRIORITY is not valid on a read.
jsc.guide.priorities.problem3: The result says unknown priority level, and lists the five names.
jsc.guide.priorities.step1: Open the Processes tab of the Network Manager, and click the row of the Operation.
jsc.guide.priorities.step2: Press > to raise its level one step, or < to lower it.
jsc.guide.priorities.text1: Every Operation has a priority, which decides which waiting Operation gets a free queue first. There are five levels, from the lowest to the highest. A new Operation starts at MEDIUM, unless you choose another level.
jsc.guide.priorities.text2: When two Operations have the same level, the one that came first goes first.
jsc.guide.priorities.text3: Keywords are not case-sensitive, and you can write medium-low or medium-high with a hyphen. The keyword normal means MEDIUM. The short label is what dense lists show.
jsc.guide.priorities.text4: An Operation that is ready but gets no free queue climbs one level for every 30 seconds it waits. By default, that is 600 ticks. It climbs no higher than HIGH, so low work is delayed, but it is never left behind for good. The mod's configuration sets this period, and a period of 0 switches aging off.
jsc.guide.priorities.text5: Aging does not change the level you chose. Each tick, the Mainframe works out the level it uses for that tick: the chosen level, plus what aging has added.
jsc.guide.priorities.text6: In IQL, end a statement with PRIORITY and a level, such as SELECT 64 iron_ingot PRIORITY HIGH. In the Network program, the popup of a request has a PRIORITY setting that raises or lowers the level one step at a time. A CRAFT takes its level from the statement or from its request ([](jsc:asking_for_a_craft)).
jsc.guide.priorities.title: Priorities
jsc.guide.processes_and_jobs.definition1: A program that is running. Every running program has a number, which ps lists as its PID.
jsc.guide.processes_and_jobs.definition2: A line that the machine runs by itself, at a set hour, every day or on named days.
jsc.guide.processes_and_jobs.fix1: Give the number of the process from the ps list, not its name.
jsc.guide.processes_and_jobs.fix2: The jobs command shows the current job numbers. Use one of them after the percent sign.
jsc.guide.processes_and_jobs.fix3: Write the hour as "06:00" or as "6".
jsc.guide.processes_and_jobs.problem1: The kill command says kill: not a process id.
jsc.guide.processes_and_jobs.problem2: The kill command says there is no such job.
jsc.guide.processes_and_jobs.problem3: The crontab command says the word you gave is not an hour of the day.
jsc.guide.processes_and_jobs.table1_1_2: Lists the lines the machine runs, and when.
jsc.guide.processes_and_jobs.table1_2_2: Removes the line with that number.
jsc.guide.processes_and_jobs.table1_3_2: The hour the line runs. The form 6 also works.
jsc.guide.processes_and_jobs.table1_4_2: The days, separated by commas. Leave them out to run every day.
jsc.guide.processes_and_jobs.text1: A process is a program that is running now. Each process has a number, its process ID (PID), and the ps command lists them with it. It lists the system's own processes first. Number 1 is the first process, which starts every other one: systemd on most Linux distributions, and init on Gentoo, FreeBSD and UNIX. Each service the system runs comes next, and the programs you start are numbered from 1000.
jsc.guide.processes_and_jobs.text2: The kill command stops a process by its number. The process stops where it stands, and any work it had not finished stays not done. A signal can come before the number, such as -9 or -KILL, and kill -l lists the signals. A service you stop stays stopped until the computer starts again. Stopping process 1 takes the whole system down: the kernel panics, prints why on the screen, and the computer starts over by itself.
jsc.guide.processes_and_jobs.text3: A job is a background command you started with an ampersand. You list your jobs with jobs, and you stop one with kill %1, where 1 is its number in that list.
jsc.guide.processes_and_jobs.text4: When the computer runs out of memory, the kernel, the core of the system, ends the process that holds the most, then the next, until everything left fits. The dmesg command prints what the kernel has logged since the computer started: what it found as it came up, and a line for each process it ended. On a desktop, a window the kernel ends closes with a balloon, "Out of memory", that names it. A program ended in front of the terminal leaves the word Killed. Only when nothing is left to end does the kernel panic, and then the computer starts over by itself.
jsc.guide.processes_and_jobs.text5: The crontab command sets a line that the machine runs by itself, at an hour you choose, every day or on named days. Such a line is a schedule.
jsc.guide.processes_and_jobs.title: Processes, jobs and scheduling
jsc.guide.processors.definition1: One unit of work a processor does at the same time as its other cores.
jsc.guide.processors.definition2: How fast each core runs, in GHz (gigahertz): billions of beats of the clock a second.
jsc.guide.processors.fix1: Its socket or its era is not the board's. Use a processor with the board's socket and era.
jsc.guide.processors.fix2: Use processors of one instruction set.
jsc.guide.processors.fix3: Take processors out, or use a board with more CPU slots.
jsc.guide.processors.problem2: The build says the CPU instruction set does not match.
jsc.guide.processors.problem3: The build says there are too many CPUs.
jsc.guide.processors.table2: Word size and item size by era
jsc.guide.processors.text1: The processor, or CPU, does the actual computing. Every program you run is the processor following its instructions, one after the other, very fast.
jsc.guide.processors.text2: Two numbers say how much a processor can do: its cores, and its clock speed in GHz. Your processor's cores are the units of work that run at the same time.
jsc.guide.processors.text3: Hover a processor and its tooltip shows its capacity, in items a tick (it/t), and its power in watts. On a Mainframe, the capacity of its processors adds up to how many items a tick the whole network handles ([Mainframes](jsc:mainframes)).
jsc.guide.processors.text4: A processor also has to fit the board. Its socket must be the board's socket, and its era must be the board's era. With no board in place yet, a processor goes into any slot, so you can set up your parts first.
jsc.guide.processors.text5: Every processor belongs to an instruction set. A program built for one set runs on it and on every newer set, never on an older one. Processors of two sets never share a computer.
jsc.guide.processors.text6: The word size of a processor depends on its era, and so does the size of one item. You will see the same sizes on the disks ([Units and ticks](jsc:units_and_ticks)).
jsc.guide.processors.text7: There are more than 170 processors in the mod, from the Integra and Velocion makers. A processor with graphics built in says so on its tooltip, and it lights a monitor without a graphics card.
jsc.guide.processors.title: Processors
jsc.guide.profiler.definition1: One recording session in the Profiler. It starts, pauses and stops, and its rows can be saved as a file.
jsc.guide.profiler.fix1: Press Start. The Profiler records only what happens after the trace starts.
jsc.guide.profiler.fix2: A trace ends when the player who started it leaves the game, and when the server stops. Use New Trace to start a new one.
jsc.guide.profiler.fix3: Record a shorter trace, or choose fewer groups, so that fewer rows are kept.
jsc.guide.profiler.fix4: Select a StatementStarting or a StatementCompleted row first.
jsc.guide.profiler.fix5: Save is off until the trace has rows. Start the trace and let some events come in.

jsc.guide.profiler.text1: The IQL Server Profiler records the network's work as it happens, one row for each event. When a craft or a query does something you did not expect, the Profiler shows you what the network did, row by row.
jsc.guide.profiler.text10: Replay Statement, in the Replay menu, runs a recorded statement again. It is on only when you have selected a StatementStarting or a StatementCompleted row. It opens the studio and runs the statement in a new query.
jsc.guide.profiler.text11: Save As... writes the rows to a file. The file name is the trace's name, with spaces replaced by underscores, and the extension .log. The file has a header line with the seven column names, then one line for each row, and its values are separated by tabs.
jsc.guide.profiler.text12: The detail lines of a row are joined with " | ", and a line break inside a row becomes a space.
jsc.guide.profiler.text2: Open it from the studio's Tools menu, with the item IQL Server Profiler, or from the desktop. It opens in its own window, not as a tab of the studio.
jsc.guide.profiler.text3: Recording is done in a trace: one session that you start, pause, stop and save as a file. Each new trace is numbered.
jsc.guide.profiler.text4: Each row has the columns EventClass, TextData, Requester, Computer, Items, Duration and StartTime.
jsc.guide.profiler.text5: Changing the groups while a trace runs restarts it with the new groups. A group that is not chosen records nothing.
jsc.guide.profiler.text6: The status line reads "Trace is running.", "Trace is paused." or "Trace is stopped." A new trace with no rows says "No events yet. Start the trace to record what the network does."
jsc.guide.profiler.text7: Under the grid, the detail lines of the row you choose appear. An event shows who asked for it, as "asked by: <requester> on <computer>", and how long it took, as "took <n> ticks (<n> s)". Twenty ticks make one second. When nobody asked, the requester reads "network".
jsc.guide.profiler.text8: The Profiler keeps at most 2,000 rows. When the trace is full, the oldest rows are dropped. The bottom bar shows "Ln <n>, Col 1" for the selected row, where Ln is the row number, and "Rows: <n>" for the count of rows.
jsc.guide.profiler.text9: Find searches the rows as text. Find Next moves to the next match, and Escape closes the find strip. When nothing else matches, it says "Nothing more holds <text>."
jsc.guide.profiler.title: The IQL Server Profiler
jsc.guide.program_messages.fix1: The program has finished or halted, or its waiting calls are full. Try again later, or send less text.

jsc.guide.program_messages.fix13: Write the path in the form host, then share, then the rest of the path: \\host\share\folder.
jsc.guide.program_messages.fix2: Switch that computer on, then try again.
jsc.guide.program_messages.fix3: Its remote setting is off. Turn that setting on at that computer. It is on by default.
jsc.guide.program_messages.fix4: That computer does not run programs, so no program starts there. Start the program on a computer that runs programs.
jsc.guide.program_messages.fix5: The name is wrong, or the computer is not on this network. Network.Computers lists the computers on it.
jsc.guide.program_messages.fix6: Use the host name of one machine, or its node id, which is its [network identity](jsc:network_identity).
jsc.guide.program_messages.fix7: The folder was shared without write. Its owner runs config unshare on it, then config share with write.
jsc.guide.program_messages.fix8: Unshare a folder with config unshare to make room for another share.
jsc.guide.program_messages.fix9: A share takes the folder's name, so only one folder can have it. Unshare the other folder first.

jsc.guide.program_messages.text1: Programs talk to each other with messages. A message is a line of text that one program sends to another program's number. The other program can run on the same computer, on another computer of the network, or be a [ComputerCraft](jsc:computercraft_side) computer reached through a [Network Gateway](jsc:network_gateway).
jsc.guide.program_messages.text10: A computer shares a folder with the network from its prompt, with the config command. The share takes the folder's own name. It is read only, unless you add write.
jsc.guide.program_messages.text11: The prompt answers with the address of the share, such as \\host\name, and says whether it is read only or read and write. A path on another computer starts with two backslashes, then the host name, then the share and the rest of the path: \\host\share\folder\file. The other computer answers for its own disks.
jsc.guide.program_messages.text12: A copy may use a shared folder at either end. The file is read where it is and written where it goes. The shares of a computer are also covered in [Shared folders](jsc:shared_folders).
jsc.guide.program_messages.text2: A program sends a message with Process.Send, giving the number of the other program and the text. To receive messages, a program sets a handler with Program.OnMessage: the steps that run for each message. The handler gets the number of the sender (From), the text (Text) and the tick it arrived on (Tick).
jsc.guide.program_messages.text3: If the program you send to has no handler, it takes the message and throws it away, so Process.Send still gives true. Process.Send gives false when no running program has that number.
jsc.guide.program_messages.text4: A message is refused when the program it is sent to has finished or halted, or when its waiting calls are full: 256 calls, or 64 KB of text. Then Process.Send gives false.
jsc.guide.program_messages.text5: A message to a Gateway reaches every program on the computer that is listening for it. A computer where no program listens drops the message.
jsc.guide.program_messages.text6: Network.Computers lists the computers on the network. Network.Computer(name) gives one of them by its name. Each one has a host name, a name, a type, an operating system and an online state.
jsc.guide.program_messages.text7: A program on another computer is reached with the remote calls below. Before any of them works, the other computer must be on the network and switched on. It must also take programs from other computers: the remote setting decides that, and it is on by default. Set it to on or off. A remote Start also needs a computer that runs programs.
jsc.guide.program_messages.text8: A program started on another computer records the caller as its parent. When it ends, the caller is told. The caller reads its output and its exit code with Process.Output and Process.ExitCode, while that program is still there to be read.
jsc.guide.program_messages.text9: A remote program's Process value carries the other computer's host name in Process.Host, and calls on that value go to that computer. If the host is unknown or switched off, Process.Running gives false and Process.Kill does nothing.
jsc.guide.program_messages.title: Programs talking to each other

jsc.guide.programming_buses.text1: Programs can set a bus, as well as the window can. A program finds a bus by its name, on the same network. Give the bus its name first, in its window ([](jsc:bus_window)).
jsc.guide.programming_buses.text2: Programs set a bus in IQL or in Sigma. IQL is the network's query language ([](jsc:iql)). Sigma is a programming language, and its sister language is Sigma#. The Book of Sigma covers both ([](jsc:sigma_two_languages)).
jsc.guide.programming_buses.text3: A name matches regardless of capital letters, and the first bus with that name on the network is the one used. Put a name in quotes when it has spaces.
jsc.guide.programming_buses.text4: Vanilla items are written by their short name, such as iron_ore. Items from other mods are written in full, as namespace:path. Fluids are written with the word FLUID before them, as in FLUID water.
jsc.guide.programming_buses.text5: The SOFTWARE tab of a bus shows the IQL and SIGMA lines that would set it as it is now, so you can copy them ([](jsc:bus_window)). It writes an HOURS condition in job form, such as CREATE JOB bus_hours AS SET BUS 'Ore in' ON WHEN TIME BETWEEN 18:00 AND 06:00. The engine keeps that job as the bus's HOURS condition.
jsc.guide.programming_buses.title: Programming buses
jsc.guide.programs.definition1: Software that a system runs for you, in a window or at a prompt.
jsc.guide.programs.definition2: The graphical face of a system: its windows, icons, menus and the programs you start from it.
jsc.guide.programs.definition3: A program as the network's repository keeps it, ready to install by name.
jsc.guide.programs.definition4: The program that fetches a package and records what is installed on the computer, such as apt, dnf, pacman, emerge, pkg or pckmgr.

jsc.guide.programs.text1: A program is software that does one job for you, such as drawing a picture, playing a game or keeping a list of files. Every system comes with some programs, and you can install others. Each program has a name, runs on some kinds of system, and needs some disk space and memory.
jsc.guide.programs.text10: On Frames, the pckmgr command also has the verbs remove, search and list. The list verb with --available shows every program the Mirror offers.
jsc.guide.programs.text11: Some programs are services that run on a Mainframe. When you install one there, the service switches on, and the Mainframe keeps a record of its version. Some programs also need an IQL engine on the network ([](jsc:engines)).
jsc.guide.programs.text12: You can publish your own packages to the Mirror, for other players to install, with the Sigma package tool ([](jsc:sigma_publish_mirror)).
jsc.guide.programs.text13: The programs of the other chapters have their own pages: the Crafting Manager ([](jsc:crafting_manager)), the Pattern Studio ([](jsc:pattern_studio)) and the Workshop ([](jsc:workshop)).
jsc.guide.programs.text14: The desktop programs follow on the next pages: the Network window, This PC, Files, the Editor, Settings, the System Monitor, the Task Manager, a Calculator, Paint, Exceed, and the games. The books of the series, one for each family of systems, go deeper into install and use ([](jsc:library)).
jsc.guide.programs.text2: There are two ways to install a program. You can install it from install media: the disc or stick the program ships on, such as a CD (compact disc), a DVD (digital versatile disc) or a USB (universal serial bus) stick. Or you can install it from [the Mirror](jsc:mirror), by name, with no media at all.
jsc.guide.programs.text3: From media, you put the program's install medium in a linked drive of the computer, and then you start its setup.
jsc.guide.programs.text4: On a Frames desktop you can also open This PC, where each linked drive shows its program with an Install button beside it. The computer answers with a line that starts with Setting up, then the program's name, then from and the medium, such as the floppy or the CD.
jsc.guide.programs.text5: The systems come on the same media, by their era: a Vintage system on a floppy, a Legacy system on a CD, a Transition system on a DVD, and a Standard or Advanced system on a USB stick. Read more about the drives on their own page ([](jsc:drives)).
jsc.guide.programs.text6: From the Mirror you install by name, and the computer needs a network whose Mainframe runs the Mirror. The Mirror is the package service of that Mainframe: it keeps the network's packages, and each computer installs from it with its package manager.
jsc.guide.programs.text7: Gentoo builds each program from its source code. When the computer has room for the build, the install runs as a script in front of the terminal, and the answer comes later.
jsc.guide.programs.text8: The store command lists every program that is not preinstalled, one line each, with the install command beside it. You can also type available. The list does not depend on your computer: a program in the list may still refuse to install here, and the install says why. When nothing is left, store answers "nothing else to install".
jsc.guide.programs.text9: The update command brings the installed programs up to their newest version. It never installs a new program, and it answers "All packages are up to date." when there is nothing to do.
jsc.guide.programs.title: Programs
jsc.guide.programs_and_processes.definit: A value that refers to a process by its number.
The memory a program has for its own values. 1 MB by default when another program starts it.
The part of your program that runs when an event arrives.
Something the program is told about: a message, a click, or a change it watches.
jsc.guide.programs_and_processes.fix1: Start a compiled program, or compile the source file first.
jsc.guide.programs_and_processes.fix2: Close a program to free memory, then start it again.
jsc.guide.programs_and_processes.fix3: Read the error the compiler gives, and fix the line it names. The errors are explained in [](jsc:sigma_reading_an_error).
jsc.guide.programs_and_processes.fix4: The process has ended, so it is no longer on the machine. Read its output while the process is still running.
jsc.guide.programs_and_processes.fix5: The receiving program has no room in its queue. Send again later.
jsc.guide.programs_and_processes.fix6: Read the error in the console. The program's work stops with that error.
jsc.guide.programs_and_processes.heading: Process
Messages and events
jsc.guide.programs_and_processes.problem: Program.Start stops the program: nothing installed runs a file of that kind.
Program.Start stops the program: the program needs more memory than is free.
The start stops with the compiler's text, because the source file does not compile.
Process.Output or Process.ExitCode stops the program: there is no process here.
The program stops with an error, and its files close.
jsc.guide.programs_and_processes.table1_: Names the program. The machine's process list shows that name. A program without a name gets one from the runtime.
The name the program has, as text.
The arguments the program was started with, as a list of text.
Ends the program with that status.
How many events the program lost, because its queue was full. Sigma# only.
Starts the program at the path, with optional arguments and priority, and gives a Process. Sigma# only.
The program itself, as a Process. Sigma# only.
Runs one line at this machine's own prompt, waits for it to end, and gives back the lines it printed. Sigma# only.
Sets the handler that runs for each message other programs send this one. Sigma# only.
jsc.guide.programs_and_processes.table2_: Sends a message to the process with that number. Gives false when its queue has no room.
The name of the process, as text.
Empty on this machine, and the host name of a machine on the network for a remote one. Sigma# only.
The status the process ended with.
Waits at most that many ticks. Gives yes when the process ended in that time.
The lines the process printed, as a list.
jsc.guide.programs_and_processes.table3_: The process has turns to run.
The process waits for something outside itself.
jsc.guide.programs_and_processes.text1: A program can start other programs, ask which programs run on its machine, and hear from them. A program you start becomes a process ([](jsc:running_programs)), with its own number, its own memory and its own work to do.
jsc.guide.programs_and_processes.text10: A program keeps at most 256 waiting calls. An event that finds no room is dropped and counted in Program.DroppedEvents. A message is the exception: it is refused, and its sender is told. Closing a window always gets in.
jsc.guide.programs_and_processes.text2: Program is the type for the program itself and for the programs it starts. Program.Start gives you a handle: a value that refers to the new process by its number.
jsc.guide.programs_and_processes.text3: Program.Start compiles a file of source (.sg or .sgs) before it starts it. A compiled file runs as it is.
jsc.guide.programs_and_processes.text4: Start takes the path, then optional arguments, then an optional priority. The priority is a name: low, medium or high, in any case. Any other name, or none, gives medium. A low program gets a turn only every other round, and a high program runs like a medium one.
jsc.guide.programs_and_processes.text5: A program started from another program gets 1 megabyte (MB) of memory, its heap. The most a heap can be is 64 MB.
jsc.guide.programs_and_processes.text6: A Process is a handle to a program on a machine. You get one from Start, from Current, and from Processes on another machine.
jsc.guide.programs_and_processes.text7: A wait ends early when the program that waits, or the one it waits for, ends. Times are in ticks, and a tick is explained in [](jsc:credits_per_tick).
jsc.guide.programs_and_processes.text8: A message is text one program sends to another. The receiver gets it as a ProcessMessage, with the number of the sender (ProcessMessage.From), the text (ProcessMessage.Text) and the tick it was sent (ProcessMessage.Tick).
jsc.guide.programs_and_processes.text9: A program does not act on a message at the moment it arrives. Each message, each click, and each change to a watched total waits in a queue as an event. The program runs the handlers in the order the events arrived.
jsc.guide.programs_and_processes.title: Programs, processes and messages
jsc.guide.prompt_editors_and_sigma.fix1: Install the program or the package that brings it, then type it again.
jsc.guide.prompt_editors_and_sigma.fix2: Put the computer on a network whose Mainframe runs the Mirror ([](jsc:mirror)).
jsc.guide.prompt_editors_and_sigma.probl: The prompt says it does not know vim, emacs or a verb of Sigma.
pckmgr says it could not resolve mirror://.
jsc.guide.prompt_editors_and_sigma.step1: Install the packages you need, such as sgsc and sigma.
jsc.guide.prompt_editors_and_sigma.step2: Write your program in a file that ends in .sgs, such as HELLO.SGS.
jsc.guide.prompt_editors_and_sigma.step3: Type sgsc HELLO.SGS to compile it. The compiler writes the listing beside it.
jsc.guide.prompt_editors_and_sigma.step4: Type sigma run and the listing's name to run it.
jsc.guide.prompt_editors_and_sigma.table: Press Esc, then type :w and press Enter.
Press Esc, then type :q and press Enter. :wq saves and leaves at once.
Compiles a Sigma file, which ends in .sg, into a listing that ends in .asm.
Compiles a Sigma# file, which ends in .sgs, into a listing.
Runs a listing with sigma run, stops one with sigma stop, and lists what runs with sigma ps.
Starts a package, builds it, and puts it on the Mirror or takes it back.
jsc.guide.prompt_editors_and_sigma.text1: Some programs work inside the Command Prompt window instead of opening their own. Two editors take over the window while you change a file, and the tools of Sigma compile and run your programs there. Install each one first ([](jsc:software_verbs)).
jsc.guide.prompt_editors_and_sigma.text2: Type vim or emacs, a space and the name of a file. The editor takes the whole window, and gives it back when you leave. The file does not have to exist: it is made when you first save it.
jsc.guide.prompt_editors_and_sigma.text3: vim starts in normal mode, where a letter is a command. Press i to type into the file, and Esc to stop typing. The Linux Desk Reference lists every key of both editors ([](jsc:vim)).
jsc.guide.prompt_editors_and_sigma.text4: Sigma and Sigma# are the programming languages of these computers. The Book of Sigma teaches them ([](jsc:sigma_two_languages)). Their tools are verbs of the prompt, once you install their packages.
jsc.guide.prompt_editors_and_sigma.text5: On the Frames editions, pckmgr install fetches these packages from the Mirror. MC-DOS installs them from their media only. The Sigma# compiler and the runtime need a Legacy computer or later, and on Frames they need Frames XP or later, so Frames 95 holds the Sigma compiler alone ([](jsc:sigma_installing)).
jsc.guide.prompt_editors_and_sigma.title: Editors and Sigma at the prompt
jsc.guide.prompt_mainframe_verbs.definit: The Mainframe's list of which disks of the network hold which items.
An item the storage index still lists, though no disk holds it any more.
jsc.guide.prompt_mainframe_verbs.fix1: Type it at the prompt of the computer the table names for it.
jsc.guide.prompt_mainframe_verbs.fix2: It is serving already. Type iqlengine status to check it.
jsc.guide.prompt_mainframe_verbs.fix3: Type iqlengine start to start it.
jsc.guide.prompt_mainframe_verbs.fix4: Type mirror status to see whether it serves.

The Mirror

mirror says the Mirror is already installed.
jsc.guide.prompt_mainframe_verbs.table1_: A computer with ports, for its Network Gateways
jsc.guide.prompt_mainframe_verbs.table2_: Checks the index against the disks.
Reads every disk again and builds the index anew. The new index takes over a tick or two later.
jsc.guide.prompt_mainframe_verbs.text1: A few verbs work on the network itself, so the prompt offers them only on the computer that keeps that part of the network. Type one anywhere else, and the prompt says it does not know the command.
jsc.guide.prompt_mainframe_verbs.text2: The Mainframe's verbs are there only while it is on a network. A Mainframe running MC-DOS or Frames offers them at its Command Prompt.
jsc.guide.prompt_mainframe_verbs.text3: iqlengine starts and stops the Midsoft IQL Server, the engine that plans the network's work ([](jsc:midsoft_iql_server)). Type iqlengine start, iqlengine stop or iqlengine status. services lists the network's services, each with its state. The prompt offers both only while the Midsoft IQL Server is installed on the Mainframe.
jsc.guide.prompt_mainframe_verbs.text4: The Mainframe keeps the storage index: its list of which disks hold which items, so the network finds an item without reading every disk. Three verbs look after it.
jsc.guide.prompt_mainframe_verbs.text5: When you pull a drive out of a running bay that has no Integrity Monitor, the index stops trusting that bay until you type reindex ([](jsc:network_services)). Learning IQL explains the same three jobs as statements ([](jsc:maintenance_analyze_vacuum_reindex)).
jsc.guide.prompt_mainframe_verbs.text6: mirror install puts the Mirror on the Mainframe: the service that pckmgr fetches packages from ([](jsc:mirror)). mirror status says whether it serves. It answers serving, installed (Mainframe off) or not installed.
jsc.guide.prompt_mainframe_verbs.text7: cluster does at the prompt what the Cluster Manager does in its window ([](jsc:cluster_management_computers)). It lists the network's supercomputers and datacenters, shows the nodes of one, turns them on or off, and installs a system or a program on them.
jsc.guide.prompt_mainframe_verbs.text8: gateway does what the Gateway Manager does for the Network Gateways on this computer's ports, the bridge to ComputerCraft ([](jsc:network_gateway)). It lists them, shows the status, permissions, computers and log of one, and changes its settings.

jsc.guide.prompt_window.definition1: A program that you call by its name, with the words after the name that say what it works on.
jsc.guide.prompt_window.definition2: A set of instructions that the computer runs when you call it by name.
jsc.guide.prompt_window.definition3: The output that the window keeps above the prompt, so that you can read back what has scrolled off the top.
jsc.guide.prompt_window.definition4: Filling in the rest of a command's name from the letters you have typed, so that you need not type the whole name.
jsc.guide.prompt_window.definition5: A signal that asks a running tool to stop.
jsc.guide.prompt_window.fix1: A line holds at most 256 characters. Split it into two lines.
jsc.guide.prompt_window.fix2: While a tool runs, the window reads only Ctrl+C. Wait for the tool to finish, or press Ctrl+C.
jsc.guide.prompt_window.fix3: The tool must be running in this window. A tool left running in the background does not answer Ctrl+C.
jsc.guide.prompt_window.fix4: An editor that uses Esc keeps the key. Leave the editor with its own exit key ([](jsc:editors_overview)), then press Esc.
jsc.guide.prompt_window.problem2: Typing does nothing while a tool runs.
jsc.guide.prompt_window.problem3: Ctrl+C does not stop a tool.
jsc.guide.prompt_window.problem4: Esc does not close an editor.
jsc.guide.prompt_window.table1_2_2: Fills in the rest of a command's name from the letters you typed. When several names fit, a second Tab in a row lists every candidate above the prompt.
jsc.guide.prompt_window.table1_3_2: Shows the line you typed before it, one step back.
jsc.guide.prompt_window.table1_4_2: Shows the line you typed after it, one step forward.
jsc.guide.prompt_window.table1_5_2: Closes the window. An editor that is open takes the key first, when the editor uses it.
jsc.guide.prompt_window.table1_6_2: Copies the text you have picked out. With nothing picked out, it interrupts a tool that is running.
jsc.guide.prompt_window.table1_7_2: Pastes text: up to 16 lines, each cut to 512 characters. Every line but the last runs as it arrives.
jsc.guide.prompt_window.text1: The Command Prompt is the window where you type a command and read what the machine answers. A command is a word that names a program, followed by the words that say what it works on. You press [[Enter]] to run the line.
jsc.guide.prompt_window.text2: A monitor opens the screen made for its system. A Frames monitor, or a monitor with no system, opens the Command Prompt screen. MC-DOS, the disk operating system (DOS), opens its own text screen, MC-NET opens the network terminal, and Linux and the other Unix systems open their own terminal.
jsc.guide.prompt_window.text3: On a Frames desktop, the Command Prompt is one of the desktop's apps, so you can open it from there too.
jsc.guide.prompt_window.text4: Above the line you type, the window keeps what the machine has answered. That kept output is the scrollback, and the mouse wheel scrolls back through it. On a monitor, the scrollback holds 512 lines.
jsc.guide.prompt_window.text5: While a tool runs, the window reads only Ctrl+C. Wait for the tool to finish, or press Ctrl+C to interrupt it. The bottom line of the window reminds you of the keys: while you type, it reads "ENTER run    UP/DOWN history    wheel scroll    ESC close", and while a tool runs, it reads "CTRL+C interrupt    wheel scroll    ESC close".
jsc.guide.prompt_window.text6: When you have scrolled back, the bottom line shows "scrolled +" and a number of lines. Once the first word is a command the machine knows, its usage appears dimmed on the right of your line, cut short with two dots if it does not fit.
jsc.guide.prompt_window.text7: A line holds at most 256 characters. The window keeps the lines you type as history for this machine, so that the Up and Down keys bring them back. An empty line is never kept, and a line typed twice in a row is kept once. Opening the window starts an empty scrollback, but the line history stays.
jsc.guide.prompt_window.title: The Command Prompt window and its keys
jsc.guide.prophet_console.definition1: One item the network is told to keep. In the States list, each state is one KEEP line.
jsc.guide.prophet_console.definition2: The range that a state is kept inside: at least a number, or between two numbers.
jsc.guide.prophet_console.definition3: What the network counts for an item: the amount held, plus the amount on its way, plus the amount arriving.
jsc.guide.prophet_console.fix1: Run the YourIQL engine on the Mainframe ([](jsc:engine_services)).
jsc.guide.prophet_console.fix10: Open the Settings tab and set "React to changes" to On.

jsc.guide.prophet_console.fix7: Write SHOW STATES to see the number of each watch.
jsc.guide.prophet_console.fix8: Forget that watch with FORGET WATCH, then set it again with a statement that works.
jsc.guide.prophet_console.fix9: Wait: the engine tries again after 600 ticks (30 seconds). Check that the network holds the items the craft needs.

jsc.guide.prophet_console.table5_5_1: watch <n> fired with nothing to make
jsc.guide.prophet_console.table5_5_2: A watch fired, and there was nothing to make.
jsc.guide.prophet_console.table6_1_1: Look at the network every <n> s
jsc.guide.prophet_console.table6_2_1: Ask for at most, in one craft
jsc.guide.prophet_console.text1: The Prophet Reactive Console keeps the network's stock where you want it. You tell it which items to keep. When a level falls, it asks the network for what is missing, on its own.
jsc.guide.prophet_console.text10: The Reactions tab lists what the engine did lately, with how long ago, as "<n> s ago" or "<n> min ago". It keeps at most 32 reactions.
jsc.guide.prophet_console.text11: The Settings tab sets how often the engine looks at the network, how much it asks for at once, and whether it reacts at all.
jsc.guide.prophet_console.text12: When React to changes is Paused, the engine makes no reactions at all. The states are still shown.
jsc.guide.prophet_console.text2: The console needs the YourIQL engine, version 3.23, running on the Mainframe. Its own statements are explained in [the YourIQL engine](jsc:prophet_youriql).
jsc.guide.prophet_console.text3: Type a YourIQL statement at the prompt, then press Check or Apply. Check reads the statement without changing anything, and answers "The statement reads well." when it is right. Apply runs the statement.
jsc.guide.prophet_console.text4: A statement that does not start with KEEP, WATCH, FORGET or SHOW STATES goes to the normal IQL engine, explained in [the engines](jsc:iql_engines_overview).
jsc.guide.prophet_console.text5: A number is a whole number, zero or more. An upper end in a band only says where the level stops being where it should be: nothing is thrown away to bring it down. The recipe [keep a stock of an item](jsc:recipe_keep_stock) shows a KEEP line at work.
jsc.guide.prophet_console.text6: The States tab lists each state, with where it stands and what is being done for it. Under the list, the graph of the selected state shows its level.
jsc.guide.prophet_console.text7: When the level is below its band, the engine asks the network for the difference as a craft. If nothing could be set going, the state reads Cannot hold, and the engine tries again after 600 ticks (30 seconds).
jsc.guide.prophet_console.text8: A state above its band, with nothing on its way, reads Over. With work on its way, it reads Working.
jsc.guide.prophet_console.text9: The Subscriptions tab lists the watches. Each watch shows its number, its status, Armed or Fired, and how many times it fired, as "fired <n> times". Press Forget to remove a watch. The number is the one that FORGET WATCH uses.
jsc.guide.prophet_console.title: Prophet Reactive Console
jsc.guide.prophet_watch.fix1: Write WATCH, the item, one comparison, a number, DO, and the action.
jsc.guide.prophet_watch.fix2: Read the reason, fix the statement, let the watch go with FORGET WATCH, and set it again.
jsc.guide.prophet_watch.fix3: The network already holds the target, so nothing is wrong.
jsc.guide.prophet_watch.fix4: Check the item's name in SHOW STATES.
jsc.guide.prophet_watch.fix5: Check the number in SHOW STATES.
jsc.guide.prophet_watch.problem1: The answer is "syntax: WATCH item < n DO statement (the comparison one of <, <=, >, >=)".
jsc.guide.prophet_watch.problem2: The answer says the watch fired, and was refused, with a reason after the colon.
jsc.guide.prophet_watch.problem3: The answer says the watch fired with nothing to make.
jsc.guide.prophet_watch.problem4: FORGET says the item is not kept.
jsc.guide.prophet_watch.problem5: FORGET WATCH says no watch is numbered that number.
jsc.guide.prophet_watch.step1: Type WATCH, the item, the comparison and the number.
jsc.guide.prophet_watch.table2_1_2: Makes up to n of the item, counting what the network holds, batch by batch.
jsc.guide.prophet_watch.table2_2_2: Runs as a statement, and its answer is shown, up to 64 rows.
jsc.guide.prophet_watch.table3: Forgetting an item or a watch
jsc.guide.prophet_watch.table3_1_2: The item is no longer kept.
jsc.guide.prophet_watch.table3_2_2: The watch with that number is let go.
jsc.guide.prophet_watch.table4_1_2: The state as you wrote it, or the WATCH statement for a watch.
jsc.guide.prophet_watch.table4_2_2: The status word from the table below.
jsc.guide.prophet_watch.table4_3_2: What the network holds of the item.
jsc.guide.prophet_watch.table4_4_2: The Operations on their way for the item.
jsc.guide.prophet_watch.table4_5_2: The last thing the engine did for it; left empty on a watch row.
jsc.guide.prophet_watch.table5_2_2: In its band, with nothing on its way.
jsc.guide.prophet_watch.table5_3_2: Work is on its way to bring it into its band or keep it there.
jsc.guide.prophet_watch.table5_4_2: Below its band, and nothing could be set going.
jsc.guide.prophet_watch.table5_5_2: Above its band; nothing is thrown away to bring it down.
jsc.guide.prophet_watch.table5_6_2: A watch waiting for its condition.
jsc.guide.prophet_watch.table5_7_2: A watch whose condition came true.
jsc.guide.prophet_watch.text1: A watch runs an action when a condition comes true. You write the condition as an item, a comparison and a number. After DO you write the action, as you would write any statement.
jsc.guide.prophet_watch.text2: The first watch you set is number 1, and the next ones count up from it. The answer says watch 1 set, and then writes the watch back in full, so you can check it.
jsc.guide.prophet_watch.text3: A watch fires once, when its condition comes true. It is armed again only after the condition has stopped being true.
jsc.guide.prophet_watch.text4: FORGET takes the name you wrote for the item. Forgetting an item also clears its record of recent Operations.
jsc.guide.prophet_watch.text5: SHOW STATES lists what the engine keeps and watches. Type it as two words, in any capitals. The answer counts the states and the watches, and then shows a table.
jsc.guide.prophet_watch.text6: Holding is the good state. Cannot hold and Over need your attention. The others wait, or are in progress.
jsc.guide.prophet_watch.text7: The engine does not react to watches while it is stopped, so no watch fires then.
jsc.guide.prophet_watch.title: Prophet YourIQL: watches, forgetting and SHOW STATES
jsc.guide.prophet_youriql.definition1: A level the engine is told to keep, written as one KEEP statement.
jsc.guide.prophet_youriql.definition2: The range between a lower and an upper level, which a state keeps.
jsc.guide.prophet_youriql.definition3: A statement that waits for a condition, then runs one action when the condition comes true.
jsc.guide.prophet_youriql.fix1: Write KEEP with >= and a number, or with BETWEEN and its two numbers.
jsc.guide.prophet_youriql.fix2: Check the spelling of the item's short name.
jsc.guide.prophet_youriql.fix3: Nothing on the network can make the item. Look at the state in SHOW STATES, and check that the network can make it.
jsc.guide.prophet_youriql.fix4: Nothing is wrong. The engine does not remove items to bring a level down.
jsc.guide.prophet_youriql.heading4: How the engine keeps a level
jsc.guide.prophet_youriql.problem1: The answer is "syntax: KEEP item >= n, or KEEP item BETWEEN a AND b".
jsc.guide.prophet_youriql.problem2: The answer is "no item is called" and the name you typed.
jsc.guide.prophet_youriql.step1: Type KEEP, the item's short name, >= and a number.
jsc.guide.prophet_youriql.step2: Read the answer, which names the item and its level.
jsc.guide.prophet_youriql.table2_1_2: Keeps at least n of the item.
jsc.guide.prophet_youriql.table2_2_2: Keeps the item within a band, from a to b.
jsc.guide.prophet_youriql.table2_3_2: Runs an action once when a condition comes true.
jsc.guide.prophet_youriql.table2_5_2: Removes the watch with that number.
jsc.guide.prophet_youriql.table2_6_2: Lists the kept states and the watches in a table.
jsc.guide.prophet_youriql.text1: Prophet YourIQL is the engine that keeps a level for you. Instead of asking for a craft each time, you write KEEP steel_ingot >= 10000 once. The engine then works out what it must make to keep that many steel ingots on the network.
jsc.guide.prophet_youriql.text10: If nothing on the network can make the item, the state shows Cannot hold. The engine tries again every 600 ticks, which is 30 seconds.
jsc.guide.prophet_youriql.text11: The Prophet Reactive Console sets three things for this engine.
jsc.guide.prophet_youriql.text12: A value that is not on the list falls back to its default. The engine reacts only while it runs, so a stopped or replaced engine stops reacting.
jsc.guide.prophet_youriql.text13: The states and the watches are saved with the Mainframe. The engine keeps 48 level samples for each state's graph, the 32 latest reactions, and up to 4 Operations for each state in the console.
jsc.guide.prophet_youriql.text2: Its own tool is the Prophet Reactive Console ([](jsc:prophet_console)), which needs YourIQL 3.23 or newer.
jsc.guide.prophet_youriql.text3: Any other statement goes to the core language unchanged.
jsc.guide.prophet_youriql.text4: KEEP with >= takes exactly four words, and >= must stand as a word of its own, with spaces around it. KEEP with BETWEEN takes exactly six words, and its upper number must not be below its lower number.
jsc.guide.prophet_youriql.text5: Numbers are whole numbers written in digits, with no minus sign. The answer says that the item is "kept at" a level "or more", or "kept between" two levels.
jsc.guide.prophet_youriql.text6: Keeping the same item again replaces its band.
jsc.guide.prophet_youriql.text7: KEEP BETWEEN makes the engine craft when the level falls below its band. The upper number only shows where the level stops being right. Nothing is thrown away to bring a level down, so going over the band is never corrected by removing items.
jsc.guide.prophet_youriql.text8: Each time it looks, the engine counts what the network holds and what is already on its way. Work on its way is an Operation that has started and not yet finished.
jsc.guide.prophet_youriql.text9: When the level is below its band, the engine asks the network to craft what is missing. It asks for at most one batch per craft, and the batch size is a setting. The request goes through the network's crafting door, under the name Prophet YourIQL ([](jsc:how_autocrafting_works)).
jsc.guide.prophet_youriql.title: Prophet YourIQL: keeping a level
jsc.guide.query_and_select.fix1: A QUERY has no FROM. Move the server into WHERE, as in QUERY items WHERE server = "Main Storage".
jsc.guide.query_and_select.fix2: The WHERE kept no row for the item, so the reply says unknown item even though the item exists. Check the WHERE, the server after FROM and the stock with QUERY items.
jsc.guide.query_and_select.fix3: Put a field name before the operator, such as qty.
jsc.guide.query_and_select.fix4: Use one of the operators in the table above.
jsc.guide.query_and_select.fix5: Check the server's name: QUERY servers lists them.
jsc.guide.query_and_select.problem1: FROM is not valid on a read
jsc.guide.query_and_select.step1: Type SELECT, a quantity and the item, such as SELECT 64 iron_ingot.
jsc.guide.query_and_select.step2: To take from one server only, add FROM and the server's name as one word.
jsc.guide.query_and_select.table1_3_2: The Operations that run or wait.
jsc.guide.query_and_select.table2_1_2: The items are on their way to this computer.
jsc.guide.query_and_select.table2_2_2: The same, taken from that one server.
jsc.guide.query_and_select.table2_3_2: You typed SELECT *, and the network holds no item.
jsc.guide.query_and_select.table2_4_2: No server has that name. Check its spelling.
jsc.guide.query_and_select.table3_1_2: Equal. Numbers compare as numbers; words compare without regard to capitals.
jsc.guide.query_and_select.table3_3_2: Less than, more than, at most, at least.
jsc.guide.query_and_select.table3_4_2: The text holds the word, without regard to capitals.
jsc.guide.query_and_select.table3_6_2: A pattern, where * stands for any run of characters.
jsc.guide.query_and_select.table4_2_2: By word, without regard to capitals.
jsc.guide.query_and_select.table4_4_2: Not sorted: the order stays as it was.
jsc.guide.query_and_select.text1: QUERY reads the network and shows you what it holds. It moves nothing. SELECT is an Operation that brings items out of the network into this computer's own storage, its [local storage](jsc:local_storage). Both take WHERE, ORDER BY and LIMIT, which choose the rows you work on.
jsc.guide.query_and_select.text10: For SELECT and the other actions, WHERE, ORDER BY and LIMIT choose which item types the statement works on. The sort uses the item fields listed above, and LIMIT then takes the first item types.
jsc.guide.query_and_select.text2: Name the object after QUERY: the table you want to read. You can also write an item, or a star for every item.
jsc.guide.query_and_select.text3: Any other name gives 0 rows and no error. After a QUERY, the reply counts the rows, such as "12 rows" or "1 row". To read the rows themselves, open the table view in the Management Studio ([](jsc:studio_queries)).
jsc.guide.query_and_select.text4: SELECT takes items out of the network. You type a quantity, the item and, if you want, a server. A quantity of ALL, or no quantity at all, asks for everything the network can give. SELECT 64 iron_ingot and SELECT ALL iron_ingot do the same thing.
jsc.guide.query_and_select.text5: A star asks for every item type at once: SELECT * queues one move for each item type the network holds, up to 256 types. The reply then says "12 item types" or "1 item type".
jsc.guide.query_and_select.text6: WHERE keeps only the rows that match a condition. A condition compares a field with a value, with an operator between them. qty > 100 keeps the rows whose quantity is over 100.
jsc.guide.query_and_select.text7: Combine conditions with AND and OR, reverse one with NOT, and use brackets to group them. NOT binds tightest, then AND, then OR. A condition can have at most 64 levels of NOT and brackets, and at most 256 comparisons. A condition ends at the first word it cannot use, such as IF, ORDER or LIMIT.
jsc.guide.query_and_select.text8: ORDER BY sorts the rows by one field: smallest first, or A to Z for words. ASC is the default, and DESC sorts the other way. LIMIT keeps only the first rows. It takes a row count, not a percentage.
jsc.guide.query_and_select.text9: With ORDER BY and LIMIT together, the rows are sorted first, and LIMIT keeps the first ones of the sorted list. By default a QUERY reads up to 4,096 rows before it sorts them.
jsc.guide.query_and_select.title: QUERY and SELECT
jsc.guide.rack_cooling_and_heat.definiti: The watts of heat that a rack can carry before its machines slow down.
jsc.guide.rack_cooling_and_heat.fix1: Switch off the bays of the machines you do not need, or add a Cooling Unit ([](jsc:rack_equipment)).
jsc.guide.rack_cooling_and_heat.table2: Share of speed for some loads
jsc.guide.rack_cooling_and_heat.table2_5: 2,500 W, with one Standard Cooling Unit
jsc.guide.rack_cooling_and_heat.text1: When you fill a rack, it can carry only so much heat before its machines slow down. Every Cooling Unit in the rack counts toward that limit, wherever it sits.
jsc.guide.rack_cooling_and_heat.text2: The heat budget is 1,000 W plus what each Cooling Unit adds, by its era. The load is the power draw of every machine whose bay is on: its processors and cards, added up.
jsc.guide.rack_cooling_and_heat.text3: When the load is over the heat budget, every machine slows down by the same share. The share is 100 times the budget, divided by the load, as a percent, and it never falls below 25%. A hot rack slows down; it does not stop.
jsc.guide.rack_cooling_and_heat.text4: The rack screen shows THROTTLED and the share while the rack is over its budget. The slowdown cuts the capacity of each server, including the bonus from its graphics cards.
jsc.guide.rack_cooling_and_heat.title: Cooling and heat
jsc.guide.rack_drive_bays.definition1: Taking a part out of a machine, or putting one in, while the machine stays on.
jsc.guide.rack_drive_bays.definition2: A way of joining several drives into one volume, with or without a copy of the data.
jsc.guide.rack_drive_bays.fix1: A drive bay takes only a disk of the rack's era or an older one. Hold the item over the bay to read which rule keeps it out.
jsc.guide.rack_drive_bays.fix2: A RAID 0 array keeps no copy, so it loses everything when a drive is lost. Use RAID 1 or RAID 5 for a copy ([](jsc:raid_arrays)).
jsc.guide.rack_drive_bays.table1_1_2: It leaves with the items on it.
jsc.guide.rack_drive_bays.table1_2_2: The whole array loses its items.
jsc.guide.rack_drive_bays.table1_3_2: The array keeps working while a replacement drive rebuilds it.
jsc.guide.rack_drive_bays.text1: A drive bay holds one disk. You can pull the disk out of its bay and put it back while the machine is on, which is called hot-swap.
jsc.guide.rack_drive_bays.text2: The bays belong to the rack, not to the server. A drive stays in its bay when the server is pulled out, and the next server mounted over those rows inherits its drives.
jsc.guide.rack_drive_bays.text3: A drive bay takes only a disk of the rack's era or an older one, as a computer's disk slots do ([](jsc:disks)).
jsc.guide.rack_drive_bays.text4: Drives can join into one volume, called RAID. Depending on the mode, a RAID array keeps working when a drive is lost ([](jsc:raid_arrays)).
jsc.guide.rack_drive_bays.text5: What happens when you pull a drive depends on the bay it is in.
jsc.guide.rack_drive_bays.text6: In a RAID 1 or RAID 5 array, a pulled drive's contents move to the drives that stay, as far as those drives have room for them.
jsc.guide.rack_drive_bays.text7: A rebuild takes 20 ticks for each 1,000 items of array capacity. It never takes less than 40 ticks, which is 2 seconds, or more than 3 minutes. While it runs, the rack shows REBUILD and a percentage. The rack also marks an array DEGRADED or FAILED.
jsc.guide.rack_drive_bays.title: Drive bays and hot-swap
jsc.guide.rack_equipment.fix1: Mount a KVM Switch in the rack. It takes one rack unit.
jsc.guide.rack_equipment.fix2: The unit is of a newer era than the rack. Use the rack's own era's unit or an older one.
jsc.guide.rack_equipment.fix3: The rack holds the Standard Fibre Optic Interface, which takes only the Fibre Optic Cable. Mount the Advanced one, in an Advanced rack.
jsc.guide.rack_equipment.fix4: Its server has no mode set, or fewer drives than the mode needs ([](jsc:raid_arrays)).
jsc.guide.rack_equipment.problem1: A rack with several computers has no way to pick one on the monitor.
jsc.guide.rack_equipment.problem2: A unit does not go in, and the rack says it belongs in a newer rack.
jsc.guide.rack_equipment.problem3: The OM5 Fibre Cable does not join the rack.
jsc.guide.rack_equipment.table1: Rack units that are not computers
jsc.guide.rack_equipment.table1_1_3: Lets one monitor reach every machine in the rack
jsc.guide.rack_equipment.table1_2_3: Takes the rack unit, and adds nothing to the heat budget
jsc.guide.rack_equipment.table1_3_3: Adds to the heat budget, more in each newer era
jsc.guide.rack_equipment.table1_4_3: Lets the rack's back take the Fibre Optic Cable
jsc.guide.rack_equipment.table1_5_3: Lets the rack's back take the Fibre Optic Cable and the OM5 Fibre Cable
jsc.guide.rack_equipment.text1: Not everything in a rack computes. Some units serve the rack: the KVM Switch (keyboard, video, mouse), the Rack UPS (uninterruptible power supply), the Cooling Unit and the Fibre Optic Interface take rack units, as a server does.
jsc.guide.rack_equipment.text2: The KVM Switch, the Rack UPS and the Cooling Unit come in every era, from the Vintage to the Advanced. A rack seats the units of its own era and of the earlier ones, as it does servers: a Vintage KVM Switch goes in a Standard rack, a Standard one never in a Vintage rack.
jsc.guide.rack_equipment.text3: The KVM Switch lets one monitor reach every machine in the rack, so you do not need a screen for each. A rack with two or more computers needs one to choose between them.
jsc.guide.rack_equipment.text4: The Cooling Unit raises the heat the rack can carry, a newer era's more than an older one's, as explained in ([](jsc:rack_cooling_and_heat)).
jsc.guide.rack_equipment.text5: From the Standard on, the backbone is fibre, and a rack takes it only through a Fibre Optic Interface. The Standard one takes the Fibre Optic Cable; the Advanced one, which only an Advanced rack seats, takes the OM5 Fibre Cable as well. One in any row of the rack is enough, and the servers in it need no network card ([](jsc:data_cables)).
jsc.guide.rack_equipment.text6: A server's storage cards go in its expansion slots, not in the rack: the RAID controller joins the server's drives into one array, and the read cache cuts the time each read from them takes ([](jsc:raid_arrays)).
jsc.guide.rack_equipment.title: Rack equipment
jsc.guide.raid_arrays.fix1: No mode is set, so the drives stay independent. Set a mode on the storage page.
jsc.guide.raid_arrays.fix2: Seat a Vaultis Array card in one of this machine's expansion slots.
jsc.guide.raid_arrays.fix3: Add drives to the server's bays, or choose a mode that needs fewer.
jsc.guide.raid_arrays.problem1: The server's drives do not join.
jsc.guide.raid_arrays.problem2: The firmware says "No storage controller fitted."
jsc.guide.raid_arrays.problem3: The firmware says the mode needs more drives, such as "needs 3 drives".
jsc.guide.raid_arrays.step1: Open the Setup of the server and go to its storage page.
jsc.guide.raid_arrays.step2: Press Up or Down until the mode you want shows under ARRAY MODE.
jsc.guide.raid_arrays.text1: A RAID controller is an expansion card: the Vaultis Array of each era, in a server's expansion slot. It joins the server's drives into one array, and until a mode is set, the drives stay separate. You set the array mode in the server's firmware, on the storage page of the Setup ([](jsc:firmware)). The card keeps the mode, so it goes with the card.
jsc.guide.raid_arrays.text2: The usable space depends on the mode. RAID 0 uses the space of all its drives. RAID 1 gives the space of its smallest drive. RAID 5 gives the space of its drives but one, at the size of the smallest. RAID 0 never rebuilds, since it keeps no copy. The screen shows "+25% throughput" for RAID 0, and "survives to 1 drive" for RAID 1.
jsc.guide.raid_arrays.text3: The read cache, the Vaultis Cache of each era, needs no mode. In a server's expansion slot it cuts the read latency of the server's drives, by more in each newer era, as the table shows. Outside a server, a storage card sits in its slot and does nothing.
jsc.guide.raid_arrays.title: RAID modes
jsc.guide.rc_services.definition1: A program that runs in the background, such as cron for scheduled jobs or sshd for remote login.
jsc.guide.rc_services.definition2: The startup scripts of FreeBSD. They read the settings to decide which services start.
jsc.guide.rc_services.fix1: The sshd box was left unticked. Type config remote on.
jsc.guide.rc_services.fix2: The cron setting is off. Type config cron on.
jsc.guide.rc_services.fix3: The remote setting is off. Type config remote on.
jsc.guide.rc_services.fix4: The value was not on or off. Use config cron on or config cron off.
jsc.guide.rc_services.problem1: sshd did not start after the installation.
jsc.guide.rc_services.problem3: Other computers cannot run programs here.
jsc.guide.rc_services.problem4: The computer answers unknown setting: cron.
jsc.guide.rc_services.step1: Type config to list the settings.
jsc.guide.rc_services.step2: Type config cron on to turn cron on.
jsc.guide.rc_services.step3: Type config cron off to turn cron off.
jsc.guide.rc_services.step4: Type config remote on to let other computers reach this one.
jsc.guide.rc_services.step5: Type config remote off to refuse the remote calls of other computers.
jsc.guide.rc_services.table1_1_3: Runs scheduled jobs. On by default.
jsc.guide.rc_services.table1_2_3: Lets other computers reach this one.
jsc.guide.rc_services.table2_2_2: The cron setting, shown as on or as off.
jsc.guide.rc_services.text1: A service is a program that runs in the background, without a window of its own. FreeBSD asks about two of them, at the installer and at each boot: cron, which runs scheduled jobs, and sshd, which lets other computers reach this one.
jsc.guide.rc_services.text2: The sshd service and the remote setting are one setting. Turning remote on starts sshd at boot, and the sshd box of the installer sets the same setting. The box is not ticked by default, so a computer installed by bsdinstall starts with remote off unless you tick it.
jsc.guide.rc_services.text3: A computer that was not installed by bsdinstall starts with remote on.
jsc.guide.rc_services.text4: You change both settings with the config command. The values are on and off, and true and false also work.
jsc.guide.rc_services.text5: A successful change answers with the name of the setting and the word set, such as cron set. Typing config alone lists both settings, one line for each.
jsc.guide.rc_services.text6: Without a value, config cron answers "usage: config <key> <value>  (or 'config' to list)". A value that is not on or off is refused with unknown setting: cron. The key is known, so the value is the part that is wrong.
jsc.guide.rc_services.text7: The rc scripts read /etc/rc.conf at boot. On FreeBSD that file is generated from your settings, not kept on the disk, so change the settings with config. It holds these lines:
jsc.guide.rc_services.text8: The ifconfig_em0 line appears only when the computer is networked. The cron and sshd lines read YES or NO from the two settings.
jsc.guide.rc_services.text9: With cron off, scheduled jobs wait instead of running. A job you put in the background with & keeps running. With remote off, the remote calls of other computers to this one are refused.
jsc.guide.rc_services.title: Services at boot: cron and sshd
jsc.guide.reboot_checklist.definition1: The list of what the new system still needs, which the live shell builds before it restarts the machine.
jsc.guide.reboot_checklist.fix1: Use 1 to 15 letters, digits or hyphens, and start with a letter or a digit.
jsc.guide.reboot_checklist.fix2: Enter the new system first ([](jsc:arch_chroot) on Arch, [](jsc:mounts_and_chroot) on Gentoo), then set the name there.
jsc.guide.reboot_checklist.problem1: hostname: the specified hostname is invalid
jsc.guide.reboot_checklist.problem2: hostname: you cannot change the host name of the live medium
jsc.guide.reboot_checklist.step2: If the shell prints "The new system will not boot:", read the lines under it.
jsc.guide.reboot_checklist.step3: Do the step that each line names.
jsc.guide.reboot_checklist.table1_1_3: Unpack the stage 3 archive onto the disk ([](jsc:stage_three)).

jsc.guide.reboot_checklist.text1: When the new system is installed, you restart the machine into it with the reboot command. Before it restarts the machine, the shell checks a short list of what the new system needs to start. If something on the list is missing, the machine does not restart: the shell names the missing items, and your live session stays open.
jsc.guide.reboot_checklist.text2: The reboot step of each guide ([](jsc:arch_reboot), [](jsc:gentoo_reboot)) runs this check. The list has two parts. The always-asked part holds the steps that every installation needs. The optional part holds the rest of the handbook, and the shell checks it only when a setting asks for it.
jsc.guide.reboot_checklist.text3: Each row names one missing item, the line the shell prints for it, and the step that clears it.
jsc.guide.reboot_checklist.text4: Gentoo checks its table by the content of the file, not by running a tool. A line that does not start with a hash sign needs at least three fields, and its second field must be a slash. The hint names blkid, the tool that shows each partition's details. The stage 3 writes a table with only comments in it, so this item stays on the list until you write the root line. On Arch the item goes as soon as genfstab has run.
jsc.guide.reboot_checklist.text5: The shell asks for the optional part only when the world's setting for that system is on. Both settings are off by default, so a world asks for the basics alone. The settings are install_by_hand.gentoo_every_step and install_by_hand.arch_every_step, in the server configuration.
jsc.guide.reboot_checklist.text6: A name has 1 to 15 characters. It uses letters, digits and hyphens, and it starts with a letter or a digit. You give it with the hostname command, or by writing it to /etc/hostname inside the new system. Either way, the checklist counts it.
jsc.guide.reboot_checklist.title: What the new system needs before the reboot

jsc.guide.recipe_keep_stock.text1: A stock is how many of an item the network holds. Often you want a number to stay where it is: 512 iron ingots ready for the next build, and never fewer. IQL has three ways to ask for that, and they work differently. Choose the one that fits what you need.
jsc.guide.recipe_keep_stock.text10: A job is a saved statement that the network runs by itself ([](jsc:iql_jobs)). The Automation Engine keeps the jobs and fires them on time, and it does so only while the Mainframe is on.
jsc.guide.recipe_keep_stock.text11: A job with a WHEN trigger fires on the rising edge of its condition: the moment the condition turns from false to true. It fires once for that moment, and not again while the condition stays true.
jsc.guide.recipe_keep_stock.text12: The job crafts an item from a pattern, the recipe the network holds for that item.
jsc.guide.recipe_keep_stock.text13: The reply reads "job restock_iron created". The job checks the stock about every half second. If the stock is already below 512 at its first check, the job fires at once.
jsc.guide.recipe_keep_stock.text14: The job looks only at the stock on the network, not at what is on its way. It fires again only after the stock has reached 512 or more and fallen below it once more.
jsc.guide.recipe_keep_stock.text15: The Automation Manager writes the same job for you, without any IQL. Its form is called Restock below: you give it an item and an amount, and it creates a job that crafts that amount when the stock falls below the same amount ([](jsc:automation_manager)).
jsc.guide.recipe_keep_stock.text16: An IF clause on one action runs that action once, and only if its condition holds. It does not come back by itself, so use it for one order, not for a standing rule.
jsc.guide.recipe_keep_stock.text17: The IF reads the network's whole stock of the item the action names. When the condition does not hold, the reply reads "the IF did not hold, so the CRAFT was not run". That is not an error: the line went through and did nothing.
jsc.guide.recipe_keep_stock.text2: KEEP belongs to Prophet YourIQL ([](jsc:prophet_youriql)). You name the item and the level, and the engine works out the crafts that reach the level and keep it there.
jsc.guide.recipe_keep_stock.text3: The engine counts what is already on its way: the items being crafted or moved toward the stock. So it orders only what is still missing.
jsc.guide.recipe_keep_stock.text4: The spaces around >= are required, and so are the words BETWEEN and AND. A name with no colon means minecraft:, so iron_ingot is the vanilla iron ingot. A mod's item needs its full name, with the mod's name before the colon.
jsc.guide.recipe_keep_stock.text5: When the level is kept, the console confirms it with a line that ends in "kept at 512 or more".
jsc.guide.recipe_keep_stock.text6: The engine looks at the network in ticks. One tick is one step of the game, and 20 ticks make one second.
jsc.guide.recipe_keep_stock.text7: Two settings change how Prophet works: the look interval and the batch per craft. Prophet reacts only while the Mainframe is on, and only when reacting is turned on.
jsc.guide.recipe_keep_stock.text8: A watch, written WATCH item < n DO statement, runs that statement once when a level crosses the line you set. Inside a watch, CRAFT item TO n makes the item up to a level.
jsc.guide.recipe_keep_stock.text9: Type SHOW STATES to see each state's status. Cannot hold means the network cannot reach the level right now.
jsc.guide.recipe_keep_stock.title: Keep a stock of an item

jsc.guide.recipe_nightly_craft.text1: This recipe has the network craft an item again and again, with a gap between each craft. You set the gap as an interval, written as a duration after EVERY, such as 30s or 1h ([](jsc:iql_jobs)).
jsc.guide.recipe_nightly_craft.text2: The interval counts game ticks, so it measures game time, not the time of day. A job fires only while the Automation Engine is installed and the Mainframe is on.
jsc.guide.recipe_nightly_craft.text3: A craft cannot be set to a time of day. The only time window in IQL belongs to a bus ([](jsc:bus_conditions)).
jsc.guide.recipe_nightly_craft.text4: The Automation Manager has the same feature as a form, called Batch Craft. Its field is labelled Every (30s), and it takes a duration such as 30s or 5m.
jsc.guide.recipe_nightly_craft.text5: A bare number counts seconds. A letter after the number changes the unit: s for seconds, m for minutes, h for hours and t for ticks. There are 20 ticks in a second.
jsc.guide.recipe_nightly_craft.text6: Always write the number. A CRAFT with no number asks the network for as much as it can make, every time the job runs.
jsc.guide.recipe_nightly_craft.title: Craft on an interval

jsc.guide.recipe_redstone_door.text1: A Redstone Interface lets a computer read a redstone signal, or send one. You place it, link it to the computer with a peripheral cable, and it reads the redstone beside it or emits a signal there ([](jsc:redstone_interfaces)).
jsc.guide.recipe_redstone_door.text2: A SET REDSTONE line makes the interface emit a strength. A door that reacts to redstone next to the interface receives that signal. A strength of 15 is the strongest, and 0 turns the signal off.
jsc.guide.recipe_redstone_door.text3: The reply names the interface and what it did, such as "Redstone Interface Gate emits 15". Quote the name in single quotes when it has a space.

jsc.guide.recipe_report.definition1: One line of a result. In the items table, one line is one kind of item.

jsc.guide.recipe_report.table1_3_2: The Midsoft IQL Server running, which every Mainframe has
jsc.guide.recipe_report.text1: A report is a query you save under a name, so you can read the same numbers again later. In IQL a saved query is a view ([](jsc:iql_views)). Each time you run it, the view reads the network again, so the numbers are current.
jsc.guide.recipe_report.text2: Only the Midsoft IQL Server keeps views. On a network whose engine is Prophet YourIQL or NextgreIQL, CREATE VIEW is refused.
jsc.guide.recipe_report.text3: The view's name can be at most 64 characters long. Do not name a view after a table: QUERY items would then run your view, not the items table.
jsc.guide.recipe_report.text4: Results to File writes the grid of results as a comma-separated values (CSV) file, a plain text table that spreadsheets open.
jsc.guide.recipe_report.text5: The items table also reads name, count, amount, damaged and durability in a WHERE or an ORDER BY, though they do not show as columns. The name is the item's name as the game shows it.
jsc.guide.recipe_report.text6: The tag column shows one tag: the first c: tag of the item, in alphabetical order. An item with two c: tags shows only one, so a WHERE on tag can miss the other. An item with no c: tag shows its first tag.
jsc.guide.recipe_report.text7: A job can run a query too, but it throws the rows away, so a job gives you no report. Run the view yourself. A script file cannot hold a report either, because run refuses QUERY.
jsc.guide.recipe_report.title: A saved report

jsc.guide.recipe_store_by_type.text1: Sometimes a network should take in only some kinds of item, such as iron ore and coal and nothing else. You set that with an Import Bus, which brings items into the network from the inventory it faces ([](jsc:buses)).
jsc.guide.recipe_store_by_type.text2: A bus moves only the items on its filter. You set the filter with a SET BUS line ([](jsc:set_bus)). Write the bus's name in single quotes when it has a space in it.
jsc.guide.recipe_store_by_type.text3: Advanced buses can filter by tag. The c: prefix marks the tags that many mods share.
jsc.guide.recipe_store_by_type.text4: A filter holds 5 items, and a bus holds 4 tags. Conditions are the WHEN lines: they keep a bus waiting until the network meets them ([](jsc:bus_conditions)).
jsc.guide.recipe_store_by_type.text5: A filter decides what a bus moves, not where the items go. The network decides which server keeps them.
jsc.guide.recipe_store_by_type.title: Store items by type

How strong a redstone signal is, from 0 to 15.
jsc.guide.redstone_interfaces.figure1: A Redstone Interface, its lens toward a redstone lamp that it lights, cabled to its computer. Drag the scene to see the back.
