jsc.guide.redstone_interfaces.text1: A Redstone Interface is a small block that lets a program read the redstone signal at one of its faces, or emit a signal from that face. Redstone is the wiring of Minecraft. A computer reaches the interface through a peripheral cable, as it reaches its other devices ([](jsc:peripheral_cables)).
jsc.guide.redstone_interfaces.text2: Place it the way you place an observer. Its lens points toward what you look at. Its back, where the cable plugs in, can face any way. Only the lens reads or emits.
jsc.guide.redstone_interfaces.text3: The interface has two modes. Its signal strength runs from 0 to 15 in either mode.
jsc.guide.redstone_interfaces.text4: A program sets the mode and the strength. The window says which program set them last.
jsc.guide.redstone_interfaces.text5: Name the interface in its window, with up to 32 characters. Programs find an interface by that name, and no two interfaces of one computer can share a name.
jsc.guide.redstone_interfaces.text6: The interface has no power of its own. With no computer at the other end of its cable, its window says "Off, no power", and it reads and emits nothing. It keeps its mode and its strength until a computer is linked to it again.
jsc.guide.redstone_interfaces.title: Redstone Interfaces
jsc.guide.redstone_library.definition1: A strength from 0 to 15: strength 0 is off, and strength 15 is the strongest.
jsc.guide.redstone_library.definition2: Powered and linked to the machine. A live interface shows its strength; one that is not live shows strength 0.
jsc.guide.redstone_library.fix1: Give Out a whole number from 0 to 15.
jsc.guide.redstone_library.fix2: Link the interface to the machine with cable, and check its name in its window.
jsc.guide.redstone_library.fix3: No enabled interface linked to this machine has that name. Check the name in its window.
jsc.guide.redstone_library.fix4: The interface is not live. Check that it is powered and linked to this machine.
jsc.guide.redstone_library.problem1: The program stops and says the number is not a redstone strength.
jsc.guide.redstone_library.problem2: The program stops and says no Redstone Interface with that name is linked to this machine.
jsc.guide.redstone_library.table1_1_2: The interface with that name, or null when no interface linked to this machine answers to it, ignoring capitals.
jsc.guide.redstone_library.table1_3_2: Sets the interface to read the signal. It stops emitting.
jsc.guide.redstone_library.table1_4_2: Sets the interface to emit that strength, from 0 to 15.
jsc.guide.redstone_library.table1_5_2: The strength the interface shows now.
jsc.guide.redstone_library.text1: A Redstone Interface reads redstone signal for a machine, or emits it, and it is linked to the machine by cable. Your program reads and sets it through Redstone. The block itself is explained in [](jsc:redstone_interfaces).
jsc.guide.redstone_library.text2: In sets the interface to read, and Out sets it to emit. The last one you call wins. Each setting is marked with the name of the program that made it, or with Sigma when that program has no name of its own.
jsc.guide.redstone_library.text3: Level shows the strength that is emitted while the interface is live, or the strength it reads when it does not emit. It gives 0 when the interface is not live.
jsc.guide.redstone_library.text4: An interface with no name of its own answers to Redstone Interface. A name is up to 32 characters long, and two interfaces of one machine cannot share a name.
jsc.guide.redstone_library.title: Redstone Interfaces from a program
jsc.guide.redstone_programs.fix1: Check the spelling of the name in the interface's window. Check that its cable reaches this computer, and that the interface is not disabled.
jsc.guide.redstone_programs.fix2: Check the name, and check the cable and the disabled setting, as above.
jsc.guide.redstone_programs.fix3: Write IN, or OUT followed by a number from 0 to 15.
jsc.guide.redstone_programs.fix5: Pass a number from 0 to 15 to Out.
jsc.guide.redstone_programs.fix6: The interface is not live. Check its peripheral cable, and check that the interface is not disabled.
jsc.guide.redstone_programs.problem1: IQL says "no Redstone Interface named Gate is linked to this machine".
jsc.guide.redstone_programs.problem2: Sigma stops the program and says the interface is not linked to this machine.
jsc.guide.redstone_programs.problem3: IQL says "SET REDSTONE needs IN, or OUT and a strength from 0 to 15".
jsc.guide.redstone_programs.problem4: IQL says the strength is not a redstone strength, which runs from 0 to 15.
jsc.guide.redstone_programs.problem5: Sigma stops the program, because the strength is not from 0 to 15.
jsc.guide.redstone_programs.problem7: The window refuses a name with "Another interface already has this name".
jsc.guide.redstone_programs.table1_1_2: Makes the interface named Gate read.
jsc.guide.redstone_programs.table1_2_2: Makes the interface named Gate emit a strength of 15.
jsc.guide.redstone_programs.table1_3_2: The same, for a name with a space. Quotes go round the name.
jsc.guide.redstone_programs.table2_1_2: Finds the interface named Gate on the computer the program runs on.
jsc.guide.redstone_programs.table2_3_2: Makes the interface emit 15, from 0 to 15.
jsc.guide.redstone_programs.table2_4_2: Returns the strength it reads or emits, or 0 while it has no power.
jsc.guide.redstone_programs.text1: A program can read a redstone signal, or make one, through a Redstone Interface ([](jsc:redstone_interfaces)). You place the interface, cable it to your computer, and let a program read it or set it.
jsc.guide.redstone_programs.text2: Name the interface in its window first. A program finds the interface by that name. The name takes up to 32 characters, and it must be unique on its computer, whatever the capitals. An empty name answers to "Redstone Interface".
jsc.guide.redstone_programs.text3: If you name a second interface with a name the first one has, the window refuses it with "Another interface already has this name".
jsc.guide.redstone_programs.text4: The SET REDSTONE statement makes an interface read or emit. The IQL book explains it in full ([](jsc:set_redstone)).
jsc.guide.redstone_programs.text5: The strength runs from 0 to 15. A statement typed at a prompt marks the setting as made by IQL, and the window then shows "Set by IQL".
jsc.guide.redstone_programs.text6: A Sigma program reaches an interface through redstone("Gate"). The Sigma book explains its library ([](jsc:redstone_library)).
jsc.guide.redstone_programs.text7: Each call marks the setting with the name of the program that made it, so the window shows that program.
jsc.guide.redstone_programs.text8: A program reaches only the interfaces on its own computer. An interface on another computer is not found, even when both are on the same network.
jsc.guide.redstone_programs.text9: A SET REDSTONE statement in a job runs each time the job fires, so a job can open a door on a timer ([](jsc:automation_engine)).
jsc.guide.redstone_programs.title: Redstone in programs
jsc.guide.remote_access.definition1: The desktop program that takes over another machine of the network and shows it on your screen.
jsc.guide.remote_access.fix1: Check the name with ssh alone, or in the Devices tab of the Network Manager. The machine must be on the same network.
jsc.guide.remote_access.fix3: The other computer has config remote off. Turn it on there with config remote on.
jsc.guide.remote_access.problem1: host not found on this network
jsc.guide.remote_access.step1: Type ssh on its own to see the machines you can reach.
jsc.guide.remote_access.step2: Type ssh and the host name of the machine you want.
jsc.guide.remote_access.step3: Type exit to leave it. Closing the window leaves it too.
jsc.guide.remote_access.table1_1_1: Connected to <machine>. Type exit to return.
jsc.guide.remote_access.table1_1_2: The session is open on the other computer.
jsc.guide.remote_access.table1_2_1: <name>: host not found on this network
jsc.guide.remote_access.table1_2_2: No machine on your network has that name; type ssh alone to see the names.
jsc.guide.remote_access.table1_3_1: <name> matches <n> machines (<names>) - use the host name or node id
jsc.guide.remote_access.table1_3_2: Use the host name or the start of the node id instead.
jsc.guide.remote_access.table1_4_1: connect to host <name>: machine is powered off
jsc.guide.remote_access.table1_4_2: The machine is off. Switch it on.
jsc.guide.remote_access.table2_1_2: Other computers may run programs here. This is the default.
jsc.guide.remote_access.table2_2_2: Other computers cannot run programs here.
jsc.guide.remote_access.text1: Being on the same network is what lets you reach another computer. The secure shell (ssh) command opens a shell on another computer of your network, from the terminal you are at.
jsc.guide.remote_access.text2: A machine answers to its host name, the name its owner gave it, the start of its node id, or the name of its system, as long as that name picks out exactly one machine. You can reach the Mainframe, the Personal Computers of the network and the servers in the racks. You cannot reach the computer you sit at.
jsc.guide.remote_access.text3: Access needs no password: being on the same network is what grants it.
jsc.guide.remote_access.text4: Commands you run on another computer use that computer's own budget, and they carry its name. A computer can refuse programs from others: its remote setting decides it.
jsc.guide.remote_access.text5: Remote Control is the point-and-click way into the network's other machines ([](jsc:remote_control)).
jsc.guide.remote_access.title: Remote access: ssh and Remote Control
jsc.guide.remote_computers.definition1: The name a machine answers to on the network.
jsc.guide.remote_computers.definition2: The machine's own identifier. Use it in place of a host name that matches several machines.
jsc.guide.remote_computers.fix1: Turn the computer on, then call it again.
jsc.guide.remote_computers.fix2: Choose another computer on the network for the program.
jsc.guide.remote_computers.fix3: Start the program on another computer, or run it on that computer yourself.
jsc.guide.remote_computers.fix4: No computer of that name is on the network. Look at the names in Network.Computers.
jsc.guide.remote_computers.fix5: Use the node id, or the full host name.
jsc.guide.remote_computers.problem1: The program stops and says the computer is powered off.
jsc.guide.remote_computers.problem2: The program stops and says the computer cannot run programs.
jsc.guide.remote_computers.problem3: The program stops and says the computer does not take programs from other computers.
jsc.guide.remote_computers.problem5: The host name matches several machines.
jsc.guide.remote_computers.table1_3_2: Mainframe, Computer, Crafting Computer, Personal Computer or Cluster Management Computer.
jsc.guide.remote_computers.table1_5_2: Yes when the computer is on.
jsc.guide.remote_computers.table2_1_2: Starts a program on that computer, as Program.Start does, and gives a Process; Start also takes (path, args) or (path, args, priority).
jsc.guide.remote_computers.table2_2_2: Runs a line at that computer's prompt, and gives back the lines it printed.
jsc.guide.remote_computers.table2_3_2: Sends a message to a process on that computer. Gives false when it cannot.
jsc.guide.remote_computers.table2_4_2: The processes on that computer, as a list of Process.
jsc.guide.remote_computers.table3_1_2: That machine does not run programs.
jsc.guide.remote_computers.table3_2_1: The computer does not take programs from other computers
jsc.guide.remote_computers.table3_2_2: That machine refuses programs sent from others.
jsc.guide.remote_computers.table3_4_1: No such computer on this network
jsc.guide.remote_computers.table3_4_2: No machine of that name is on this network.
jsc.guide.remote_computers.text1: A program can start a program on another computer of the same network, and ask that computer what it runs. The other computer is a RemoteComputer, and you get one from Network.Computer or Network.Computers.
jsc.guide.remote_computers.text2: The computer must be on the same network. A host name that matches several machines is refused, so use the node id or the full host name instead.
jsc.guide.remote_computers.title: Other computers on the network
jsc.guide.remote_control.fix1: Switch the machine on before you can take it over.
jsc.guide.remote_control.fix2: Check that this computer is on the network whose machines you want to reach.
jsc.guide.remote_control.problem1: A machine is listed as off.
jsc.guide.remote_control.problem2: The list says No other machine is reachable.
jsc.guide.remote_control.table1_2_2: The machine's kind and its system, and whether it is up or off.
jsc.guide.remote_control.table1_3_2: Take over, or Select a machine when no row is chosen.
jsc.guide.remote_control.text1: Remote Control takes over another machine of the network, and puts its screen on this monitor. It is the point-and-click twin of [ssh](jsc:remote_access), the secure shell. It matters most for a server in a rack, which has no screen of its own ([](jsc:server_racks)).
jsc.guide.remote_control.text2: The window lists the machines on this network under the heading Machines on this network. Each row shows the machine's kind and its system, and whether it is up or off. Select a machine, and press Take over. Taking over puts the machine's session on this monitor: its power-on self-test, its firmware, its terminal, or its full desktop ([](jsc:monitors)).
jsc.guide.remote_control.title: Remote Control
jsc.guide.routers.balloon1_detail: It joins the access line to the backbone.
jsc.guide.routers.balloon2_detail: It carries the backbone far, but only straight.
jsc.guide.routers.balloon3_detail: Lay it in a long run to renew the range of the cable.
jsc.guide.routers.balloon4_detail: Turn and branch the fibre here.
jsc.guide.routers.balloon5: The router at the far end
jsc.guide.routers.balloon5_detail: The access cables of the far computers join it.
jsc.guide.routers.figure1: Routers, a repeater and optical fibre carrying a network far. The fibre runs straight, so the Optical Router turns it. Drag it to see it from the other side.
jsc.guide.routers.fix1: Put a router of the newer era between them.
jsc.guide.routers.fix2: A run on one side of the repeater is still longer than its range. Add a repeater inside it.
jsc.guide.routers.problem1: An older machine will not join a newer network.
jsc.guide.routers.problem2: The far end is still off the network.
jsc.guide.routers.table1_2_3: The Legacy cables, and the Vintage ones
jsc.guide.routers.table1_3_3: The Transition cables, and the older ones
jsc.guide.routers.table1_4_3: The Standard cables, and the older ones
jsc.guide.routers.table1_5_3: The Advanced cables, and the older ones
jsc.guide.routers.text1: A router is where the lines of a network meet. Each era has its own, and a router joins its era's access line to its backbone: your small computers on one side, the Mainframe and the racks on the other. It takes the cables of its own era and of every earlier one, on any of its six faces, and all of them become one network. A router extends a network; it never splits one. When your network must reach further, you add a router.
jsc.guide.routers.text2: Eras matter here. A port takes its own era's cable and every older one, never a newer one. Two eras of one line that touch do not join: they meet at a router of the newer era. So an old machine on a new network needs a router between them.
jsc.guide.routers.text3: From the Standard on, the backbone's fibre runs only straight. An optical router takes only the backbone's fibre, from the Standard's era up to its own, and it is the block that turns and branches fibre.
jsc.guide.routers.text4: A repeater renews a cable's range. Lay it in a run of cable, and the cable after it starts counting its range again, so the run can go on past its first range. A repeater takes every line of its era and of every earlier one, except the long distance line. It carries each line on its own and never joins one line to another; that is a router's work.
jsc.guide.routers.text5: Hubs are not data blocks. A hub belongs to the peripheral line: it takes one of its computer's device ports and offers ports of its own, so one computer can reach more devices. A hub does not carry the network ([](jsc:peripheral_cables)).
jsc.guide.routers.text6: The Server Router is a different block, with its own page ([](jsc:server_router)).
jsc.guide.routers.title: Routers and repeaters
jsc.guide.running_programs.definition1: A program that is running on a computer, with its own number, name and memory.
jsc.guide.running_programs.definition2: One beat of the game's clock. Twenty ticks make a second.
jsc.guide.running_programs.definition3: One simple step of a program's work. Each step a program takes costs one instruction.
jsc.guide.running_programs.fix1: No installed language runs files of that kind. Compile a source file with sgsc or scc first, or install the package that runs that kind of file ([the programs page](jsc:programs)).
jsc.guide.running_programs.fix2: The prompt gave no reason. Run the compiler on the file yourself to see its messages. [Reading an error line](jsc:sigma_reading_an_error) shows how to read them.
jsc.guide.running_programs.fix3: sigma run starts only files that end in .asm, .sgs or .sg. Start one of those instead.
jsc.guide.running_programs.fix4: The number is wrong, or that program has already ended. Type sigma ps to see the numbers that are running.
jsc.guide.running_programs.heading2: Starting a program at the prompt
jsc.guide.running_programs.problem1: The prompt answers with the file's name and extension, in the form "name: nothing installed runs a .ext".
jsc.guide.running_programs.problem2: The prompt answers with the file's name and "does not compile", and gives no reason.
jsc.guide.running_programs.problem3: The prompt says "<file> is not a <language> program".
jsc.guide.running_programs.problem4: The prompt answers "sigma: nothing is running as <id>".
jsc.guide.running_programs.step1: Type sigma run, the file's name and any arguments, then press [[Enter]].
jsc.guide.running_programs.step2: Type sigma ps to see the program's number and what it is doing.
jsc.guide.running_programs.table1_1_2: Starts the program from its file, and passes the words after the file's name to it as arguments.
jsc.guide.running_programs.table1_2_2: Sets the memory the program is given, in megabytes: write 16M or 16.
jsc.guide.running_programs.table1_3_2: Lists the running programs, the same as sigma list or a bare sigma.
jsc.guide.running_programs.table1_4_2: Stops the program with that number, the same as sigma kill.
jsc.guide.running_programs.table2_1_2: The program's number, which sigma stop takes.
jsc.guide.running_programs.table2_2_2: The program's name, cut to 20 characters, with a tilde (~) at the end when it is cut.
jsc.guide.running_programs.table2_3_2: What the process is doing, as the table below explains.
jsc.guide.running_programs.table2_4_2: The memory it holds, out of the memory it was given: bytes below one kilobyte (KB), kilobytes above.
jsc.guide.running_programs.table3_1_2: It stopped on a read and waits for a line you type.
jsc.guide.running_programs.table3_2_2: It has instructions left to run.
jsc.guide.running_programs.table3_3_2: It waits for something outside itself, and uses no turns until that is done.
jsc.guide.running_programs.table3_5_2: It stopped because of a mistake, and its message is written to its console.
jsc.guide.running_programs.table4_1_2: Starts another thread, which runs the action you give it.
jsc.guide.running_programs.table4_2_2: Waits that many ticks, then goes on.
jsc.guide.running_programs.table4_3_2: Gives up the rest of its turn.
jsc.guide.running_programs.table4_5_2: Waits up to that many ticks, and gives false if the thread has not ended by then.
jsc.guide.running_programs.table4_7_2: The thread's number, which is 1 for the main thread.
jsc.guide.running_programs.text1: A program is a file that the computer runs for you. You write it in Sigma or Sigma#, and the compiler turns it into a listing (a file that ends in .asm) that the computer runs. See [Compiling with sgsc and scc](jsc:sigma_compile).
jsc.guide.running_programs.text10: When you stop a program, it gets a goodbye: it may run its own closing steps before it is removed. Its parents are told that it ended. The goodbye has a budget, described in [How much a machine runs each tick](jsc:credits_per_tick).
jsc.guide.running_programs.text11: A finished process leaves the list once nothing waits for it. A process that another program started keeps its output and its exit code until that parent is gone.
jsc.guide.running_programs.text12: A program has one of two shapes, console or script. A console program starts at its entry method, keeps the prompt while it runs, writes to the terminal that started it, and is gone when it returns.
jsc.guide.running_programs.text13: Any other shape is a script. A script is set up once, is called again on every tick while the computer is on, and is told when it is stopped. After the world loads again, it comes back.
jsc.guide.running_programs.text14: A process starts with one thread, the main thread, which always has the number 1. A program makes more threads with Thread.Start, and each new thread gets the next number: thread 2, then thread 3, and so on. The threads of a process share its memory, but each one keeps its own place in the calls it is making.
jsc.guide.running_programs.text15: The computer gives the process its turns, and the process shares them among its threads that are ready to run. Each turn is a slice of at most 64 instructions. A thread that waits for something gets no turn until it can go on.
jsc.guide.running_programs.text16: Starting a thread costs 49 instructions on top of the call, because each thread keeps a stack of calls of its own.
jsc.guide.running_programs.text17: Each object can have a lock. Releasing a lock that you do not hold halts the program. [Threads and locks](jsc:threads_and_locks) explains how to take and release one.
jsc.guide.running_programs.text2: While it runs, the program is a process: one entry in the computer's list of running programs, with its own number, its own name and the memory it was given. The list lives on the computer, not on its disks. A program you have installed sits on a disk and does nothing until it starts.
jsc.guide.running_programs.text3: A process leaves the list when it ends. Switching the computer off stops all of them. What happens to them after a save is in [Programs and the world's save](jsc:saved_with_world).
jsc.guide.running_programs.text4: Each process has a number, and the first is number 1. The computer counts up from 1 and skips every number that a running process still holds. Past the largest number it can hold, it starts again at number 1. A program can give itself a name with Program.SetName. Until it does, its name is sigma.
jsc.guide.running_programs.text5: Once the runtime is installed ([Installing the compilers and the runtime](jsc:sigma_installing)), the prompt knows the sigma command. Its commands are these:
jsc.guide.running_programs.text6: A program that stays up in the background is a service. The prompt does not wait for it, and says which number it started as. Any other program keeps the prompt until it returns, and whatever you type goes to that program.
jsc.guide.running_programs.text7: The list has one row per process. With nothing running, the prompt says that no programs are running.
jsc.guide.running_programs.text8: A halt is a stop caused by a mistake in the program's own steps. The reasons for each one are in [The stops while a program runs](jsc:sigma_runtime_stops).
jsc.guide.running_programs.text9: A program ends in one of three ways: it returns from the method where it starts, it calls Program.Exit with a number, or you stop it. The number it ends with is its exit code. A program that returns on its own ends with exit code 0, unless it set another code. A halted program reports exit code 1.
jsc.guide.running_programs.title: Programs and processes
jsc.guide.saved_with_world.definition1: A number worked out from a text. The same text always gives the same number, and a changed text gives another one.
jsc.guide.saved_with_world.fix1: The save came from another version of the mod, or a listing changed since it started. Start the programs again.
jsc.guide.saved_with_world.fix2: Its language is no longer installed, so the program is left out. Install that language.
jsc.guide.saved_with_world.fix3: It was stopped, not kept. Start it again.
jsc.guide.saved_with_world.problem1: The prompt says "the programs that were running could not be brought back from the save".
jsc.guide.saved_with_world.problem2: A program in a language that is no longer installed is gone after a reload.
jsc.guide.saved_with_world.problem3: A program is gone after the computer was switched off.
jsc.guide.saved_with_world.table1: What a save keeps for each program
jsc.guide.saved_with_world.table1_1_2: Every object the program holds, and the links between them.
jsc.guide.saved_with_world.table1_2_2: Each thread, and what it was doing.
jsc.guide.saved_with_world.table1_3_2: The lines on the console, and the lines typed ahead.
jsc.guide.saved_with_world.table1_4_2: The calls that wait to run in the program.
jsc.guide.saved_with_world.table1_5_2: The windows the program has open.
jsc.guide.saved_with_world.table1_6_2: The program's listing, identified by its checksum.
jsc.guide.saved_with_world.table1_7_2: The program that started it, if another program did.
jsc.guide.saved_with_world.text1: Your programs are kept when the world is saved. The computer writes its running programs into its own save data, which is the part of the world's save that belongs to that computer. Its disks and its settings are saved there too.
jsc.guide.saved_with_world.text2: Each program is written down in full, so that it can carry on. When the world comes back, a program carries on from where it stopped. It does not start again from the beginning.
jsc.guide.saved_with_world.text3: The next free number is saved too, so no number is given out twice.
jsc.guide.saved_with_world.text4: Switching a computer off is different. Its programs are stopped, each with its goodbye, and they are not kept for when it comes back on. When you turn it on again, you start the programs again.
jsc.guide.saved_with_world.text5: When the save is read back, the computer checks it. If the save came from another version of the mod, or a listing changed since its program started, the computer leaves out every program of that computer.
jsc.guide.saved_with_world.text6: A program whose language is no longer installed is left out alone. So is a program whose language does not take what it wrote. The other programs are not affected.
jsc.guide.saved_with_world.text7: A program started from another computer keeps its link to the program that started it. After a reload, that parent is still told when the child ends.
jsc.guide.saved_with_world.title: Programs and the world's save
jsc.guide.seeing_the_disks.definition1: A disk or a partition the system can read and write, named as lsblk prints it.
jsc.guide.seeing_the_disks.definition2: The list kept at the start of a disk that says where each partition begins and ends.
jsc.guide.seeing_the_disks.definition3: The way a partition stores its files: a table of names, folders and data. Each partition holds one, and a tool named mkfs makes an empty one.
jsc.guide.seeing_the_disks.definition4: To attach a file system to a folder, so that its files appear inside that folder.
jsc.guide.seeing_the_disks.definition5: The folder that a file system is attached to.
jsc.guide.seeing_the_disks.definition6: The file system the whole new system lives in. The system sees it as its top folder, /.
jsc.guide.seeing_the_disks.fix1: Only a disk in one of the computer's disk slots, or in its hot-swap bay, is a device. Put the disk there and run lsblk again.
jsc.guide.seeing_the_disks.fix2: The letter follows the slot the disk sits in. Use the name lsblk prints for it in every later command.
jsc.guide.seeing_the_disks.problem1: Your disk is not in the lsblk table.
jsc.guide.seeing_the_disks.problem2: The disk has a different name from the one you expected.
jsc.guide.seeing_the_disks.table1_1_2: The name of the device, such as sda for a disk or sda2 for its second partition.
jsc.guide.seeing_the_disks.table1_2_2: Two numbers the kernel uses to tell devices apart, which you can ignore.
jsc.guide.seeing_the_disks.table1_3_2: Whether the device can be removed; every row here shows 0.
jsc.guide.seeing_the_disks.table1_4_2: How big the device is: 512M is 512 megabytes, 1G is 1 gigabyte.
jsc.guide.seeing_the_disks.table1_5_2: 1 when the device is read-only: the live medium is, and your disks are not.
jsc.guide.seeing_the_disks.table1_6_2: disk for a whole disk, part for a partition, and loop for the live medium.
jsc.guide.seeing_the_disks.table1_7_2: Where the device is mounted, or none when it is not.
jsc.guide.seeing_the_disks.text1: Before you change anything on a disk, look at it. The command lsblk lists every disk the computer has, and every partition on those disks, in one table. It answers at once and changes nothing.
jsc.guide.seeing_the_disks.text2: You use it at three points: first to find your disk, then after you have divided it, and then after you have made the file systems, to check that each step did what you meant. lsblk needs no words after its name.
jsc.guide.seeing_the_disks.text3: Sizes are written with M for megabytes, G for gigabytes and T for terabytes. A decimal place appears only when it is needed: 512M, 1G, 1.5G, 4T.
jsc.guide.seeing_the_disks.text4: A disk takes its name from the slot it sits in, not from how many disks you have. The first slot is sda, the second sdb, and so on. An empty slot still takes its letter, so a disk alone in the third slot is sdc. The computer's own slots come first, then the bay on the front of the case ([](jsc:case_front)).
jsc.guide.seeing_the_disks.text5: Read the name from lsblk and use that exact name in every later command. Your disk may not be sda.
jsc.guide.seeing_the_disks.text6: A partition is a part of a disk that holds its own file system. lsblk lists each partition under its disk. A vertical bar and a dash mark every partition except the last, and the last one has a back-quote and a dash instead. A disk nobody has divided shows no partition rows at all.
jsc.guide.seeing_the_disks.text7: Here your disk is sda, 1G in size, and it is divided into two partitions. You made them with fdisk in the next entry. The MOUNTPOINTS column shows where the new system is attached: sda2 is the root filesystem, mounted at /mnt, and sda1 is mounted at /mnt/boot. The loop0 row is the live medium you are working from, read-only, and it is not a disk you install onto.
jsc.guide.seeing_the_disks.title: Seeing the disks (lsblk)
jsc.guide.server_racks.balloon1_detail: Click the front of the rack with a server in your hand to mount it.
jsc.guide.server_racks.balloon2_detail: It lets one monitor reach every machine in the rack.
jsc.guide.server_racks.balloon3_detail: It takes two rack units, and its ten drive bays hold the disks.
jsc.guide.server_racks.balloon4_detail: This Standard one adds 1,500 W to the heat the rack can carry.
jsc.guide.server_racks.definition1: A computer built to sit in a Server Rack.
jsc.guide.server_racks.definition2: A cabinet, two blocks wide, three tall and two deep, that holds machines in rows.
jsc.guide.server_racks.definition3: The height a machine takes in a rack, counted in units. Each cabinet has eight.
jsc.guide.server_racks.definition4: Many computers that work as one large machine, joined by high compute cable.
jsc.guide.server_racks.figure1: A Server Rack with its rack units filled: a server, a KVM Switch, a Storage Server, another server, a Cooling Unit and a Rack UPS. Drag it to turn it.
jsc.guide.server_racks.fix1: Mount a Fibre Optic Interface in the rack: the Standard one for the Fibre Optic Cable, the Advanced one for the OM5 Fibre Cable too ([](jsc:rack_equipment)).
jsc.guide.server_racks.fix2: It is from a newer era than the rack, or the rows it needs are taken or too small for it. Use a rack of its era or a newer one, or free those rows.
jsc.guide.server_racks.fix3: Put it in the rack the message names.
jsc.guide.server_racks.fix4: Put it in a rack of its own era or a later one.
jsc.guide.server_racks.problem1: The fibre does not join the rack.
jsc.guide.server_racks.problem2: A server does not go in.
jsc.guide.server_racks.problem3: The message names another kind of rack, such as "This chassis belongs in a Server Rack".
jsc.guide.server_racks.problem4: The message says "This chassis is of a later era than this rack".
jsc.guide.server_racks.text1: Your items have to live somewhere. In J's Computers they live on the disks of servers, and the servers live in racks.
jsc.guide.server_racks.text2: A Server Rack gives eight rack units of room. A machine's height is counted in those units: most servers take one, the bigger ones take two.
jsc.guide.server_racks.text3: The Supercomputer Rack holds supercomputer nodes only, and comes in the Standard and the Advanced ([](jsc:supercomputers)).
jsc.guide.server_racks.text4: A rack seats servers of its own era or older. Each server has drive bays, which show at the front of the rack. The [server types](jsc:server_types) list how many a server has.
jsc.guide.server_racks.text5: To mount a server by hand, hold it and click the front of the cabinet. It goes into the row under the crosshair, counted from the top. Aim elsewhere, and it takes the first row that fits, from the top down. A rack unit mounts the same way.
jsc.guide.server_racks.text6: Click the cabinet with an empty hand to open the rack screen. On a Supercomputer Rack, sneak-click to take the livery panel off.
jsc.guide.server_racks.text7: Each rack unit has a power switch for its bay, and a new rack switches every bay on. The switch of a bay is the power button of the machine in it. The machine still runs its self-test and stops at its boot menu.
jsc.guide.server_racks.text8: The disks in the bays are the storage. A server item carries no disks of its own: its drives are the disks you put in its bays. Join the rack's back port to the backbone cable, which the rack takes up to its era ([](jsc:data_cables)). From the Standard on, the backbone is fibre, and the rack takes it only through a Fibre Optic Interface mounted in one of its rows ([](jsc:rack_equipment)).
jsc.guide.server_racks.title: Server racks and servers
jsc.guide.server_router.fix1: More than 8 racks sit on the router. Move some to a second Server Router, which has its own budget.
jsc.guide.server_router.problem1: The rack count shows in red.
jsc.guide.server_router.step1: Join its uplink face to the network.
jsc.guide.server_router.step2: Join a section of racks to each of its other faces.
jsc.guide.server_router.step3: Open it to see each section and its rack count.
jsc.guide.server_router.text1: The Server Router is how you organise a datacenter. It groups Server Racks into sections, one for each of its faces besides the uplink ([](jsc:datacenters)). Its faces take any data cable, of any era ([](jsc:data_cables)).
jsc.guide.server_router.text2: A Server Router manages up to 8 Server Racks in all, across sections. Racks past that are counted as unmanaged, and the router shows its rack count in red.
jsc.guide.server_router.text3: The Cluster Manager runs each section as one machine, as far as its card reaches ([](jsc:cluster_management_computers)).
jsc.guide.server_router.title: Server Router
jsc.guide.server_types.fix1: Mount a unit in that row that cables those slots, or pick a chassis that fits the row.
jsc.guide.server_types.fix2: Use a chassis with more drive bays.
jsc.guide.server_types.problem1: A slot is blocked: "Blocked - no unit in this row cables these slots".
jsc.guide.server_types.problem2: A slot is blocked: "Blocked - the chassis does not cable this slot".
jsc.guide.server_types.text1: Each server is a chassis of its own kind. The chassis sets its height, its drive bays, and how many processors and expansion slots it has. When you pick a server, this table tells you what you get. Every server and server case comes from the creative tabs of J's Computers.
jsc.guide.server_types.text2: Every era has three: a 1U server, a 2U Storage Server with the most drive bays and a 2U Compute Server with the most processors. A newer era's has more of what it is built for. A server still runs only as many processors as its board has sockets.
jsc.guide.server_types.text3: A server fits a rack of its own era or a newer one. A Vintage Server seats in a Standard Server Rack, but a Standard server never seats in a Vintage rack. Supercomputer Nodes go in a Supercomputer Rack, and the Advanced Supercomputer Node goes in an Advanced Supercomputer Rack.
jsc.guide.server_types.text4: A server's expansion slots take its cards, the storage cards among them: a RAID controller that joins its drives into one volume and a read cache that answers them faster ([](jsc:raid_arrays)).
jsc.guide.server_types.text5: Each rack unit has five front slots. A machine fills the slots of its rows in order with its drive bays, and the rest are blocked. When a slot is blocked, the screen says why, with one of two fixed messages.
jsc.guide.server_types.title: Server types

jsc.guide.set_bus.text1: SET BUS changes the settings of a [bus](jsc:buses) from the prompt. It does what the bus's window does: it switches the bus on or off, choose the items it moves, how many, and when ([](jsc:bus_window)).
jsc.guide.set_bus.text2: Write the bus's name as its window shows it, in quotes when it has spaces. Each statement changes one setting, so you type one statement for each setting you need.
jsc.guide.set_bus.text3: After WHEN STOCK, the only comparison allowed is the < sign. KEEP and MAX take a whole number that is not negative. The hours after WHEN TIME are whole numbers from 0 to 23. A list of items is separated by commas, and a fluid is written with its kind first, as in FLUID water.

jsc.guide.setup_utility.text1: The Setup is the firmware's own settings screen. You open it with [[DEL]] while the self-test runs ([](jsc:turning_on)). The title of the screen ends with BIOS Setup Utility.
jsc.guide.setup_utility.text2: The Setup has pages. Press [[Tab]] to move to the next one.
jsc.guide.setup_utility.text3: The Hardware page lists Processor, Instruction Set, Cores, Memory, Graphics, Video, Board, Monitors, Hardware Era, Boot Disk and Install Target. The Memory line shows the size in megabytes (MB) and how many of the slots hold a module.
jsc.guide.setup_utility.text4: The Storage page shows ARRAY MODE with four options for the RAID array ([](jsc:raid_arrays)). Each one needs drives. Enter applies the mode, and changing it erases the array.
jsc.guide.setup_utility.text5: The Exit row leaves the Setup.

jsc.guide.shared_folders.text1: A folder on your computer can be shared with the other computers of the network. A shared folder is seen by its path, which starts with two backslashes, then the computer's name, then the share's name: \\computer\name.
jsc.guide.shared_folders.text2: A share takes its name from the last part of its folder's path, and a drive root such as C: is named c. Two folders cannot share one name, and a computer shares at most 16 folders.
jsc.guide.shared_folders.text3: Another computer's share is reached through its path. The path below a share is followed on the owner's computer, exactly as it would be at that computer's own prompt.
jsc.guide.shared_folders.title: Shared folders
jsc.guide.shell_prompt.definition1: The program that reads the lines you type and runs the commands in them.
jsc.guide.shell_prompt.definition2: The text before the cursor, which names who you are, on which computer and in which folder.
jsc.guide.shell_prompt.definition3: The all-powerful account of a system. On FreeBSD the prompt names that account and ends in the sign #.
jsc.guide.shell_prompt.definition4: The text screen of a computer, with a keyboard, where you type commands and read the answers.
jsc.guide.shell_prompt.definition5: A program you call by its name, with the words after the name that say what it works on.
jsc.guide.shell_prompt.fix1: Type help on Linux or UNIX System V to list the commands; FreeBSD has no help command. The apropos command with one word finds commands by what they do ([](jsc:whatis_and_apropos)).
jsc.guide.shell_prompt.fix2: apropos with one word finds the command you want. man intro reads a manual entry on FreeBSD only.
jsc.guide.shell_prompt.fix3: The command belongs to a package you have not installed. The which command says whether it is here and what put it there ([](jsc:software_commands)).
jsc.guide.shell_prompt.problem1: I cannot find the command I need.
jsc.guide.shell_prompt.problem2: The shell says the name is not found, and suggests apropos or man intro.
jsc.guide.shell_prompt.problem3: A command the manual lists says it is not found.
jsc.guide.shell_prompt.text1: A shell is the program that reads the line you type, runs the command named in that line, and prints what the command answers. You type into the terminal, the text screen of a computer, at the prompt: the short line of text that waits for you.
jsc.guide.shell_prompt.text2: Each computer has one prompt, and you type into it from the computer's own screen. Linux, FreeBSD and UNIX System V share one set of commands and one way of reading a line. A command that one of these systems lacks is not in its list, so it cannot run there.
jsc.guide.shell_prompt.text3: You log in as player on all three systems, and the prompt shows that name first. The part after the at sign is the computer's own name, which you change with the config command ([](jsc:system_commands)).
jsc.guide.shell_prompt.text4: The folder part shows where you are. The sign ~ stands for your home folder, the folder your files live in: /home/player on Linux and FreeBSD, and /usr/player on UNIX System V.
jsc.guide.shell_prompt.text5: On FreeBSD the prompt shows root and ends in #, because a fresh FreeBSD machine opens as root. These systems have no sudo and no su command, so you do not change accounts with a command.
jsc.guide.shell_prompt.title: What a shell is, and its prompt
jsc.guide.shell_verbs.definition1: A name that the machine keeps with a value. You give it a value with set, and read it back between percent signs.
jsc.guide.shell_verbs.fix1: The full-screen help is on MC-DOS and MC-NET only. On the Frames editions, help prints the list ([](jsc:help_on_a_computer)).
jsc.guide.shell_verbs.fix2: The command is not on this machine. Type help to see the list, or listcmd if the server allows it ([](jsc:finding_a_command)).
jsc.guide.shell_verbs.fix3: Start the name with a letter, and use only letters, digits and underscores.
jsc.guide.shell_verbs.fix4: Put an equals sign between the name and the value: set NAME=value.
jsc.guide.shell_verbs.fix5: exit only closes an ssh session. To leave this window, press [[Esc]].

jsc.guide.shell_verbs.problem3: set says a name is not allowed.
jsc.guide.shell_verbs.problem5: exit says it is not connected.
jsc.guide.shell_verbs.step1: Type set BASE=C:\work to give BASE a value.
jsc.guide.shell_verbs.step2: Type set to list the names, and BASE is in the list.
jsc.guide.shell_verbs.step3: Type dir %BASE% to read the value back, which the prompt replaces before dir runs.
jsc.guide.shell_verbs.step4: Type set BASE= to forget the name again.
jsc.guide.shell_verbs.table1: Where the prompt's own commands run
jsc.guide.shell_verbs.table1_1_2: MC-DOS, MC-NET, the Frames editions, and the Linux and UNIX systems. Not FreeBSD.
jsc.guide.shell_verbs.table2_1_2: Picks a button or a link.
jsc.guide.shell_verbs.table2_2_2: Follows the button or link that is picked.
jsc.guide.shell_verbs.text1: A few commands belong to the prompt itself. help lists the commands and explains each one, cls clears the window, echo prints the words you give it, and set gives a name a value. Most of them are on every system, and the table shows where each one runs.
jsc.guide.shell_verbs.text10: A value set here belongs to the machine. It stays set at the monitor, in a session opened from another machine, and after a restart.
jsc.guide.shell_verbs.text2: help with no words lists the commands this machine can run, one line each, with a summary of each. At the foot it says "'help <command>' for details". The list shows only the commands this machine has, not every command of its family.
jsc.guide.shell_verbs.text3: help <command> prints the page of one command. On MC-DOS and MC-NET, help takes the whole screen, with the series' manuals beside the commands. On the Frames editions, help prints. help dir opens the page of dir. The page ends with an also line that lists the other names of the command.
jsc.guide.shell_verbs.text4: cls clears the window, and the scrollback goes with it.
jsc.guide.shell_verbs.text5: version prints the line "J's Computers Shell v1.0" in the accent colour.
jsc.guide.shell_verbs.text6: echo prints the words that you give it. On MC-DOS and on the Frames editions, the text prints as you typed it.
jsc.guide.shell_verbs.text7: whoami prints this computer's name, its type and its node, one row each. A computer with no name shows (unnamed).
jsc.guide.shell_verbs.text8: exit closes a remote session that you opened with ssh ([](jsc:network_verbs)). On the prompt of this computer, exit only says that it is not connected. To leave the window, press [[Esc]].
jsc.guide.shell_verbs.text9: set with no words lists every name this machine knows. set NAME=value gives a name a value. set NAME= with nothing after the equals sign forgets the name. Names use letters, digits and underscores, and do not start with a digit.
jsc.guide.shell_verbs.title: The prompt's own commands

jsc.guide.shutting_down.text1: When you have finished, you can log off, shut the machine down, or restart it. Each edition has its own control for this, and most of them open the same Power dialog.
jsc.guide.shutting_down.text2: The Power dialog is a short list with the title "Power". It has three rows, in this order, and each row shows a short hint under its name.
jsc.guide.shutting_down.text3: A click outside the list closes the dialog without doing anything. The Escape key closes it too.
jsc.guide.shutting_down.text4: On Frames XP, the footer's Log Off closes the desktop at once, without the Power dialog. The machine keeps running.
jsc.guide.shutting_down.text5: The desktop closes first. Then the machine acts on your choice: a shutdown turns it off, a restart starts it again, and a log off leaves it running. To open the firmware setup, use the button Restart to firmware on the System page of [Settings](jsc:frames_settings).

jsc.guide.sigma_at_the_prompt.text1: Sigma and Sigma# are the programming languages of these computers. Their tools are commands at the prompt, once you install their packages. The Book of Sigma teaches the languages themselves ([](jsc:sigma_two_languages)).
jsc.guide.sigma_at_the_prompt.text2: You install a package by its name, with your system's package manager ([](jsc:software_commands)). The packages come from the Mirror, so your computer must be on a network whose Mainframe runs it.

jsc.guide.sigma_build_package.fix1: Run sgpack init in this folder, or go to the folder that holds your manifest.
jsc.guide.sigma_build_package.fix2: Copy that file into the folder, or remove its file line from package.cpk.

jsc.guide.sigma_build_package.problem2: The build says sgpack: a file is named in the manifest but not here.
jsc.guide.sigma_build_package.problem3: The build says package.cpk: files: and a name, then "is not a file name a package may carry; it must stay inside the package's own folder".

jsc.guide.sigma_build_package.step3: Read the line the build prints.
jsc.guide.sigma_build_package.text1: Building turns the manifest and its files into one package file. Nothing is compiled in this step: the listing the manifest names must already exist, made by the compiler ([](jsc:sigma_compile)). Build only reads your files and joins them.
jsc.guide.sigma_build_package.text2: A built package is one text file, named after the package, such as mypkg-1.0.0.cpk. It starts with the line ".pkg 1", then the manifest lines, then each file in a block that starts with three dashes and the file's name. Because it is plain text, you can read every line before you install it.
jsc.guide.sigma_build_package.text3: Build marks any line of a file that starts with three dashes or with a backslash, so the reader does not mistake it for the start of another file. The reader takes the mark off again, so your file comes back unchanged.
jsc.guide.sigma_build_package.text4: A successful build prints a line such as built mypkg-1.0.0.cpk (2 files, 512 bytes): the file name, how many files it holds and the size of the text in characters. The built file lands in the same folder, next to the manifest, so you can publish it at once.
jsc.guide.sigma_build_package.text5: Each file in a package keeps a name that stays inside the package's own folder: plain names separated by slashes, with no . or .. parts, no backslash and no colon. The game refuses any other name.

jsc.guide.sigma_classes.definition6: A list of method signatures that a class promises to write.
jsc.guide.sigma_classes.definition7: The class that another class inherits from, written after a colon.
jsc.guide.sigma_classes.definition8: A class-like type made of readonly fields, which is compared by its values.
jsc.guide.sigma_classes.definition9: A named shape of method. A value of a delegate type can hold any method of that shape.

jsc.guide.sigma_classes.text1: A class is a blueprint, and an object is a thing made from it. You declare a class with the word class, and you make an object of it with new. A program declares its types at the top of a namespace, and each type can hold fields, constructors and methods.
jsc.guide.sigma_classes.text2: A struct is a value type. Its values are copied when you store them or hand them over, so a change to the copy does not change the original. An enum is a list of named numbers. Each name is a value of the enum type, and you write Level.Mid to use one. The first name gets the number 0, and each name after it gets the next number, unless you write its number yourself.
jsc.guide.sigma_classes.text3: A constructor has the name of its class and gives nothing back. It runs when you make an object with new, and it sets the object up. Till till = new Till(100); makes a Till that starts with 100 cents. A class with no constructor gets an empty one. A constructor can hand over to another constructor of its own class with the keyword this, or to the base class with the keyword base.
jsc.guide.sigma_classes.text4: You reach a member with a dot. An object's member is written with the object's name, as till.Total(). A static member is written with the type's name, as Level.Mid for an enum value. The keyword this means the current object, and base means the base class. A field marked readonly can be written only where it is declared or in a constructor. The word const is kept for a later version of the language: for now, write a static readonly field.
jsc.guide.sigma_classes.text5: The words public, private, protected and internal say who may reach a member, as in C#. A public or an internal member is reached from anywhere in the program. A private one is reached only from inside its own type and the types nested in it, and a member written with no word of access is private. A protected one is reached from its own type and from the types that stand on it. Reaching a member from where its word does not let you is the error S3060.
jsc.guide.sigma_classes.text6: Sigma# has interfaces, records and delegates as well, which are explained in [Interfaces and records](jsc:sigma_interfaces_records) and [Properties, events, delegates and lambdas](jsc:sigma_delegates_events).

A program is a list of statements. A statement is one instruction, such as storing a number in a variable or calling a method. Most statements end with a semicolon. Before you write one, you need the small pieces that statements are built from: comments, names, keywords and literals.

A comment is a note for the people who read the program, and the machine skips it. A line comment starts with two slashes and runs to the end of the line. A block comment starts with a slash and a star, and it ends at the first star and slash after that. Block comments do not nest: you cannot put one inside another.

A name is a word you choose for a variable, a method or a type. It starts with a letter or an underscore, and then holds letters, digits or underscores. Any letter counts, so accented and Greek letters are allowed in names. The keywords below are reserved: you cannot use them as names.

Sigma refuses some of these words, even though the language knows them. The table "What Sigma has, and what Sigma# adds" shows which features each language has. The words kept for a later version are refused in both languages until that version brings them, and none of them can be a name.

A literal is a value written out in the program, such as the number 42, the number 0.5, true, or a text in double quotes. Each literal has a type, and the table shows which one. Numbers are written in plain decimal digits. A number with an exponent, such as 1e5, or with underscores, such as 1_000, is not a number the language can read.
Inside a text or a character, a backslash starts an escape. The letter after the backslash says what goes into the text, as the table shows.
A text must close on the line where it starts. A text can also have holes filled from values, written with a dollar sign in front of the quotes, and that form belongs to Sigma# only.

jsc.guide.sigma_compile.text1: Compiling turns your source file into a listing that a computer can run. You compile on the command line with the compiler of your language: sgsc for Sigma#, and scc for Sigma.
jsc.guide.sigma_compile.text2: Both commands take the same options. Type the command with no file, and it shows its usage line.
jsc.guide.sigma_compile.text3: The full page of each compiler follows.
jsc.guide.sigma_compile.text4: A successful compile prints the compiler's name and version first, then what it wrote. Here it compiles a file called hello.sgs:
jsc.guide.sigma_compile.text5: Compiling does not run the program. The last line says how to run it, with the sigma command ([](jsc:sigma_run)).
jsc.guide.sigma_compile.text6: A warning looks the same, but it says warning instead of error, and it is shown in dim text. When the build fails, the compiler prints the number of errors last, such as "sgsc: 1 error, nothing was written". You get no listing from a failed build.

jsc.guide.sigma_compile_errors.definitio: A mistake in the shape of the text: a missing bracket, a word where a symbol belongs, or a line that is not finished.
One run of the compiler over a program: it gives a listing, or the messages when the program has mistakes.
What the names and the types of a program stand for, checked once its shape is right.
The machine instructions a computer's processor runs. Each computer has one, and a program is built for one.
jsc.guide.sigma_compile_errors.fix1: That is expected: the steps hide each other's mistakes. Fix the first line of the new list, then compile again.
jsc.guide.sigma_compile_errors.fix2: The listing is written only when no mistake is left. Fix every line in the list, then compile again.
jsc.guide.sigma_compile_errors.problem1: The list changed after you fixed one line, and new mistakes appeared.
jsc.guide.sigma_compile_errors.problem2: The compiler gives you a list of mistakes and no listing.

jsc.guide.sigma_compile_errors.table1_2_: The shape of each line: its brackets, its keywords and its punctuation.
jsc.guide.sigma_compile_errors.table1_3_: Whether every feature the file uses exists in its language level.

jsc.guide.sigma_compile_errors.text1: The compiler does not check a file all at once. It goes through a few steps in order, and each step can find mistakes. A mistake in one step can hide the mistakes of the steps after it, so the list can change as you fix things.
jsc.guide.sigma_compile_errors.text2: The compiler checks meaning only when the earlier steps found no mistake at all. So a file with a syntax error shows its syntax errors first, and its meaning errors appear after you have fixed them. The editor checks a file while you type, and it is looser: it can report meaning errors while a line is still broken. Treat those as less certain, and check them again once the syntax errors are gone.
jsc.guide.sigma_compile_errors.text3: The compiler builds a program for the oldest instruction set that runs every instruction the program uses. If you ask for a newer instruction set, the compiler keeps your choice.
jsc.guide.sigma_compile_errors.text4: The compiler reads at most 128 levels of nesting, which means blocks inside blocks inside blocks. Deeper than that, it reports code S2013 and does not read the rest of the file.
jsc.guide.sigma_compile_errors.title: How the compiler reads a file
jsc.guide.sigma_console.definition1: The screen a program is started in: the machine's prompt or a window.
jsc.guide.sigma_console.definition2: A program waiting on something outside itself. A parked program spends no credits while it waits.
jsc.guide.sigma_console.fix1: Type a whole number. To keep going on bad input, read a line with ReadLine and convert it with Convert.ToInt(text, fallback).
jsc.guide.sigma_console.fix2: ReadBool takes only true, yes, y, on or 1 for true, and false, no, n, off or 0 for false. Type one of those.
jsc.guide.sigma_console.fix3: It waits for a line. Type one in the terminal the program is in front of.
jsc.guide.sigma_console.fix4: The console keeps only the last 200 lines. Print less, or write what you need to a file.
jsc.guide.sigma_console.fix5: A line keeps 4,096 characters. Split long text into several lines.

jsc.guide.sigma_console.text1: The console is a program's line to the terminal: the screen the program is started in. Whatever you print appears there, and whatever you read is a line the player typed there. Most programs start by printing a question and reading the answer.
jsc.guide.sigma_console.text2: Console calls cost nothing. Printing does not end the line, but PrintLine does. A read waits until a line is typed, and a program that waits is parked.
jsc.guide.sigma_console.text3: After Read or Scan, the rest of the line waits for the next read. When Scan fails on a string variable, the variable becomes empty text.
jsc.guide.sigma_console.text4: ReadBool takes true, yes, y, on or 1 for true, and false, no, n, off or 0 for false. It ignores case and spaces, so you can type Yes or OFF.
jsc.guide.sigma_console.text5: The terminal keeps at most 16 typed lines waiting. Output is kept too: the last 200 lines, 4,096 characters at most for each line, and 64,000 characters in all. Older lines go first, and a line that is cut ends with a marker.
jsc.guide.sigma_console.title: Console: reading and writing the terminal
jsc.guide.sigma_control_flow.definition1: A group of statements between a pair of braces, which counts as one statement.
jsc.guide.sigma_control_flow.definition2: A statement that repeats another statement, such as while, do or for.
jsc.guide.sigma_control_flow.definition3: An expression that must give a true or false value, such as count > 0.
jsc.guide.sigma_control_flow.definition4: A fixed row of values of one type, numbered from 0. You write its type with brackets, such as int[].
jsc.guide.sigma_control_flow.definition5: A growable row of values of one type, from the List type of Sigma#. Its items are numbered from 0 as well.
jsc.guide.sigma_control_flow.fix1: Move the break inside a loop or a switch, or remove it.
jsc.guide.sigma_control_flow.fix2: Move the continue inside a loop, or remove it.
jsc.guide.sigma_control_flow.fix3: End the method with a return that gives a value, such as return total;
jsc.guide.sigma_control_flow.fix4: Remove the value after return, or change the method so that it gives back a value of some type, such as int.
jsc.guide.sigma_control_flow.problem1: The compiler says 'break' only means something inside a loop or a switch.
jsc.guide.sigma_control_flow.problem2: The compiler says 'continue' only means something inside a loop.
jsc.guide.sigma_control_flow.problem3: The compiler says a method that gives back 'int' must return a value.
jsc.guide.sigma_control_flow.problem4: The compiler says a method that gives back nothing cannot return a value.
jsc.guide.sigma_control_flow.text1: Some statements hold other statements inside them. They decide whether the inside runs, or how many times it runs. Most of them test a condition: an expression that is true or false.
jsc.guide.sigma_control_flow.text2: A block can stand wherever one statement can. A variable declared inside a block exists only until the closing brace.
jsc.guide.sigma_control_flow.text3: The if statement runs its statement when the condition is true. The optional else runs its statement when the condition is false. A loop repeats a statement: while checks the condition before each run, and do checks it after each run. The for loop keeps a counter. For example, for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) runs three times, with i at 0, 1 and 2.
jsc.guide.sigma_control_flow.text4: The foreach statement runs its statement once for each item of an array or a list, in order. It gives each item to a variable of your choice. Sigma refuses foreach and asks you to write a for over the array's Length instead.
jsc.guide.sigma_control_flow.text5: The switch statement compares a value with each case label, and runs the section whose label matches. A section does not stop by itself. Without a break or a return at its end, the program goes on into the next section. Put break at the end of each section unless you want that.
jsc.guide.sigma_control_flow.text6: The break statement leaves the nearest loop or switch. The continue statement skips to the next turn of the nearest loop. The return statement ends a method. A method that gives back a value must return one on every way out, so the code cannot reach the end of the method without a return.
jsc.guide.sigma_control_flow.text7: The lock statement, in Sigma# only, takes an object, and a number cannot be locked. How locks are used with threads is explained in [Threads and locks](jsc:threads_and_locks).
jsc.guide.sigma_control_flow.title: Statements: if, loops, switch, break and return
jsc.guide.sigma_delegates_events.definit: A way for an object to announce that something happened. Other code subscribes to it with += and unsubscribes with -=.
A short method written in place, which takes its shape from the delegate it is given to.
jsc.guide.sigma_delegates_events.fix1: Give the event a delegate type, such as Action.
jsc.guide.sigma_delegates_events.fix2: Call a method of the class that declares the event, and let that method raise it.
jsc.guide.sigma_delegates_events.fix3: Give the lambda the same parameters and the same result as the delegate.
jsc.guide.sigma_delegates_events.fix4: Declare the variable before the loop starts, so the lambda keeps a variable of its own.
jsc.guide.sigma_delegates_events.fix5: Write Ring() with its brackets, or hand the method to a delegate of its shape.
jsc.guide.sigma_delegates_events.problem: The compiler says an event's type must be a delegate.
The compiler says an event can only be raised inside the type that declares it.
The compiler says this lambda does not have the shape 'Pick' takes.
The compiler says a lambda that keeps a variable a loop declares is not built yet.
The compiler says 'Ring' is a method: call it, or hand it over where a delegate of its shape is wanted.
jsc.guide.sigma_delegates_events.text1: Sigma has none of the features on this page. Sigma# has all of them. Sigma refuses lambdas as well, so this page is for Sigma#.
jsc.guide.sigma_delegates_events.text2: A property is a named value of an object that runs code when it is read or written. You write it with get and set accessors, as in int Size { get; set; }. A property with only get can be read but not written. Sigma refuses properties: write a field, or a method that gives the value back.
jsc.guide.sigma_delegates_events.text3: A delegate is a named shape of method. A value of a delegate type can hold any method of that shape, and you call the value as if it were a method. The line delegate int Pick(int a, int b); declares a shape that takes two ints and gives back an int. The System namespace has three ready-made delegates: Action takes nothing and gives nothing back, Action<T> takes one value and gives nothing back, and Func<T, R> takes one value and gives one back.
jsc.guide.sigma_delegates_events.text4: A class declares an event with the word event and a delegate type, as in event Action Changed;. Other code subscribes with += and unsubscribes with -=. Only the class that declares the event can raise it, by calling it.
jsc.guide.sigma_delegates_events.text5: A lambda is a short method written in place. x => x * 2 takes one value, and () => { statements } takes none, with a block of statements for its body. The shape comes from the delegate that the lambda is given to, so its parameters and its result must match that delegate. A lambda can use the local variables of the method it sits in, and it can use this.
jsc.guide.sigma_delegates_events.title: Properties, events, delegates and lambdas
jsc.guide.sigma_dispose.definition1: A part of a machine that finds objects nothing uses any more, and frees them. This language has none.
jsc.guide.sigma_dispose.fix1: Dispose only objects made with new. A value of an enum is not an object.
jsc.guide.sigma_dispose.fix2: Make a new object with new when you need one again.
jsc.guide.sigma_dispose.fix3: Dispose of the objects you no longer need, so that the program holds less.
jsc.guide.sigma_dispose.problem1: The compiler says only an object can be disposed, not 'Level'.
jsc.guide.sigma_dispose.problem2: The program stops and says this was disposed and cannot be used.
jsc.guide.sigma_dispose.problem3: The program stops with an out of memory message.
jsc.guide.sigma_dispose.text1: A program makes objects with new, and each object takes some of the memory the program may use. This language has no garbage collector. Here, an object stays until your program disposes of it, or until the program ends.
jsc.guide.sigma_dispose.text2: The dispose statement says that you have finished with an object. You write the word, then the name of the object, as in dispose scratch;. The name must hold an object: dispose of an enum value is refused.
jsc.guide.sigma_dispose.text3: After dispose, the object cannot be used again. A later use stops the program with the message "this was disposed and cannot be used." Memory is counted to the byte: each new takes bytes from the memory your program may use, and a program that asks for more stops with an out of memory message.
jsc.guide.sigma_dispose.title: Freeing objects with dispose

jsc.guide.sigma_editors.text1: You write a Sigma program in a text editor. Five programs open Sigma code: the Editor, vim, Virtual Studio, Virtual Studio Code and Exposure. They differ in where they run and how much they help you.
jsc.guide.sigma_editors.text2: vim takes over the terminal it was started from, so it works where there is no desktop. Virtual Studio, Virtual Studio Code and Exposure are installed like any other program ([](jsc:programs)). All three need a Legacy computer or later. On Frames, they also need Frames XP or later.
jsc.guide.sigma_editors.text3: Virtual Studio is the whole Sigma# workshop in one window, and it runs on Frames only. It works with projects and solutions, and you can read about it in [](jsc:virtual_studio).
jsc.guide.sigma_editors.text4: Virtual Studio Code is a light editor with the terminal built in, so you can write, compile and run without leaving it. It runs on Frames, Linux and FreeBSD.
jsc.guide.sigma_editors.text5: Exposure compiles every program in a folder at once, so a change shows what else it broke. It offers nothing while you type, and that is its trade.
jsc.guide.sigma_editors.text6: The window of Exposure shows PROBLEMS, a count of the problems the survey found, and WHAT THE COMPILER SAID, the compiler's own words about the problem. The Rebuild all button compiles everything again.

jsc.guide.sigma_entry_points.definition1: The place where a program starts running.
jsc.guide.sigma_entry_points.definition2: A program that runs its Main method once, and ends when Main returns.
jsc.guide.sigma_entry_points.definition3: A program that starts and then stays up, running its methods each game tick until it is stopped.
jsc.guide.sigma_entry_points.fix1: Add a class with a static method named Main, or a class that stands on Script, or implements IScript in Sigma#.
jsc.guide.sigma_entry_points.fix2: Write the Main that your project's version has, or change the version the project names.
jsc.guide.sigma_entry_points.problem1: The compiler says the program needs exactly one place to start, and this one has none.
jsc.guide.sigma_entry_points.problem2: The compiler says 'Main' needs version 2; this project is version 1.
jsc.guide.sigma_entry_points.table1_2_2: A class that stands on Script, or, in Sigma#, a class that implements IScript.
jsc.guide.sigma_entry_points.table1_2_3: It calls Program.Exit, or the program is removed.
jsc.guide.sigma_entry_points.table2_1_3: Runs once, takes nothing and gives nothing back.
jsc.guide.sigma_entry_points.table2_2_3: Gives back an exit code, a whole number, when it ends.
jsc.guide.sigma_entry_points.table2_3_3: Receives the arguments that the program was started with.
jsc.guide.sigma_entry_points.table2_4_3: Receives the arguments, and gives back an exit code.
jsc.guide.sigma_entry_points.text1: Every program has exactly one place to start. When you run a program, the machine runs that place first. There are two kinds of start. A console program runs a method named Main once and ends. A resident program stays up after it starts, and runs code each game tick until it is stopped.
jsc.guide.sigma_entry_points.text2: A class that both stands on Script and implements IScript is a resident program, because writing the interface is a deliberate act. A file with no start place is refused, and so is a file with more than one.
jsc.guide.sigma_entry_points.text3: Main must be static, in the class that holds it. A project is held to the version it names, so a form of Main that a later version adds is refused in an earlier project.
jsc.guide.sigma_entry_points.text4: A resident program has three methods that the machine calls. OnInit runs once when the program starts. OnTick runs once per game tick, and a new tick waits until the last OnTick has finished, so a slow OnTick never piles up. OnDestroy runs when the program is stopped, if the machine still has time to run it. In Sigma#, write public void for each of them in an IScript class. In Sigma, write public override void for the ones you use, in a class that stands on Script.
jsc.guide.sigma_entry_points.text5: A console program in Sigma looks like this, with one line that prints when it runs.
jsc.guide.sigma_entry_points.text6: A resident program in Sigma stands on Script, and it overrides only the methods it needs. Each game tick, the machine calls OnTick, as the [credits page](jsc:credits_per_tick) explains.
jsc.guide.sigma_entry_points.title: Where a program starts: Main and resident programs

jsc.guide.sigma_example_buses.text2: Each setting gives back the same bus, so the calls chain: one setting is followed by the next on the same line. The buses themselves, with their filters and tags, are explained in ([](jsc:buses)).

jsc.guide.sigma_example_crafting.text1: Crafting is the network's work of making items from patterns. This example sets up two crafting interfaces and two routers, then asks the network to smelt raw iron.
jsc.guide.sigma_example_crafting.text2: The network's own language, IQL, carries crafting too ([](jsc:iql)). The words of that language are not needed here: this program uses only the library's calls.
jsc.guide.sigma_example_crafting.text3: Patterns and jobs are explained in ([](jsc:how_autocrafting_works)). Routers are explained in ([](jsc:input_routers_and_receiving_buses)).
