jsc.guide.software_verbs.step2: Type store to see the programs that you can install.
jsc.guide.software_verbs.step3: Put the program's disc in a linked drive, if the program needs one.
jsc.guide.software_verbs.step4: Type install and the program's id.
jsc.guide.software_verbs.step5: Wait for the lines that say Setting up. The last line says Installation complete. Rebooting into the new system.
jsc.guide.software_verbs.table1_1_2: No words. Lists the programs installed on this computer, each with its id.
jsc.guide.software_verbs.table1_2_2: A program's id. Installs the program from its medium.
jsc.guide.software_verbs.table1_3_2: No words. Lists the programs that you can install on this computer.
jsc.guide.software_verbs.table1_4_2: A program's id. Removes an installed program.
jsc.guide.software_verbs.table1_5_2: install, remove, search, list or update, and a name. Works from the Mirror, on the Frames editions only.
jsc.guide.software_verbs.table1_head2: Words after it, and what it does
jsc.guide.software_verbs.table2_1_2: Fetches and sets up a package.
jsc.guide.software_verbs.table2_3_2: Finds the packages that the Mirror offers. With no text, it lists what is offered.
jsc.guide.software_verbs.table2_4_2: Lists the installed packages, or everything on offer with --available.
jsc.guide.software_verbs.table2_5_2: Brings the installed packages to the current build.
jsc.guide.software_verbs.text1: A program reaches the computer in two ways: from a medium, such as a disc in a linked drive ([](jsc:installing)), or from the Mirror, the network's package service. programs lists the programs installed here. store lists the ones you can install, install and uninstall change them, and on the Frames editions pckmgr fetches packages from the Mirror.
jsc.guide.software_verbs.text2: When a program needs a disc that is not in a linked drive, install says that the program needs its install disc in a linked drive.
jsc.guide.software_verbs.text3: pckmgr fetches packages from the Mirror on the Frames editions. MC-NET calls the same manager netgetter. MC-DOS has no pckmgr: it installs programs from media only.
jsc.guide.software_verbs.text4: screenfetch is a small program for the Frames editions. Once you install it, typing screenfetch at the Command Prompt prints the logo of Frames, with a summary of your machine beside it: the system, its kernel, its uptime, its packages and its shell.
jsc.guide.software_verbs.title: Installing and removing programs
jsc.guide.sound_cards.definition1: The small beeper of the computer. On a Vintage or Legacy board with no sound card, it is the only sound.
jsc.guide.sound_cards.fix1: Use a sound card of the board's era.
jsc.guide.sound_cards.fix2: Take one of the two sound cards out.
jsc.guide.sound_cards.fix3: It has no sound card, and no monitor or speaker is linked to carry its sound. Put in a sound card of the board's era, or link a monitor or speakers.
jsc.guide.sound_cards.problem1: The build says a sound card of one era does not sit on a board of another.
jsc.guide.sound_cards.problem2: The build says "one sound card per machine".
jsc.guide.sound_cards.problem3: A Vintage or Legacy computer only beeps.
jsc.guide.sound_cards.text1: Sound comes from the board or from a sound card. A Vintage or Legacy board has no sound of its own, so it needs a sound card for anything more than a beep.
jsc.guide.sound_cards.text2: The Artisan Tone Blaster family gives you the sound cards. Each one fits one era and one bus.
jsc.guide.sound_cards.text3: A computer takes one sound card, of its board's era, and the card's bus must belong to the board's bus family ([the bus family](jsc:build_refusals)).
jsc.guide.sound_cards.text4: From the Transition on, a board has sound of its own, so the card is no longer needed. Its tooltip says "Sound on the board: plays everything". The earlier boards say "PC speaker: beeps only".
jsc.guide.sound_cards.text5: The sound you hear comes out through the monitors linked to the computer, and through speakers joined to it by peripheral cable ([the speakers](jsc:speakers)). With no monitor and no speaker linked, the sound goes to the PC speaker. Otherwise the sound card plays if there is one, then the board's own sound if it has any, and otherwise the PC speaker.
jsc.guide.sound_cards.title: Sound cards
jsc.guide.sound_library.definition1: The number of times a sound wave repeats each second. A higher number is a higher pitch.
jsc.guide.sound_library.definition2: One sound that the sound card can play at once.
jsc.guide.sound_library.definition3: A song file on the machine's disk.
jsc.guide.sound_library.definition4: A named pitch: a letter from A to G, an optional sharp or flat, and an octave from 0 to 8.
jsc.guide.sound_library.fix1: Write each item as a note, a pitch in hertz, or R for a rest.
jsc.guide.sound_library.fix2: The machine's sound is off, or the machine makes no sound. Check that its sound is on.
jsc.guide.sound_library.fix3: Check that the file is a recording, that the volume is above 0, and that the server keeps the recording.
jsc.guide.sound_library.fix4: No speaker linked to this machine has that exact name. Check the name, because it must match exactly.
jsc.guide.sound_library.problem1: The program stops and says that the item is not a note.
jsc.guide.sound_library.table1_1_2: Beeps at that pitch, for that many milliseconds (ms).
jsc.guide.sound_library.table1_2_2: Plays a tune of notes. Gives true when it plays.
jsc.guide.sound_library.table1_3_2: Plays a recording from the machine's disk. Gives true when it plays.
jsc.guide.sound_library.table1_4_2: Stops the recordings the programs are playing.
jsc.guide.sound_library.table2_1_2: The speaker with that name, linked to this machine, or null when there is none.
jsc.guide.sound_library.table2_3_2: Plays a recording out of that speaker alone. Gives true when it plays.
jsc.guide.sound_library.table3_1_2: A note: a letter from A to G, then its octave from 0 to 8.
jsc.guide.sound_library.table3_2_2: A sharp with #, or a flat with b, in a note.
jsc.guide.sound_library.table3_3_2: A pitch in hertz, above 0 and up to 20000.
jsc.guide.sound_library.table3_4_2: A rest: silence for the item's length.
jsc.guide.sound_library.table3_5_2: Notes played together as a chord, up to 16 notes.
jsc.guide.sound_library.table3_6_2: A length in milliseconds, from 1 to 60,000, after the item.
jsc.guide.sound_library.text1: A machine makes sound through the speaker in its case, and through the sound cards you fit. Sound is the type for the machine as a whole, and Speaker is one speaker you can name. The hardware is explained in [](jsc:sound_cards) and [](jsc:speakers).
jsc.guide.sound_library.text2: Beep comes out of the speaker in the machine's case. A new beep cuts off the one before it. Its pitch stays between 20 and 20,000 hertz (Hz), and its length between 1 and 60,000 milliseconds (ms).
jsc.guide.sound_library.text3: A tune is written as items separated by spaces or commas. A tune such as C4:250 E4 G4 C4+E4+G4:500 plays three notes and then a chord.
jsc.guide.sound_library.text4: An item with no length lasts as long as the item before it. The first item lasts 250 milliseconds. A tune holds at most 1,024 items.
jsc.guide.sound_library.text5: Each note of a chord takes a voice of the sound card. A machine with no sound card plays only the first note of each chord, through the speaker in its case.
jsc.guide.sound_library.text6: Play reads a recording from the machine's disks. It gives false when the file is not a recording, when the machine plays no recordings, when the volume is 0, or when the server does not keep the recording. A new Play replaces the recording the programs were playing.
jsc.guide.sound_library.text7: A sound comes out at the machine's volume. A sound that finds no voice free takes the voice of the oldest sound.
jsc.guide.sound_library.text8: A speaker is found by its exact name. A speaker with no name cannot be found this way.
jsc.guide.sound_library.title: Sound: beeps, tunes, recordings and speakers
jsc.guide.soundfoundry.definition1: The list of songs queued to play, in order.
jsc.guide.soundfoundry.definition2: A song sent while it plays, instead of kept on the computer first.
jsc.guide.soundfoundry.definition3: A song sent to the server's library, so that the others on the network can play it.
jsc.guide.soundfoundry.definition4: The service on a rack server that streams the network's music to every Soundfoundry you play it on.
jsc.guide.soundfoundry.fix1: Install a sound card in the computer.
jsc.guide.soundfoundry.fix2: No Soundfoundry Server is on the network, or the server has no memory to spare for the stream. Install a Soundfoundry Server on a server in a rack of the network.
jsc.guide.soundfoundry.problem1: The song line says NO SOUND CARD INSTALLED.
jsc.guide.soundfoundry.problem2: A network song does not play.
jsc.guide.soundfoundry.text1: Soundfoundry plays songs on the computer, from a file or from the network. It is on the Frames, Linux and FreeBSD desktops, but not on UNIX. It needs a Legacy computer or newer.
jsc.guide.soundfoundry.text2: Soundfoundry needs a sound card. Without one, the song line says NO SOUND CARD INSTALLED, and the volume, balance and playlist buttons turn grey. Install a sound card in the computer ([](jsc:sound_cards)), and choose where the sound goes ([](jsc:speakers)).
jsc.guide.soundfoundry.text3: The window also has SHUFFLE and REPEAT buttons, and a PL button that shows the playlist. ADD, REM and SEL work on the playlist. NET opens the network share window. The volume and the balance are sliders, and the song line shows MONO or STEREO, and its bit rate and sample rate.
jsc.guide.soundfoundry.text4: The menu holds the ways to fill the playlist: open a file or a folder, add to the playlist, remove or keep the selected songs, sort the list, and save or open a playlist. A playlist holds at most 500 songs, and its name is at most 32 characters.
jsc.guide.soundfoundry.text5: The network tabs are SEARCH, DOWNLOADS and SHARED. A search finds every word you type in a song's title, artist, album or file name, in any order and any case. A query holds at most 64 characters. Songs from the network arrive at the speed of the slowest cable on the way, and several downloads at once share that speed.
jsc.guide.soundfoundry.text6: A song plays from one of three places: a file on this computer's disk, a song of the library that this computer already has on its own disk, or a stream from the Soundfoundry Server the computer picked. A downloaded or imported song is kept in the music folder of the computer.
jsc.guide.soundfoundry.text7: The Soundfoundry Server runs on a server in a rack. It streams the music catalogue to every Soundfoundry on the network ([](jsc:server_racks)). Its library is the songs in its own music folder, and each computer's shared songs sit in a folder named after that computer.
jsc.guide.soundfoundry.text8: The server streams only while it has the memory to hold the stream open. So a computer asks to listen before it plays, and asks again every little while.
jsc.guide.soundfoundry.title: Soundfoundry
jsc.guide.speakers.definition1: A recording with two channels: a left side and a right side.
jsc.guide.speakers.definition2: The small speaker of the Transition set, which plays everything but the bass.
jsc.guide.speakers.definition3: A box, with no cable of its own, that plays the bass the satellites leave out.
jsc.guide.speakers.fix1: Stand a Transition subwoofer against one of the linked Transition speakers.
jsc.guide.speakers.fix2: Join the speaker to the computer with a peripheral cable ([](jsc:peripheral_cables)).
jsc.guide.speakers.fix3: Pick another name for this speaker.
jsc.guide.speakers.problem3: Another speaker already has this name.
jsc.guide.speakers.table1_1_2: Both sides, as the only speaker of the computer.
jsc.guide.speakers.table1_2_2: Both sides, as one of several speakers.
jsc.guide.speakers.table1_3_2: The left side, from its place beside the monitor.
jsc.guide.speakers.table1_4_2: The right side, from its place beside the monitor.
jsc.guide.speakers.table1_5_2: No sound from this speaker: the computer's sound plays only out of the monitor.
jsc.guide.speakers.table1_6_2: No sound at all, for a speaker that is not linked to the computer.
jsc.guide.speakers.text1: A speaker plays a computer's sound somewhere other than the monitor. The Vintage has no speaker; the Legacy and the later eras do. Join a speaker to the computer with a peripheral cable. It takes an audio output of the sound card, or of the board from the Transition on, and each audio output drives two speakers.
jsc.guide.speakers.text2: Two speakers beside a monitor play a stereo recording: the one on the left, as you face the monitor, plays the left side, and the one on the right plays the right side. A speaker on its own, or one that is not beside a monitor, plays both sides.
jsc.guide.speakers.text3: The speaker's window has a CHANNEL, with one of these settings:
jsc.guide.speakers.text4: The speaker's window also shows what it PLAYS. A Legacy speaker plays "22 kHz, bass and treble cut", so the bass and the treble are cut. A Transition satellite plays "Bass cut: no subwoofer". A Standard or Advanced speaker plays "The whole range".
jsc.guide.speakers.text5: Stand a subwoofer against one of the computer's linked Transition speakers, on any of that speaker's six faces. Then the Transition speakers of the computer play the bass too. A computer needs only one subwoofer: a second one adds nothing.
jsc.guide.speakers.text6: Give each speaker a name of up to 32 characters. Programs find a speaker by its name, so no two speakers of one computer can share a name.
jsc.guide.speakers.title: Speakers and the subwoofer
jsc.guide.stage_three.definition1: A tar archive of a base Gentoo system, ready to unpack in place of building it.
jsc.guide.stage_three.definition2: The file of build settings that Portage reads before it compiles a program.
jsc.guide.stage_three.fix1: No Mainframe running the Mirror is on this network, or the address does not begin with mirror://mainframe.
jsc.guide.stage_three.fix2: The address must end in /gentoo/stage3-vel64-openrc.tar.xz, spelled exactly like that.
jsc.guide.stage_three.fix3: The command names no stage 3 file. Type the whole command, with stage3 in the file name.
jsc.guide.stage_three.fix4: The archive is in /root, the folder you started in. Type cd /mnt/gentoo, then download the stage 3 again there.
jsc.guide.stage_three.fix5: The disk is not mounted at /mnt/gentoo, or you are not in that folder. Mount it ([](jsc:mounts_and_chroot)), then type cd /mnt/gentoo.
jsc.guide.stage_three.problem1: The download says "Name or service not known".
jsc.guide.stage_three.problem3: tar says "Cowardly refusing to create an empty archive".
jsc.guide.stage_three.problem4: tar says "Cannot open: No such file or directory".
jsc.guide.stage_three.problem5: tar says "refusing to unpack a whole system over the live medium".
jsc.guide.stage_three.step3: Type tar xpvf stage3-*.tar.xz --xattrs-include='*.*' and press [[Enter]].
jsc.guide.stage_three.step4: Wait for the prompt to come back. Unpacking takes longer on a slow disk.
jsc.guide.stage_three.text1: A stage 3 is a ready-made archive of a base Gentoo system: the basic files, the tools and the libraries, before the kernel and before any program you chose. You download it and unpack it into the new system's disk, so you do not build the base from source yourself.
jsc.guide.stage_three.text2: Its name tells you what it holds. In stage3-vel64-openrc.tar.xz, vel64 is the processor architecture, and openrc is the init system, the program that starts the services at boot.
jsc.guide.stage_three.text3: The disk must be mounted first ([](jsc:mounts_and_chroot)). The download saves the file in the folder you stand in, and the live medium starts you in /root, so you move to /mnt/gentoo before you download.
jsc.guide.stage_three.text4: The first line of the answer carries the date. A progress bar then fills while the archive downloads, and the screen says when the file is saved.
jsc.guide.stage_three.text5: The letters after tar matter. x unpacks the archive, p keeps the file permissions, and f names the archive that follows. The v letter prints each path as it is unpacked. Without v, the screen stays quiet until the unpacking ends. --xattrs-include keeps the extra file information that some programs need.
jsc.guide.stage_three.text6: When the unpacking ends, the new system has its folders, among them /etc, /boot, /usr and /var. It also has two starting files: /etc/portage/make.conf, and an /etc/fstab that holds only a header. Unpacking the archive again undoes every later step, so the checklist asks for them again.
jsc.guide.stage_three.title: The stage 3 archive
jsc.guide.standard_functions.definition1: An old-style name, such as printf or rand, that the library answers with a member you can also call by its full name.
jsc.guide.standard_functions.definition2: A place in a format text, starting with a percent sign, that is filled with a value.
jsc.guide.standard_functions.definition3: A file the program has opened, which it works on a piece at a time.
jsc.guide.standard_functions.definition4: No value at all: the program holds nothing, and a call that gives null answers with nothing.
jsc.guide.standard_functions.fix1: Use one of the holes listed above, such as %d for a whole number or %s for text.
jsc.guide.standard_functions.fix2: Write the number into the format, as in %5d, instead of a star.
jsc.guide.standard_functions.fix3: Put the format between quotes in the call, not in a variable.
jsc.guide.standard_functions.fix4: Use a hole from the list above.
jsc.guide.standard_functions.problem1: The compiler says a hole is not one printf has.
jsc.guide.standard_functions.problem2: The compiler says a width or a precision cannot come from a value here.
jsc.guide.standard_functions.problem3: The compiler says the format must be written out.
jsc.guide.standard_functions.problem4: The program stops and says that the hole is not one this machine's printf can write.
jsc.guide.standard_functions.table1_1_2: Console.Print, filled from the values after the format.
jsc.guide.standard_functions.table1_2_2: Gives the text back instead of printing it.
jsc.guide.standard_functions.table1_3_2: Console.PrintLine: prints and ends the line.
jsc.guide.standard_functions.table1_6_2: Console.Read: the next character as a number.
jsc.guide.standard_functions.table2_10_2: The place of the part inside the text, as IndexOf.
jsc.guide.standard_functions.table2_11_2: string.Compare: the order of two texts.
jsc.guide.standard_functions.table2_13_2: Adds the text to the end of dest.
jsc.guide.standard_functions.table2_14_2: The upper or lower case of one character.
jsc.guide.standard_functions.table2_1_2: Program.Exit: ends the program with the status.
jsc.guide.standard_functions.table2_4_2: Convert.ToInt(text, 0): 0 when the text is not a number.
jsc.guide.standard_functions.table2_9_2: The length of the text, as string.Length.
jsc.guide.standard_functions.table3_15_2: Bus.Named: the bus with that name.
jsc.guide.standard_functions.table3_16_2: Redstone.Named: the Redstone Interface with that name.
jsc.guide.standard_functions.table3_3_2: File.Open: gives a FILE, or null.
jsc.guide.standard_functions.table3_9_2: FILE.Read(), the next character as a number.
jsc.guide.standard_functions.text1: Programs written in the old style call bare names such as printf, rand and strlen. Sigma and Sigma# still accept them. Each bare name is a call on a library member, so puts(s) does the same as Console.PrintLine(s).
jsc.guide.standard_functions.text2: printf is version 1. Every other name on this page is version 2, so a version 1 build refuses it. Each table row names the member the old name calls, so you can read that member's entry in this book.
jsc.guide.standard_functions.text3: The formats of printf, sprintf, scanf, fprintf and fscanf work the same way. A hole starts with a percent sign and a letter: %d for a whole number, %f for a decimal number, %s for text, %c for a character and %% for a percent sign.
jsc.guide.standard_functions.text4: The compiler knows %d, %i, %u, %x, %X, %o, %f, %e, %E, %s, %c and %%. A version 1 hole takes only the plain letters d, i, f, s and c, with nothing between the percent sign and the letter. Flags, widths and precisions came in version 2.
jsc.guide.standard_functions.title: The old names: printf, rand and the rest
jsc.guide.start_menus.definition1: The face a system shows after it starts: the wallpaper, the windows, the taskbar and the Start menu.
jsc.guide.start_menus.definition2: The menu that opens from the Start button, with your programs, the places of the system and the power controls.
jsc.guide.start_menus.definition3: The bar along the bottom of the screen, with the Start button, a button for each open program and the status area.
jsc.guide.start_menus.definition4: A box on the desktop that holds one open program.
jsc.guide.start_menus.definition5: A square on the Frames 10 Start menu that stands for one program, and starts that program when you click it.
jsc.guide.start_menus.definition6: Keeping a program on a tile, a square in the grid or a button on the taskbar, so that it stays there when the program is closed.
jsc.guide.start_menus.fix1: Check the spelling, or clear the search box and look through the list.
jsc.guide.start_menus.fix2: A machine keeps up to 24 tiles. Right-click a tile, choose "Unpin from Start", then pin the new program.
jsc.guide.start_menus.problem1: The menu says "No results" while you type.
jsc.guide.start_menus.problem2: You want a 25th tile on a Frames 10 menu.
jsc.guide.start_menus.step1: Click the Start button in the taskbar.
jsc.guide.start_menus.step2: Find the program in the list, or type part of its name.
jsc.guide.start_menus.step3: Click the program with the left button.
jsc.guide.start_menus.table1_1_2: Start, at the left corner of the taskbar
jsc.guide.start_menus.table1_1_3: One vertical list of programs, under a side band that carries the name of the system.
jsc.guide.start_menus.table1_2_3: Two columns: programs on the left, places on the right.
jsc.guide.start_menus.table1_3_2: A round glass button at the left end
jsc.guide.start_menus.table1_3_3: Two columns in a frame of glass: programs on the white side, places on the glass side.
jsc.guide.start_menus.table1_4_3: A rail, a list of programs and a set of tiles.
jsc.guide.start_menus.table1_5_3: A floating panel: a search box, a grid of pinned programs and a power button.
jsc.guide.start_menus.text1: The Start menu is where you find the programs of your Frames. Click the Start button on the taskbar, and the menu opens above it. The general idea is on the page [Desktops](jsc:desktops).
jsc.guide.start_menus.text10: The tiles at the right of the menu are squares, each standing for one program. The tile sizes are these:
jsc.guide.start_menus.text11: A Frames 10 machine keeps up to 24 tiles. A new machine starts with File Explorer, Calculator, System Monitor, Settings, Editor, Command Prompt, Paint, Minesweeper and Network Manager on its tiles.
jsc.guide.start_menus.text12: Two tiles are live. The Network Manager tile reads "Connected to a network" or "No network". The System Monitor tile shows the processor in use, marked "CPU" (central processing unit), and the memory in use, marked "Memory". A live tile turns over every 7 seconds, between its picture and its reading.
jsc.guide.start_menus.text13: You arrange the tiles with the mouse. A right click on a tile unpins it or changes its size. A right click on a program in the list pins it, with "Pin to Start". Drag a tile onto another tile to take its place.
jsc.guide.start_menus.text14: Frames 11 uses a compact floating panel. It has a search box that reads "Type here to search", a grid of pinned programs under the heading "Pinned", and a footer. The account is at the left of the footer, and the power button at the right. The grid is 5 columns wide.
jsc.guide.start_menus.text15: Whatever the edition, the search box starts empty each time you open the menu. The search keeps the programs whose name contains the text you typed, and capital letters do not matter. It takes up to 24 characters.
jsc.guide.start_menus.text16: A left click starts the program you point at. A right click opens that program's own menu.
jsc.guide.start_menus.text2: Each Frames edition draws its Start menu in its own style. Every one of them lists your programs, and each has a power control at its foot.
jsc.guide.start_menus.text3: The menu of Frames 95 is a single vertical list, one row for each program. Below the programs, a row labelled "Shut Down" opens the [power controls](jsc:shutting_down).
jsc.guide.start_menus.text4: Frames XP splits its menu into two columns. The left column lists your programs, and the first two are in bold, because they are pinned. The right column holds the places: This PC, Files, Settings and Network. The header shows your own name, and the footer holds "Log Off" and "Turn Off Computer".
jsc.guide.start_menus.text5: The menu of Frames 7 is drawn in glass. Its left column is white and lists your programs, with the first two in bold. A search box at the foot of that column filters the list as you type.
jsc.guide.start_menus.text6: The right column is the glass itself. At its head is the picture of your account, and under it are the places in white: Files, Computer, Network, Settings and Device Manager. Frames 7 calls This PC "Computer". "Shut down" sits at the foot of the column.
jsc.guide.start_menus.text7: The menu opens over the corner of the screen, level with the top of the bar. The round button stays in the bar beneath it.
jsc.guide.start_menus.text8: The menu of Frames 10 has three parts. The narrow rail at the left holds the menu's own button at the top. At the foot of the rail are your account, your files, Settings and the power button.
jsc.guide.start_menus.text9: Beside the rail is the list. It shows the programs you used most in this session, up to 4 of them, under the heading "Most used". Then it lists every program from A to Z under its letter. When you type in the search box, the list keeps only what matches.
jsc.guide.start_menus.title: The Start menu of each edition
jsc.guide.states_and_queues.definition1: The program on the Mainframe that reads IQL and plans the network's work.
jsc.guide.states_and_queues.definition2: How many items a queue or the Mainframe moves in one game tick.
jsc.guide.states_and_queues.fix1: Look at the Mainframe first. Its processor and its graphics cards set how many Operations run at once, and how fast ([](jsc:mainframes)).
jsc.guide.states_and_queues.table1_2_2: The lower of the processor's capacity and the card's speed.
jsc.guide.states_and_queues.text1: A queue is one lane that moves items for one Operation at a time. The Mainframe has one queue for its processor, and one more for each graphics card in it. A Mainframe with a processor and three graphics cards works four queues at the same time.
jsc.guide.states_and_queues.text2: Subframes on the same network lend their graphics card queues too, if they run the same engine. A Subframe that runs another engine lends none ([](jsc:subframes)).
jsc.guide.states_and_queues.text3: Each queue runs at its own speed, measured in items a tick (it/t). The processor's queue runs at the processor's capacity. A graphics card's queue runs at the lower of the processor's capacity and the card's own speed. A weak card, or a card in an older slot, is slower.
jsc.guide.states_and_queues.text4: The queues do not share their capacity among themselves. A second graphics card gives you a second lane. It does not make the first lane faster.
jsc.guide.states_and_queues.text5: The pace of the whole Mainframe is the lower of two figures. One is its orchestration capacity: how many items a tick the Mainframe, with its Subframes, can move. The other is its random-access memory (RAM) buffer, the working memory of the Mainframe in items a tick ([](jsc:memory)).
jsc.guide.states_and_queues.text6: The Network Manager shows the queues in use, as Parallel queues, and the Orchestration capacity, in items a tick. A machine step of an autocraft does not take one of these queues ([](jsc:how_autocrafting_works)).
jsc.guide.states_and_queues.text7: You can hot-swap a graphics card without losing work. The number of queues changes in place, and the Operations keep running.
jsc.guide.states_and_queues.title: Queues and graphics cards
jsc.guide.storage_insights.definition1: The count under which an item type is listed as running low. It starts at 64 items.
jsc.guide.storage_insights.fix1: No item type fits the search. Try a shorter word.
jsc.guide.storage_insights.fix2: The network holds no items yet. Put items on the network, and the numbers will follow.
jsc.guide.storage_insights.table1_1_2: The number of item types the network holds.
jsc.guide.storage_insights.table1_2_2: The total of the network's contents.
jsc.guide.storage_insights.table1_3_2: The number of item types running low.
jsc.guide.storage_insights.table2_1_2: The biggest types, as a bar chart.
jsc.guide.storage_insights.table2_2_2: The types under the threshold, or all stocked when none are.
jsc.guide.storage_insights.text1: Storage Insights shows where the network's storage went. It is a dashboard of the network's contents: the totals, the biggest types of item, the types that are running low, and how full each server is. You open it when you want to know what the network is short of.
jsc.guide.storage_insights.text2: Use the control labelled Threshold to change the count. Click a type to see its detail view. The detail view has a Back button, the total of the type, the places it is STORED IN, what it is USED TO MAKE, and the [buses](jsc:buses) that filter it. A type no bus filters is marked as not on any bus filter.
jsc.guide.storage_insights.text3: The search field, which says search item..., narrows the list. The dashboard asks the network again on its own, every so often, so the numbers keep up with the network.
jsc.guide.storage_insights.title: Storage Insights
jsc.guide.storage_priority.definition1: The number that orders the storages when items go in. The highest fills first, and the network's own storage counts as priority 0.
jsc.guide.storage_priority.definition2: The ticks a storage waits before it gives items out. Fewer ticks is faster.
jsc.guide.storage_priority.fix1: Priority starts at the Standard era. Use a Standard or newer External Storage Bus.
jsc.guide.storage_priority.problem1: The bus has no priority setting.
jsc.guide.storage_priority.step1: Look at the free room of every storage, and skip any that refuse the item.
jsc.guide.storage_priority.step2: Give the items to the storage with the highest priority, up to its free room.
jsc.guide.storage_priority.step3: Between storages with the same priority, prefer the faster one, then the one with more room.
jsc.guide.storage_priority.step4: Give the rest to the next storage in that order, and write them.
jsc.guide.storage_priority.table1: Read latency of the network's disks
jsc.guide.storage_priority.text1: When the network stores items, it must choose a storage for them, and the storage priority decides the order. The storage with the highest priority fills first. This is not the priority of an Operation ([](jsc:states_and_queues)), which orders the jobs themselves.
jsc.guide.storage_priority.text2: Some items go back to the server they came from first, as far as that server has room. This is how the results of a craft return ([](jsc:asking_for_a_craft)).
jsc.guide.storage_priority.text3: Taking items out uses another order: the fastest storage first, then the fuller one.
jsc.guide.storage_priority.text4: These are the default values, and the mod's configuration can change them.
jsc.guide.storage_priority.text5: Only an External Storage Bus has a storage priority, and only from the Standard era on. Servers, racks and computers always count as 0. You set a bus's priority from -99 to 99. The same number also decides which bus claims an item first ([](jsc:bus_keep_max_and_priority)).
jsc.guide.storage_priority.text6: A bus with a negative priority fills after the network's own storage, and a bus with a positive one fills before it.
jsc.guide.storage_priority.text7: A read cache card, the Vaultis Cache of the era, in a server's expansion slot cuts the read latency of the server's disks, by more in each newer era ([](jsc:raid_arrays)). The Predictive Cache service cuts it by 15%. Their cuts add together.
jsc.guide.storage_priority.text8: Inside one server, the Load Balancer service changes the write order. New items go to the emptiest disk first, instead of filling the disks in turn ([](jsc:network_services)).
jsc.guide.storage_priority.title: Storage priority
jsc.guide.storage_servers.balloon1_detai: Right-click its front to open the bays.
jsc.guide.storage_servers.balloon2_detai: The Standard storage server has 10 of them.
jsc.guide.storage_servers.balloon3_detai: Pull one out and push another in while the server runs.
jsc.guide.storage_servers.definition1: A server built for disks, with the most disk bays in 2 rack units (U). Its disks give the network room for items.
jsc.guide.storage_servers.definition2: One slot of height in a Server Rack. A server takes one or more of them.
jsc.guide.storage_servers.figure1: A Server Rack with a storage server in its top rack units: ten disks in the drive bays, joined as a RAID 5 array by the Vaultis Array card inside the server. Drag it to see the rack from the side.
jsc.guide.storage_servers.fix1: That slot cannot hold a disk. Use another slot.
jsc.guide.storage_servers.fix2: Use a slot that a unit in this row cables.
jsc.guide.storage_servers.problem1: A slot says "Blocked - the chassis does not cable this slot".
jsc.guide.storage_servers.problem2: A slot says "Blocked - no unit in this row cables these slots".
jsc.guide.storage_servers.text1: The network's room for items is on disks, and the disks sit in servers. A server lives in a Server Rack, a cabinet with slots called rack units (U), and each rack unit is one slot of height. A storage server is the server built for disks: it is 2 rack units tall and has more disk bays than any other server of its era. Every era has one, from the Vintage's five bays to the Standard's and the Advanced's ten.
jsc.guide.storage_servers.text2: Each disk goes into a drive bay on the front of the server. The bays are hot-swap: you can pull a disk out and push another in while the server runs.
jsc.guide.storage_servers.text3: Every server's bays, processors and slots are in [](jsc:server_types).
jsc.guide.storage_servers.text4: RAID (redundant array of independent disks) joins the disks of one server into one disk for the network. You seat a RAID controller card, the Vaultis Array of the era, in an expansion slot of the server, and you choose the mode on the STORAGE page of the server's Setup ([](jsc:setup_utility)). The modes and their numbers are in [](jsc:raid_arrays).
jsc.guide.storage_servers.text5: The network counts the room of every disk in every server of a rack. A server with no disks adds nothing to the network's room.
jsc.guide.storage_servers.title: Storage servers
jsc.guide.storage_trouble.fix1: Its filter lets nothing through, its mode is ON DEMAND with no redstone signal on its cable, or it is on no network. Check each of these.
jsc.guide.storage_trouble.fix2: Add disks or servers. A bigger disk holds more items. A newer era's disk holds more megabytes.
jsc.guide.storage_trouble.fix3: Delete files you do not need, or use a bigger disk.
jsc.guide.storage_trouble.fix4: Use a bigger disk. The number is the room in megabytes (MB) that the system needs.
jsc.guide.storage_trouble.problem2: An Operation says "the network had no room left for the <item>".
jsc.guide.storage_trouble.problem3: A file does not fit, and the computer says "Not enough free space".
jsc.guide.storage_trouble.problem4: Installing a system says "The target disk has no room for <system> (<number> MB needed)."
jsc.guide.storage_trouble.table1_1_1: "the network had no room left for the <item>"
jsc.guide.storage_trouble.table1_1_2: Not all of the items fit. Add disks or servers to the network.
jsc.guide.storage_trouble.table1_2_2: The network had less of the item than you asked for. Stock more of it, or ask for less.
jsc.guide.storage_trouble.table1_3_1: "another Operation was holding the <item> it needed"
jsc.guide.storage_trouble.table1_3_2: Another Operation reserved the items this one needs. Wait for it, or cancel it ([](jsc:cancelling_and_the_log)).
jsc.guide.storage_trouble.table1_head2: What it means, and the fix
jsc.guide.storage_trouble.table2: Messages at a bus and an inventory
jsc.guide.storage_trouble.table2_1_2: The inventory has no free room. Take items out of it.
jsc.guide.storage_trouble.table2_2_2: The bus's cable is not on a network. Join it to one ([](jsc:data_cables)).
jsc.guide.storage_trouble.table2_3_2: The bus faces nothing. Put it on a data cable beside an inventory.
jsc.guide.storage_trouble.table2_4_1: ON DEMAND, with "Moves only while its cable has a redstone signal"
jsc.guide.storage_trouble.table2_4_2: The bus moves only when its cable has a signal. Give the cable a redstone signal, or change the bus's mode.
jsc.guide.storage_trouble.table2_head2: What it means, and the fix
jsc.guide.storage_trouble.table3_1_2: The bay has fewer disks than that RAID mode needs, so the change is refused. Add disks, then set the mode again.
jsc.guide.storage_trouble.table3_2_2: The array lost disks but still serves its items. Put a replacement disk in the bay ([](jsc:raid_arrays)).
jsc.guide.storage_trouble.table3_3_2: More disks are gone than the mode can lose, so the array gives no room. Put the missing disks back.
jsc.guide.storage_trouble.table3_4_2: A replacement disk is copying the array's items back. The array serves again when the copy is done.
jsc.guide.storage_trouble.table3_5_1: "Blocked - the chassis does not cable this slot"
jsc.guide.storage_trouble.table3_5_2: That slot cannot hold a disk. Use another slot.
jsc.guide.storage_trouble.table3_head2: What it means, and the fix
jsc.guide.storage_trouble.text1: Storage goes wrong in a few known ways, and the game says which. An [Operation](jsc:what_operations_are) that does not finish its whole job shows its status in the Network Manager ([](jsc:network_manager)): "partial" when some of the job was done, "failed" when none was, and "locked" when it gave up waiting.
jsc.guide.storage_trouble.text2: Each Operation reserves the items it will take, and another Operation that needs the same items waits for it. In the messages below, <item> stands for the name of the item.
jsc.guide.storage_trouble.text3: Pulling a disk out of a RAID 1 or RAID 5 array keeps its items on the other disks. The array keeps working while it waits for a replacement, and it rebuilds when the replacement goes into the bay ([](jsc:raid_arrays)).
jsc.guide.storage_trouble.title: When storage goes wrong
jsc.guide.storage_trouble.warning1: Pulling any disk out of a RAID 0 array erases the data on every disk of the array. RAID 0 keeps no second copy.
jsc.guide.studio_activity.fix1: Start a query or a craft. Its Operation appears in this list.
jsc.guide.studio_activity.fix2: That Operation has no id yet. Wait for it to get one, or press [[Alt]]+[[Break]] in the query tab that started it.
jsc.guide.studio_activity.problem1: The list says "No Operations in flight."
jsc.guide.studio_activity.problem2: Cancel Operation cannot be chosen on a row.
jsc.guide.studio_activity.text1: The Activity Monitor shows the Operations in flight on the network: the work that the network is doing right now. Open it from the Tools menu, and you see the list refresh by itself while it stays open.
jsc.guide.studio_activity.text2: The top line reads "Craft slots <used> / <total>": the craft slots in use out of the total. On the right it reads "<n> running". When nothing runs, the list says "No Operations in flight."
jsc.guide.studio_activity.text3: Each group has a colour of its own, so you can see at a glance which Operations go on and which are held up or stopped. The statuses are explained in [the Operation states](jsc:operation_states).
jsc.guide.studio_activity.text4: Click an Operation row to open a menu with one item, Cancel Operation. The item works only for an Operation that has an id. Cancel Operation asks the network to stop that Operation.
jsc.guide.studio_activity.title: The Activity Monitor
jsc.guide.studio_explorer.definition1: The network's record of what each storage holds. ANALYZE, REINDEX and VACUUM keep it fresh.
jsc.guide.studio_explorer.definition2: A hold on items, so that other Operations cannot take them.
jsc.guide.studio_explorer.fix1: Click a node in the tree, then open the details again with F7.
jsc.guide.studio_explorer.fix2: Connect the studio to a network first. The studio says "Not connected: <name>" until it is.
jsc.guide.studio_explorer.problem1: The details say "Nothing is picked in the explorer."
jsc.guide.studio_explorer.problem2: Stop and Restart of the engine need a connection to the network.
jsc.guide.studio_explorer.table1_1_2: The tables of the network. Each table has its columns below it.
jsc.guide.studio_explorer.table1_2_2: The views you saved with CREATE VIEW.
jsc.guide.studio_explorer.table1_3_2: The procedures you saved with CREATE PROCEDURE, under Programmability.
jsc.guide.studio_explorer.table1_4_2: One server for each storage server on the network.
jsc.guide.studio_explorer.table1_5_2: The Index, the Locks and the Operations Log. On the Legacy look this folder is called Maintenance.
jsc.guide.studio_explorer.table1_7_2: The jobs you made with CREATE JOB. A paused job shows (paused) beside its name.
jsc.guide.studio_explorer.table2_2_2: Hot events left entries the index has not re-read.
jsc.guide.studio_explorer.table2_3_2: Mass removals left ghost entries pointing at storage that is gone.
jsc.guide.studio_explorer.table3_1_2: New Query, Refresh, Start, Stop and Restart the engine, Properties
jsc.guide.studio_explorer.table3_2_2: Query Top 100 Rows, Count Rows, Script Table as, Properties, Refresh
jsc.guide.studio_explorer.table3_3_2: Query View, Script View as, Properties
jsc.guide.studio_explorer.table3_4_2: Execute Stored Procedure, Modify, Script Procedure as, Properties
jsc.guide.studio_explorer.text1: The Object Explorer is the tree at the side of the studio. Its top node is the network, and folders hang below it. When you open a folder, you see what the network holds.
jsc.guide.studio_explorer.text2: Every folder holds one kind of thing. Right-click a node, and you see the menu of that kind of node. The next table names the folders.
jsc.guide.studio_explorer.text3: The Index note tells you how healthy the Index is. The next table shows each note and the statement that fixes it.
jsc.guide.studio_explorer.text4: Each entry under Locks shows the item and its quantity, as an item name with x and a number.
jsc.guide.studio_explorer.text5: Script Table as and Script View as open a submenu. Each item writes a statement into a new query tab, or copies it to the clipboard. Delete on a job asks first: "Delete the job <name>?"
jsc.guide.studio_explorer.text6: Object Explorer Details (F7) lists the children of the picked node in columns: Name, Kind, Rows, Columns, What it holds, Last change, State, Trigger, Quantity and Version. It has a Search box and counts its items. Properties (F4) lists the facts of the picked node. A running job shows as running there.
jsc.guide.studio_explorer.title: The Object Explorer
jsc.guide.studio_keys.table1_13_2: Replace. Searches the tab and replaces the text.
jsc.guide.studio_keys.table1_14_2: Go To Line. Moves to a line you choose.
jsc.guide.studio_keys.table1_15_2: Comment / Uncomment. Turns the lines into comments, or back.

jsc.guide.studio_keys.table1_3_2: Close. Closes the current query tab.
jsc.guide.studio_keys.table1_6_2: Undo. Takes back the last change.
jsc.guide.studio_keys.table1_head2: Menu item and what it does

jsc.guide.studio_keys.table2_3_2: Cancel Executing Query. Stops the query that is running.
jsc.guide.studio_keys.table2_4_2: Parse. Checks the syntax without running anything.
jsc.guide.studio_keys.table2_5_2: Display Estimated Plan. Shows the plan of a CRAFT statement without running it.
jsc.guide.studio_keys.table2_8_2: Results Pane. Shows the results pane.
jsc.guide.studio_keys.table2_9_2: Results to File. Saves the results as comma-separated values.

jsc.guide.studio_keys.text1: Most actions have a key. The menu writes that key beside the item, and the studio answers to the same key. The first table lists the keys for files and text.
jsc.guide.studio_keys.text2: When you read a key written with a plus sign, press the keys together: [[Ctrl]]+[[Shift]]+[[S]] means hold Ctrl and Shift, then press S.
jsc.guide.studio_keys.text3: The Break key is sometimes printed as Pause, and Alt+Pause also cancels a running query. The Keyboard Shortcuts page lists every key of the studio's menus. The Help menu opens it.

jsc.guide.studio_overview.definition1: The statements in one query tab. The statements are separated by semicolons and run one at a time.
jsc.guide.studio_overview.fix1: Put a Mainframe that runs the Midsoft IQL Server on this network ([](jsc:midsoft_iql_server)).
jsc.guide.studio_overview.fix2: Use the tools of the engine that runs, or switch the engine in the Network Manager ([](jsc:network_manager)).
jsc.guide.studio_overview.fix3: Install the engine from the Network Services of the Network Manager ([](jsc:network_manager)).
jsc.guide.studio_overview.fix4: Connect the studio to a network whose Mainframe runs the engine, then try again.
jsc.guide.studio_overview.problem1: The studio says "No compatible Midsoft IQL Server was found on this network."
jsc.guide.studio_overview.problem2: The studio says "<computer> runs <engine>. Use the tools of that engine, or ask whoever runs the Mainframe to switch it in the Network Manager."
jsc.guide.studio_overview.problem3: The studio says "<computer> has no Midsoft IQL Server installed."
jsc.guide.studio_overview.table1_1_2: The 2000 look. The name in the window is "IQL Query Analyzer".

jsc.guide.studio_overview.text1: The IQL Server Management Studio (ISMS) is the program where you write IQL, run it, and read what the network answers. Use it when you want to query the network by hand.
jsc.guide.studio_overview.text2: The studio is a desktop program. Open it from its desktop icon: typing a command at the prompt does not open it. The console answers "Open the ISMS from its desktop icon."
jsc.guide.studio_overview.text3: The studio works with the Midsoft IQL Server, the engine that runs on the [Mainframe](jsc:mainframes) and reads your IQL. You need a network with that engine before the studio can work: [the Midsoft IQL Server](jsc:midsoft_iql_server).
jsc.guide.studio_overview.text4: The studio runs from the Legacy era on, and it needs 128 MB of memory.
jsc.guide.studio_overview.text5: The studio's look follows the era of your computer. Every look has the same functions. Only the appearance and a few names change.
jsc.guide.studio_overview.text6: The Object Explorer Details, the Activity Monitor, the Template Explorer and the IQL Reference open beside the queries. The Profiler opens in its own window.
jsc.guide.studio_overview.text7: The studio keeps its settings in the file isms.cfg at the top of the computer's disk. When it starts, it opens an empty query tab, unless you turn off "Open a new query when the studio starts" in Tools > Options.
jsc.guide.studio_overview.title: The IQL Server Management Studio
jsc.guide.studio_queries.fix1: Type a statement in the tab first, or select the text you want to run.
jsc.guide.studio_queries.fix2: Split the statement into shorter statements, each ending with a semicolon.
jsc.guide.studio_queries.fix3: Press [[Ctrl]]+[[S]] to save the tab first, then close it.
jsc.guide.studio_queries.fix4: Read the Messages tab, fix the line it names, and run the script again.
jsc.guide.studio_queries.fix5: Fix the line that the message names, then parse again with [[Ctrl]]+[[F5]].
jsc.guide.studio_queries.fix6: Run a query first, then save its results.
jsc.guide.studio_queries.fix7: Put a CRAFT statement in the tab, then press [[Ctrl]]+[[L]].
jsc.guide.studio_queries.problem1: The studio says "There is nothing to run."
jsc.guide.studio_queries.problem2: The studio marks a line: "Line <n>: the statement is <length> characters long, more than the 512 a statement may be."
jsc.guide.studio_queries.problem3: The studio asks "<tab> has changes that are not saved. Close it anyway?"
jsc.guide.studio_queries.problem4: The run answers "Query completed with errors".
jsc.guide.studio_queries.problem5: Parse answers "Parse found an error" beside a line.
jsc.guide.studio_queries.problem6: Save answers "There are no results to save."
jsc.guide.studio_queries.problem7: The studio answers "Display Estimated Plan works on a CRAFT statement."
jsc.guide.studio_queries.step1: Press [[Ctrl]]+[[N]] to open a new query tab.
jsc.guide.studio_queries.step2: Type a statement and end it with a semicolon, for example QUERY items LIMIT 10;
jsc.guide.studio_queries.step3: Press [[F5]] to run the whole script.
jsc.guide.studio_queries.step4: Read the results under the script. Press [[Ctrl]]+[[D]] to see them as a grid.
jsc.guide.studio_queries.table1_1_1: Ask before a statement that cannot be undone
jsc.guide.studio_queries.table1_1_3: Asks before each statement that cannot be undone. Tools > Options.
jsc.guide.studio_queries.table1_2_1: Open a new query when the studio starts
jsc.guide.studio_queries.table1_2_3: Opens an empty query tab at the start. Tools > Options.
jsc.guide.studio_queries.table1_3_3: Shows a number beside each line of a script. Tools > Options.
jsc.guide.studio_queries.table1_4_1: Stop the script at the first error
jsc.guide.studio_queries.table1_4_3: Stops the run at the first failed statement. Query > Query Options.
jsc.guide.studio_queries.text1: Each query tab holds one script: the statements you write, and the results of the last run. The tabs are named Query 1, Query 2 and so on. [[Ctrl]]+[[Tab]] moves to the next tab.
jsc.guide.studio_queries.text10: Save writes the tab to its file. Save As... writes a new script file. Scripts are saved with the extension .iql, and a file typed as IQL opens in the studio.
jsc.guide.studio_queries.text2: Statements run one at a time. The studio sends the next one only when the last one has come back.
jsc.guide.studio_queries.text3: Each Operation that a run starts is listed in the Messages tab, as "Operation #<id> started - Cancel Executing Query stops it". Press [[Alt]]+[[Break]], or the toolbar's Cancel, to stop the run. The studio then answers "Query was cancelled by user."
jsc.guide.studio_queries.text4: Some statements cannot be undone: every DROP statement, and a DELETE of ALL. Before one runs, the studio asks "This statement cannot be undone:", shows the statement and asks "Run it?". Its buttons are Yes, No and a box named "Don't ask again". Ticking that box turns the question off.
jsc.guide.studio_queries.text5: A statement may be 512 characters long. A longer one is refused, and the studio marks the line where it starts.
jsc.guide.studio_queries.text6: Results appear in a grid by default. [[Ctrl]]+[[T]] shows them as text, and [[Ctrl]]+[[Shift]]+[[F]] saves them to a file as comma-separated values.
jsc.guide.studio_queries.text7: The Messages tab, next to Results, lists what the run did. It keeps at most 200 messages for each tab.
jsc.guide.studio_queries.text8: [[Ctrl]]+[[E]] runs only the selected text. [[Ctrl]]+[[F5]] checks the syntax without running anything. A clean check answers "Commands completed successfully."
jsc.guide.studio_queries.text9: [[Ctrl]]+[[L]] shows the estimated plan of a CRAFT statement. For any other statement the studio answers "Display Estimated Plan works on a CRAFT statement." The plan lists the steps chosen to make the craft.
jsc.guide.studio_queries.title: Writing and running queries
jsc.guide.studio_templates.definition1: A saved statement with blanks in it. The blanks are filled in before the statement runs.
jsc.guide.studio_templates.fix1: Open a template from the Template Explorer, or write the statement by hand.

jsc.guide.studio_templates.text1: A template is a statement with blanks, which you fill in before it runs. The Template Explorer, in the View menu, lists eight of them. Click one, and you open it in a new query.
jsc.guide.studio_templates.text2: A blank has three parts in its angle brackets: a name, a type and a default value. For example, <quantity, number, 64> is a blank named quantity, of the type number, whose value starts as 64.
jsc.guide.studio_templates.text3: Press [[Ctrl]]+[[Shift]]+[[M]] to fill in the blanks of the current query. The dialog Specify Values for Template Parameters asks for each value, and shows each blank as its name and type.
jsc.guide.studio_templates.text4: Press [[F1]] to open the IQL Reference. It lists each statement with what it does. The table below gives the same list, with the meaning the studio gives each line.
jsc.guide.studio_templates.title: Templates and the IQL Reference
jsc.guide.subframes.fix1: The network has no Subframe, so the Mainframe does all the work by itself.
jsc.guide.subframes.fix2: Make it run the same engine as its Mainframe ([](jsc:engines)).
jsc.guide.subframes.problem1: The screen says "No Subframes on this network."
jsc.guide.subframes.problem2: The screen says a Subframe will take no work until it runs the same engine too.
jsc.guide.subframes.text1: A Subframe is a computer that helps the Mainframe of its network carry the work. When your Mainframe is alone, it does all the work itself, with its own capacity and queues.
jsc.guide.subframes.text2: A Subframe lends a share of its capacity. By default that share is 60%, set by the Subframe share in the mod's config. It lends its queues too, which are its graphics cards, so a Subframe without graphics cards lends capacity only.
jsc.guide.subframes.text3: A Subframe works only for a Mainframe that runs the same engine as it does ([](jsc:engines)). A Subframe without a Mainframe lends nothing.
jsc.guide.subframes.title: Subframes
jsc.guide.supercomputers.balloon1_detail: A full computer of two rack units, with its own co-processor.
jsc.guide.supercomputers.balloon3_detail: It ties every rack of the supercomputer to the interface.
jsc.guide.supercomputers.balloon4_detail: The one point where the supercomputer meets the network.
jsc.guide.supercomputers.definition1: A card that adds extra processing to a node, such as the Integra Phi series.
jsc.guide.supercomputers.figure1: A supercomputer: two Supercomputer Racks of nodes, joined by High Compute Cable to the HBW Interface, which meets the network. Drag it to see the cables behind the racks.
jsc.guide.supercomputers.fix1: Check the slots: each needs a node with a Phi that fits, is assembled, and has its bay on.
jsc.guide.supercomputers.fix2: Use a Phi whose rated slots reach that far.
jsc.guide.supercomputers.fix3: Only the first six nodes count, in rack order from the top. Put the ones you want first.
jsc.guide.supercomputers.problem3: A node past six adds nothing.
jsc.guide.supercomputers.table2_2_2: The Phi is rated only for the slots before this one.
jsc.guide.supercomputers.table2_3_2: The node's bay is switched off.
jsc.guide.supercomputers.table2_4_2: No node sits in that slot.
jsc.guide.supercomputers.text1: A supercomputer is every Supercomputer Rack tied together by a fabric cable, meeting the network at one HBW Interface ([](jsc:hbw_interface)). The Standard and the Advanced have an interface of their own.
jsc.guide.supercomputers.text2: The fabric cables are the InfiniBand Cable (Transition), the High Compute Cable (Standard) and the OSFP Cable (Advanced).
jsc.guide.supercomputers.text3: Each Supercomputer Rack holds Supercomputer Nodes, which are full computers. A node adds crafts only when it holds a Phi that fits its slot, is assembled, and has its bay on. The Integra Phi co-processors come in four models.
jsc.guide.supercomputers.text4: A Phi's tooltip gives its slots as "Supercomputer slots 1-2" for the Integra Phi 5100. The nodes are counted across the racks on the run, from the top down, and the first six nodes are the rated slots, numbered 1 to 6.
jsc.guide.supercomputers.text5: Each slot gives parallel crafts: slot 1 gives 8 crafts, slot 2 gives 16 crafts, doubling up to slot 6 with 256 crafts. Together the six slots give up to 504 parallel crafts. Each slot shows its state:
jsc.guide.supercomputers.text6: The supercomputer is ONLINE when its interface is on a network and at least one slot runs crafts. A slot runs crafts when its node holds a Phi that fits, it is assembled, and its bay is on. An operation can hold several slots, as many as are free, and the Mainframe shows the crafts in use out of the total.
jsc.guide.supercomputers.title: Supercomputers

jsc.guide.system_commands.text1: These commands tell you about the computer you use: its system, its name, its power and its settings. Some work on every machine, and the others only on the Unix systems, as each block says.
jsc.guide.system_commands.text2: The config command shows and changes the settings of the computer. With no argument it lists them. With a key and a value, as in config name <name>, it changes one setting.
jsc.guide.system_commands.text3: The config command has more settings, such as wallpaper and theme.
jsc.guide.system_commands.text4: The reboot command can open the firmware instead of the system: its --firmware option enters the setup of the [firmware](jsc:firmware).
jsc.guide.system_commands.text5: You will not find a version command on these systems. It belongs to MC-DOS and the Frames systems, where it shows the shell's version.
jsc.guide.system_commands.title: Machine and system information
jsc.guide.system_monitor.definition1: How busy a part of the machine is, in percent.
jsc.guide.system_monitor.definition2: Memory that programs have taken for themselves. Free memory is what is left.
jsc.guide.system_monitor.fix1: The window reads the machine again about every 40 frames of the screen. Wait a moment, then look again.
jsc.guide.system_monitor.problem1: A bar shows a figure a moment late.
jsc.guide.system_monitor.text1: The System Monitor is a dashboard of this machine at a glance: its processor, its memory, its graphics, and a bar for every disk. It only reads the machine and shows it, so you cannot change anything in it.
jsc.guide.system_monitor.text2: Open it before you start a big program, to see whether the machine has memory to spare. The memory part shows the random-access memory (RAM) that programs hold, and how much is free.
jsc.guide.system_monitor.text3: The processor load is how busy the processor is, in percent. Memory shows the memory held, out of the total in MB, and the free memory below it.
jsc.guide.system_monitor.text4: Graphics shows "no GPU" when the machine has no graphics processor (GPU). Otherwise it shows the video memory held, out of the total, and the load of the card in percent.
jsc.guide.system_monitor.text5: Storage draws a bar for each disk, and marks the system disk with the word (system). It also counts the programs installed on the machine.
jsc.guide.system_monitor.title: The System Monitor

The System Monitor and the Task Manager show what the machine is doing. The first only reads: it shows the load on the processor, the memory, the graphics and the storage. The second lists what is running, and it lets you end a program.
The System Monitor is on the desktop systems. It reads the machine as it works, and it changes as the load changes.
Right-click the panel and open the Task Manager from its menu. It is not on the Start menu or the desktop. Each desktop has its own manager, so what you see depends on your system.

On Frames XP the tabs are Applications, Processes, Performance and Networking. The Performance tab shows the use of the processor and the memory, as numbers and as a history, and the graphics card when there is one. The Networking tab shows whether the machine is Connected or Not connected, and the link activity over the last minute.
Next to the buttons the window warns: "Ending a program may lose unsaved work." and "Ending the system restarts the machine." A system, a desktop or a service cannot be ended from here.
The System Monitor and the Task Manager

jsc.guide.system_sounds.text1: Frames plays short sounds for the events of the machine: startup, shutdown, an error, a notice, a beep, and a device that you plug in or take out. Each edition has its own chimes, so a Frames 95 startup sounds different from a Frames 11 startup. Each sound has a subtitle: the caption that names it on the screen, such as "Frames 95 chimes".
jsc.guide.system_sounds.text2: Frames 7 has no error sound of its own, so it uses the one of Frames XP. Frames 10 uses the one of Frames 11. A shutdown plays the startup chime of the same edition again.
jsc.guide.system_sounds.text3: The machine plays the sound through its monitor, its speakers, or both. The Output setting on the Sound page of [Settings](jsc:frames_settings) chooses: Monitor, Speakers or Both.
jsc.guide.system_sounds.text4: The same Sound page holds the Volume, which changes in steps of 10 percent from 0 to 100 percent, and the Mute switch, which shows On or Off. On Frames 10, Quiet hours also stops the notice sound, as the [notices](jsc:notices) entry explains.

jsc.guide.system_v_installer.step3: Type the name of the computer in the Computer name box.

jsc.guide.system_v_installer.step5: Wait for the copy. Closing the monitor does not stop it.
jsc.guide.system_v_installer.step6: On the done page, remove the floppy and press [[Enter]] to reboot.

jsc.guide.system_v_installer.text1: You install UNIX System V from its floppy, with the System V installer. The installer asks two things, the disk and the name of the computer, then copies the system onto the disk. It runs in a window with one banner in reverse video the whole way through.
jsc.guide.system_v_installer.text2: You need a computer of the Vintage era or newer, with a Floppy Drive linked to it, and a disk with at least 10 MB of free space. When you finish, the disk holds UNIX System V, and the computer starts it after the reboot.
jsc.guide.system_v_installer.text3: The settings page asks "Choose the disk to install the UNIX System V on:" and shows each disk on a line. A line starts with the slot number and the label of the disk, and then gives its size, its free space and what it holds, or "Nothing".
jsc.guide.system_v_installer.text4: A disk that already holds a system asks you first. The question reads "<disk label> holds <what it holds>. What should happen to it?"
jsc.guide.system_v_installer.text5: While the copy runs, the copy page names the disk you chose. Open the monitor again to see its progress.
jsc.guide.system_v_installer.text6: The done page says "The UNIX System V is installed on <disk>." and then gives the name of the computer and the space used on the disk.

jsc.guide.system_v_overview.definition1: An item that carries the files of a system or a program. It goes into a drive linked to the computer, and the system reads it from there.
jsc.guide.system_v_overview.definition2: The menu system of UNIX System V, with its menus in frames over one another.
jsc.guide.system_v_overview.fix1: Check the table above: some commands belong to other systems. Use the command this system has.
jsc.guide.system_v_overview.fix2: A desktop is a program you install. On a Legacy computer or a newer one, install CDE ([](jsc:cde_on_system_v)), then restart the computer. The desktop shows at the next boot.

jsc.guide.system_v_overview.problem2: The system starts at a prompt, and you expect a desktop.

jsc.guide.system_v_overview.text1: UNIX System V is the oldest of the UNIX systems you meet at a prompt, and the one that a computer of the first era runs. Its release is 3.2. You work in it the way you work in any UNIX system: you type a command, the system answers, and your files sit in folders.
jsc.guide.system_v_overview.text2: The system was built for a small machine. It takes 10 megabytes (MB) of disk, and it keeps 2 megabytes (MB) of memory for itself while it runs, yet it runs several programs at once. It takes its programs from media and from nowhere else: there is no Mirror to install from, only media ([](jsc:programs)).
jsc.guide.system_v_overview.text3: Starting the system prints a few lines in order, and the last one says the system is ready.
jsc.guide.system_v_overview.text4: When you shut the system down, it prints a warning first: "THE SYSTEM IS BEING SHUT DOWN NOW ! ! !", then "Log off now or risk your files being damaged."
jsc.guide.system_v_overview.text5: The last line says "The system is down.", or "The system is being restarted." when the system comes straight back up.
jsc.guide.system_v_overview.text6: Your home folder is /usr/player, and the people of the system live under /usr. The installation makes bin, etc, mnt and tmp under the root, and bin, lib and player inside usr. Inside your home it makes Desktop and Documents.
jsc.guide.system_v_overview.text7: Programs go to /usr/bin. When a drive holds a medium, its files appear under /mnt with the letter of the drive, such as /mnt/d.
jsc.guide.system_v_overview.text8: Most commands of the shell work here, and [the shell](jsc:shell_prompt) explains them. Two commands exist only on this system: installpkg, which installs a program from a medium, and pace, the menu system. Both have their own entries ([](jsc:installpkg), [](jsc:pace)).

jsc.guide.system_v_tools_notes.text1: Three commands of this group are explained in full in other chapters, because the UNIX systems share them. This page says only what UNIX System V does on its own.
jsc.guide.system_v_tools_notes.text2: vi comes with the system, so it is always there, and you never install it. It uses the same engine as [vim](jsc:vim), with the messages of System V. The screen has no colour and no ruler in the corner. Its keys and colon commands are in [](jsc:vi).
jsc.guide.system_v_tools_notes.text3: lp sends a file to a printer linked to the computer ([](jsc:peripheral_cables)). Its options and messages are on the printing page, [](jsc:printing). Unless you name a printer with -d, lp uses the default one.

On this system it also reads the wider manuals: man graphics-cards opens the manual's entry on graphics cards, as a page of section 7. jsc.guide.task_manager.text1: The Task Manager shows what the machine is running and what each thing uses: the windows open, the processes, the processor (CPU) and the memory, and the disks. You use it to end a program that will not close.
jsc.guide.task_manager.text2: Open it from the taskbar ([](jsc:taskbar)): right-click the taskbar and choose Task Manager. It is kept off the desktop and off the Start menu.
jsc.guide.task_manager.text3: End Task is unavailable when the selected row is neither a window nor a process. Ending a window closes that program. Ending a process stops the script or service it names.
jsc.guide.task_manager.text4: The Performance page shows CPU Usage and Memory Usage as figures and as histories. The graphics part shows video memory, with its dedicated and shared parts. A computer with no graphics says "This computer has no graphics."
jsc.guide.task_manager.text5: The Networking page says whether the machine is Connected or Not connected, and shows the link activity over the last minute.
jsc.guide.task_manager.text6: The Task Manager does not show the Operations of a network. You watch those in the Network Manager ([](jsc:network_manager)). The eight states an Operation can be in are on their own page ([](jsc:operation_states)).

jsc.guide.taskbar.text1: The taskbar is the bar along the bottom of the screen. It holds the Start button, a button for every open program, and the status area at the right. Every Frames edition has a taskbar that is 24 pixels tall, but each one looks different.
jsc.guide.taskbar.text2: What happens depends on the state of the program's windows.
jsc.guide.taskbar.text3: Click a program's button with the right button to open its menu. The items you see depend on its windows.
jsc.guide.taskbar.text4: A closed program has a shorter menu: Open, and Unpin from taskbar if it is pinned.
jsc.guide.taskbar.text5: Right-click the empty part of the bar to open its menu. A line separates Show the Desktop from Task Manager.
jsc.guide.taskbar.text6: At the right of the bar, the status area shows the network, the sound, the memory and the clock, and on some editions the day. The memory is random-access memory (RAM).
jsc.guide.taskbar.text7: The [Task Manager](jsc:task_manager) lists the programs that are running. It also shows the processor, the memory, the network and the disks, and it ends a program that stops answering. Its pages are Applications, Processes, Performance, Networking, Services and Storage.
jsc.guide.taskbar.text8: Frames 95 gives its Task Manager the shape of a close box. Frames XP and Frames 7 use tabs, and Frames 10 and Frames 11 use a modern shape with graphs.
jsc.guide.taskbar.title: The taskbar and its menu
jsc.guide.taskbar.warning1: Ending a program may lose unsaved work.
jsc.guide.tasks_and_jobs.definition1: A program that the computer is running right now.
jsc.guide.tasks_and_jobs.definition2: The process identifier: the number that names one task.
jsc.guide.tasks_and_jobs.definition3: A line the computer keeps to run later or at an hour. It holds memory while it waits.
jsc.guide.tasks_and_jobs.definition4: The list of jobs, each with its hour and its days.
jsc.guide.tasks_and_jobs.fix1: No program is running on the computer right now. Start a program, then run tasklist again.
jsc.guide.tasks_and_jobs.fix2: Write /PID, then the number that tasklist shows for the task.
jsc.guide.tasks_and_jobs.fix3: Stop a task with taskkill, or add memory ([](jsc:frames_memory)).
jsc.guide.tasks_and_jobs.fix4: Write the hour as 06:00 or 6. Write the days as M, T, W, Th, F, Sa or Su, separated by commas.
jsc.guide.tasks_and_jobs.fix5: Only the hour is kept. Schedule the job for the hour you need.
jsc.guide.tasks_and_jobs.problem1: tasklist says No tasks are running.
jsc.guide.tasks_and_jobs.problem2: taskkill says /PID takes the number of a task.
jsc.guide.tasks_and_jobs.problem3: start says Not enough memory to start another task.
jsc.guide.tasks_and_jobs.problem4: at says The time is not in the right format.
jsc.guide.tasks_and_jobs.problem5: A job did not run at the minute you asked.
jsc.guide.tasks_and_jobs.table1_1_2: Lists the jobs, with their hours and days.
jsc.guide.tasks_and_jobs.table1_2_2: Runs the command every day at that hour.
jsc.guide.tasks_and_jobs.table1_3_2: Runs the command only on the days named: M, T, W, Th, F, Sa and Su.
jsc.guide.tasks_and_jobs.text1: A task is a program that the computer is running right now. A job is a line the computer keeps to run later, or at an hour of every day. These verbs list and stop the tasks, start commands in the background, and keep the schedule of the jobs.
jsc.guide.tasks_and_jobs.text2: tasklist lists the tasks the computer is running. Its columns are PID, NAME, FILE, STATE and MEM. MEM shows the memory that each task holds of the memory promised to it. When nothing runs, it says "No tasks are running."
jsc.guide.tasks_and_jobs.text3: On the Frames editions, tasklist works from Frames XP on. Frames 95 does not have it.
jsc.guide.tasks_and_jobs.text4: taskkill stops a task. Give it the number with /PID, as in taskkill /PID 12, or write /PID:12. The number is the one that tasklist shows. Like tasklist, it works on Frames XP and later.
jsc.guide.tasks_and_jobs.text5: where looks up a command by its name and reports where the machine has it. If it finds nothing, it says INFO: Could not find "NAME". With no name, it prints its usage. It works on Frames XP and later.
jsc.guide.tasks_and_jobs.text6: start runs a command and gives you the prompt back at once, while the command keeps running. On a machine that runs one thing at a time, it takes the started commands in turn. Each started command holds 1 MB of memory while it runs.
jsc.guide.tasks_and_jobs.text7: at runs a command at an hour of the day, every day or only on the days that you name. The smallest time step a job can use is one hour of the world's clock.
jsc.guide.tasks_and_jobs.text8: For example, AT 06:00 INTERAC GET 64 COAL /LOCAL brings 64 coal into this computer every morning at six. Only the hour counts: the minutes after the colon are not kept, so write 06:00.
jsc.guide.tasks_and_jobs.text9: When at adds a job, it prints "Added a new job with ID = " and the number. Deleting a job prints "Deleted job" and its number. A job number that does not exist gets "The job ID does not exist." With no jobs, at says "There are no entries in the list."
jsc.guide.tasks_and_jobs.title: Tasks, starts in the background and the schedule
jsc.guide.text_tools.definition1: A program that shows one screen of text at a time, so you can read a long file.
jsc.guide.text_tools.fix1: grep matches the exact text you type, so check the spelling. Add -i to ignore upper and lower case.
jsc.guide.text_tools.fix2: Type less alone, with a file name. To read only some lines, first pick them with grep, then read the result in a file with less.
jsc.guide.text_tools.problem1: grep shows no lines at all.
jsc.guide.text_tools.problem2: less says it cannot be piped.
jsc.guide.text_tools.table1_3_2: Move one line at a time.
jsc.guide.text_tools.table1_4_2: Searches the text for what you type next.
jsc.guide.text_tools.table1_5_2: Goes to the next match of the search.
jsc.guide.text_tools.table1_6_2: Leaves less and gives you back the prompt.
jsc.guide.text_tools.text1: Text tools read lines of a file, or the lines that a pipe brings in. They count the lines, pick some out, put them in order, or show them one screen at a time.
jsc.guide.text_tools.text2: A line is the text between two line breaks. Most of these tools count or choose by line.
jsc.guide.text_tools.text3: less shows a file one page at a time. These keys move you through it, and each one works while less holds the whole terminal.
jsc.guide.text_tools.title: Reading and sorting text
jsc.guide.the_systems.fix1: The hardware is older than the system's first era, or the disk is too small for it ([](jsc:installing)).
jsc.guide.the_systems.table2: The help book of each system
jsc.guide.the_systems.text1: The operating system is what a computer starts into, and what every program runs on. You choose a system when you install it ([](jsc:installing)).
jsc.guide.the_systems.text2: Each system needs hardware of its era or newer, takes room on the disk it is installed on, and takes memory while it runs.
jsc.guide.the_systems.text3: MC-DOS is a command prompt. UNIX System V is a shell, with no desktop of its own.
jsc.guide.the_systems.text4: Each Frames edition runs on its own era and every newer one. Frames 10 needs Standard hardware, and Frames 11 needs Advanced.
jsc.guide.the_systems.text5: The programs you open take memory on top of the system's. What a program takes grows with the era of the computer: 8 times as much on a Transition computer as on a Legacy one, 32 times on a Standard one and 128 times on an Advanced one ([](jsc:frames_memory)).
jsc.guide.the_systems.text6: Arch Linux and Gentoo are installed by hand, step by step. The other systems have a guided installer ([](jsc:installing)).
jsc.guide.the_systems.text7: Each book is in the library ([](jsc:library)). Help on a computer opens on the book of its system first ([](jsc:help_on_a_computer)).
jsc.guide.the_systems.title: Operating systems
jsc.guide.the_walkthrough.definition1: A command that takes time and holds the terminal until it ends, such as pacstrap, or emerge on Gentoo.
jsc.guide.the_walkthrough.fix1: Each line names what is missing and the step that provides it, in brackets. Do that step, then type reboot again.
jsc.guide.the_walkthrough.fix2: Type exit to leave the new system, then type reboot.
jsc.guide.the_walkthrough.problem1: reboot answers: "The new system will not boot:", with a list under it.
jsc.guide.the_walkthrough.problem2: reboot answers: "reboot: you are inside the new system. exit first."
jsc.guide.the_walkthrough.step3: Read the step you are on, then type it at the prompt.
jsc.guide.the_walkthrough.step4: Check what the shell answered, and only then type the next step.

jsc.guide.the_walkthrough.table2_1_3: The hardware clock set, and a name for the machine.

jsc.guide.the_walkthrough.table2_head3: When it is on, reboot also asks for
jsc.guide.the_walkthrough.text1: The medium carries its own walkthrough: the steps of the distribution's guide, written out in order, as a plain file. You do not need a guide from outside the game to follow it.
jsc.guide.the_walkthrough.text2: The walkthrough is kept in /root/install.txt, on the medium and not on your disk, so it is there whatever the disk holds. To find it and read it:
jsc.guide.the_walkthrough.text3: The walkthrough lists the commands in order. Some steps carry a mark, and the table shows what each mark means.
jsc.guide.the_walkthrough.text4: The medium greets you when it starts: "Type 'help' for the installation walkthrough." It logs you in as root on its own, so you type no name and no password.
jsc.guide.the_walkthrough.text5: On Gentoo, the same help names Gentoo, and the prompt reads livecd instead of root@archiso.
jsc.guide.the_walkthrough.text6: The server can ask for more before a reboot. Each distribution has one setting, off by default, kept in jscomputers-server.toml beside the world. The table lists what each one adds.
jsc.guide.the_walkthrough.text7: These settings change only what reboot refuses. Every command still answers the way the real tool does, so you type the same commands either way. The basic list that reboot always checks is in [When the reboot refuses](jsc:when_reboot_refuses).

jsc.guide.this_pc.definition1: A piece of hardware attached to the machine, such as a drive or a monitor.
jsc.guide.this_pc.definition2: The name a disk or medium carries. This PC and the Files tree show it.
jsc.guide.this_pc.fix1: Install a disk in the computer, or link a drive to it ([](jsc:drives)).
jsc.guide.this_pc.fix3: The field was blank once its spaces were trimmed, and a blank name is ignored. Type a name.
jsc.guide.this_pc.fix4: The field stops at 32 characters. Use a shorter name.

jsc.guide.this_pc.problem3: The name does not change after you press Enter.
jsc.guide.this_pc.problem4: You cannot type more than 32 characters.
jsc.guide.this_pc.step2: Type the new name in the field.
