jsc.guide.this_pc.table1_3_2: Takes the medium out of the drive ([](jsc:drives)).
jsc.guide.this_pc.text1: This PC is the window that shows the machine itself: its name, its disks, the drives linked to it, the hardware seated in it and the programs installed on it. Open it when you want to know what the computer holds. On Frames 7 the same window is called Computer.
jsc.guide.this_pc.text2: The top of the window is a card for the machine. It shows the machine's name, its kind, its era, its system and whether it is on a network. A machine with no system says "No system installed".
jsc.guide.this_pc.text3: You can give the machine a name of your own. The name can be 32 characters long at most, and the machine trims the spaces at both ends before it keeps the name.
jsc.guide.this_pc.text4: A disk or medium has a name too. Select its row and press Rename: the name is cut to 32 characters, and a blank name is ignored.
jsc.guide.this_pc.text5: Under the card, Devices and drives lists each disk with a bar that shows how full it is, and the system it holds. Each linked drive names what is in it. For an installer, the row says what it would install.
jsc.guide.this_pc.text6: Install appears only on an installer. Eject appears only on a drive that holds a medium.
jsc.guide.this_pc.text7: Further down, the window lists the hardware seated in the machine. Installed programs follows, as a grid of the programs on the machine.
jsc.guide.this_pc.title: This PC

jsc.guide.this_pc_and_desktop_tools.text: Some programs come with every desktop, under the names its system gives them. This page covers four of them: This PC, which shows the machine and its drives; Files, which holds your files; the Editor, which writes text; and Settings, which changes the way the desktop and the machine behave. The Network window has its own page ([](jsc:network_interactor)).
The eight pages are Personalize, System, Network, Storage, Display, Programs, Sound and Users. The Programs page holds the line Uninstall a program.

This PC is the page of the machine itself. A card shows the computer's name, its kind, its era, its system and its network. Below it are the devices and drives: each disk with a bar that shows how full it is, and each linked drive with what is in it. For an installer in a linked drive, This PC names the program it would install.
This PC is on Frames, Linux and FreeBSD. UNIX has [Workstation Info](jsc:cde_workstation_info) in its place.
Files is the program for your files. Its toolbar has back, forward and up buttons. An address trail shows the folder you are in, and each part of it is clickable. A search box sits beside it.

The drive tree on the left holds the quick-access shortcuts and every volume, each with its letter. A removable disk has an eject control. The list in the middle shows the files of the folder, with an icon for each type, and you sort it by name, type or size.

Double-click a folder to open it. Double-click an installer to run its setup, or a text file to open it in the Editor. The right-click menu offers cut, copy, paste, rename, delete, new file, new folder and properties, and it greys out what the volume forbids. An archive opens with 67ark ([](jsc:archiver)).
The Editor edits plain text. It is not an integrated development environment (IDE). It has no syntax highlighting, no completion and no compiler, so it only edits the text.
You can have several files open at once. Open and Save As use the system's own file window. The Editor is the default for text files, so a .txt file opens there.
Settings is the control panel. A list on the left holds its pages, and the page you pick fills the pane on the right. A change takes effect as soon as you make it.
jsc.guide.this_pc_and_desktop_tools.titl: This PC, Files, the Editor and Settings
jsc.guide.threads_and_locks.definition1: A line of work inside one program, sharing its memory with the program's other threads.
jsc.guide.threads_and_locks.definition2: A claim on an object, so that only one thread at a time runs the steps that hold it.
jsc.guide.threads_and_locks.fix1: Give Thread.Start a method with a body of steps to run.
jsc.guide.threads_and_locks.fix2: The thread already ended, or it was never started here. Check Thread.Running first.
jsc.guide.threads_and_locks.fix3: Use the lock statement, which takes and lets go of the lock in turn.
jsc.guide.threads_and_locks.fix4: Lock an object, such as a value of a class you write, not a plain number.
jsc.guide.threads_and_locks.fix5: Use Sigma#, or write the program so that its steps run one after another.
jsc.guide.threads_and_locks.problem1: The program stops and says there is no body to run on the thread.
jsc.guide.threads_and_locks.problem2: The program stops and says there is no thread here.
jsc.guide.threads_and_locks.problem3: The program stops and says that this thread is letting go of a lock it does not hold.
jsc.guide.threads_and_locks.problem4: The compiler says only an object can be locked.
jsc.guide.threads_and_locks.problem5: The compiler refuses Thread or lock in Sigma.
jsc.guide.threads_and_locks.step1: Write lock, then the object in brackets.
jsc.guide.threads_and_locks.step2: Write the statement the lock covers after the brackets.
jsc.guide.threads_and_locks.table1_1_2: Starts a new thread that runs the method the action points at.
jsc.guide.threads_and_locks.table1_2_2: The thread that is running this part of your program.
jsc.guide.threads_and_locks.table1_3_2: Stops the thread for that many ticks.
jsc.guide.threads_and_locks.table1_4_2: Gives the turn to the next thread.
jsc.guide.threads_and_locks.table1_8_2: Waits at most that many ticks. Gives yes when the thread ended in that time.
jsc.guide.threads_and_locks.text1: A thread is a line of work inside one program. Threads of one program share its memory, and only one of them runs at a time: the machine gives each a turn in turn.
jsc.guide.threads_and_locks.text2: Thread exists only in Sigma#. Sigma has no threads, and it has no lock statement either.
jsc.guide.threads_and_locks.text3: A thread runs a few instructions at a time, and 64 at most before another thread of the same program has its turn. Sleep and Join count ticks, and 20 ticks make one second.
jsc.guide.threads_and_locks.text4: A lock stops two threads from running the same steps on one object at once. The lock statement takes the object's lock while its body runs, and lets go when the body ends.
jsc.guide.threads_and_locks.text5: Only an object can be locked. A thread that finds the lock held by another thread waits, and asks again when the lock is free. A thread that already holds a lock can take it again, and then it must let go as many times as it took it.
jsc.guide.threads_and_locks.title: Threads and lock
jsc.guide.tour.step4: Read what a network is ([](jsc:what_a_network_is)), then build your first one ([](jsc:first_network)).
jsc.guide.tour.text1: This mod has many parts. Before you pick one, it helps to see the whole, from the computers you build to the network they make together.
jsc.guide.tour.text10: Each computer's help opens on the book of its own system ([](jsc:help_on_a_computer)).
jsc.guide.tour.text2: The computers come in kinds. A Personal Computer ([](jsc:personal_computers)) is the one you build first. A Mainframe ([](jsc:mainframes)) directs a network.
jsc.guide.tour.text3: Others are made for other jobs. A Crafting Computer ([](jsc:crafting_computers)) carries the crafting cards, and servers stand in a server rack ([](jsc:server_racks)). A Cluster Management Computer ([](jsc:cluster_management_computers)) helps you run many machines at once.
jsc.guide.tour.text4: Computers are built from parts, one by one: a motherboard, a processor, memory, a graphics card, a disk and a power supply. [Building your first computer](jsc:first_computer) shows how they fit.
jsc.guide.tour.text5: A computer shows its picture on a Monitor. A monitor is joined to a computer by standing right against it, or by a [Peripheral Cable](jsc:peripheral_cables) when it stands further away.
jsc.guide.tour.text6: Drives read the media that systems are installed from ([](jsc:drives)). The Dock Station ([](jsc:dock_station)) reads USB sticks. Printers print, speakers play sound, and a Redstone Interface ([](jsc:redstone_interfaces)) links a computer to redstone.
jsc.guide.tour.text7: Computers of one network are joined by data cable ([](jsc:data_cables)). J's Computers has no channels and no subnetworks at all: one network is one Mainframe and its computers. Routers and repeaters ([](jsc:routers)) help the network reach further.
jsc.guide.tour.text8: [Operations](jsc:what_operations_are) are jobs the network does, such as selecting, moving or crafting items. You send them in IQL ([](jsc:iql)), the network's query language.
jsc.guide.tour.text9: Items live on the disks as data ([](jsc:items_as_data)). Buses ([](jsc:buses)) move them in and out, and autocrafting ([](jsc:how_autocrafting_works)) crafts what you ask for, from patterns.
jsc.guide.tour.title: A tour of J's Computers
jsc.guide.turning_on.definition1: The check the firmware runs each time the computer starts. It lists each part it finds, one line at a time.
jsc.guide.turning_on.definition2: The firmware's own settings screens. Its pages show the disks and the hardware the firmware found.
jsc.guide.turning_on.definition3: The list the firmware opens with F12 to start a disk or medium, for this start only.
jsc.guide.turning_on.fix1: The computer has no motherboard or no power supply, so it has no build at all. Add them ([](jsc:first_computer)).
jsc.guide.turning_on.fix2: The parts do not make a valid build. See what each refusal means in ([](jsc:build_refusals)).
jsc.guide.turning_on.fix3: DEL works only while the self-test runs. Turn the computer off and on again, and press DEL in time.
jsc.guide.turning_on.fix4: The Boot Menu opens only when a disk or medium can start the computer ([](jsc:no_bootable_device)).
jsc.guide.turning_on.problem1: Nothing starts when you press the power button.
jsc.guide.turning_on.problem2: The switch goes on, but the computer does not run.
jsc.guide.turning_on.step1: Press the power button on the front of the case ([](jsc:case_front)).
jsc.guide.turning_on.step2: Watch the monitor while the self-test runs.
jsc.guide.turning_on.step3: Press [[DEL]] during the self-test to enter the Setup, or [[F12]] to open the Boot Menu.
jsc.guide.turning_on.table1: The keys while the computer starts
jsc.guide.turning_on.table1_1_2: Enters the Setup, while the self-test runs.
jsc.guide.turning_on.table1_2_2: Opens the Boot Menu, when a disk or medium can start the computer.
jsc.guide.turning_on.table1_3_2: After a self-test that finds nothing to start, goes to the Setup.
jsc.guide.turning_on.table2_1_2: The processor's name and its cores and clock speed, or "not detected". Legacy machines say Main Processor.
jsc.guide.turning_on.table2_2_2: The motherboard's name. Legacy machines do not show this line.
jsc.guide.turning_on.table2_3_2: The memory counted so far, which climbs while it is tested, and then OK.
jsc.guide.turning_on.table2_4_2: The graphics card's name, or none when there is no card. Legacy machines say Video Adapter.
jsc.guide.turning_on.table2_5_2: The firmware looks for disks and drives, and lists each one it finds.
jsc.guide.turning_on.table2_6_2: The disk the computer starts from, once it has found a system to start.
jsc.guide.turning_on.text1: Turning a computer on starts a sequence that you can watch on its monitor. It begins with a check of the hardware, and then it looks for a system to start.
jsc.guide.turning_on.text2: The check is the power-on self-test (POST). The firmware ([](jsc:firmware)) checks each part it finds, and lists it on the screen, one line after another.
jsc.guide.turning_on.text3: If you switch the computer off during its self-test, its screen stays up until you press [[Esc]].
jsc.guide.turning_on.text4: A new line appears about every 0.15 seconds. These are the lines, in order.
jsc.guide.turning_on.text5: The self-test takes between 2 and 12 seconds. The more memory modules and devices it finds, the longer it takes, and a newer era finishes sooner.
jsc.guide.turning_on.text6: After the self-test the system loads, which takes between 2 and 20 seconds. A big system and short memory make it longer. Shutting down takes a third of the boot time, but never less than 1 second or more than 5 seconds.
jsc.guide.turning_on.title: Turning the computer on
jsc.guide.two_systems.definition1: The program that lists the systems on a computer, so you can pick one to start.
jsc.guide.two_systems.definition2: The list of systems that a Frames machine shows when it starts, so you can pick one.
jsc.guide.two_systems.definition3: The order the firmware tries the disks in when the computer starts. The first disk with a system on it starts.
jsc.guide.two_systems.fix1: Pick the system you want at the Midsoft Boot Manager, or change the boot order in the firmware ([](jsc:firmware)).
jsc.guide.two_systems.fix2: Install it on another disk with room, or on a bigger disk ([](jsc:disks)).
jsc.guide.two_systems.fix3: The server's boot menu setting is off. Turn it on, with the setting boot.show_boot_menu.
jsc.guide.two_systems.problem1: The computer starts into the wrong system.
jsc.guide.two_systems.problem2: The screen says "The target disk has no room for", then the name of the second system and the megabytes it needs.
jsc.guide.two_systems.problem3: The computer starts at once, with no list, although it has two systems.
jsc.guide.two_systems.text1: Why choose? Install a second system on another disk of the same computer, and you have both.
jsc.guide.two_systems.text2: Unless the server's boot menu is turned off, each start of a computer with two systems stops at a boot manager, so you pick which system to start: the Midsoft Boot Manager on Frames, GRUB on Linux, FreeBSD's own loader. With one system only, a Frames machine goes straight through ([](jsc:midsoft_boot_manager)). The boot order in the firmware sets which disk the firmware tries first ([](jsc:firmware)).
jsc.guide.two_systems.text3: The installer proposes a default disk for the new system: the first disk with no system on it. When every disk has a system, it proposes the first disk. A disk holds up to 16 systems, as long as it has room for each one.
jsc.guide.two_systems.text4: The new system becomes the one the computer boots by default. Installing a system that the disk already carries does not add a second copy: the setup rewrites the system's boot loader, which is how a damaged system is repaired.
jsc.guide.two_systems.text5: A server setting can turn the boot menu off, so the computer boots its default system at once, with no list. The setting is boot.show_boot_menu.
jsc.guide.two_systems.title: Two systems on one computer
jsc.guide.units_and_ticks.definition1: One of the game's beats. 20 ticks make a second, so a tick is one twentieth of a second.
jsc.guide.units_and_ticks.definition2: How many items a processor handles in one tick. A faster processor handles more items each tick.
jsc.guide.units_and_ticks.table1_1_2: One unit of everything the network keeps. Disk room is counted in items.
jsc.guide.units_and_ticks.table1_2_2: The real size of a disk or a memory module, in megabytes, gigabytes and terabytes.
jsc.guide.units_and_ticks.table1_3_2: Items a tick: a processor's tooltip shows it.
jsc.guide.units_and_ticks.table1_4_2: Watts: how much power a power supply gives, and how much a part draws.
jsc.guide.units_and_ticks.table1_5_2: Seconds. The boot manager counts down in them.
jsc.guide.units_and_ticks.text1: Several units appear in this manual and on the screens. This page explains each one, so the numbers mean something to you.
jsc.guide.units_and_ticks.text2: The game counts time in ticks, too. The boot manager waits 5 seconds, which is 100 ticks ([](jsc:boot_menu)).
jsc.guide.units_and_ticks.text3: Memory is counted in items as well. Each memory module's buffer holds one item for every 4 MB of its size, and the disks count by the era of each disk ([](jsc:items_as_data)).
jsc.guide.units_and_ticks.title: Units and ticks

jsc.guide.update_cards.step2: Type UPDATE, the item, SET and the action, such as UPDATE iron_sword SET REPAIR.
jsc.guide.update_cards.table1_1_2: Furnace Card, for an item that smelts, with no experience cost and no WITH.
jsc.guide.update_cards.table1_2_2: Enchanting Card, for an item that takes an enchantment, paid with experience, and OFFER picks one of the offers.
jsc.guide.update_cards.table1_3_2: Anvil Card, for a damaged item, paid with experience, and WITH may name the material.
jsc.guide.update_cards.table1_4_2: Anvil Card, paid with experience, and WITH names the item it combines with.
jsc.guide.update_cards.table1_5_2: Anvil Card, paid with experience, for a name in quotes of at most 50 characters.

jsc.guide.update_cards.table2_4_2: The network did not start the change.
jsc.guide.update_cards.text1: UPDATE changes an item the network holds. A card does the work: it sits in a Personal Computer ([](jsc:personal_computers)), and you run the statement from that computer. The cards are explained on their own page ([](jsc:workshop)).
jsc.guide.update_cards.text2: Only the Personal Computer's own cards change items for the network. A Furnace Card smelts, an Enchanting Card enchants and an Anvil Card repairs, combines and names.
jsc.guide.update_cards.text3: A paid action takes the experience of the player who sent the statement, so somebody has to send it. The Crafting Table Card has no UPDATE action: a grid filled from the network is what CRAFT is for ([](jsc:iql_craft)).
jsc.guide.update_cards.text4: Without OFFER, ENCHANT lists the three offers and changes nothing. Each offer shows a clue, the level it needs and the levels it costs. Type OFFER with 1, 2 or 3 to take one.
jsc.guide.update_cards.text5: An item can exist in several copies, with different damage, enchantments or names. With no ORDER BY, REPAIR picks the most worn copy, and the other actions pick the copy the network holds most of. With no quantity, UPDATE changes one item.
jsc.guide.update_cards.text6: REPAIR without WITH uses the material the network holds most of.
jsc.guide.update_cards.title: UPDATE with the cards
jsc.guide.vi.fix1: vi comes only with FreeBSD and UNIX System V. On other systems, use [vim](jsc:vim).
jsc.guide.vi.fix2: Type :w to save, then :q. Or type :q! to leave without saving.
jsc.guide.vi.problem1: You type vi and the prompt says "command not found: vi".
jsc.guide.vi.problem2: The bottom row says E37: no write since last change (add ! to override).
jsc.guide.vi.table1_1_1: You open a file that exists
jsc.guide.vi.table1_2_1: You open a file that does not exist yet
jsc.guide.vi.text1: vi is the editor that comes with FreeBSD and UNIX System V. It is the same engine as [Vim](jsc:vim): the same keys, the same modes and the same colon commands.
jsc.guide.vi.text2: The machine chooses which vi you get, and you cannot change it. FreeBSD gets nvi, its own version of vi. UNIX System V gets the original, with its own words.
jsc.guide.vi.text3: The words differ from Vim's. vi keeps no name row of its own: its bottom row shows only the messages below, so there is no file name and no -- INSERT -- text. It shows no colour.
jsc.guide.vi.text4: The numbers count the lines and the characters of the text. In this example, the file has 3 lines and 42 characters.
jsc.guide.vi.text5: The keys are the same as in Vim, so the table of normal-mode keys in the Vim entry works here too. Undo and the yank of a line say the same words as in Vim, in both voices.
jsc.guide.vi.title: vi
jsc.guide.vim.definition1: The state that decides what a key does: normal, insert or command.
jsc.guide.vim.definition2: The place where dd and yy keep the line they copied, so that p and P can put it back.
jsc.guide.vim.fix1: The text has changes that are not saved. Type :w to save, then :q. Or type :q! to leave without saving.
jsc.guide.vim.fix2: The colon command is not in the table above. Check its spelling.
jsc.guide.vim.fix3: The text is more than 32,767 characters, so the file keeps its old content. Make the text shorter, or split it into more than one file.
jsc.guide.vim.fix4: Counts are not supported here. Type dd once for each line.
jsc.guide.vim.fix5: Only dd, dw, yy and gg are commands. Press [[Esc]] to cancel the wait, then type a command.
jsc.guide.vim.fix6: There is nothing left to undo. Make the change again, or leave the file as it is.
jsc.guide.vim.problem1: The bottom row says E37: no write since last change (add ! to override).
jsc.guide.vim.problem2: The bottom row says E492: not an editor command, followed by what you typed.
jsc.guide.vim.problem3: The bottom row says Too long to save.
jsc.guide.vim.problem4: You type 3 and then dd, and only one line goes.
jsc.guide.vim.problem5: After d, y or g, nothing happens.
jsc.guide.vim.problem6: The bottom row says Already at oldest change.

jsc.guide.vim.table1_2_2: Letters, digits and symbols are typed into the file.
jsc.guide.vim.table1_3_2: What you type after the colon runs when you press [[Enter]].

jsc.guide.vim.table2_12_2: Moves to the first character that is not a space.
jsc.guide.vim.table2_13_2: Moves to the end of the line.
jsc.guide.vim.table2_14_2: Moves to the last line of the file.
jsc.guide.vim.table2_15_2: Moves to the first line of the file.
jsc.guide.vim.table2_16_2: Deletes the character under the caret, unless the caret is at the end of the line.
jsc.guide.vim.table2_17_2: Deletes from the caret to the end of the line.
jsc.guide.vim.table2_18_2: Deletes the whole line and keeps it in the register.
jsc.guide.vim.table2_19_2: Deletes up to the next word. When the next word is on another line, it deletes to the end of this line.

jsc.guide.vim.table2_20_2: Copies the whole line into the register.
jsc.guide.vim.table2_21_2: Puts the register back on the line below.
jsc.guide.vim.table2_22_2: Puts the register back on the line above.
jsc.guide.vim.table2_24_2: Redoes the change that undo took back, in normal mode.
jsc.guide.vim.table2_25_2: Starts a colon command. The bottom row shows the colon and what you type.

jsc.guide.vim.table5_9_1: E37: no write since last change (add ! to override)
jsc.guide.vim.table5_9_2: You try to quit with changes that are not saved.
jsc.guide.vim.text1: Vim works in modes. A mode decides what a key does: in one mode a letter is typed into the file, and in another the same letter is a command that moves the caret or deletes text.
jsc.guide.vim.text2: The Vim here is a modern copy of the editor. It is not all of Vim. It has what you need to write and change a program: moving, typing, deleting, copying a line, undoing and a few colon commands. It has no search and no split windows.
jsc.guide.vim.text3: The bottom row shows the name of the file in quotes, with [+] after it when the text has changes that are not saved. In insert mode it also says -- INSERT --.
jsc.guide.vim.text4: You start in normal mode. Press [[Esc]] to return to normal mode from insert mode or from command mode.
jsc.guide.vim.text5: The keys d, y and g wait for a second key. Only dd, dw, yy and gg do anything. Any other second key is ignored, and the wait ends.
jsc.guide.vim.text6: Type a colon command after the colon, then press [[Enter]]. Nothing happens until you press it.
jsc.guide.vim.title: Vim
jsc.guide.virtual_studio.definition1: A folder that groups projects. It has a file that ends in .sln.
jsc.guide.virtual_studio.definition2: One program's source files, and the project file that says what to build.
jsc.guide.virtual_studio.definition3: A starting point for a new project, offered by the New Project wizard.
jsc.guide.virtual_studio.definition4: Turning the sources into a program. Start builds the startup project, then runs it.
jsc.guide.virtual_studio.fix1: It needs Frames XP or newer ([](jsc:frames_xp)).
jsc.guide.virtual_studio.fix2: Free up 512 MB of disk space, then install it.
jsc.guide.virtual_studio.fix3: The memory is past nine tenths. Close other programs, or add memory, before the system runs out and goes down ([](jsc:frames_memory)).
jsc.guide.virtual_studio.fix4: Fix the errors the build reports, then press [[Ctrl]]+[[Shift]]+[[B]] again.

jsc.guide.virtual_studio.step2: Read the result: it says Build succeeded, or Build failed with the number of errors.
jsc.guide.virtual_studio.step3: Press [[F5]] to build the startup project and run it at the terminal.
jsc.guide.virtual_studio.table1_3_2: One .sgs or .sg file, with no project.
jsc.guide.virtual_studio.table2_10_2: Shows the completions, if they are turned on.
jsc.guide.virtual_studio.table2_6_2: Builds the startup project and runs it.
jsc.guide.virtual_studio.table2_9_2: Opens the terminal, ready for typing.
jsc.guide.virtual_studio.text1: Virtual Studio is the workshop for Sigma# programs, in one window. You open a solution or a folder, write the sources, build them, and start the program. The language itself is in the Book of Sigma ([](jsc:book_of_sigma)).
jsc.guide.virtual_studio.text2: It is an installable program, for Frames XP or newer. Installing it needs 512 MB of free disk space, and it holds 256 MB of memory while it is open.
jsc.guide.virtual_studio.text4: The list of what can follow a name says what each call costs the program, before you write the line. The Book of Sigma explains the editors ([](jsc:sigma_editors)).
jsc.guide.virtual_studio.title: Virtual Studio
jsc.guide.welcome.definition1: The program on the motherboard that starts the computer. It is the first thing that runs when you turn the computer on.
jsc.guide.welcome.definition2: The system a computer starts into, and what every program runs on. MC-DOS, Frames and the Linux distributions are operating systems.
jsc.guide.welcome.definition3: A generation of hardware, such as Vintage or Standard. Parts of one era are built to fit the boards of that era.
jsc.guide.welcome.text1: J's Computers is about computers. But what is a computer here? You might expect a box that you place and switch on. It is that, but it is also built part by part, the way a real one is.
jsc.guide.welcome.text10: This book, the Guide to Operations, is one of seven books. The other six are the Frames Resource Kit, The Linux Desk Reference, Linux by Hand, The Daemon Handbook, Learning IQL and The Book of Sigma. Each book is an item in the J's Computers creative tab, and the library ([](jsc:library)) says what each one covers.
jsc.guide.welcome.text2: Computers that are joined by data cable to one Mainframe ([](jsc:mainframes)) make a network ([](jsc:what_a_network_is)). The network keeps your items on its disks, moves them, and crafts what you ask for.
jsc.guide.welcome.text3: When a computer starts, the first thing it runs is the firmware ([](jsc:firmware)): the program that checks the hardware and finds the disks. Then it hands over to an operating system, the system you use day to day.
jsc.guide.welcome.text4: To build a working computer you need parts: a motherboard, a processor (CPU), memory (RAM) and a power supply (PSU). A disk holds the system, and a graphics card (GPU) gives the monitor a picture. Each part has its own entry, and [Building your first computer](jsc:first_computer) puts them together.
jsc.guide.welcome.text5: Every part of this mod comes from the creative tabs: J's Computers has no crafting recipes of its own. J's Computers holds what every era shares, and there is one tab for each era, from J's Computers - Vintage to J's Computers - Advanced ([](jsc:eras)). A modpack can give the mod recipes, with KubeJS or a datapack; then the recipe viewer, JEI or EMI, shows how each thing is made.
jsc.guide.welcome.text6: Every entry starts on a page of its own. The row of items under an entry's title, the plate, is clickable: click an item to go to its own page. A number in brackets is a link to another entry.
jsc.guide.welcome.text7: Hold the manual key over an item and the manual opens at the item's page. The manual key is [[M]] unless you changed it.
jsc.guide.welcome.text8: The Search button finds anything in the manual by name. A search that finds nothing says "Nothing by that name".
jsc.guide.welcome.text9: The buttons Contents, Index and Glossary, and Back and Forward, move you around the book.
jsc.guide.welcome.title: Welcome to J's Computers
jsc.guide.what_a_network_is.definition1: Every computer and device joined by data cable to one Mainframe, which runs the network.
jsc.guide.what_a_network_is.definition2: A cable that carries the data of a network, in one of the lines of the data cables.
jsc.guide.what_a_network_is.definition3: A block with six faces that joins the access line of an era to its backbone, and extends the network it is part of.
jsc.guide.what_a_network_is.definition4: A block laid in a run of cable that renews the run's range, and carries each line on.
jsc.guide.what_a_network_is.definition5: The most items per tick that an Operation crossing a cable can move.
jsc.guide.what_a_network_is.definition6: How many cables a run can be before a router or a repeater renews it. A run longer than its range carries nothing.
jsc.guide.what_a_network_is.text1: J's Computers has no channels and no subnetworks at all. A network here works much like a real computer network.
jsc.guide.what_a_network_is.text2: A network is every computer and device joined by data cable to one Mainframe, its brain ([](jsc:mainframes)). The cables come in lines, by the job they do: the access line joins the small computers to a router, the backbone joins the routers, the Mainframe and the racks, the long distance line joins two networks, gateway to gateway, and the high compute line joins a supercomputer's nodes ([](jsc:data_cables)). You lay the line the job asks for, and you never count what a cable holds.
jsc.guide.what_a_network_is.text3: What a cable does have is a speed and a range: how many items per tick an Operation crossing it can move, and how many cables a run can be before a router or a repeater renews it. So a network built with the right cables in the right places is a fast network.
jsc.guide.what_a_network_is.text4: And what does the network do for you? It keeps your items as data on its servers' disks ([](jsc:items_as_data)), gives them back when you ask, and crafts what you need ([](jsc:how_autocrafting_works)). Every one of those is an Operation ([](jsc:what_operations_are)).
jsc.guide.what_a_network_is.title: What a network is here
jsc.guide.what_iql_is.definition1: Every computer and device joined by data cable to one Mainframe.
jsc.guide.what_iql_is.definition2: The one computer of a network that runs its work and keeps track of it.
jsc.guide.what_iql_is.definition3: The network's own query language: the words you type to ask it for items and to tell it what work to do.
jsc.guide.what_iql_is.definition4: One complete IQL instruction, typed on its own line.
jsc.guide.what_iql_is.definition5: A question put to the network, which it answers with rows and without changing anything.
jsc.guide.what_iql_is.definition6: One line of an answer, such as one disk or one item, with its details.
jsc.guide.what_iql_is.definition7: One action the network carries out, from the moment it is asked until it ends.
jsc.guide.what_iql_is.definition8: One beat of the game. 20 ticks make a second.
jsc.guide.what_iql_is.fix1: The Mainframe is off, or it is not on this network. Turn it on, or join the computer to its network ([](jsc:first_network)).
jsc.guide.what_iql_is.fix2: The Mainframe is busy, off, or has no processor time left for it. Wait a little, or give the Mainframe more processors or graphics cards ([](jsc:mainframes)).
jsc.guide.what_iql_is.fix3: Another Operation, or a LOCK, holds an item it needs. Wait for the other Operation to finish, or read about locks ([](jsc:lock_unlock)).
jsc.guide.what_iql_is.fix4: The network had less than you asked for. Ask for a smaller quantity. QUERY items shows how much of each item the network holds.
jsc.guide.what_iql_is.problem1: The reply says "the network has no running Mainframe".
jsc.guide.what_iql_is.table1_1_2: The word that says what to do, such as SELECT or QUERY
jsc.guide.what_iql_is.table1_2_2: How many. You may leave it out.
jsc.guide.what_iql_is.table1_3_2: The item's name, as one word.
jsc.guide.what_iql_is.table1_4_2: Words such as WHERE, which narrow the answer.
jsc.guide.what_iql_is.text1: Your items are not kept in one chest. They sit on the disks of the network: a set of computers and devices joined by data cable to one Mainframe. To get an item out, you do not open a box. You ask the network for it, and the network fetches it for you.
jsc.guide.what_iql_is.text2: You ask in IQL, the Item Query Language. IQL is the network's own language, and it looks like the languages of databases: a word for the action, then the item and how many. Its words come from SQL (Structured Query Language), the language that databases speak.
jsc.guide.what_iql_is.text3: Each line you type is a statement. A statement either asks a question, or it asks for work. QUERY asks a question, and SHOW means the same. A question gets its answer as rows, and it changes nothing.
jsc.guide.what_iql_is.text4: When a statement asks for work, the network turns it into an Operation. An Operation is one action the network carries out. It waits its turn, and the network works on it over game ticks.
jsc.guide.what_iql_is.text5: Take SELECT 64 iron_ingot. It asks the network to bring 64 iron ingots to you. That is one Operation. The reply only says that the Operation is queued. The items reach you as the network works it.
jsc.guide.what_iql_is.text6: The quantity is optional. Leave it out with SELECT, and the network brings all it holds of that item. The word ALL means the same. A quantity is a whole number: 50% is refused.
jsc.guide.what_iql_is.text7: Write an item's name as one word, with an underscore for each space. iron_ingot means minecraft:iron_ingot, the iron ingot of Minecraft. A name with a colon, such as mod:item, is taken as the full name.
jsc.guide.what_iql_is.text8: Each Operation also has a priority. It is MEDIUM unless you say otherwise. Write PRIORITY and a level such as HIGH at the end of a statement to set it ([](jsc:priorities)).
jsc.guide.what_iql_is.text9: An Operation ends in one of eight states, and the network tells you which one ([](jsc:operation_states)).
jsc.guide.what_iql_is.title: What IQL and Operations are
jsc.guide.what_is_missing.fix1: Not needed here. Install with apt install or dnf install instead.
jsc.guide.what_is_missing.fix2: There is no service command. A service is installed, and the Mirror is put on the Mainframe with mirror install.
jsc.guide.what_is_missing.fix3: There are no file permissions to change in this world.
jsc.guide.what_is_missing.table1_1_2: Not needed: install with apt install or dnf install as player.
jsc.guide.what_is_missing.table1_2_2: There are no other users. Every command runs as player.
jsc.guide.what_is_missing.table1_3_2: The shell keeps no file permissions to change.
jsc.guide.what_is_missing.table1_4_2: No service command. A service starts once its program is installed.
jsc.guide.what_is_missing.table1_6_2: Not in the shell. The shell chapter ([](jsc:shell)) lists the commands that do exist.
jsc.guide.what_is_missing.table1_7_2: Not in the shell. Use reboot to restart the computer.
jsc.guide.what_is_missing.text1: Many commands you may know from other Linux systems are not in the shell here. The table lists the common ones and what to do instead. The shell still has reboot, which restarts the computer.
jsc.guide.what_is_missing.text2: Nothing in this world logs in with a password yet, so a step that set one would be setting nothing. Every command runs as the user player, and there is no other user to switch to.
jsc.guide.what_is_missing.text3: The package commands need no sudo. apt install and dnf install run directly for player ([](jsc:apt), [](jsc:dnf)).
jsc.guide.what_is_missing.text4: When a command is missing, the shell says "command not found" with the word you typed, and adds a dim line: "type 'help' to list commands".
jsc.guide.what_is_missing.title: What a Linux here does not have, and why
jsc.guide.what_operations_are.definition: One action the network carries out, queued and then run over game ticks.
A lane on the Mainframe that moves items for one Operation at a time. More queues mean more Operations at once.
The network's own list of what each of its servers holds, kept up to date so that the network knows where each item is.
jsc.guide.what_operations_are.fix1: The Mainframe is off, or it is not on this network. Switch it on, or join it to the network ([](jsc:first_network)).
jsc.guide.what_operations_are.fix2: Install an operating system on it ([](jsc:installing)).
jsc.guide.what_operations_are.problem1: The result says "the network has no running Mainframe".
jsc.guide.what_operations_are.problem2: The Mainframe has no operating system installed, so it refuses new Operations.
jsc.guide.what_operations_are.text1: In many storage mods, storage works like a service that is always there. You put a disk in a drive, and it serves you whatever is on it. That works, but it makes the whole system feel like one huge chest that you put things in and take things out of.
jsc.guide.what_operations_are.text2: J's Computers does not work like that. Here the network does not only serve you: its computers do work to get each thing done, and every piece of that work is an Operation.
jsc.guide.what_operations_are.text3: So, what is an Operation? It is an action the network is carrying out. Its names come from SQL (Structured Query Language), the language databases speak. When you take items out of storage, you do not fetch them from a disk yourself. You send the network a SELECT, and the network works it.
jsc.guide.what_operations_are.text4: The request goes into a queue. The Mainframe picks it up, finds where the items are, and moves them to you as fast as its hardware allows. That is why the Mainframe's hardware matters so much ([](jsc:mainframes)).
jsc.guide.what_operations_are.text5: Most Operations go through the same stages. An Operation waits in a queue, runs over game ticks (20 ticks make a second), and then settles in one of eight states ([](jsc:operation_states)).
jsc.guide.what_operations_are.text6: A timed Operation does not finish on the spot. A SELECT first takes a moment to find the items, and then it streams them out over ticks. By default that moment is 10 ticks on a hard disk, 3 on a solid-state drive and 1 on a non-volatile memory express (NVMe) drive.
jsc.guide.what_operations_are.text7: Some Operations settle at once, on the spot: the index upkeep (ANALYZE, REINDEX and VACUUM), LOCK, UNLOCK and DROP.
jsc.guide.what_operations_are.text8: Operations need a Mainframe. Every computer on the network is joined by data cable to one Mainframe, which runs the work and keeps the list of what is running ([](jsc:what_a_network_is)).
jsc.guide.what_operations_are.title: What an Operation is
jsc.guide.what_the_hand_files_do.heading: What reaches the disk
jsc.guide.what_the_hand_files_do.table1: What the installation copies to the disk
jsc.guide.what_the_hand_files_do.table1_: Yes: the table of what to mount.
The kernel file you installed (/boot/vmlinuz-6.11.5-gentoo-x86_64 on Gentoo, /boot/vmlinuz-linux on Arch)
No: the bootloader's list is not copied.
jsc.guide.what_the_hand_files_do.text1: Much of a hand install happens in the live shell, in files you type or edit: the table, the name, the kernel, the bootloader's list. The installed system does not get all of them. The reboot checklist records the steps you ran, and on Gentoo it also reads the table you wrote.
jsc.guide.what_the_hand_files_do.text2: While you work, the files you type go under the new system's root folder in the live session: /mnt on Arch, and /mnt/gentoo on Gentoo.
jsc.guide.what_the_hand_files_do.text3: Then the installation writes its own boot files onto the disk: a folder named boot, and the kernel file boot/vmlinuz inside it. It writes them whatever you typed, so the machine can start even though the kernel file you installed is not copied.
jsc.guide.what_the_hand_files_do.title: Which typed files reach the installed system
jsc.guide.what_you_need.definition1: The program on the motherboard that starts the computer, before any system runs.
jsc.guide.what_you_need.definition2: A generation of hardware, such as Vintage, Legacy or Standard. A computer has the era of its motherboard.
jsc.guide.what_you_need.definition3: The computer that runs a network, which is every computer and device joined to it by data cable. It hosts the network's services, such as the Mirror.
jsc.guide.what_you_need.definition4: The network's package repository, a service on the Mainframe. Every package manager of the network installs from it.
jsc.guide.what_you_need.fix1: This machine is older than the medium needs. Put a Legacy-era or newer motherboard in the computer.
jsc.guide.what_you_need.fix2: Put the CD in a CD Drive and join that drive to the computer ([](jsc:drives)).
jsc.guide.what_you_need.fix3: Put a disk in a disk slot. Then type lsblk to list the disks the shell can see ([](jsc:disks)).
jsc.guide.what_you_need.fix4: Type mirror to see how it stands. Install it with mirror install if it is not installed, and keep the Mainframe running.
jsc.guide.what_you_need.problem1: The firmware's list shows "Legacy era or newer" beside the medium.
jsc.guide.what_you_need.problem2: The firmware says there is no installation medium in a linked drive.
jsc.guide.what_you_need.problem3: The shell says the disk does not exist.
jsc.guide.what_you_need.problem4: The package steps fail, and the Mirror does not answer.
jsc.guide.what_you_need.table1_1_3: The firmware refuses: "Arch Linux needs Legacy era hardware or newer; this machine is Vintage era."
jsc.guide.what_you_need.table1_2_1: A disk in a disk slot
jsc.guide.what_you_need.table1_2_2: The computer's disk slots, named sda, sdb and so on in slot order.
jsc.guide.what_you_need.table1_3_1: The Arch Linux or Gentoo CD in a CD Drive joined to the computer
jsc.guide.what_you_need.table1_3_2: The CD is in the Legacy creative tab, J's Computers - Legacy.
jsc.guide.what_you_need.table1_3_3: The firmware says: "No installation medium is in a drive linked to this machine."
jsc.guide.what_you_need.table1_4_1: The Mirror, running on the network's Mainframe
jsc.guide.what_you_need.table1_4_2: Installed on the network with the command mirror install.
jsc.guide.what_you_need.table1_4_3: The package steps fail, because the Mirror does not answer.
jsc.guide.what_you_need.table2_1_2: Install it on the network with the command mirror install.
jsc.guide.what_you_need.table2_2_2: It is installed, but the Mainframe is not running, so nothing answers.
jsc.guide.what_you_need.table2_3_2: The Mirror answers, and the package steps can fetch.
jsc.guide.what_you_need.text1: Four things must be ready before you start. Each one has a refusal of its own, so the machine tells you which one is missing, and the table shows where each one comes from.
jsc.guide.what_you_need.text2: First, the computer must be of Legacy era or newer. The era is the era of the motherboard in the computer, not of the parts you put on it. A Vintage computer cannot install either system.
jsc.guide.what_you_need.text3: The package steps fetch from the Mirror, so they need it. It answers only while the Mainframe is running ([](jsc:mainframes)). Type mirror on its own to see how it stands:
jsc.guide.what_you_need.text4: Last, the machine must start from the medium. In the firmware's list, choose the CD. The machine restarts, runs its self-test again, and then the medium's shell comes up ([](jsc:firmware_for_install)).
jsc.guide.what_you_need.title: What you need
jsc.guide.whatis_and_apropos.definition1: The short description a command gives of itself in one line, which whatis and apropos read.
jsc.guide.whatis_and_apropos.fix1: No name or summary holds that word. Try a shorter word, or an English word from a summary, such as disk.
jsc.guide.whatis_and_apropos.fix2: You typed whatis with no name. Type whatis and a command's name, such as whatis ls.
jsc.guide.whatis_and_apropos.fix3: You typed apropos with no word. Type apropos and the word to search for, such as apropos network.
jsc.guide.whatis_and_apropos.fix4: The search reads the English summaries only. Type the English word.
jsc.guide.whatis_and_apropos.problem1: The reply ends with "nothing appropriate." after the word you typed.
jsc.guide.whatis_and_apropos.problem4: apropos finds nothing for a word in another language.
jsc.guide.whatis_and_apropos.step1: Type whatis and a command's name, such as whatis ls.
jsc.guide.whatis_and_apropos.step2: Type apropos and a word, such as apropos network, to find commands by their job.
jsc.guide.whatis_and_apropos.step3: Type man and the name of a command you want to read in full.
jsc.guide.whatis_and_apropos.table1_1_2: The command this line is about.
jsc.guide.whatis_and_apropos.table1_2_2: The section. Every command's page is in section 1.
jsc.guide.whatis_and_apropos.table1_3_2: What the command is for, in a few words.
jsc.guide.whatis_and_apropos.text1: whatis gives the one line that says what a command is for. It is the quickest answer, and it tells you whether the full page is worth reading.
jsc.guide.whatis_and_apropos.text2: apropos is for when you know the job, not the name. It searches the name and the one-line summary of every command this computer has, and prints the commands that match.
jsc.guide.whatis_and_apropos.text3: The summaries are in English, whichever language the game shows you. Search with English words, such as network or disk.
jsc.guide.whatis_and_apropos.text4: Everything you type after apropos is the search. apropos network card looks for the whole phrase, network card, not for two words. Only the commands this computer has are searched.
jsc.guide.whatis_and_apropos.title: whatis and apropos
jsc.guide.when_a_craft_goes_wrong.fix1: Check that the Mainframe is running with an operating system, and that a Crafting Computer is switched on with a card.
jsc.guide.when_a_craft_goes_wrong.fix2: The craft settled as partial. Ask for the rest once the missing items are in storage.
jsc.guide.when_a_craft_goes_wrong.proble: A craft does not start at all.
A craft makes less than you asked.
jsc.guide.when_a_craft_goes_wrong.table1: A craft starts only while the Mainframe is running and has an operating system.
Switch the Mainframe on, and install its operating system.
The text "nothing on the network knows how to make", then the item.
No pattern on the network makes the item.
Add a bench, machine or multi-stage pattern for it ([](jsc:patterns)).
The text "no crafting computer was free to make", then the item.
No Crafting Computer is switched on with a Crafting Card, or all of them are busy.
Switch a Crafting Computer on, give it a Crafting Card, or wait until one is free.
The recipe does not appear in the plan.
The recipe is in the ROM of a Crafting Computer that is not running.
jsc.guide.when_a_craft_goes_wrong.table2: While a craft runs
The text "the machine making", then the item, and "stopped taking anything".
A machine job gave up after its timeout, while nothing moved on its interface.
Check the machine's power and its output. A Crafting Receiving Bus must face the output.
The text "no Crafting Interface holds the recipe for", then the item.
No interface holds the machine's pattern, and it was not placed in time.
Put the machine's pattern into a Crafting Interface that a Crafting Computer drives.
The text "the ingredients for", then the item, and "ran out".
The bench craft ran out of ingredients in storage.
Stock more of that ingredient.
The text "the pattern has no stages in it".
A multi-stage pattern holds no stages.
Add stages to the pipeline ([](jsc:patterns)).
The text "stage", then a number, "of", a count, and "could not be started".
The machine or the interface of that stage is not ready.
Check that stage's machine and its interface, as for a machine that stopped.
The text "stage", then a number, "of", a count, and "failed".
The stage timed out.
Check the stage's machine for power and room, and that its output faces a Crafting Receiving Bus.
What you see
What it means
The fix
jsc.guide.when_a_craft_goes_wrong.table3: A partial craft: some of the amount was made.
Ask for the rest once the missing items are in storage.
The text "timed out waiting on a locked resource".
Another operation held what this craft needed.
Ask again once that other operation has settled.
Read the step that failed above, and fix it first.
jsc.guide.when_a_craft_goes_wrong.table4: The screen says "Driven by no Crafting Computer".
The interface is not on a cable that a Crafting Computer drives, or the cards drive fewer interfaces than the cable reaches.
Put it on a cable that a Crafting Computer drives, switch the computer on, or give the computer another card.
The screen says "no router on its cable takes it: this pattern cannot run".
No router on the interface's cable takes one of the inputs.
Put a Crafting Input Router on that cable, with a filter that takes the input ([](jsc:input_routers_and_receiving_buses)).
jsc.guide.when_a_craft_goes_wrong.text1: A craft can fail before it starts, or while it runs. The network names the step that went wrong, and the messages below tell you what each one means and how to fix it.
jsc.guide.when_a_craft_goes_wrong.text2: A craft that makes part of what it asked for is partial, and the part is kept. A craft that makes nothing has failed. If one stage fails, the whole craft fails: bench stages give back the items they took, and machine stages keep what they fed into their machines.
jsc.guide.when_a_craft_goes_wrong.text3: The eight states of an operation are listed in [](jsc:operation_states).
jsc.guide.when_a_craft_goes_wrong.text4: A machine job waits for its outputs, and its clock counts only while nothing moves on its interface. When the timeout passes, the job gives up. A machine pattern's timeout is 200 ticks by default, which is 10 seconds ([](jsc:patterns)).
jsc.guide.when_a_craft_goes_wrong.text5: Outputs that come late are still credited for a short while after a job ends. After that, they go to the network as unexpected.
jsc.guide.when_a_craft_goes_wrong.text6: An interface waits until its owed outputs are in before a new recipe goes in. Its log shows draining until then ([](jsc:crafting_interfaces)).
jsc.guide.when_a_craft_goes_wrong.text7: The other messages of the routers and the buses are listed in [](jsc:input_routers_and_receiving_buses).
jsc.guide.when_a_craft_goes_wrong.text8: The planner stops at 16 levels of recipes, and it cuts a recipe that depends on itself ([](jsc:craft_planner)).
jsc.guide.when_a_craft_goes_wrong.title: When a craft goes wrong
jsc.guide.when_a_tool_refuses.fix1: Run lsblk and compare the name you typed with the name it prints. The name follows the slot the disk is in.
jsc.guide.when_a_tool_refuses.fix2: Find the tool's name at the start of the message, read that tool's table, and check the name with lsblk.
jsc.guide.when_a_tool_refuses.problem1: The same message comes back after you fix something.
jsc.guide.when_a_tool_refuses.problem2: The message is not in these tables.
jsc.guide.when_a_tool_refuses.table1_1_2: No disk was named: type fdisk /dev/sda.
jsc.guide.when_a_tool_refuses.table1_2_2: No disk of that name is in the computer: use a disk name from lsblk, not a partition name.
jsc.guide.when_a_tool_refuses.table1_3_2: Information: the disk has no partitions yet, so type g for a GPT.
jsc.guide.when_a_tool_refuses.table1_4_2: t or d needs a partition: make one with n first.
jsc.guide.when_a_tool_refuses.table1_5_2: The disk is full, an earlier partition took the rest, or there are 128 partitions: delete the last one with d.
jsc.guide.when_a_tool_refuses.table1_6_2: The size or number is outside what the disk has: use a smaller size or a number from the list.
jsc.guide.when_a_tool_refuses.table1_7_2: The type word is not known: type 1 for EFI System, 20 for Linux filesystem, or L for the list.
jsc.guide.when_a_tool_refuses.table1_8_2: The letter x is not a command of the editor: type m for the list.
jsc.guide.when_a_tool_refuses.table1_hea: What it means, and the fix
jsc.guide.when_a_tool_refuses.table2_1_2: No partition was named: give one, such as /dev/sda2.
jsc.guide.when_a_tool_refuses.table2_2_2: The partition does not exist yet: make it with fdisk, or check its number.
jsc.guide.when_a_tool_refuses.table2_3_2: The EFI system partition was named: use mkfs.fat -F 32 on it, and mkfs.ext4 on another partition.
jsc.guide.when_a_tool_refuses.table2_4_2: The whole disk was named, and it has a partition table: use one partition, such as sda2.
jsc.guide.when_a_tool_refuses.table2_hea: What it means, and the fix
jsc.guide.when_a_tool_refuses.table3_1_2: No partition was named: give one, such as /dev/sda1.
jsc.guide.when_a_tool_refuses.table3_2_2: The partition does not exist: make it with fdisk, or check its number.
jsc.guide.when_a_tool_refuses.table3_3_2: Its type is not EFI System yet: run fdisk, then t, then 1, then w, and try again.
jsc.guide.when_a_tool_refuses.table3_hea: What it means, and the fix
jsc.guide.when_a_tool_refuses.table4_1_2: Fewer than two words were given: give a partition and a folder.
jsc.guide.when_a_tool_refuses.table4_2_2: The root is not mounted yet, so mount it first.
jsc.guide.when_a_tool_refuses.table4_3_2: The folder is not a place that can be mounted: use /mnt, or the boot or efi folder under it.
jsc.guide.when_a_tool_refuses.table4_4_2: The EFI system partition is not formatted as FAT, so run mkfs.fat -F 32 on it first.
jsc.guide.when_a_tool_refuses.table4_5_2: The partition is not the one mkfs.ext4 last formatted, so run mkfs.ext4 on it first.
jsc.guide.when_a_tool_refuses.table4_hea: What it means, and the fix
jsc.guide.when_a_tool_refuses.text1: Most messages start with the tool's name, such as fdisk, mkfs.ext4 or mount. When a tool stops you, find its message in the tables below. A message in a plain sentence, such as Device does not contain a recognized partition table, is information rather than a refusal.
jsc.guide.when_a_tool_refuses.text2: lsblk never refuses anything. It always prints its table.
jsc.guide.when_a_tool_refuses.text3: A mount or a bind that works prints nothing at all, so silence is its success.
jsc.guide.when_a_tool_refuses.title: What each disk error means
jsc.guide.where_to_type_iql.definition1: A file of IQL statements that the network runs one after another.
jsc.guide.where_to_type_iql.definition2: This computer's own storage, where the items you take out of the network go.
jsc.guide.where_to_type_iql.fix10: Install the Automation Engine on the Mainframe first.
jsc.guide.where_to_type_iql.fix2: The computer has no data network under it. Join it with a data cable ([](jsc:data_cables)).
jsc.guide.where_to_type_iql.fix3: Rename the file so that it ends in .iql, or write the statements in a new .iql file.
jsc.guide.where_to_type_iql.fix4: run does not take reads, QUERY or COUNT. Type the read at the prompt, with iql or operation.
jsc.guide.where_to_type_iql.fix5: The whole file is checked first, so no line ran. Fix the line that the message names.
jsc.guide.where_to_type_iql.fix6: Make sure the Mainframe is on, and that the Midsoft IQL Server is installed and running ([](jsc:engine_services)).
jsc.guide.where_to_type_iql.fix7: Install it from the Network Manager, in its Network Services, as the message says ([](jsc:network_manager)).
jsc.guide.where_to_type_iql.fix8: The Midsoft IQL Server is stopped. Start it with iqlengine start.
jsc.guide.where_to_type_iql.fix9: Install the Automation Engine on the Mainframe, then try again.
jsc.guide.where_to_type_iql.heading1: The iql command at the prompt
jsc.guide.where_to_type_iql.problem1: You type iql alone, and the reply shows a usage line with an example.
jsc.guide.where_to_type_iql.problem10: The reply says "jobs are kept by the Automation Engine".
jsc.guide.where_to_type_iql.problem2: The reply says "not on a network".
jsc.guide.where_to_type_iql.problem3: run says "only .iql files can be run".
jsc.guide.where_to_type_iql.problem4: run says "QUERY/COUNT are not supported by 'run'".
jsc.guide.where_to_type_iql.problem5: run says "syntax error in", followed by a line.

jsc.guide.where_to_type_iql.problem7: ISMS says the Midsoft IQL Server is not installed.
jsc.guide.where_to_type_iql.problem8: A statement answers "Network Operations Service unavailable".
jsc.guide.where_to_type_iql.problem9: The Automation Manager says "No engine - install the Automation Engine on the Mainframe".
jsc.guide.where_to_type_iql.table1_1_2: Type iql at the prompt, then a statement

jsc.guide.where_to_type_iql.table1_4_2: Write a Sigma program that calls it

jsc.guide.where_to_type_iql.table2_head2: The command, as the menu writes it
jsc.guide.where_to_type_iql.table3: The members of the Iql class
jsc.guide.where_to_type_iql.table3_1_2: An IqlResult, with Ok, Message and Rows
jsc.guide.where_to_type_iql.table3_3_2: An IqlResult. It also takes a list of strings.
jsc.guide.where_to_type_iql.text1: You can type IQL in five places. Each one needs the network to be ready first, and each one reads its statements a little differently. The list below names the five places, and the parts after it show how to use each.
jsc.guide.where_to_type_iql.text10: The exact way to call it is in [Iql](jsc:iql_library), in the Book of Sigma.
jsc.guide.where_to_type_iql.text11: The Automation Manager ([](jsc:automation_manager)) does not take typed IQL. Its form makes work that repeats: Restock below, Batch Craft, Move, or IQL. For the IQL kind, you pick a .iql file from the Mainframe's system disk, and you set how often it runs in the field Every (30s).
jsc.guide.where_to_type_iql.text12: Typing IQL needs the Midsoft IQL Server running. You start and stop it with the command iqlengine ([](jsc:engine_services)).
jsc.guide.where_to_type_iql.text2: Type iql, a space, then one statement, and press [[Enter]]. The command also answers to the names operation, op and sql, so op SELECT 64 iron_ingot does the same. It needs a data network under the computer. A read on a computer with no network answers "not on a network".
jsc.guide.where_to_type_iql.text3: A read answers with rows, at most 64 of them. A write answers with one line, such as "SELECT queued: 64 Iron Ingot -> local storage". The item is named as the game shows it, such as Iron Ingot, not by its internal name.
jsc.guide.where_to_type_iql.text4: The IQL Server Management Studio (ISMS) is the program for writing scripts. A script is several statements in one file, with room to edit them. ISMS opens and saves files that end in .iql.
jsc.guide.where_to_type_iql.text5: In ISMS, each statement ends with a semicolon. A comment starts with two dashes and runs to the end of the line. Press the keys below to run what you wrote.
jsc.guide.where_to_type_iql.text6: A script can ask for values first. Its parameters are written in angle brackets with a type and a default, and the dialog "Specify Values for Template Parameters" lists each one as name (type).
jsc.guide.where_to_type_iql.text7: The run command runs a file of IQL on a computer that runs MC-NET ([](jsc:mc_net)). Type run, a space and the file's name. The computer needs a disk, and run takes only files that end in .iql.
jsc.guide.where_to_type_iql.text8: run is stricter than ISMS. It reads one statement a line, skips every line that starts with two dashes, and takes statements without semicolons. It asks you for no values. It refuses the reads, QUERY and COUNT. It checks the whole file before the first line runs, so a bad line moves nothing.
jsc.guide.where_to_type_iql.text9: Sigma, one of the programming languages of the computers, can ask the network too. Its class Iql, in the namespace System.Network, has four members.
jsc.guide.where_to_type_iql.title: Where you type IQL
jsc.guide.widgets_basic.fix1: Shorten the text, or split it between two boxes.
jsc.guide.widgets_basic.fix2: Listen for OnSubmit, which runs when the player presses Enter in the box.

jsc.guide.widgets_basic.text1: A widget is one part of a window. The simplest ones show text, and the others take what the player types or clicks. Making a widget costs nothing. Changing a value that the player sees costs credits, see [](jsc:call_costs).
jsc.guide.widgets_basic.text2: An event tells your program that something happened, and it comes with no argument. OnChange runs on every change to a text box. OnSubmit runs when the player presses Enter in the box.
jsc.guide.widgets_basic.text3: A text box keeps at most 256 characters of text.

jsc.guide.widgets_lists.text1: Lists and choices hold many entries, and the player picks one. The Selected value tells your program which one is picked. On a RadioGroup, a ComboBox or a TabView the count starts at 1, and 0 means nothing is picked on a RadioGroup or a ComboBox.
jsc.guide.widgets_lists.text2: RadioGroup.Across is yes to lay the choices out across instead of down. A ComboBox is a drop-down and has no Across. TabView.Selected runs from 1 to the count, and the first page added is the one shown first. RadioGroup, ComboBox and TabView are version 2.
jsc.guide.widgets_lists.text3: Table.AddRow takes a list of texts, or one to four texts. Table.Cell(row, column) gives the text in that place. TreeView.Add gives the number of the node it made, and TreeView.Add(text, parent) puts the node under another. TreeView.NodeText gives the text of a node by its number.
jsc.guide.widgets_lists.text4: A ContextMenu opens with the other mouse button on the widget it was made for. A menu holds 64 entries.
jsc.guide.widgets_lists.text5: TextArea keeps at most 4,096 characters. A list, a table, a tree or an item picker holds at most 1,024 rows. A tab view holds 64 pages, a table 8 columns, and a status bar 4 sections.
jsc.guide.widgets_lists.title: Lists, choices, tables, trees and menus
jsc.guide.widgets_pictures_and_data.defi: One drawing command on a canvas.
A part that a mod adds to a window, with a kind name. It holds values, not handlers.
jsc.guide.widgets_pictures_and_data.fix1: A canvas holds 4,096 strokes at most. Clear it, and draw fewer strokes.
jsc.guide.widgets_pictures_and_data.fix2: Give the component a value, and listen for its actions with OnAction.
jsc.guide.widgets_pictures_and_data.fix3: Keep the value under 32 kilobytes (KB), or split it into several components.
jsc.guide.widgets_pictures_and_data.fix4: Build a value that does not contain itself.
jsc.guide.widgets_pictures_and_data.prob: The program stops and says a component holds values, not handlers.
The program stops and says the component's value weighs too much.
The program stops and says a value that holds itself cannot be handed to a component.
jsc.guide.widgets_pictures_and_data.text: Some widgets show pictures, numbers and records. A Canvas is an area you draw on, an Image shows a picture from the disk, and a Chart plots numbers. Each colour argument is a whole number.
A chart holds 120 points, and when it is full the oldest point goes. A log view holds 256 lines, and the oldest line goes first. Image, Chart, LogView and the widgets below are version 2.

An ItemSlot shows an item the way the game shows it. An ItemPicker shows a grid of items, with a search line above it. An OperationView shows one Operation as it stands, with its text, state, done and total amounts, and computer.

A GenericComponent is a kind a mod adds. Its Data is a copy of the value you give it, and OnAction gives you a ComponentAction, with its ComponentAction.Name and ComponentAction.Value. A component's value weighs at most 32 kilobytes (KB), nests at most 16 levels deep, and has at most 4,096 parts.
jsc.guide.widgets_pictures_and_data.titl: Canvas, images, charts, logs, items and components
jsc.guide.will_not_boot_messages.fix1: Type exit, which leaves the new system, then run reboot.
jsc.guide.will_not_boot_messages.fix2: Free space on the disk, or put a disk in the computer. Then run reboot again.
jsc.guide.will_not_boot_messages.fix3: Run that step again, read what it prints, then type reboot again.
jsc.guide.will_not_boot_messages.heading: The reboot does not check the mounts
jsc.guide.will_not_boot_messages.problem: reboot says you are inside the new system.
The disk message shows, with no space or no disk.
The same list shows again after you did its steps.
jsc.guide.will_not_boot_messages.table1: The lines the reboot command prints
jsc.guide.will_not_boot_messages.table1_: You are still inside the new system, entered with chroot.
Type exit to leave the new system, then run reboot.
Items of the checklist are still missing, one for each line under it.
Do the step that each line names ([](jsc:reboot_checklist)), then run reboot again.
Nothing is missing. The installation is written to the disk, and the machine restarts.
No disk has room for the system, or there is no disk to write to.
Free space on the disk, or put a disk in the computer, then run reboot again.
jsc.guide.will_not_boot_messages.text1: A refusal is the reboot command telling you that it did not restart the machine. Nothing is lost when it refuses: your live session stays open. Type the missing step, then run reboot again.
jsc.guide.will_not_boot_messages.text2: The lines appear in the live shell after you type reboot, each one exactly as shown in the table. The table gives what each line means and what you do about it.
jsc.guide.will_not_boot_messages.text3: The reboot command does not check whether the new system's disk is still mounted. Only the checklist and the disk write decide. The Gentoo and Arch guides still tell you to unmount first with umount -R, so do that before you run reboot, as the guide says.
jsc.guide.will_not_boot_messages.text4: A chroot error about a root folder that does not exist comes from the chroot command. It is not a refusal of the reboot.
jsc.guide.will_not_boot_messages.title: The refusals and their fixes

jsc.guide.windows_and_layout.definition2: A row's or column's rule for sharing spare room among its widgets.
jsc.guide.windows_and_layout.fix1: Close a window you no longer need with Window.Close(), before you show another.
jsc.guide.windows_and_layout.fix2: Use fewer widgets. Widgets inside rows and columns count too.
jsc.guide.windows_and_layout.fix3: Do not put a row or a column inside itself, or inside a row or column that it holds.

jsc.guide.windows_and_layout.fix8: Check the kind of widget. Each kind takes only its own values.

jsc.guide.windows_and_layout.text1: A window is a box on the desktop, with a title and one widget inside it. A program makes a Window, puts a widget in it, and shows it. The taskbar lists the open windows. The screens that show them are explained in [](jsc:monitors) and [](jsc:desktops).
jsc.guide.windows_and_layout.text2: A row puts its widgets side by side, and a column stacks them. A row shares its width among its widgets, and a column shares its height.
jsc.guide.windows_and_layout.text3: MessageBox.Show(title, text) opens a window the machine makes for a title and one line of text. Sigma# only.
jsc.guide.windows_and_layout.text4: Every widget has Widget.Visible and Widget.Enabled, which are yes or no, and Widget.Width and Widget.Height, which are whole numbers. A width or height of 0 takes what the widget needs. Any other value stays between 8 and the most the window allows.
jsc.guide.windows_and_layout.title: Windows, rows and columns
jsc.guide.working_with_files.definition1: The letters after the last dot in a file name. They tell the system what kind of file it is.
jsc.guide.working_with_files.definition2: A file that you can read, but cannot change or delete.
jsc.guide.working_with_files.fix1: A .dat file is the view of the disk's items. To move items, use interac ([](jsc:network_verbs)).
jsc.guide.working_with_files.fix2: You cannot change log files by hand. For the network's log, see [](jsc:cancelling_and_the_log).
jsc.guide.working_with_files.fix3: Crafts are asked for on the network, not written by hand ([](jsc:asking_for_a_craft)).
jsc.guide.working_with_files.fix4: Delete a file you no longer need, or use a larger disk.
jsc.guide.working_with_files.fix5: This drive is flat and holds no folders. Put the folder on another drive.
jsc.guide.working_with_files.fix6: Choose another name, or delete the old file first.
jsc.guide.working_with_files.fix7: Copy or move the file into a folder that you can write to.

jsc.guide.working_with_files.table1_2_2: Takes an optional folder. Shows the folder you are in, or changes to the folder you name.
jsc.guide.working_with_files.table1_3_2: A file name. Prints the lines of the file.
jsc.guide.working_with_files.table1_4_2: A file name, then the text. Creates the file, or overwrites it, with the text.
jsc.guide.working_with_files.table1_5_2: A file name. Deletes one file from the system disk.

jsc.guide.working_with_files.table1_7_2: A source, then a folder. Moves a file or a folder tree into that folder.

jsc.guide.working_with_files.table1_9_2: A folder name. Creates the folder.
jsc.guide.working_with_files.table1_head: Words after it, and what it does
jsc.guide.working_with_files.text1: Most of the prompt's work with files is this: you list them, move between folders, copy, rename and delete them. Each verb takes its words in the order the table shows, and each one has a page of its own below.
jsc.guide.working_with_files.text10: ren changes a name in place. The new name is everything after the old name. ren does not move the file, so use move for that.
jsc.guide.working_with_files.text11: mkdir creates a folder. Some drives are flat and hold no folders at all, and mkdir refuses them.
jsc.guide.working_with_files.text12: rmdir removes a folder, but only an empty one. A folder with files in it is refused.
jsc.guide.working_with_files.text13: tree draws the folders under the one you are in. With none, it says "No subfolders exist".
jsc.guide.working_with_files.text14: run runs an .iql file, as if you had typed its statements with iql ([](jsc:network_verbs)). Only .iql files run. A result prints in green on success and in red on failure.
jsc.guide.working_with_files.text2: These verbs need a machine with a file system. MC-NET has none, so they are not on its prompt.
jsc.guide.working_with_files.text3: dir lists the folder you name, or the folder you are in. Each row shows when the item was last written, its size and its name. A folder shows <DIR> in place of a size, and a read-only file has [RO] after its name. The last line counts the files and the folders and gives the total size in mB, the unit the listing prints. An empty folder says File Not Found.
jsc.guide.working_with_files.text4: cd with no words prints the folder you are in. cd with a folder changes to it. A drive letter alone goes to the root of that drive ([](jsc:paths_and_drives)).
jsc.guide.working_with_files.text5: type prints each line of a file. An empty file prints the dim line "(empty file)". A .dat file is refused, because it is the view of a disk's items.
jsc.guide.working_with_files.text6: write takes the file name, then everything after it as the text. The extension decides the kind of file. You can write files with the extensions iql, txt, cfg, csv and cmd. You cannot write log and craft files by hand. On success write prints "wrote" and the file name.
jsc.guide.working_with_files.text7: del deletes one file and prints "deleted" and its name. A .dat file cannot be deleted.
jsc.guide.working_with_files.text8: copy copies one file, or a whole folder tree within one drive. Between drives it copies files only, and on success it prints "1 file(s) copied." A file on another machine can be copied, but not moved.
jsc.guide.working_with_files.text9: move takes the same words as copy. It moves a file or a folder tree into another folder, and between drives it moves files only. On success it prints "1 file(s) moved."
jsc.guide.working_with_files.title: Working with files and folders

jsc.guide.workshop.text1: A Personal Computer can do more than run programs. Its Workshop program works with four personal-use cards. You put a card in the computer, and the program uses it for one kind of work: the Crafting Table Card, the Furnace Card, the Enchanting Card or the Anvil Card ([](jsc:expansion_cards)).
jsc.guide.workshop.text2: The Workshop has four tabs: Crafting, Furnace, Enchanting and Anvil. A tab whose card is not in the computer is dim, and it reads "no card".
jsc.guide.workshop.text3: The speed grows with the era of the computer. Every number here is a first estimate, and it may change.
jsc.guide.workshop.text4: The Enchanting Card asks 1, 1 or 2 levels for its three offers, and it asks no lapis. The Anvil Card asks two thirds of the levels an anvil would ask, rounded up. An offer shows its level and what it costs, and an offer that cannot be made reads "no offer".
jsc.guide.workshop.text5: Repair takes a material from storage. Each piece of material mends a quarter of the item's durability, and up to 4 pieces are used.
jsc.guide.workshop.text6: An UPDATE changes an item that the network stores. It runs in three steps. First, the item leaves the storage servers for the card's drawer, as a SELECT takes it out. Then the card does its work. Last, the result goes back into the item's own server, and what has no room there stays at the card's output.
jsc.guide.workshop.text7: A smelt of more than one stack runs the three steps again, one stack at a time. A step that cannot be done sends the item back as it was.
jsc.guide.workshop.text8: An UPDATE belongs to the Personal Computer that asked for it. If that computer stops, or loses its card, the UPDATE is discarded, and what the card held is left at its output. The drawer does not survive the world being closed.
jsc.guide.workshop.title: The Workshop and the personal-use cards
